plants.name: Abrotanella forsteroides
plants.form: Hard, bright green herb forming cushions to 1m in diameter. Perennial, densely tufted.
plants.flowers: Tiny, solitary, white, growing on stem that protrudes from the leaves.
plants.habitat: Dominant in bolster heath in eastern, central and western mountains. The western populations are coarser and larger in all their parts.
plants.notes: A sunny well-drained position with plenty of moisture in well-composted soil is needed but even so this species is not easy to grow. Ideal for rockeries or containers.

plants.name: Abrotanella scapigera
plants.form: Dark green rosette herb.
plants.flowers: Green, few grouped in a terminal head.
plants.habitat: Found in all forms of alpine heath, sedgeland and in short alpine grassland. Most common in the central and western mountains. Usually grows in the shelter of boulders or low shrubby plants.

plants.name: Acacia axillaris
plants.form: Bush or densely branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Stalkless heads of 3-4 tiny flowers, light to medium yellow.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – small (3-4cm) long, brown, flat. Seed, hard, black/brown.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia dealbata subsp. dealbata
plants.form: Small to medium tree with growth varying with conditions.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow, prolific. Globular flower heads in racemes or panicles.
plants.habitat: Tolerates a wide range of soils, except poorly drained or permanently wet soils. Best growth on moist, fertile sites. Tolerates strong winds, frost and snow.
plants.notes: A hardy, widespread species. Very fast growing. Pioneer species, good “nurse” plant to shelter other species. Fixes nitrogen. Excellent wildlife habitat. Bee attracting. Bird attracting. Used for cut flower and foliage industry. Timber used for furniture and pulp. …

plants.name: Acacia derwentiana
plants.form: Medium dense prickly shrub; branches have drooping ends.
plants.flowers: Pale yellow in loose spikes.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – narrow, 3-4cm long, with constrictions between seeds.
plants.habitat: Derwent River and some other rivers in the south-east.
plants.notes: Provide shelter; require moisture.

plants.name: Acacia genistifolia
plants.form: Shrub, often low and straggling.
plants.flowers: Spherical flower heads rich yellow to creamy yellow.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant especially in dry places and on roadsides, particularly in the east and north.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia gunnii
plants.form: Small shrub, erect or procumbent.
plants.flowers: About 30 flowers in each small spherical head.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – flat, about 3cm long with margins thickened, dark brown, often hairy.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in dry heaths.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia leprosa var. graveolens
plants.form: Shrub, usually straggly.
plants.flowers: Tiny flowers which appear to be dense fluffy balls occurring singly on a flowering stem.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – brown, straight, sticky, flattened, constricted between the seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in damp shady places. Occasional in lower, drier habitats.
plants.notes: Useful in providing low level shelter (up to 4m) in mixed species windbreaks. Useful in soil erosion control as fibrous roots help bind the soil. Also useful in improving soil fertility. Will regenerate naturally from seed particularly following fire. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. …

plants.name: Acacia longifolia subsp. longifolia
plants.form: Much-branched shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Long straight yellow spikes.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – thick, narrow, 8-15cm long, tightly coiled, narrowed between seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent on sand dunes and fringing beaches.
plants.notes: This shrub has long arching branches which root and bind the sand. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia longifolia subsp. sophorae
plants.form: Much-branched shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Long straight yellow spikes.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – thick, narrow, 8-15cm long, tightly coiled, narrowed between seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent on sand dunes and fringing beaches.
plants.notes: This shrub has long arching branches which root and bind the sand. Bee attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia mearnsii
plants.form: Small tree with smooth dark grey bark.
plants.flowers: Pale yellow globular heads of 20-30 flowers.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – dark brown, flat, slightly constricted between seeds.
plants.habitat: Frost and drought tolerant but sensitive to fire when young (less than three years). Adapts to a wide range of soils including relatively infertile sites. Will tolerate occasional inundation.
plants.notes: Useful as a medium-level cover in windbreaks. A good shade tree, useful in erosion control, due to its quick growth and ability to improve soil quality. Provides important structural diversity for nesting and foraging wildlife. Bee attracting. Important food source for sugar gliders. …

plants.name: Acacia melanoxylon
plants.form: Large erect tree.
plants.flowers: Dense pale yellow globular heads of 30-50 flowers on stout stalks.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – flattish, curved or coiled, 4-12cm long.
plants.notes: Good shade tree and shelter in windbreaks. Useful in controlling erosion as it has a vigorous spreading root system and improves soil fertility. It suckers readily or regenerates from seed after disturbance such as fire, ploughing or ripping making it useful for restoration. Bird attracting. …

plants.name: Acacia mucronata subsp. mucronata
plants.form: Erect bushy shrub to small tree.
plants.flowers: Creamy yellow in axillary spikes.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – long, narrow, with thickened margins.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in moist gullies and on hillsides.
plants.notes: Hardy, quick growing. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Acacia myrtifolia
plants.form: Small dense shrub with reddish stems.
plants.flowers: Large creamy yellow balls with 2-4 balls per head.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – curved, 4-7cm long, hard leathery valves, dark brown.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in dry places; usually on dolerite sites.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia pataczekii
plants.form: Shrub or small slender tree, young branches angular.
plants.flowers: Stalked small bright lemon-yellow globular heads of about 15 flowers in spikes of up to 30 heads.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – short, wide, brown, flat, purplish when young.
plants.habitat: Local in the north-east at Tower Hill and Rose’s Tier.
plants.notes: Named after the forester Wally Pataczek who first found it. Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia riceana
plants.form: Tall shrub or small tree with slender pendulous branches.
plants.flowers: Yellow, in a loose spike.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – narrow, curved, 4-6cm long, constricted between the seeds.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in damp, shady places. Frequent in south and south-east of state. Usually on dolerite soils.
plants.notes: Can do well in very dry shade. Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia siculiformis
plants.form: Rigid shrub. Leaves 1-3cm long, shaped like a dagger, sharply pointed phyllodes.
plants.flowers: Yellow, numerous, solitary, axillary.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – linear, flat, about 2.2cm long, constricted between the seeds. Seeds 6-10 black and shining.
plants.habitat: Local in the east, north-east and on the Central Plateau. Scattered in understorey of lower open forests, in tablelands and mountain country. Well drained rocky or sandy site, common near streams. Very hardy, tolerates frost and snow.
plants.notes: Useful for providing low-level shelter (up to 3m) in windbreaks. Useful in erosion control as the fibrous roots help bind the soil. Improves soil fertility. Bird attracting. The prickly foliage provides refuge for small birds. …

plants.name: Acacia stricta
plants.form: Shrub, branches angular and erect.
plants.flowers: 20-30 yellow flowers in a spherical head.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – straight, flat, about 7cm long; not constricted between the seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common in pastures and dry places.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits. High flammability.

plants.name: Acacia suaveolens
plants.form: Shrub with few branches, usually erect.
plants.flowers: In clusters enclosed in bracts which fall early. Pleasantly fragrant.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oblong, flat, leathery, 3-4cm long, purplish-brown, glaucous.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in sandy heaths.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia terminalis
plants.form: Shrub with spreading branches.
plants.flowers: Clusters of ‘fluffy balls’, pale cream/yellow and smelling of mulberries.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oblong, straight, flattened, 6-10cm long.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent on poor stony soils especially derived from mudstone.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia ulicifolia
plants.form: Small, rigid shrub.
plants.flowers: Creamy yellow in spherical heads.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – straight or slightly curved, 2.5-4.5cm long, constricted between the seeds.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia uncifolia
plants.form: Shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: In small spherical heads forming spikes or clusters in axils, in racemes.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – usually straight and flat, 6-20cm long.
plants.habitat: Local on Flinders Island in Marshall Bay area mainly. Grows on limestone based soils.
plants.notes: Sometimes known to sucker on Flinders Island. Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Acacia verticillata subsp. verticillata
plants.form: Prickly woody shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Yellow cylindrical spikes in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – long and thin without constriction between seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread especially in damp places.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Bee attracting. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits. High flammability.

plants.name: Acaena echinata
plants.form: Perennial rosette herb with hairs on leaves but under veins only.
plants.flowers: Small green or purplish flowers in a long interrupted spike which is denser at the tip.
plants.fruit: Achene – prickly clusters of seed turn from green to greyish-brown when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant along roadsides and in native pastures.

plants.name: Acaena montana
plants.form: Perennial herb, with spreading branches.
plants.flowers: Numerous flowers form dense spherical heads under 1.5cm.
plants.fruit: Achene – prickly clusters of seed turn from green to greyish-brown when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread in alpine sedgeland and coniferous heath and bolster heath, at altitudes of 1000-1500m.

plants.name: Acaena novae-zelandiae
plants.form: Creeping herb with spreading branches that give rise to short erect flowering branches.
plants.flowers: Many small green or purplish flowers in dense spherical heads which dry to reddish burrs. Attach to animal fur and people’s clothing.
plants.fruit: Achene – prickly clusters of seed turn from green to greyish-brown when mature.
plants.habitat: Most common in the eastern mountains; abundant at all altitudes from sea level to over 1000m.
plants.notes: Leaves have been used as tea substitute. Spreads by stolons and seed – usually treated as a weed.

plants.name: Acaena pallida
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.fruit: Achene – prickly clusters of seed turn from green to greyish-brown when mature.
plants.habitat: Sand dunes and grassland on the Tasman Peninsula.

plants.name: Acaena x anserovina
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.fruit: Achene – prickly clusters of seed turn from green to greyish-brown when mature.

plants.name: Acaena x ovina
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.flowers: Flowers in globular head.
plants.fruit: Achene – prickly clusters of seed turn from green to greyish-brown when mature.

plants.name: Acianthus caudatus
plants.form: Often forms quite massive colonies, but not all plants produce flowers. Heart shaped leaves, dark green above and purple beneath.
plants.flowers: Slender raceme of small dark purplish flowers with long filamentous sepals.
plants.habitat: Sheltered sites in heathland and heathy open eucalypt forest, sheoak woodland and teatree scrub.
plants.notes: A fly from the genus Mycoma pollinates this species.

plants.name: Acianthus pusillus
plants.form: Ground-hugging leaves, often in dense colonies.
plants.flowers: Slender raceme of small pale green to dark brown flowers, labellum green to reddish.
plants.habitat: Heathy open eucalypt forest, often among bracken, teatree scrub and heathland.
plants.notes: Generally responds positively to fire, but flowering is inhibited in the first spring following a summer fire.

plants.name: Acradenia frankliniae
plants.form: Tall shrub or small tree, branches sometimes drooping.
plants.flowers: White, 5 petals with a raised yellow ovary and 10 protruding stamens, 1.5 cm in diameter in dense terminal clusters.
plants.habitat: Local at Macquarie Harbour and on banks of rivers of the west coast.
plants.notes: Very slow growing. Suited to sheltered coastal planting in gardens and parks.

plants.name: Acrothamnus hookeri
plants.form: Small shrub, usually erect and much-branched.
plants.flowers: White, the spreading lobes have bearded inner surfaces. 3-6 together in spikes.
plants.fruit: Drupe – fleshy, spherical, light yellow or reddish colour.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in upland grassland.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained in cultivation. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run of large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial. More experimental work is needed.

plants.name: Acrothamnus montanus
plants.form: Much-branched, upright shrub. Leaves upper surface green, lower, bluish-green.
plants.flowers: White, 3-6 together near ends of branches and in upper leaf axils. Inside of flower hairless.
plants.fruit: Drupe – white or red and fleshy.
plants.habitat: In heaths and grassland at moderate altitudes in the central and eastern mountains.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial. This formula is not the total answer.

plants.name: Acrotriche cordata
plants.form: Small perennial shrub.
plants.flowers: Small, greenish, in clusters of 4-6.
plants.habitat: Exposed coastal areas.
plants.notes: Needs a well-drained position without excess moisture. Useful for erosion control especially on calcareous soils.

plants.name: Acrotriche serrulata
plants.form: Low dense shrub with spreading branches.
plants.flowers: Green, tubular, 5mm long with tasty nectar. Grow in small spikes near base of shrub.
plants.fruit: Drupe – green, scarcely succulent. Seed contained in a large stone, spongy but hard.
plants.habitat: Frequent in sandy heaths and dry places.
plants.notes: Mainly for the collector. Needs a well-drained position without excess moisture.

plants.name: Actinotus bellidioides
plants.form: Small, tufted rosette herb.
plants.flowers: Small, inconspicuous flowers; small, linear petals may be present.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in the west in wet peaty soil on mountains, and at sea level in the west and south-west.
plants.notes: Grows in boggy areas/ buttongrass plains.

plants.name: Actinotus moorei
plants.form: Small herb or slightly woody undershrub.
plants.flowers: Inconspicuous flowers; petals absent.
plants.habitat: Local on mountains of the Central Plateau, west, and south-west.
plants.notes: Grows in wet sub-alpine areas.

plants.name: Actinotus suffocatus
plants.form: Small perennial rosette herb with long, rhizome-bearing roots; forms dense mats.
plants.flowers: Terminal group of 5-10 white flowers at end of an erect stem emerging from centre of rosette.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent on western mountains, in wet ground, at the margins of lakes or tarns.
plants.notes: Grows in boggy alpine herbfields.

plants.name: Actites megalocarpus
plants.form: Stout, perennial herb with long erect rootstock bearing stolons.
plants.flowers: Daisy-like in loose clusters, ligules yellow, with sometimes crimson streak on lower surface.
plants.fruit: Achene – straw-coloured or light brown, smooth with marginal wings.
plants.habitat: Local on coastal sand dunes.

plants.name: Adiantum aethiopicum
plants.form: Small fern, with creeping underground rhizomes, fronds prostrate or erect, up to 60cm long, delicate, spreading and lacy.
plants.habitat: Widespread along stream banks and rocky areas in a variety of situations but usually in sunny, moist sites. Also tolerates salt-laden winds in coastal situations.
plants.notes: May withstand sunny, dry conditions if planted amongst rocks when soil moisture and drainage requirements are met.

plants.name: Agastachys odorata
plants.form: An bushy shrub with erect branches or (in the west) may be a small tree.
plants.flowers: Creamy white in straight upright spikes 5-8cm long in leaf axils, strongly scented.
plants.habitat: Local in areas of high rainfall in scrub associated with buttongrass plains. Grows mostly on poor soils being particularly common near rocky outcrops on quartzite hillsides in the south-west.
plants.notes: In cultivation needs a well-composted soil with good drainage. Half-to three quarters shade preferred. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamoni.

plants.name: Agrostis australiensis
plants.form: Annual, tufted with slender erect stems. Leaf blade surface scabrous (rough).
plants.flowers: Open panicle
plants.habitat: Damp areas, 60m to alpine.

plants.name: Agrostis bettyae
plants.form: Loosely tufted, rarely rhizomatous, annual or perennial. Erect stems, leaves basal and sparse, blades flat or in rolled.
plants.flowers: Panicle 8-35cm long, narrowly ovoid, spikelets purplish.
plants.habitat: Highland areas – wet heath.

plants.name: Agrostis diemenica
plants.form: Loosely tufted hairless perennial, leaf blades flat or inrolled to 12cm long and 2mm wide.
plants.flowers: Panicle up to 12cm long, purplish spikelets at tips of secondary branches. Few-flowered.
plants.habitat: Only recognised in Tasmania. Open areas at the edges of wetlands in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Agrostis joyceae
plants.form: Loosely tufted annual. Stems erect and very fine. Leaves basal and crowded.
plants.flowers: Panicle open, ovoid to pyramidal, to 12cm, sometimes drooping. Spikelets often purplish.

plants.name: Agrostis muelleriana
plants.form: Small annual, or perhaps perennial, grass in small tufts, leaves slightly in rolled or flat with roughened margins.
plants.flowers: Panicles 1-6cm long, narrow, contracted, dark brown or blackish; spikelets 0.2-0.3cm, purplish.
plants.habitat: Widespread in sub-alpine grassland sometimes growing in wet situations. North-east, Central Highlands and south-west at altitudes from 1100m to 1500m.

plants.name: Agrostis parviflora
plants.form: Tufted annual grass with leaves 2-4cm long, in rolled.
plants.flowers: Panicle 3-10cm, open with stiffly spreading branches, spikelets 1.5-2mm, green or purplish.
plants.habitat: Occasional throughout the mountains of Tasmania, especially in the east.

plants.name: Agrostis propinqua
plants.form: Loosely tufted hairless perennial.
plants.flowers: Panicles up to 30cm, pyramidal; spikelets 2.5- 2.75mm long clustered near ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Found on the east coast from sea level to 480m and on kunanyi/Mt. Wellington at about 900m.

plants.name: Agrostis thompsoniae
plants.form: Tufted stoloniferous grass with leaves flat, up to 13cm long, 2.5mm wide.
plants.flowers: Panicle up to 12 cm long, open, with stiffly spreading branches, spikelets 1.5-2.5mm.
plants.habitat: Known only from Tasmania where it is occasional in eastern mountains (Ben Lomond).

plants.name: Agrostis venusta
plants.form: Tufted annual grass with leaves in rolled, 2-4cm long.
plants.flowers: Panicle open with thin spreading branches, spikelets 2.5-3mm; brown awn from bracts.
plants.habitat: Occurs in open and frequently damp areas from sea level to over 1400m in all regions except the Midlands, north-east and north-west.

plants.name: Ajuga australis
plants.form: Spreading perennial herb with rosettes of soft hairy leaves up to 12 cm long.
plants.flowers: Erect stalks with clusters of approximately 10 blue, purple, mauve, or pink flowers, to 30 cm high.
plants.habitat: Occasional at lower altitudes in grassland and grassy heath in the eastern mountains.
plants.notes: Hardy, spreading plant for coastal sites; good for control of erosion.

plants.name: Allittia cardiocarpa
plants.form: Small, tufted perennial with dark green or purplish, grass-like leaves in a rosette.
plants.flowers: Flower heads about 4cm across with white or blue florets.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in swamps.
plants.notes: A very handsome specimen well worth cultivating. Prefers a sunny aspect.

plants.name: Allocasuarina crassa
plants.form: Sprawling shrub
plants.flowers: Red-brown ‘tufts’ of stigmas.
plants.fruit: Woody cone. Seed a winged nut in cones.
plants.habitat: Known only from the Cape Pillar and Tasman Island areas of the Tasman Peninsula.
plants.notes: crassa’ means thick or stout and refers to the relatively longer, thicker branchlets compared with other species. Bird attracting. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Allocasuarina duncanii
plants.form: Very erect, narrow-crowned tree.
plants.flowers: Red-brown ‘tufts’ of stigmas.
plants.fruit: Woody cone. Seed a winged nut in cones. Female cones, up to 7cm and quite narrow.
plants.habitat: Officially only known from a small population at Snug Plains. However a few other small populations are thought to exist in similar localities elsewhere in south-east Tasmania. It grows in heavy clay soils in moist forest communities dominated by Eucalyptus tasmaniensis.
plants.notes: First collected in l979 but it was not until 1994 that it was described and named. Bird attracting. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Allocasuarina littoralis
plants.form: Shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers on different trees. Female: tiny brush-like clusters of reddish stigmas. Male: stamens in spikes at tips of branches.
plants.fruit: Woody cone – smooth cylindrical cones 2-2.5 cm long enclosing seed – a winged nut.
plants.habitat: On dry hills and in the understorey of forests along the east coast. It is most common on sandy soils but also occurs in grassy forests on dolerite. Will tolerate moderate exposure.
plants.notes: Suitable for control of erosion and to provide soil stabilization. Also suitable for street planting. Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Allocasuarina monilifera
plants.form: Erect shrub
plants.flowers: Male flowers in spikes at ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant from coastal heaths to sub-alpine scrub. Often only 50cm high in coastal heaths but small tree on the Central Plateau.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamoni. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Allocasuarina paludosa
plants.form: Small erect shrub
plants.flowers: In terminal spikes 1-2 cm long.
plants.fruit: Woody cone – cylindrical cones 1-1.5cm long, valves with margins rounded, enclosing winged nut.
plants.habitat: Local in the north-east of the state.
plants.notes: Will grow in most soils in a sunny position. Plenty of moisture required. Bird attracting. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Allocasuarina verticillata
plants.form: Small much-branched tree.
plants.flowers: Stamens only in spikes up to 12cm long. Male flower spikes yellow-brown and red female flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody cone – prickly, enclosing winged nuts.
plants.habitat: Forms close to pure stands along the margins of coastal cliffs and on dry, rocky, north-facing slopes, especially on dolerite. Also grows inland on dry rocky sites. Probably the most drought-resistant tree species in Tasmania. Only moderately tolerant of fire. …
plants.notes: A long-lived species (50-100 years), moderately slow-growing. Plants are highly palatable to livestock and rabbits and usually require protection to establish. Good for medium level windbreaks, useful for erosion control due to its ability to shoot from the roots and the leaf litter. …

plants.name: Allocasuarina zephyrea
plants.form: Shrub with waxy, bead-like foliage.
plants.flowers: Red-brown” tufts” of stigmas.
plants.habitat: The first specimens were collected at Ocean Beach, Strahan and it occurs in heaths and rocky outcrops from sea-level in the west to central and south-east Tasmanian highlands as well as on King Island.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Almaleea subumbellata
plants.form: Slender shrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, almost stalkless, with deep orange-yellow petals and purple markings on wings.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – small, broadly oval and inflated, valves hard.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant in wet heaths and margins of streams and tarns, sea level to 1000m.

plants.name: Alternanthera denticulata
plants.form: Scrambling perennial herb with a tough, slender tap-root and numerous branches arising at ground-level. Leaves 1.5-3.5cm long with a bluntly pointed tip.
plants.flowers: Small and papery, white or pinkish, occurring in the leaf axils either singly or in clusters of 2-3.
plants.fruit: Heart shaped achene, small, translucent and flattened, containing one seed.
plants.habitat: Damp grasslands, Melaleuca ericifolia forest, river edges and boulder gaps, around Launceston and Longford in the north of the state.
plants.notes: Seedlings will establish on heavy clay.

plants.name: Althenia bilocularis
plants.form: Annual herb with slender, 1-2cm long leaves.
plants.flowers: Male flowers solitary, all flowers on 5mm long stalks.
plants.habitat: Known from only a fragment collected from Swanport in the 1800s.
plants.notes: Aquatic herb in brackish water.

plants.name: Althenia cylindrocarpa
plants.form: Annual herb with threadlike leaves, 0.1-0.4mm wide and 2-6cm long.
plants.flowers: Male flowers often occur in pairs, with the flower stalks elongating to 6mm long; the flower stalks of female flowers elongate from 5-10mm to 20mm.
plants.fruit: Achene – cylindrical, brown, smooth and shining, and about 2mm long when mature.
plants.habitat: Fresh to brackish coastal lagoons and creeks in the north-east and east coast.
plants.notes: Semi-aquatic herb from brackish water.

plants.name: Althenia marina
plants.form: Annual herb with underground stems and linear leaves ending in a narrow, hard point.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers on separate plants. Male flowers on dense, leafy shoots; females on slender leafy shoots that are often longer than the vegetative shoots.
plants.fruit: Achene – small, brown, oblong-shaped, dry and leathery, 1.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Sandy and muddy tidal flats, with Zostera muelleri. Historically collected from Blackman Bay, the Swan River Estuary and Boomer Marsh; the only available current records are from Boomer Marsh.
plants.notes: Semi-aquatic herb from brackish water.

plants.name: Althenia patentifolia
plants.form: Variable herb with horizontal underground stems and flat, narrow-bladed leaves held at right angles to the plant.
plants.flowers: Male flowers are usually together in pairs, and female flowers solitary; all flowers are borne in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Achene – dry, leathery, 1.5-2.25mm long, with warty protrusions.
plants.habitat: Coastal lagoons, creeks, inlets and estuaries, and inland brackish lagoons. Historically recorded from King Island, the Midlands, north-east, east coast and south-west, however the only available records are from the south-west, at Moulting Lagoon and New River Lagoon.
plants.notes: Semi-aquatic plant.

plants.name: Althenia preissii
plants.form: Slender annual herb with horizontal stems and thread-like leaves 1-6cm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers are either male or female, and solitary or in clusters.
plants.fruit: Achene – dry, leathery and oblong, 1.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Fresh and brackish lagoons, and estuaries in the north-east, east coast and King and Flinders Island. Key sites include Calverts Lagoon, South Arm, and the Macquarie River.
plants.notes: Semi-aquatic annual herb.

plants.name: Alyxia buxifolia
plants.form: Sprawling shrub, many spreading branches. Shiny oval, dark green leaves.
plants.flowers: Scented, white, 2-7 in terminal clusters, 5 windmill petals, orange tube.
plants.fruit: Fleshy drupes – 6-10mm diam, often 2 end-to-end, orange to red at maturity.
plants.habitat: Among rocks in salt spray zone, cliffs and old dunes, harshly exposed sites. Local on rocks and cliffs northern Tasmania and north-west coasts.

plants.name: Amperea xiphoclada var. xiphoclada
plants.form: Undershrub with greyish-green stems, usually leafless, arising from a hard woody base.
plants.flowers: Small clusters of tiny cream flowers borne in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Capsules, small green, egg-shaped, about 4mm long.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant, especially in poor soils and sandy heaths.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Amphibolis antarctica
plants.form: A seagrass

plants.name: Amphibromus archeri
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial often with corm-like swelling at the base.
plants.flowers: Spikelets 12-18mm long. 3-flowered +/- several hairless husks with bristle arising from apex.
plants.habitat: Occurs in lagoons, waterholes, swamps and winter-wet situations in the East Coast, Midlands, north-east and Central Highlands.

plants.name: Amphibromus macrorhinus
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial grass.
plants.flowers: Spikelets 11-15mm long, 4-5 flowered +/- several hairless husks with bristle arising from apex.
plants.habitat: Occurs at waterholes and in low-lying wet places in the Midlands.

plants.name: Amphibromus neesii
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial. Leaves linear, apex acute and often hooded.
plants.flowers: Spikelets narrow, ellipsoid to 15mm long (excluding awn), 3-5-7 flowered.
plants.habitat: Occurs in marshes, lagoons and river flats on the east coast, north-east, Midlands and west coast.

plants.name: Amphibromus nervosus
plants.form: Annual or perennial, tufted. Rhizomes short.
plants.flowers: Open panicle, 12cm long.
plants.habitat: Central Highlands and Ben Lomond.

plants.name: Amphibromus recurvatus
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial. Leaves with lower surface smooth, upper surface ribbed, ribs with short hairs.
plants.flowers: Spikelets 7-11mm long excluding awns, 3-6 flowered. Lower bract ending in 4 rough teeth.
plants.habitat: Occurs in dune swales, lagoons, swamps and mountain tarns from sea level to about 1100m in the north-west, north-east, west coast, east coast, south-west, Central Highlands and Mt. Field.

plants.name: Amphibromus sinuatus
plants.form: Decumbent and ascending aquatic perennial rooting at the lower nodes.
plants.flowers: Spikelets 9-15mm long, 4-5 flowered.
plants.habitat: Occurs in farm dams in the Midlands and on the margin of Lake Crescent.

plants.name: Androstoma verticillata
plants.form: Small shrub with ascending, spreading branches.
plants.flowers: 2 or 3 together in short spike which appears terminal but pushed aside by new leaf growth.
plants.fruit: Drupe – spherical, red, with the fleshy part thin; the stone in 5 parts, or fewer by abortion.
plants.habitat: Local on mountains near west coast.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial.

plants.name: Anemone crassifolia
plants.form: Rosette herb, base leaves on long stems with thick, almost succulent blades, purplish underneath with toothed lobes.
plants.flowers: White, open, to 3cm diameter at end of stem. Centre crowded with yellow stamens and immature seeds.
plants.fruit: A cluster of achenes, without hairs and with persistent style 3-4mm long and hooked at the end.
plants.habitat: Local at altitudes of about 1200m on mountains towards the west coast. Found in alpine heaths and sedgeland.
plants.notes: Australia’s only Anemone. In cultivation requires moist, well drained, peaty acid soils with partial sun. May tolerate full sun in milder climates. Best planted amongst logs and rocks or as a container plant.

plants.name: Angianthus preissianus
plants.form: Annual herb, usually with many slender, wiry stems spreading from base.
plants.flowers: In clusters forming compound heads each surrounded by downy leaves.
plants.fruit: Achene covered with tiny protuberances and with the pappus ring-shaped and very finely toothed.
plants.habitat: Sandy flats near the coast, especially in the north and in the islands of Bass Strait.

plants.name: Anisotome procumbens
plants.form: Procumbent, perennial herb; forms a dense tuft up to 2 m in diameter.
plants.flowers: Small white to cream flowers form a dense cluster on a stem slightly taller than the leaves.
plants.habitat: Local on west, central, and south-west mountains.
plants.notes: Difficult to grow, prefers wet high elevation areas.

plants.name: Anodopetalum biglandulosum
plants.form: Slender tree which bends, sends up vertical branches which in turn bend down.
plants.flowers: Small, with 4 pale green pointed petals.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 6mm, fleshy and green with one seed.
plants.habitat: South and west in rainforest, mostly on poor soils, particularly favouring gullies and creeks. Also in sub-alpine areas near rocky outcrops on quartzite.

plants.name: Anogramma leptophylla
plants.form: Tiny ferns growing in clumps; pale green fronds erect, delicate, thin-textured.
plants.habitat: Very Rare in Tasmania. Found growing in thin, mossy soil layer on rock ledges and under boulders. May co-exist with mosses, liverworts and small annual or perennial angiosperms.
plants.notes: Dies back during the dry season and shoots again with the onset of rain.

plants.name: Anopterus glandulosus
plants.form: Tall shrub, straggly ,with branches tending to layer when growing in shady positions.
plants.flowers: Cup-shaped with 6 concave white or pink petals in terminal sprays.
plants.fruit: Capsule, 12-18mm long, containing two winged elongated seeds.
plants.habitat: Frequent in wet sclerophyll and rainforests from sea level to about 900m. Also found on sandy soils near the south coast.
plants.notes: In cultivation this species forms a dense rounded shrub which is slow growing. Good drainage is essential. Bee attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Anthosachne scabra
plants.form: Highly variable perennial grass, erect or abruptly bent, with stems much longer than the leaves. Leaves are flat or weakly in rolled, and up to 30cm long.
plants.flowers: Flower head up to 35cm long with alternate spikelets.
plants.habitat: Widespread in open situations or under light woodland, from sea level to 1200m altitude. North-west, Midlands, Furneaux Group, Ben Lomond, Central Highlands, east coast and west coast.

plants.name: Aotus ericoides
plants.form: Much branched shrub, occasionally prostrate.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, golden yellow with red markings.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant. Well drained coastal heathlands and open forest.
plants.notes: Bee attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Apalochlamys spectabilis
plants.form: Stout aromatic herb.
plants.flowers: Very numerous in loose clusters, pyramidal in shape and 20-40cm long.
plants.fruit: Achene – striated, non-hairy and with pappus bristles minutely barbed.
plants.habitat: Local near the coasts.
plants.notes: Plants usually only last for two years.

plants.name: Aphelia gracilis
plants.form: A slender annual ephemeral herb with scapes.
plants.habitat: Local in damp sandy ground and wet places in the Midlands and north-east.

plants.name: Aphelia pumilio
plants.form: A slender annual herb with scapes.
plants.habitat: Rare – recorded from damp places in the Midlands.

plants.name: Apium annuum
plants.form: A small annual herb.
plants.habitat: Prefers saline/saltmarsh areas.

plants.name: Apium prostratum var. filiforme
plants.form: Perennial, scrambling herb with branches 30-70cm long and divided leaves resembling Italian parsley. Leaflets can be entire or divided; leaflets 2-3 times as long as wide.
plants.flowers: Very small flowers with white petals, in flower heads.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – circular, 1.3-2.5mm long, somewhat succulent and with 5 thick longitudinal ridges.
plants.habitat: Sunny beaches, saltmarsh and sandy coastal foreshores, often in tidal areas.
plants.notes: Captain Cook’s party is said to have used it as a substitute for domestic celery.

plants.name: Apium prostratum var. prostratum
plants.form: Perennial, scrambling herb with branches 30-70cm long and divided leaves resembling Italian parsley. Leaflets can be entire or divided; undivided leaflets are 6-15 times as long as wide.
plants.flowers: Very small flowers with white petals, in flower heads.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – circular, 1.3-2.5mm long, somewhat succulent and with 5 thick longitudinal ridges.
plants.habitat: Sunny beaches, saltmarsh and sandy coastal foreshores, often in tidal areas.
plants.notes: Captain Cook’s party is said to have used it as a substitute for domestic celery.

plants.name: Apodasmia brownii
plants.form: Rhizome creeping
plants.flowers: Female spikelets
plants.habitat: Coastal heaths and dunes.

plants.name: Archeria comberi
plants.form: Much-branched shrub, erect or ascending, branchlets with scattered hairs.
plants.flowers: Pink, tubular, on short stalks near the ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Uncommon. Found on a few western and central mountains and favours sheltered positions. A component of heaths and alpine sedgelands.

plants.name: Archeria eriocarpa
plants.form: Straggling shrub with slender branches; branchlets having stiff hairs.
plants.flowers: White or pink, tubular on short hairy stalks, either solitary or in short spikes.
plants.habitat: Occasional in temperate rain forests of the west and south-west, reaching an altitude of 100m.
plants.notes: Relatively slow growing. Could tolerate full shade.

plants.name: Archeria hirtella
plants.form: Slender, untidy shrub with small leathery leaves which end in a point.
plants.flowers: White or pink, arranged along the stems in leaf axils and at the end of branches.
plants.fruit: Capsule – smooth, hairless, opening by 5 valves.
plants.habitat: South and west, mostly in rainforest. Extends into sub-alpine habitats on the south coast ranges.
plants.notes: Grow in a shady place. Some success has been reported from container-grown plants.

plants.name: Archeria minor
plants.form: Leaves and flowers much smaller than type variety.

plants.name: Archeria serpyllifolia
plants.form: Stout, rigid bushy shrub, erect or prostrate pressed against the surfaces of boulders.
plants.flowers: White or light pink at ends of branches in dense groups.
plants.habitat: Local among boulders on summits of mountains of the Central Plateau and west.
plants.notes: Requires moist, well-drained soils. Will grow in dappled shade but will tolerate full sun if it has a cool root system such as near logs or boulders.

plants.name: Argentipallium dealbatum
plants.form: Perennial herb with small tufts of leaves springing from perennial rhizomes.
plants.flowers: Terminal, 2.5cm in diameter. White with red- purple flush on outside bracts. Daisy eye white.
plants.habitat: Common in wet peaty soils.

plants.name: Argentipallium obtusifolium
plants.form: Perennial herb or undershrub, much-branched and woody at the base.
plants.flowers: Flower heads solitary at ends of branches, white, outer florets with pistils.
plants.fruit: Achene with pappus bristles finely barbed.
plants.habitat: Local near the north coast and in the islands of Bass Strait.

plants.name: Argentipallium x spiceri
plants.form: Perennial herb or undershrub, much-branched and often woody at base.
plants.flowers: Flower heads of white florets sometimes solitary but usually in clusters.
plants.fruit: Achene – slender but slightly thicker towards the tips with pappus bristles minutely barbed.
plants.habitat: Known only from material collected in southern Tasmania in the Huon district between Longley and Cairns Bay. No known surviving plants in the wild.

plants.name: Argyrotegium fordianum
plants.form: Mat-forming perennial herb, stems creeping, leaves silvery grey and felt-like.
plants.flowers: Flower heads small, shining, 5-15, surrounded by bracts.
plants.habitat: An alpine or sub-alpine species found on grasslands or slopes near creeks and rivers.
plants.notes: Usually slow growing in cultivation. Does not tolerate extended dry periods.

plants.name: Argyrotegium mackayi
plants.form: A perennial mat-forming herb with much-branched rhizomes, leaves hairy; stems 3-10cm long.
plants.flowers: Flower heads large for size of plant; in irregular terminal, leafy clusters of 4-7.
plants.habitat: Occasional in grassy vegetation in the eastern mountains and in swampy places on mountains of the Central Plateau.

plants.name: Argyrotegium nitidulum
plants.form: Mat or cushion forming perennial daisy with thick, much branched creeping rhizomes.
plants.notes: Difficult to grow. Requires high elevation.

plants.name: Argyrotegium poliochlorum
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender creeping stems bearing short leafy branches; stems 5-10cm long.
plants.flowers: Usually 3 in a terminal cluster, compact at first but loosening in the fruiting stage.
plants.fruit: Achene with pappus bristles in ring at base.
plants.habitat: Local in acid, waterlogged soil between tussocks of button grass in alpine and sub-alpine heaths.

plants.name: Aristotelia peduncularis
plants.form: Straggling shrub with slender branches.
plants.flowers: White, bell-shaped with four 3-lobed petals which hang singly from axils.
plants.fruit: Berry – dark pink or red, sometimes white through to brown or black, heart-shaped, 1-1.5cm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Common in moist shady forests and fern gullies often on mountains. Grows especially in the south.
plants.notes: The fruit, stems and leaves are relished by wildlife.

plants.name: Arthropodium milleflorum
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.flowers: Blue to violet (rarely white).
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – small, round, turn from soft and green to brown and brittle. Ripe seeds are black and firm.
plants.habitat: Often on dry rocky slopes in open situations or under light eucalypt cover to 800m, north-west, Midlands, north-east, east coast and south-west.
plants.notes: Various insects are attracted to the flowers.

plants.name: Arthropodium minus
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.flowers: Purple, 1-3 per node, with long yellow or purple anthers recurved after flowering.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – small, round, turn from soft and green to brown and brittle. Ripe seed are black and firm.
plants.habitat: Open, dry, rocky areas in north-west, Midlands, north-east and east coast to 280m.
plants.notes: Various insects are attracted to the flowers.

plants.name: Arthropodium strictum
plants.form: Dwarf perennial herb with basal grass-like leaves and erect stem.
plants.flowers: Mauve flowers, chocolate scented, with purplish-black conspicuous anthers.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – small, round, turn from soft and green to brown and brittle as the seed ripen. The ripe seed are black and firm.
plants.habitat: Grows on dry hillsides, open forest and grasslands in the Midlands, north-east, and east coast to 300m. Likes well-drained to heavy, seasonally inundated soils. Common in the Tamar region.
plants.notes: Various insects are attracted to the flowers.

plants.name: Asperula conferta
plants.form: Perennial herb, stems short and densely crowded. Internodes shorter than leaves.
plants.flowers: White, borne on short stalks.
plants.habitat: Known only from the north-west coast in sandy soil at Woolnorth.

plants.name: Asperula gunnii
plants.form: Herb forming mats with ascending stems.
plants.flowers: Sweet smelling, cream or white in small clusters arising from upper whorls.
plants.habitat: Widespread in grassy vegetation in the eastern and central mountains. Often colonises banks by sides of roads and tracks.
plants.notes: Should withstand some waterlogging during the colder months.

plants.name: Asperula minima
plants.form: Prostrate, dense carpeting herb.
plants.flowers: Small, white, solitary or in 3’s borne on stalks longer than leaves.
plants.habitat: Local near the north coast.
plants.notes: Moss-like species. Prefers dappled shade or partial sun and moist, well drained soils.

plants.name: Asperula pusilla
plants.form: Perennial densely tufted hairy herb, between A. gunnii and A. minima in size.
plants.flowers: Cream or white, single or in small clusters from upper whorls and ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Occasional in grassy vegetation in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Asperula scoparia subsp. scoparia
plants.form: Low spreading, perennial, moss-like herb. Stems rough and hairy.
plants.flowers: White, in small terminal, axillary clusters to 0.6cm long.
plants.habitat: Occasional but widespread.
plants.notes: Ideal for planting around boulders and underneath other plants. Needs moist but relatively well drained soil, partial sun or dappled shade.

plants.name: Asperula subsimplex
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender quadrangular hairless stems.
plants.flowers: White, in axils of leaves of upper whorls, solitary or in 2 or 3-flowered clusters.
plants.habitat: Occasional but widespread on river banks and in marshy places.

plants.name: Asplenium appendiculatum subsp. appendiculatum
plants.form: Lithophytic, occurs on logs. Fronds leathery and lanceolate, never with bulbils. Lamina dark green with pinnules close together.

plants.name: Asplenium decurrens
plants.form: Small fern in compact clumps; fronds, 10-35cm long, thick, smooth, fleshy, greyish green, once divided. Form varies with habitat.
plants.habitat: Common on Tasmanian coastline and offshore islands amongst stable rock. Occasionally inland away from salt spray e.g. in gorges of the Serpentine R. and Gordon R. on sheltered rock ledges near the base of cliffs. May also occur in coastal fern gullies as a lithophyte or an epiphyte on Dicksonia.
plants.notes: Very hardy. As lithophyte or epiphyte, salt influenced.

plants.name: Asplenium flabellifolium
plants.form: Small fern forming large spreading patches, fronds pale green, once divided.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in dry rocky places and occasional in fern gullies in all parts except western Tasmania. Grows in a thin soil layer on rock ledges, crevices and amongst boulders and rubble in sunny and exposed sites and as a terrestrial fern in sheltered conditions. …
plants.notes: Epiphytic on dicksonia. Quite hardy but eagerly attacked by slugs and snails.

plants.name: Asplenium flaccidum subsp. flaccidum
plants.form: Medium fern forming pendulous clumps, fronds weeping, 2-3 divided, leathery.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in Tasmania but locally abundant in rainforest in the north-west and west and with scattered distribution in the north, east and south in rainforest, wet sclerophyll forest and fern gullies. Mostly occurs near sea level but known as high as 550m. …
plants.notes: Not common in cultivation. Needs humid conditions and does best in a bush house or glasshouse.

plants.name: Asplenium gracillimum
plants.form: Epiphytic on rocks and logs; epiphytic on Dicksonia and trees. Large, soft, elliptical fronds, 20-120cm long. Bulbils present on the lamina.
plants.habitat: Most common in near coastal gullies.

plants.name: Asplenium hookerianum
plants.form: Small fern growing in clumps; fronds once or twice divided, pale green, thin stalks.
plants.habitat: Very rare in Tasmania known only from the Hellyer Gorge and Drys Bluff. Typically grows in heavily shaded side creeks or channels and amongst exposed riparian tree roots which fill only during heavy rain. Occasional on wet rock faces.
plants.notes: Resents disturbance, needs cool humid conditions. Eagerly attacked by slugs and snails. Slow growing.

plants.name: Asplenium trichomanes subsp. quadrivalens
plants.form: Small fern, upright clumps; fronds narrow, dark green, once divided, in rosette.
plants.habitat: Usually found growing on limestone. Growing in Mount Field, Southwest National Park and Hastings Caves State Reserve.
plants.notes: May need lime.

plants.name: Asplenium trichomanes subsp. trichomanes
plants.form: Small fern, upright clumps; fronds arise in clusters from short thick rhizome.
plants.habitat: Found at three sites in the north-east, with the majority of plant at Mt Durham.
plants.notes: May need lime.

plants.name: Astelia alpina var. alpina
plants.form: Densely tufted plant with stiff rosettes of leaves, green above and silver below, forming large mats.
plants.flowers: Small, greenish yellow, at the end of flower spikes which arise from the centre of the leaves.
plants.fruit: Berry – bright red, egg-shaped, 12mm long; containing 5 black, shiny seeds. Fruits only found on female plants.
plants.habitat: Wet places, peaty heaths, moors, bogs and around water courses on mountains.
plants.notes: Berries edible.

plants.name: Asterotrichion discolor
plants.form: Medium to tall shrub or small tree, branches covered with stellate hairs when young, leaves alternate, many stellate hairs below.
plants.flowers: Small, creamy white clusters. Male and female usually on separate plants, delicately perfumed.
plants.fruit: Capsule – remains enclosed in persistent calyx.
plants.habitat: Common in moist eucalypt forests and gullies of southern Tasmania.
plants.notes: Fast growing and appreciates moist, well-drained soils with shade. Flowers in late autumn and winter and sporadically at other times of the year.

plants.name: Atherosperma moschatum subsp. moschatum
plants.form: Evergreen shrub or conical tree with aromatic bark and leaves and spreading, rather drooping branches.
plants.flowers: White; male with 12 short, thick stamens; female, less showy with hairy carpels in centre.
plants.fruit: Dry, a blackish woody knob with feathery styles protruding and gradually decaying.
plants.habitat: A rainforest tree found also in the understorey of some tall eucalypt forests. Occurs from sea level to the alpine zone where it is an infrequent shrub. Also occupies gullies in drier areas in the east.
plants.notes: Requires sheltered area with constant moisture. Grows slowly. Crushed leaves have a pleasant aroma. Bee attracting. Moderate flammability.

plants.name: Athrotaxis cupressoides
plants.form: Conical tree with markedly tapering trunk.
plants.flowers: Inconspicuous. Several years often pass between successive flowerings.
plants.fruit: Cone – male and female cones on same tree. Male – terminal hardly wider than foliage. Mature fertile cones 1 cm cross, spherical, at end of twigs.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in alpine and sub-alpine habitats around lakes and in wet but well-aerated soil sometimes forming pure stands. Dominates closed and open forests at high altitude in the west of the state.
plants.notes: Prefers moist (well drained) humus rich soils which do not become too dry in summer and with a cool root run. Grows well in partial or full sun. Slow growing. Specimen plant in public and domestic gardens.

plants.name: Athrotaxis selaginoides
plants.form: Tree, often stunted and twisted in high exposed places.
plants.flowers: Inconspicuous
plants.fruit: Cone – spherical, about 1.5cm in diameter at the ends of branchlets, on female plants.
plants.habitat: Found on valley slopes in high rainfall areas between 800 and 1400m often in association with Nothofagus cunninghamii. A shrub when extending into the alpine zones.
plants.notes: Requires very well drained, moist soils with partial or full sun. May be very slow growing. Suitable for public and large domestic gardens and forests. Timber is valuable for joinery, cabinet work and boat-building. Has been grown for many years in the British Isles.

plants.name: Athrotaxis x laxifolia
plants.form: Tree, similar to A. cupressoides but leaves slightly spreading with apex incurved.
plants.fruit: Cone – spherical or slightly ovoid, 1.5-2cm in diameter on female plants.
plants.habitat: Rare; found as isolated trees near Athrotaxis cupressoides or Athrotaxis selaginoides.
plants.notes: This species has been cultivated in the British Isles for over 100 years and some trees have reached about 20m in height. It will withstand slightly alkaline soils but soils need to be moist, well drained and in partial or full sun. Suitable for public and domestic gardens.

plants.name: Atriplex billardierei
plants.form: Prostrate, much-branched herb, forming 20-50cm wide mats. The leaves have blunt tips and are covered with shining protuberances, as are the branches.
plants.flowers: 2-5 flowers clustered together in the axils of upper leaves, and flowers in the axils of the lower leaves are solitary or in groups of 2-5.
plants.habitat: Sandy beaches near the high-tide mark.

plants.name: Atriplex cinerea
plants.form: Dense shrub to 6m wide, with white, stout, grooved branches and 5-6cm long, silvery-grey, leathery leaves.
plants.flowers: Shrubs are either male or female; males can be identified by dense brown spikes of flowers up to 5cm long. Female flowers are cryptic, and are single or occur in small clusters in the leaf axils.
plants.habitat: Frequent in saltmarshes and on coasts.
plants.notes: Edible foliage, mistaken as a ‘sort of sage’ by members of the First Fleet. Tolerant of salt spray.

plants.name: Atriplex paludosa subsp. paludosa
plants.form: Erect, silvery-grey shrub covered with woolly hairs, with bluntly pointed, 1-2cm long leaves. Leaves are green on the upper surface and whitish on the lower surface.
plants.flowers: Cream, yellow or brown. Male flowers in spherical clusters and female flowers in spikes.
plants.habitat: Coastal sand dunes in the north-west, at Coles Bay on the east coast and possibly elsewhere.

plants.name: Atriplex suberecta
plants.form: Sprawling herb that branches from the base, with thin, narrow, coarsely toothed leaves which are hairless on the upper surface and scaly or flaky on the undersurface, 1.5-3cm long.
plants.flowers: Male flowers in clusters near the top of the branch; female flowers in clusters in the leaf axils. Flowers are small and pale green, 2mm wide.
plants.habitat: Wide range of habitats on most soil types, but most commonly in disturbed areas, on the outer islands of the Furneaux Group.

plants.name: Australina pusilla subsp. muelleri
plants.form: Loosely branched perennial shrub, stems creeping at the base, then erect, leaves dark green, coarsely toothed and scattered with hairs.
plants.flowers: Flowers are hairy, petal-less and small, and either male or female.
plants.fruit: Achene – ellipsoid, asymmetric, smooth, brown, 1.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Wet forests and wet rocky gullies on kunanyi/Mt. Wellington and King Island.

plants.name: Australina pusilla subsp. pusilla
plants.form: Loosely branched perennial shrub, stems creeping at the base, then erect, leaves dark green, coarsely toothed and scattered with hairs.
plants.flowers: Flowers are hairy, petal-less and small, and either male or female.
plants.habitat: Widespread – found from sea level to 750m.

plants.name: Australopyrum pectinatum
plants.form: Erect, densely tufted, short-leaved perennial grass, extremely prickly.
plants.flowers: Heads 5cm long, each holding 8-15 spikes of flowers. Spikelets at right angles to stem.
plants.habitat: Alpine and sub-alpine grasslands, wet, rocky and shady places, in open situations or under light eucalypt cover, forest clearings and roadsides from sea level on the west coast to 1300m altitude, north-west, Midlands, Ben Lomond, Central Highlands and east coast.

plants.name: Australopyrum velutinum
plants.form: Erect, few-stemmed perennial.
plants.flowers: Spikes 2-5.5cm long, dense, the lowest spikelets sometimes distant.
plants.habitat: Recorded only from the Middlesex Plains area and south of Lake Augusta, Central Highlands.

plants.name: Austrofestuca littoralis
plants.form: Stiffly erect tufted yellowish green perennial, branching rhizomes, sharply pointed leaf blades.
plants.flowers: Dense spike-like panicle, frequently partly in sheath of upper leaf. Straw-coloured.
plants.habitat: Found in sandy coastal dunes.

plants.name: Austrostipa aphylla
plants.form: Tufted perennial. Leaf blades absent or very small at flowering.
plants.flowers: Panicle up to 25cm x 3cm. Contracted at maturity and often a tangled mass by entwining awns.
plants.habitat: To 350m altitude.

plants.name: Austrostipa bigeniculata
plants.form: Tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Spikelets green or purplish, lemma reddish-brown.
plants.habitat: East coast, open woodland/grassland up to 100m.

plants.name: Austrostipa blackii
plants.form: Tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Red-brown to dark brown.
plants.habitat: East coast, open woodland up to 100m.

plants.name: Austrostipa flavescens
plants.form: Tufted or shortly rhizomatous perennial.
plants.flowers: Spikelets green or purplish. Brownish-yellow, dark brown.
plants.habitat: Coastal up to 100m, commonly on dunes. North-west, King Island, Furneaux, north-east, east coast, west coast.

plants.name: Austrostipa mollis
plants.form: Tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Spikelets green or purplish.
plants.habitat: Predominantly east coast, dry situations, often under light forest, up to 350m; also north-west, north-east, Ben Lomond and Midlands.

plants.name: Austrostipa nodosa
plants.form: Tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Spikelets purplish.
plants.habitat: East coast and Midlands to 400m in open grassland or under light forest, dry habitats.

plants.name: Austrostipa pubinodis
plants.form: Tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Red-brown
plants.habitat: Predominantly east coast, open grasslands and sedgelands and under light forest cover; also north-east, north-west, Midlands, kunanyi/Mt. Wellington, sand dunes on the west coast.

plants.name: Austrostipa rudis subsp. australis
plants.form: Robust erect perennial.
plants.flowers: Greenish or purplish, dark-brown or yellow-brown.
plants.habitat: Open grassland and under light forest cover from sea level on the east coast to 740m in the Central Highlands; also Ben Lomond and north-west.

plants.name: Austrostipa scabra subsp. falcata
plants.form: Tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Erect panicle, 25 cm.

plants.name: Austrostipa scabra subsp. scabra
plants.form: Tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Purplish, honey brown, whitish.
plants.habitat: Apparently uncommon, east coast to 270m, dry open habitats.

plants.name: Austrostipa semibarbata
plants.form: Robust tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Dark brown to almost black.
plants.habitat: Open grassland and under light forest cover in dry situations, north-east, Midlands, east coast and Central Highlands, sea level to 360m.

plants.name: Austrostipa stipoides
plants.form: Tufted perennial. Leaf blades tightly in rolled, stiff, smooth, shiny, sharply pointed tips.
plants.flowers: Whitish yellow inflorescence up to 22cm long.
plants.habitat: All coasts.

plants.name: Austrostipa stuposa
plants.form: Tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Lemma reddish-brown, hairs whitish or pale gold.
plants.habitat: Grassland, open woodland, scrub and heath, sea level to 550m, north-east, Midlands, east coast, Central Highlands.

plants.name: Azolla rubra
plants.form: Sparsely branched aquatic fern forming free floating masses, roots unbranched.
plants.habitat: Occurs in still or slow-moving waters of agricultural dams, lagoons, creeks and rivers.
plants.notes: Normally light green in colour under shade but in full sun changes to a conspicuous purplish red which is believed to protect leaves from ultra violet. Bird attracting. Commonly grown on ponds or dams as a cover for fish and food for water birds. Also used in cold water aquaria.

plants.name: Baeckea gunniana
plants.form: Erect, densely branched shrub, or prostrate and spreading over boulders.
plants.flowers: Petals, white, 5-7 stamens, not opposite petals. Often numerous at ends of branchlets.
plants.fruit: Capsule – insignificant cup-like capsules turn from green to pale brown when ripe. Fruits are not persistent and open to release seed from 3 valves when ripe.
plants.habitat: Abundant in sub-alpine habitats. Frequent in bog and wetter alpine heaths, sometimes dominant. More common in the east of Tasmania than the west.
plants.notes: Foliage has a strong lemony eucalyptus-like smell when crushed.

plants.name: Baeckea leptocaulis
plants.form: Shrub with slender erect branches.
plants.flowers: Petals white, almost orb-shaped, 5 stamens, irregularly spaced and not opposite petals.
plants.fruit: Capsule – small and cup-like, turn from green to pale brown when ripe. Fruits are not persistent and open to release seed from valves when ripe.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant on wet heaths near the north-west, west and south-west coasts.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Similar to Baeckea gunniana but has larger fragrant leaves and forms a less dense shrub.

plants.name: Baloskion australe
plants.form: Rhizomatous graminoid with many erect dark reddish-green flowering stems. Leaves reduced to sheaths on flowering stems
plants.flowers: One to few flowered reddish terminal inflorescence.
plants.habitat: Occurs in mountainous areas in bolster heaths and other wet heath alpine and sub-alpine sites.
plants.notes: Frog habitat. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Baloskion tetraphyllum subsp. tetraphyllum
plants.form: Rhizome
plants.flowers: Male and female spikelets red-brown.
plants.habitat: Peaty heaths, river flats, margins of rainforest, seal level to 450m.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Banksia marginata
plants.form: Variable shrub to small tree.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence cylindrical spikes, 10cm long, of soft yellow flowers.
plants.fruit: Seed follicles clustered in woody cones
plants.habitat: This widespread species occurs as a shrub in heath, coastal scrub, dry sclerophyll forest, grassy forest and sub-alpine forest. As a tree it is relatively common on sheltered coastal sand dunes and in the grassy woodlands of the Midlands.
plants.notes: Very useful for providing medium-level cover (up to 8m) in windbreaks. May be used as a sheltering species in timber belts. Bird attracting. Bee attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi. High flammability. …

plants.name: Banksia serrata
plants.form: Tall shrub in poor soils or gnarled branching tree.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence oblong-cylindrical spikes, large up to 20cm long, 10cm wide, flowers pale yellow to golden.
plants.fruit: Seed follicles clustered in woody cones
plants.habitat: Very local at Sisters Hill, Rocky Cape, where it forms woodlands and extends into the understorey of dry sclerophyll forest.
plants.notes: Good drainage essential. Bird attracting. Bee attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Barbarea australis
plants.form: Dwarf herb with pinnate basal leaves and upper stem leaves with wavy margins.
plants.flowers: Small, yellow, borne in racemes and with 6 stamens. Flowers sporadically throughout year.
plants.fruit: Capsule (siliqua) elongated, 4-angled, to 5cm long, slender on stalks to 1cm long.
plants.habitat: Recorded by J. D. Hooker from moist or marshy districts in the centre of Tasmania and near Launceston.
plants.notes: May be short-lived but grows readily from seed with plants grown in the ground or in containers.

plants.name: Bauera rubioides
plants.form: Wiry shrub with long spreading branches.
plants.flowers: 5 or 6 petals on slender stalks, pink or white. Stamens very numerous with long filaments.
plants.fruit: Capsule opens by 2 valves. Seed very fine.
plants.habitat: Abundant from sub-alpine woodland downwards wherever sufficient light and moisture are available. In areas of high rainfall on the west coast can grow to 6m high growing with and over other shrubs.
plants.notes: Bee Attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Bedfordia arborescens
plants.form: Robust tree
plants.habitat: Associated with cloud forest, a term referring to vegetation that strips moisture from mist and cloud enveloping mountains for many days of the year.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Bedfordia linearis subsp. linearis
plants.form: Shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow, white-stalked, one or two in each axil of leaves near the ends of branches.
plants.fruit: Achene with long white parachute bristles.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet eucalypt forests and on well drained rocky hillsides, on the Central Plateau, in the islands of Bass Strait and in south-west Tasmania. Intergrades with Bedfordia salicina on drier rocky slopes on dolerite.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Bedfordia linearis var. curvifolia
plants.form: Bushy shrub or small slender tree.
plants.flowers: Small yellow daisy, 1-2 in leaf axils near end of stem.
plants.habitat: Wet eucalypt forest and rocky hillsides of Central Plateau and south of the state.
plants.notes: Well drained soil with constant moisture. Tolerates part shade.

plants.name: Bedfordia linearis var. oblongifolia
plants.form: Bushy shrub or small slender tree.
plants.flowers: Small yellow daisy, 1-2 in leaf axils near end of stem.
plants.habitat: Wet eucalypt forest and rocky hillsides of Central Plateau and south of the state.
plants.notes: Well drained soil with constant moisture. Tolerates part shade.

plants.name: Bedfordia salicina
plants.form: Shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Yellow, 5-25 or more in dense clusters in the axils of the leaves.
plants.fruit: Long cylindrical achene with pappus bristles finely toothed.
plants.habitat: Widespread in the understorey of tall eucalypt forest. It also forms a dense scrub on cliffs in areas of high rainfall and in gullies and extends into sub-alpine eucalypt forest. Is also found on dry, rocky sites on dolerite.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Moderate flammability.

plants.name: Bellendena montana
plants.form: Small shrub with branches erect or decumbent.
plants.flowers: White to pale pink in showy clusters above the foliage.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – brilliant red or yellow, flattened and hanging.
plants.habitat: Almost exclusively an alpine plant, widespread and locally abundant on mountain plateaux.
plants.notes: Grows well at higher elevations, extremely slow/difficult nearer to sea level.

plants.name: Bertya tasmanica subsp. tasmanica
plants.form: Erect, much-branched, heath-like shrub with long, narrow, alternate leaves 8-20cm long. Leaf margins rolled under, and lower surface covered with dense white woolly hairs.
plants.flowers: Small, golden and bell-shaped. Solitary, in the leaf axils or a few together on very short stalks.
plants.fruit: Capsule – dry, oval-shaped, and densely hairy, 6-8mm long, containing one smooth seed.
plants.habitat: In the north and east, in the understorey of wet sclerophyll forest on river and stream banks. One near-coastal population is known from near Coles Bay, within low she oak forest or wind-pruned coastal heath/scrub.

plants.name: Beyeria viscosa
plants.form: Tall shrub or small tree.
plants.fruit: Paper capsule – oblong, smooth; 3 seeds or fewer in capsule.
plants.habitat: A pyramidal tree found in gullies in the east of the state, usually as an understorey to eucalyptus. Locally abundant especially on shady, rocky banks.
plants.notes: Moderate flammability. Crushed leaves have a strong turpentine aroma.

plants.name: Billardiera longiflora
plants.form: Slender undershrub with stems twining, to vigorous open climber. Stems up to 2m long.
plants.flowers: Tubular, green-yellow, fairly showy, up to 2.5cm long.
plants.fruit: Berry – blue, but, rarely, white on kunanyi/Mt. Wellington. Up to 12 seeds per fruit. Seed is dark brown or maroon when ripe.
plants.habitat: Quite common, climbing in the shrubby understorey of all but the driest forest communities.
plants.notes: If planting in the home garden support on trellis or dead branch/shrub as this plant will eventually strangle and kill its supportive “host”. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Billardiera macrantha
plants.form: Strongly climbing and branching vines often forming leafy blankets over supporting understorey shrubs, to 5–6m tall; stems shining brown.
plants.flowers: Flowers solitary in upper leaf axils, pendulous; petals greenish yellow with bright green tips in bud.
plants.fruit: Berry – firm, glossy, blue, oblong, 10–18mm long. Seeds numerous, oval, 2 mm long, surrounded by soft pulp.
plants.habitat: Widespread in forest margins and in sheltered gullies among non-forest habitats.

plants.name: Billardiera mutabilis
plants.form: Shrubby, slender climber.
plants.flowers: Pendulous bell-shaped, green-yellow turning purplish with age. Tube with 5 petals.
plants.fruit: Berry – slender, cylindrical, olive green becoming yellow when ripe, sometimes red. The berry is pulpy and seeds red-brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Common in the north in dry woodland. Becomes shrubby if grown in the open. Tolerates light to moderate frosts.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Birds, including honeyeaters and silvereyes, feed on the flowers and/or fruit. Flowers through spring and summer, fruits at various stages of development and flowers are often on the plant at the same time. Prefers well-drained sites in full sun or partial shade.

plants.name: Billardiera ovalis
plants.form: Slender undershrub with stems twining, to vigorous open climber.
plants.flowers: Tubular, green-yellow, fairly showy, up to 2.5cm long.
plants.fruit: Berry – pink. Up to 12 seeds per fruit.
plants.habitat: Among rocks near the shore, and a little inland, spreading into the first line of trees. Grows on a variety of soils.

plants.name: Blandfordia punicea
plants.form: Robust tufted perennial herb arising from thickened rootstock.
plants.flowers: Brilliant red, pendulous on short stalks. Inside of flower and reflexed tips bright yellow.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – long, triangular. Each capsule has numerous seeds that are brown and hairy.
plants.habitat: Wet heaths, moors and hillsides, sea level to sub-alpine in high rainfall areas of north-west, west and south.
plants.notes: Unreliable as a garden plant. Fire seems to stimulate growth and flowering. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Blechnum cartilagineum
plants.form: Fern with pale green fronds crowded, erect broad, leathery, young fronds may be pink.
plants.habitat: Extremely rare in Tasmania. Favours sheltered sites along creeklines in northern and eastern Tasmania. Hardy enough to withstand clay soils and dry areas under established eucalypts. Tolerant of a range of soil types and positions.
plants.notes: Very hardy; clump forming; suitable for growing in large container.

plants.name: Blechnum chambersii
plants.form: Fern which forms clumps of semi-erect or weeping fronds, dark green, thin textured; dimorphic, sterile fronds 15-55cm long.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in rainforest, wet sclerophyll forest and fern gullies from sea level to rarely more than 500m. The species likes dark, moist and sheltered sites and can hang in masses from waterfalls and other wet rock faces. …
plants.notes: Resents disturbance and is slow to establish.

plants.name: Blechnum deltoides
plants.form: Fern with dark green leathery fronds, 20-50cm long, on long stalks, segments sickle-shaped.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in western half of state and in a few locations elsewhere. Grows in cool, moist habitats in rainforest or on rock outcrops in high rainfall areas. Grows from rock overhangs, cliff faces and waterfalls or along watercourse margins. …
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Blechnum fluviatile
plants.form: Small fern forming a low rosette, 20-75cm; fronds prostrate or spreading, pale green thin-textured.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in rainforest, wet sclerophyll and fern gullies, from sea level to exposed sub-alpine creeks. Rare as a lithophyte of waterfalls and wet rock-faces, more common as a terrestrial species of creek and river banks or amongst boulders in riverbeds. Intolerant of dryness.
plants.notes: Fast growing when in a suitable position. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Blechnum minus
plants.form: Fern forms rosettes or clumps; fronds, usually 40-75cm long but can be up to 200cm, shiny green, thin textured, erect or semi, crowded.
plants.habitat: Widespread in a range of vegetation but needs good light. In wet forest it grows where there is a broken canopy such as on riverbanks. Found in discontinuously inundated parts of creeks and rivers from coastal swamps to over 1000m. Re-colonises disturbed, badly drained sites. …
plants.notes: Forms dense patches bushy to ground level. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Blechnum neohollandicum
plants.form: Terrestrial fern with clustered erect fronds.
plants.habitat: Known from a single site near Chain of Lagoons.

plants.name: Blechnum nudum
plants.form: Fern with dark green fronds, commonly 40-60cm long but can be up to 120cm, erect spreading in rosette, segments linear, joined.
plants.habitat: Abundant and widespread in moist soils in a range of vegetation types from sea level to over 1000m. Seems to be absent only from the Midlands. Frequent coloniser of disturbed areas. Grows in large colonies in semi-shade or shade. Tolerates boggy soils.
plants.notes: Very hardy; clump forming; suitable for growing in large container. Bird attracting. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Blechnum parrisiae
plants.form: Terrestrial fern with underground stolons. Fronds erect, 20-70cm long, stiff and rough.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in Tasmania and mostly restricted to the mid-east coast and Tamar estuary. Grows in thin soil layers over rock but more typically on the margins of small permanent creeks where it grows from the rubble of the creekbank. Intolerant of deep shade.
plants.notes: Hardy and readily grown in any partially protected situation in the garden. New fronds are often an attractive purplish pink.

plants.name: Blechnum patersonii subsp. patersonii
plants.form: Terrestrial, occasionally lithophytic.
plants.habitat: Found in dark locations beside running water.
plants.notes: Very hardy; clump or slow spreading; red new growth. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Blechnum pennamarina subsp. alpina
plants.form: Fern with fronds prostrate or spreading, dark green. Dimorphic with short sterile fronds and taller fertile fronds. Segments almost triangular.
plants.habitat: Widespread in the highlands of Tasmania, occasional near sea-level. Low altitude populations are typically in open, grassy sites beside waterways originating at higher altitudes. On mountain plateaux found in bogs, watercourse margins and amongst rocks.
plants.notes: Red new growth. Grows during summer months and becomes dormant in winter. Useful in cultivation because it forms a compact mat of low ground cover foliage.

plants.name: Blechnum spinulosum
plants.form: Terrestrial fern. Fronds rough; segments with terminal pinnae joined in a tail.
plants.habitat: Extremely rare in Tasmania with scattered small populations reported from only a few sites, including the banks of the River Leven, Pipers River and Cataract Gorge, Launceston.

plants.name: Blechnum wattsii
plants.form: Medium sized coarse fern, fronds, up to 125cm long, dark green, erect, bearing dark scales.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant from sea level to 1000m in a range of vegetation types. May be dominant groundcover in rainforest and wet eucalypt forest. Grows in extensive colonies. Will not tolerate dryness but will tolerate salt-laden winds in coastal situations.
plants.notes: Very hardy; clump forming; suitable for growing in large container; red new growth. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Bolboschoenus caldwellii
plants.form: Summer-green, perennial plant with lime-green, tufted, leafy stems which are triangular in cross-section.
plants.flowers: In heads of 2-6 chestnut-brown, many-flowered spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nut – greenish to golden-brown, smooth and shining, 3.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Shallow standing water, sometimes brackish water, growing in heavy black mud. North-east, Midlands and east coast.

plants.name: Bolboschoenus medianus
plants.form: Summer-green perennial with lime-green, often solitary stems and alternate leaves.
plants.flowers: In compact heads of mid-brown, many-flowered spikelets.
plants.habitat: Known only from two sites in the Midlands, growing in heavy black mud.

plants.name: Boronia citriodora subsp. citriodora
plants.form: Small, low-growing and much branched shrub with aromatic strongly lemon-scented leaves.
plants.flowers: Four-petalled star-like flowers are more pink in bud than when open.
plants.habitat: Abundant in sub-alpine moors and on mountains in central and south-eastern areas.
plants.notes: Needs well drained soil and full sun. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Boronia citriodora subsp. orientalis
plants.form: Prostrate to erect, woody shrub.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence axillary and terminal; flowers solitary, petals white to pink.
plants.habitat: Found in alpine heath at Mt Barrow and Ben Lomond.

plants.name: Boronia citriodora subsp. paulwilsonii
plants.form: Erect shrub
plants.flowers: Inflorescence axillary and terminal, 1–7-flowered.
plants.habitat: Found in a variety of usually wet habitats including, Eucalyptus/Nothofagus woodland.

plants.name: Boronia elisabethiae
plants.form: Semi-erect to weakly spreading, woody sub-shrub to 50 cm long.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence terminal or axillary, 1–3-flowered; petals white to pink.
plants.habitat: Found in western Tasmania from sea level to 960m in exposed areas with poor and rocky or peaty soils; also in wet and dry conditions in button grass and sedge moorland.

plants.name: Boronia gunnii
plants.form: Erect, multi-branched woody shrub.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence is situated in the leaf axils, 1- to 7-flowered; 4 pink or white petals.
