plants.habitat: Usually found in exposed, rocky riverine areas prone to flooding.

plants.name: Boronia hemichiton
plants.form: Erect to somewhat straggly shrub.
plants.flowers: Flowers in clusters of 1 to 5 in the upper leaf axils; pointed petals pink to white.
plants.fruit: Capsule – glabrous. The seeds are dark brown to black and about 2 mm long.
plants.habitat: Grows in wet heath or scrub; found only on Mt Arthur and in upper catchment of Pipers River.

plants.name: Boronia hippopala
plants.form: Erect woody shrub.
plants.flowers: White to pink flowers occur in clusters of 1 to 3 in the upper leaf axils. The flowers occur in four parts.
plants.habitat: Grows in wet heaths.

plants.name: Boronia parviflora
plants.form: Small, weak shrub with elliptical leaves to 2 cm. May be prostrate, trailing.
plants.flowers: White or pale pink flowers axillary or terminal, crowded towards the tops of stems.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in wet heaths in Tasmania.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Boronia pilosa subsp. pilosa
plants.form: Small shrub; leaves have mildly unpleasant smell when crushed.
plants.flowers: Pink or white flowers with four petals at ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant, widespread throughout the lowlands.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Boronia pilosa subsp. tasmanensis
plants.form: Erect shrub
plants.flowers: Inflorescence 1–10-flowered; petals white to pink.
plants.habitat: Confined to the Tasman and Forestier Peninsulas; found in dense or open and usually wet heath or bushland.

plants.name: Boronia rhomboidea
plants.form: Loose, slender, much-branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Pink flowers, 4 petals, solitary or 2 to 3 together; terminal or in a few upper leaf axils.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent on mountains of the Central Plateau, heaths in the north-west, and North West Bay River at Longley.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Boronia rozefeldsii
plants.form: Erect woody shrub.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence axillary, 3–7-flowered; petals pink.
plants.habitat: Confined to Schouten Island; found in sparsely vegetated areas or bare granitic outcrops and ridgelines.

plants.name: Bossiaea cinerea
plants.form: Much-branched shrub, erect or spreading.
plants.flowers: Brown and yellow pea, long-stalked with two upper lobes broader than the three lower.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – flattened, about twice as long as broad. Pod contains several to many pale or yellow-brown seeds.
plants.habitat: Abundant in coastal heaths and light coastal forest.
plants.notes: Variable in habit but prefers a little shade. Very floriferous.

plants.name: Bossiaea cordigera
plants.form: Prostrate, slender shrub, branches spread or straggle over other plants. Leaves fern-like.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers with yellow petals, solitary on slender stems.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – several to many seeds, black when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread and occasional in the north and east mainly in shady places from sea level to 1000m.

plants.name: Bossiaea heterophylla
plants.form: Semi-prostrate to erect shrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, yellow with a red flare, flushed pink on the back.
plants.habitat: Only known on the north coast.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Bossiaea prostrata
plants.form: Small prostrate undershrub.
plants.flowers: Yellow streaked with crimson pea flowers.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – 2-2.5cm long, flat, has several to many seeds, black when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in dry and stony places. Common in dry woodlands.

plants.name: Bossiaea riparia
plants.form: Undershrub, sometimes erect, usually trailing, base of stem stout and woody.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, solitary in upper axils, petals yellow and crimson.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – without hairs, on a small stalk, has several to many seeds, black when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread and occasional in a wide range of habitats, from river banks at sea level to mountains at 1000m. Occasional in dry alpine heath and tussock grassland at lower altitudes.

plants.name: Bossiaea tasmanica
plants.form: Prostrate or low-growing rigid shrub with smaller branches ending in spines.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers with greenish-yellow petals, solitary or two together in axils of upper leaves.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – several to many seeds, black when mature.
plants.habitat: Primarily in inland areas in the north-east. Local at The Rocks near New Norfolk.

plants.name: Botrychium lunaria
plants.form: Sterile frond, once divided bright green; fertile frond 1-2 divisions taller, bearing sporangia.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in Tasmania but locally abundant in sub-alpine or alpine grassland up to 1220m.

plants.name: Brachyloma ciliatum
plants.form: Small woody plant with tough slender rhizomes and spreading branches.
plants.flowers: White, tubular, solitary in leaf axils and formed early in growing season. 5 tufts of hairs in throat of tube.
plants.fruit: Drupe – fleshy with 5 parts, surrounding a seed which has a woody coat.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in sandy heaths near the east and north coasts.

plants.name: Brachyloma depressum
plants.form: Much- branched shrub with slender wiry branches.
plants.flowers: White, tubular, solitary in axils at base of the dwarf shoots. 5 tufts of hairs at throat of tube.
plants.fruit: Drupe – fleshy with 5 parts surrounding a hard seed.
plants.habitat: Local on the east and north coasts and in the islands of Bass Strait.

plants.name: Brachyscome aculeata
plants.form: Tufted perennial herb with slender woody rootstock. Leaves in a rosette.
plants.flowers: Blue, sometimes white, daisy-like flowers, 2cm in diameter with yellow centres.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in a large range of vegetation types, especially on dry or rocky hillsides.
plants.notes: Prefers a sunny or semi-shaded position and withstands wet conditions but reasonable drainage preferred. Seedlings transplant easily. Can be grown as a bog plant. Makes an excellent rockery plant.

plants.name: Brachyscome decipiens
plants.form: Small, tufted perennial herb, leaves with a toothed margin.
plants.flowers: Flower heads about 4cm across, light blue daisy flowers.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in grassy places; often growing in colonies.
plants.notes: A useful small plant for a rockery or moist position.

plants.name: Brachyscome diversifolia
plants.form: Tufted perennial herb. Robust variety with thick, blunt, oblong leaves.
plants.flowers: Flower heads 2-4cm across with numerous white ray florets.
plants.habitat: Confined to the islands of Bass Strait.

plants.name: Brachyscome graminea
plants.form: Small, spreading, perennial herb in a basal rosette or scattered on grass-like stems.
plants.flowers: Stem branched, flower heads about 2cm across with numerous deep blue ray florets.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet places, especially brackish marshes.
plants.notes: A very attractive species well worth cultivating.

plants.name: Brachyscome parvula
plants.form: Small tufted perennial herb.
plants.flowers: White daisy flowers, flower heads about 1cm across.
plants.habitat: Flinders Island; elsewhere recorded only three times; from the west coast at the Gordon River, at Strahan and from swampy ground near Cradle Mountain.
plants.notes: Resembles Brachyscome graminea.

plants.name: Brachyscome perpusilla
plants.form: A very tiny annual herb.

plants.name: Brachyscome radicans
plants.form: Dwarf perennial herb with stolons.
plants.flowers: White or mauve daisy flowers borne on long stalks. Flower heads to 2cm.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent in swampy ground.
plants.notes: Highly suitable for cultivation as a ground cover and as a container plant. Should adapt to most soils.

plants.name: Brachyscome radicata
plants.form: Perennial with short, stout rootstock and hairy glandular, erect/ascending branches.
plants.flowers: Flower heads 1-2cm across with white or mauve florets.
plants.fruit: Achene – almost black, slightly thickened, very hairy and with short pappus.
plants.habitat: Present in the foothills of kunanyi/Mt. Wellington and on the Middlesex Plains near Cradle Mountain.

plants.name: Brachyscome rigidula
plants.form: Small, perennial herb. Plants may be erect or prostrate, compact or straggling.
plants.flowers: Flower heads 1-1.8cm across with white, pink or various shades of blue daisy flowers.
plants.fruit: Achene – light to dark brown with lighter coloured wings.
plants.habitat: Local in dry pastures in eastern and central parts of the state.
plants.notes: Prefers a sunny aspect and well-drained soil. It tolerates dry conditions but should not be allowed to dry out.

plants.name: Brachyscome spathulata
plants.form: Rosette of toothed leaves arising from a rhizomatous base.
plants.flowers: Solitary purple-mauve flower head, 3cm across, eye yellow.
plants.habitat: Found in grasslands and open ground in forests from sea level to 1200m.

plants.name: Brachyscome tenuiscapa
plants.form: Tufted perennial with basal cluster of toothed leaves.
plants.flowers: Mauve, daisy-like 2-3cm across, singly on slender stems usually with one stem leaf.
plants.fruit: Achene – black, smooth, wedge shaped with very short white pappus (sometimes absent).
plants.habitat: Occurs in open forest and on granite outcrops and has been recorded only once in Tasmania.
plants.notes: Plants spread by suckering. In cultivation plants prefer sun in winter, dappled shade in summer and an enriched soil. Roots should be protected by deep mulch. Plants will die back if they dry out but will regenerate after rains.

plants.name: Bromus arenarius
plants.form: Erect annual, loosely tufted or solitary stems.
plants.flowers: Panicle 12cm long, open.

plants.name: Brunonia australis
plants.form: Small herb, perennial under favourable conditions.
plants.flowers: One or more on separate stalks. Small individual florets have 5 deep sky blue petals.
plants.fruit: Each seed head contains individual fruits (nuts), about 3 mm long, tightly clustered together. These turn grey with a small white feathery tip; 4-10 seeds per head.
plants.habitat: Sandy or gravelly soil in dry forests in the north.

plants.name: Bulbine bulbosa
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.flowers: Erect stalk 8-60cm long, unbranched, bears numerous yellow 6-petalled flowers in a spike.
plants.fruit: Rounded capsule – turns brown and brittle when mature; mature seed is angular and dark brown or black.
plants.habitat: Launceston Field Naturalists Club: says it is widespread in open rocky, sandy or grassy areas from sea level to mountains; Curtis: says it is rarely collected and apparently confined to the north-east and Midlands, dry material difficult to distinguish from Bulbine glauca. Sensitive to drought.
plants.notes: Koori (mainland) use: the bulbous roots were eaten year-round, and were probably cooked. Leaves are toxic to stock.

plants.name: Bulbine crassa
plants.habitat: Only occurs on off-shore Bass Strait Islands.

plants.name: Bulbine glauca
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.flowers: Yellow flowers in a large spike, stamens densely bearded with yellow hairs. Few flowers at a time.
plants.fruit: Rounded capsule – about 5mm in diameter; turns brown and brittle when mature. Mature seed is angular and dark brown or black.
plants.habitat: Common in rocky places, especially moss-covered rocky ledges liable to dry out in summer. Also on sand dunes. Often found growing in a group of similar plants. Common in damp sandy soils under light forest cover, sea level to about 250m; north-west, north-east, Midlands and east coast.
plants.notes: Plants can be short-lived but regenerates readily from seed.

plants.name: Bulbine semibarbata
plants.form: Annual herb
plants.flowers: Yellow, star-like.
plants.fruit: Rounded capsule – small capsules and flower stems turn from orange brown to light brown. Seed is dark brown blackish or silvery-grey when mature.
plants.habitat: Open, frequently damp situations in coastal areas or under light eucalypt or allocasuarina forest and occasionally inland on dry, stony hillsides up to 400m; north-west, north-east, Furneaux Group and east coast.
plants.notes: May be short-lived but regenerates readily from seed.

plants.name: Burchardia umbellata
plants.form: Tufted herb
plants.flowers: White with 6 petals. Flowers grow in umbels.
plants.fruit: Triangular capsule – becomes red-brown and brittle as it matures. Seed is dark brown and hard when mature.
plants.habitat: Coastal heaths and swampy areas or under light dry sclerophyll cover sea level to 350m.
plants.notes: Dies down to a bulb annually.

plants.name: Burnettia cuneata
plants.form: Leafless with a dark purplish brown stem.
plants.flowers: 1-4 (rarely 7) white or pink flowers 25mm across, strongly hooded dorsal sepal, red striped labellum covered with numerous short calli. Flower only fully open when weather is warm and humid.
plants.habitat: Damp button grass moorland, sedgeland, damp heathland and paperbark or teatree scrub.
plants.notes: Strong response to high intensity summer fires in the preceding season, appearing as a leafless flowering plant, often in very large numbers.

plants.name: Bursaria spinosa subsp. spinosa
plants.form: Shrub or small tree. Very variable in size and form. In west and south-west a tree to 18m.
plants.flowers: Prolific cream-white scented flowers.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – seeds like coins in a papery heart-shaped purse.
plants.habitat: Grows on a range of soils, including acidic and moderately alkaline soils. Dislikes very poorly-drained sites. Tolerates wind and frost, although young plants may be susceptible.
plants.notes: Very useful plant; for erosion control (fibrous roots), shelter belts, and as wildlife habitat. Bursaria flowers attract many insects, including some that feed on the saw-fly larvae that infest eucalypts, and wasps that parasitise pasture grubs. Bird attracting. …

plants.name: Caesia alpina
plants.form: Tufted perennial herbaceous plant, often with curved leaves, and fleshy-fibrous roots.
plants.flowers: Yellowish-green to greenish-white flowers, on stalks 5mm long.
plants.fruit: Capsule – strongly lobed and green, even when the seeds are mature. 6-8 seeds are enclosed in each capsule. Seeds are black and firm when ripe.
plants.habitat: Wet heaths and swamp margins, Central Highlands, north-east, east coast and south-west.

plants.name: Caesia calliantha
plants.form: Erect, tufted herbaceous plant with thick, fibrous roots with tuberous swellings towards the tips.
plants.flowers: 1-3 flowers, with blue or purple petals with darker nerves, petals 6-9mm long.
plants.fruit: Capsule – strongly lobed and green, even when the seeds are mature. 6-8 seeds are enclosed in each capsule. Seeds are black and firm when ripe.

plants.name: Caesia parviflora var. minor
plants.form: Tufted herbaceous plant.
plants.flowers: White or tinged blue, petals less than 5mm long, stamens are greenish-white.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 3-lobed, up to 5mm wide. The capsule is green, even when the seeds are mature. 6-8 seeds are enclosed in each capsule. Seeds are black and firm when ripe.

plants.name: Caladenia alata
plants.form: Leaf erect, narrowly linear, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2 short lived, white to pink with dark red bands, mid-lobe orange to yellow, calli yellow, column green with red bands.
plants.habitat: Heathy open forest, teatree scrub and heathland.
plants.notes: Short lived and self-pollinating, occurs where habitat has moderate to high fire frequency.

plants.name: Caladenia alpina
plants.form: Robust species with broad leaves.
plants.flowers: 1-4 flowers 35mm across, white internally and pink to red externally, broad strongly hooded dorsal sepal. Labellum white with red bars.
plants.habitat: Open, sunny sites above 400m in alpine and sub-alpine open eucalypt forest, grasslands and moorlands.
plants.notes: Tolerates fire, but occurs in mountain habitats with low fire frequency. Occurs on areas with prolonged snow cover.

plants.name: Caladenia angustata
plants.form: Leaf erect, filiform to very narrowly linear, sparsely hairy. Scape very slender and wiry, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2 intensely white to pinkish internally, reddish or greenish-brown externally, petals curving up, labellum white with reddish striae and spots, mid-lobe purple, calli yellow to purplish, column greenish with red markings.
plants.habitat: Grassy and heathy open eucalypt forest and woodland.
plants.notes: Moderate to high fire frequency habitat.

plants.name: Caladenia anthracina
plants.form: Leaf narrowly lanceolate, base purple blotched, densely hairy. Scape, wiry, densely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flower single, white to cream with pale reddish lines and prominent black tails, labellum white to cream, calli dark reddish purple, column translucent with reddish markings.
plants.habitat: Grassy woodland with silver wattle and bracken.
plants.notes: Much of its habitat has been lost to agriculture; has a restricted distribution in the Midlands area. Very dry and fire prone.

plants.name: Caladenia atrata
plants.form: Leaf erect and linear, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Intensely white flowers with exterior covered with black to reddish black glands. Strongly hooded dorsal sepal. Lemon scented.
plants.habitat: Open eucalypt forest and woodland, heathy understorey, sunny slopes.
plants.notes: Flowers open for only a few days. Responds well to fire and disturbance.

plants.name: Caladenia atrochila
plants.form: Leaf erect, narrowly linear, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2, short lived, white or pinkish internally, yellowish green externally, labellum mid-lobe and lateral lobes cream with deep crimson coalescing bars, apex of mid-lobe yellowish, calli yellow with dark red stalks, column green with crimson bars and suffusions.
plants.habitat: Eucalyptus obliqua woodland with heathy and scrubby understorey dominated by Leptospermum species and Bauera rubioides and in tall open Eucalyptus obliqua forest.
plants.notes: The flowers open for only a few days before self pollinating. Responds well to fire and disturbance.

plants.name: Caladenia aurantiaca
plants.form: Leaf erect, narrowly linear, very thin and wiry, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Small white flowers with widely spreading petals, lateral sepals held close together, orange labellum tip and calli. Self pollinating.
plants.habitat: Found on Deal Island and possibly islands in Furneaux Group. Occurs in fire prone habitat.

plants.name: Caladenia australis
plants.form: Leaf lanceolate, sparsely hairy. Scape, hairy.
plants.flowers: Flower usually single, creamy with red streaks, sepals with dark red osmophores, labellum red with maroon margins, calli dark red, shiny, column green with red markings.
plants.habitat: Heathy coastal forest, grasslands and scrub.
plants.notes: Fire prone habitat. Restricted to Furneaux Group.

plants.name: Caladenia brachyscapa
plants.form: Leaf linear, base purple blotched, hairy, underside densely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flower single, reddish pink, with thick blackish osmophores on all the segments, labellum white to reddish with darker veins and maroon apex, calli dark reddish purple, column translucent with reddish markings.
plants.habitat: Among grasses and low shrubs in sparse coastal scrub.
plants.notes: Fire prone habitat. Very rare because of grazing. Not observed since 1979; possibly extinct.

plants.name: Caladenia campbellii
plants.form: Leaf narrowly linear, erect, dark green, sparsely hairy. Scape relatively thick, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2, short-lived, cream internally, pinkish externally, labellum cream with orange tipped apex, calli yellow to orange, column cream with red bars.
plants.habitat: Among coastal and near coastal scrub.
plants.notes: Probably very rare due to its suitable range being converted to agriculture and the remaining land under threat.

plants.name: Caladenia carnea
plants.form: Leaf narrowly linear, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: 1-2 (occasionally up to 5) pink to bright pink internally, often white to greenish-white externally.
plants.habitat: Grassy and heathy open eucalypt forest, woodland and heathland.
plants.notes: Common

plants.name: Caladenia caudata
plants.form: Leaf broadly linear, base reddish-purple, densely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers usually single 40-50mm across. Pinkish-red flowers, dark red to blackish osmophores on all perianth segments. Labellum tip tapering to a long tail.
plants.habitat: Heathy and grassy eucalypt forest and woodlands, often with sheoaks. Sunny north facing slopes.
plants.notes: Flowers are pollinated by male Thynnine wasps. Fire frequency moderate to high.

plants.name: Caladenia clavigera
plants.form: Leaf lanceolate, red spotted at base, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: 1-2 flowers 40mm across, greenish-yellow with red stripes. Short dark red osmophores (clubs) on lateral sepals.
plants.habitat: Grassy open eucalypt forest, sheoak woodland and teatree scrub on Flinders Is.
plants.notes: Only smooth lipped spider orchid commonly seen in Tasmania. Fire frequency moderate to high.

plants.name: Caladenia congesta
plants.form: Slender, slightly hairy cap orchid with erect flowering stem; very narrow leaf, shorter than stem.
plants.flowers: 1-3 bright deep pink or pale reddish-purple, 3cm diameter, narrow sepals and petals. Protruding labellum. 2 broad rows of black shiny calli in a congested mass.
plants.habitat: Widely spread, localised sites on coastal sandy heathland to open sub-alpine bushland in Tasmania’s east and north.
plants.notes: Fire frequency moderate to high. Flowers may last up to 10 weeks if not pollinated.

plants.name: Caladenia cracens
plants.form: Small cap orchid with leaf narrowly linear, dark green, base reddish purple. Scape sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: 1-2 flowers, white to pale pink, pink to reddish externally, labellum whitish, heavily suffused and barred with red, mid-lobe cream, calli cream or yellow, column whitish with red suffusions and bars. Sweetly scented.
plants.habitat: Shrubby and heathy open eucalypt forest, teatree shrubland and heathland below 400m. Often favouring damp and poorly drained sites.
plants.notes: Relatively high fire frequency habitat.

plants.name: Caladenia dienema
plants.form: A shorter sturdy spider orchid.
plants.flowers: 1-2 flowers, 70-110mm across, cream with darker red lines and black caudae on all the segments; labellum wholly maroon or white to cream with a maroon apex, fringed; calli dark reddish purple; column translucent with reddish markings.
plants.habitat: Windswept low heathland among dwarfed shrubs and sedges.
plants.notes: Habitat has been reduced due to agricultural development, with the remainder subject to grazing.

plants.name: Caladenia dilatata
plants.form: Leaf lanceolate, base red purple, densely hairy.
plants.flowers: 1-2 flowers, 30mm across, yellowish-green with reddish stripes. Labellum has unusually large side lobes with long green comb-like teeth.
plants.habitat: Heathy open forest, coastal shrub, heathland, teatree scrub.
plants.notes: Widespread and locally common in east, north-west and Bass Strait Islands. The only green and red green-combed spider orchid found in Tasmania.

plants.name: Caladenia echidnachila
plants.form: Leaf narrowly lanceolate, base purple blotched, hairy. Scape wiry, hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2, 70-110mm across, fawn to pale tawny yellow, with pale reddish lines and darker sepaline caudae, labellum cream to yellowish, sometimes with red suffusions, calli dark red, column translucent with reddish markings.
plants.habitat: Coastal scrub, heathland and open eucalypt forest.
plants.notes: Labellum likened to the tongue of the echidna. Fire frequency moderate to high.

plants.name: Caladenia filamentosa
plants.form: Leaf tall, hairy.
plants.flowers: 10-40 maroon flowers with long thread-like tails (50-70mm long) on the flower segments. Labellum small, red with cream stripes.
plants.habitat: Coastal scrub, heathland and open eucalypt forest.
plants.notes: Tasmania’s only wispy spider orchid.

plants.name: Caladenia fuscata
plants.form: Leaf narrowly linear, dark green, sparsely hairy. Scape very thin and wiry, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flower single, white to pink internally, the exterior darker and heavily glandular, often with a prominent broad, darker central stripe, labellum white to pink with red bars, mid-lobe cream to yellowish, calli yellow, column greenish with narrow red bars.
plants.habitat: Heathy open eucalypt forest and woodland.
plants.notes: Tends to favour drier habitats and to flower earlier than Caladenia carnea. Moderate to high fire frequency.

plants.name: Caladenia gracilis
plants.form: Leaf erect, narrowly linear, moderately hairy. Scape slender and wiry, moderately hairy.
plants.flowers: Small cap orchid. Flowers white to pinkish interior, reddish brown to greenish-brown externally, labellum wholly white or cream.
plants.habitat: Heathy open eucalypt forest and woodland.
plants.notes: Some populations of Caladenia gracilis produce a strong musky scent while others hardly have any. Moderate to high fire frequency.

plants.name: Caladenia helvina
plants.form: Leaf linear-lanceolate, base reddish, hairy. Scape wiry, densely hairy.
plants.flowers: Tall tailed-spider orchid, 1-2 flowers, greenish to yellow with dark glandular tips, greenish-yellow labellum, reddish-purple calli, yellowish column.
plants.habitat: Grassy and heathy open eucalypt forest and sheoak/hakea heathland. Widely distributed from south-west coastal areas to higher altitudes in south and north-east.
plants.notes: Habitat with low to high fire frequency.

plants.name: Caladenia latifolia
plants.form: Leaf broadly lanceolate, bright green, very hairy on both surfaces, usually lax on the ground. Scape wiry and hairy.
plants.flowers: 1-4 pale pink or bright pink internally, externally duller and hairy, labellum pink, calli yellow and column pale pink with a dark pink toned anther.
plants.habitat: Windblown salt-spray areas near the sea, coastal scrub, grassland, teatree scrub and sheoak woodland.
plants.notes: Responds well to fire, often with vigour. Unlike most Caladenia species, Caladenia latifolia produces several tubers on the end of stolonoid roots.

plants.name: Caladenia lindleyana
plants.form: Medium sized long-tail spider orchid. Leaf narrowly lanceolate 60-110mm long, hairy. Scape wiry, hairy.
plants.flowers: 1-2 flowers, greenish-yellow with reddish slender caudae.
plants.habitat: Open eucalypt forest and woodland.

plants.name: Caladenia mentiens
plants.form: Leaf narrowly linear, sparsely hairy. Scape thin and wiry, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flower single pale pink to bright pink, labellum cream with dark red bars, mid-lobe pale yellow, calli yellow, column green with irregular red bars.
plants.habitat: Heathland, shrubland, woodland and open eucalypt forest, often in damper soils.
plants.notes: Scattered and uncommon.

plants.name: Caladenia pallida
plants.form: Leaf lanceolate, densely hairy. Scape densely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2 yellowish to bright rosy pink, calli cream, whitish or slightly reddish, column yellowish.
plants.habitat: Little known. Railton Hills area.
plants.notes: Lost habitat.

plants.name: Caladenia patersonii
plants.form: Long-tailed spider orchid. Leaf lanceolate, base red to purple blotched, densely hairy. Scape wiry, densely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2 commonly creamy white with darker red lines and reddish brown caudae, labellum wholly white to cream, sometimes the apex maroon, calli reddish, column translucent with reddish markings. Scented.
plants.habitat: Grows in sandy and clay soils in low shrubby and sedgy heathland.
plants.notes: Abundant flowering after fire, diminishing with shrubby regrowth. Restricted distribution due to habitat loss.

plants.name: Caladenia prolata
plants.form: Medium sized finger orchid. Leaf linear, dark green, red base, sparsely hairy. Scape relatively stout, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2, dull white internally, greenish with red bands and densely hairy externally, labellum pink with narrow dark red transverse bars, apex pale yellow, calli lemon coloured, column greenish with red transverse bars. Self pollinating.
plants.habitat: Highly localised, growing on coastal sandy soils, often in association with grasstrees on islands in the Furneaux group.
plants.notes: Maybe intolerant of high fire frequency.

plants.name: Caladenia pusilla
plants.form: Tiny finger orchid. Leaf narrowly linear, 30-60mm long, sparsely hairy. Scape relatively sturdy hairy.
plants.flowers: Flower single often not opening widely, usually pink internally, commonly paler towards the centre, brownish pink externally, labellum white or pink narrow red bars, mid-lobe cream to pale yellow, calli yellow, column green with red bars.
plants.habitat: Mainly heathland, occasionally open forest.
plants.notes: Caladenia pussila has smallest flower of the Caladenia genus in Tasmania. Flowering promoted by fire.

plants.name: Caladenia saggicola
plants.form: Tall long-tailed spider orchid. Leaf narrowly lanceolate, base purple blotched, densely hairy. Scape wiry, densely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2 white to cream with very pale reddish lines and dark grey to blackish petal and sepal tips, labellum white to cream, sometimes the mid-lobe maroon, calli reddish-purple, column translucent with reddish markings.
plants.habitat: Grows abundantly in association with Lomandra longifolia (sagg – namesake) in sparse woodland with old Eucalyptus viminalis, trees and scattered shrubs. This type of woodland has been greatly reduced since European settlement. …
plants.notes: Tasmania’s only white long-tailed spider orchid.

plants.name: Caladenia sylvicola
plants.form: Small finger orchid. Leaf narrowly linear, dark green, sparsely hairy. Scape very slender and wiry, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flower single, white internally, greenish externally, labellum white with apex yellow to orange, calli yellow to orange, column green and white. Self pollinating.
plants.habitat: Heathy Eucalyptus terminalis forest on a sunny hillside. Also on moist sheltered slopes growing amongst leaf litter and dense shrubs in tall open forest dominated by Eucalyptus obliqua. Seems to be restricted to one site on the lower slopes of kunanyi/Mt Wellington.

plants.name: Caladenia tonellii
plants.form: Tall, robust finger orchid. Leaf narrowly linear, dark green, base reddish purple. Scape relatively thick, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-3, bright pink internally, brownish pink externally, labellum white to pink with reddish bars, apex yellowish to orange, calli yellow, column green with broad red bars.
plants.habitat: Eucalyptus amygdalina forest with a shrubby understorey.
plants.notes: Distribution is likely to be very restricted because of conversion of its habitat to forestry plantations.

plants.name: Caladenia transitoria
plants.form: Small cap orchid. Leaf narrowly linear, base slightly reddish, densely hairy. Scape very slender and wiry, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-3 short lived, sometimes not opening, creamy-green to yellowish green internally, greenish-brown externally, labellum pink with purple bars and blotches, the apex calli dark purplish black, column greenish, spotted and blotched with red. …
plants.habitat: Occurs in shrubby and heathy open eucalypt forest and teatree shrubland. Grows in soils covered with bracken and heavy leaf litter.
plants.notes: Fires are relatively infrequent in this habitat, and flowering plants have been found one or two years after fire.

plants.name: Caladenia vulgaris var. nunguensis
plants.form: Small finger orchid. Leaf narrow 30-80mm long.
plants.flowers: 1-2 flowers, pale pink internally with dark pink bands on tepals. Labellum cream with widely gaping lobes, yellow apex. Calli with yellow tips.

plants.name: Caladenia vulgaris var. vulgaris
plants.form: Leaf narrowly linear, dark green, red base, sparsely hairy. Scape slender and wiry, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers 1-2 dull pink or whitish internally, with brownish central bands externally, labellum white or pink with prominent red transverse bars and yellow apex, calli yellow to orange, column whitish with red transverse bars. Self pollinating.
plants.habitat: Found in damp, sandy coastal heathland and scrub but more commonly in deep, damp litter in tall open eucalypt forest and eucalypt woodlands.
plants.notes: Main habitat tends to be damp with few fires; may be intolerant to high fire frequency.

plants.name: Calandrinia calyptrata
plants.form: Small annual herb with slender tap root, branched from the base.
plants.flowers: Small white or pink terminal flowers in loose groups on stalks up to 15 cm long.
plants.habitat: Common, especially on granite rocks of the east coast.

plants.name: Calandrinia eremaea
plants.form: Decumbent to erect annual herb; stems to 20 cm long.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence a loose terminal raceme. Flower petals white or pale pink.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 4mm long, narrow, 3-valved. Seeds red-brown to black with a metallic lustre when fully mature.
plants.habitat: Known only from the catchment of the Derwent River from 200–400 m altitude on dolerite or basalt rocks.

plants.name: Calandrinia granulifera
plants.form: Annual herb which branches from the base, with very fleshy egg or club-shaped leaves, 5cm long.
plants.flowers: Flower heads are dense, and contain few small flowers with white or pink petals.
plants.fruit: Capsule – egg-shaped or almost spherical, opens by 3 valves, and contains black, shining seeds.
plants.habitat: Gravelly and sandy soils, often granitic, in dry sclerophyll forest or woodland around the north-east.

plants.name: Caleana major
plants.form: Broad reddish, often spotted leaf, tall wiry scape.
plants.flowers: Usually bearing 1-3 flying-duck-shaped reddish shiny flowers with a sensitive hinged, smooth, broad labellum that snaps into the broad reddish column wings when touched.
plants.habitat: Heathy open eucalypt forest, sheoak woodland, teatree scrub and heathland. Widespread and locally common in lowland areas below 250m in the north, east and south-east and on Flinders Island.

plants.name: Callitriche brachycarpa
plants.form: Terrestrial annual or perennial herb with prostrate stems growing in tangled mats.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers occur together in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – light brown, four-lobed and 1mm wide. Separates into 4 fruitlets at maturity.
plants.habitat: Damp areas or near the water line of creeks and rivers. Recorded from Gould’s Country, and the Kindred, Picton and Forth Rivers.

plants.name: Callitriche sonderi
plants.form: Small semi-aquatic, mat-forming herb with stalked, 3-veined, opposite leaves.
plants.flowers: Paired, one female, one male, often in opposite leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – small (less than 1mm long and wide), dark brown, heart-shaped and present for most of the year.
plants.habitat: Known only from the Sea Elephant River on King Island.

plants.name: Callitriche umbonata
plants.form: Annual or perennial herb with slender stems, lower leaves with one vein, upper leaves with 3-5 veins.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers occur together in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – dark brown, and about 1mm long and wide, with a continuous wing around the base.
plants.habitat: Creeping or rooted in mud, or floating in shallow water. Recorded from the South Esk River and from a small pool near Jericho.

plants.name: Callitris oblonga subsp. oblonga
plants.form: Tall shrub or tree, occasionally to 8m. Can be varied in form, mostly growing as a tight columnar tree but will occasionally spread.
plants.fruit: Cone – pollen cones terminal on foliage. Mature cones, usually clustered, grey, oval but pointed with 2 rings of 3 scales; open to shed numerous angular 1-3 winged seeds.
plants.habitat: Local on banks of St. Pauls, Apsley and South Esk Rivers. Fire sensitive and largely confined to riverine scrub and woodland in the central east of the state. Likes dry sandy soils.
plants.notes: Fire sensitive. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Callitris rhomboidea
plants.form: Tall shrub or tree.
plants.flowers: Pollen bearing male cones may be seen easily in winter. Female flowers are less obvious.
plants.fruit: Cone – clustered on short branches, turn grey brown when ripe. Cones can contain up to 30 winged black seeds.
plants.habitat: Found in dry sclerophyll forest, grassy forest, scrub and heath in those parts of the east coast and the Furneaux Group where fire frequency is low. It forms pure stands in some places but is usually found in rocky situations mixed with eucalypts. Hardy in most soils.
plants.notes: Often forms an elegant dense tree in suburban gardens. High flammability. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Calocephalus citreus
plants.form: Tufted herb with silvery-grey linear leaves.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow flower heads on erect stems.
plants.habitat: Occasional in dry places. Has been found mainly along the eastern shores of the River Derwent between Bellerive and Bridgewater.
plants.notes: Needs a dry, well-drained site in full sun.

plants.name: Calocephalus lacteus
plants.form: Perennial herb forming dense patches 60cm or more in diameter.
plants.flowers: White flower heads in clusters which are ovoid or almost spherical.
plants.habitat: Occasional in open situations along roadsides and on river flats.

plants.name: Calochilus campestris
plants.form: Robust beard orchid with a large ribbed leaf.
plants.flowers: Widely spreading floral segments and a labellum with dense bushy beard, recurved apex and 2 prominent broad blue plates completely covering the base. Column with eye spots.
plants.habitat: Habitat in mainland states including open forest, heathy forest and heathland on moist but well drained sandy loams.

plants.name: Calochilus herbaceus
plants.form: Slender beard orchid narrow, short leaf.
plants.flowers: 1-10 green flowers with reddish stripes, often cupped. Oval-shaped labellum covered with purple bristly hairs with a visible tapered glandular tail and a greenish column with false eye spots.
plants.habitat: Prefers sedgeland and heathland on poorly drained or damp peats, clays and sandy soils. Also in teatree scrub. Widespread and common in lowland areas except for much of the east coast. Also occurs on King Island and Furneaux Group.
plants.notes: Grows on wet sandy or peaty soils, often colonising banks and the edge of tracks after disturbance. Often found around old logging sites. Flowers without fire.

plants.name: Calochilus paludosus
plants.form: Narrow keeled leaf.
plants.flowers: 1-9 flowers that open in warm weather. Slender beard orchid , widely spreading perianth segments that are usually bronze or reddish. The labellum has long, coarse, non-glandular reddish hairs with the lowest ones reduced to small calli, and a prominent long naked strap on the apex.
plants.habitat: Heathy and sedgy open eucalypt forest, teatree scrub, sedgeland and heathland on poorly drained peats and sandy soils, often near sheoaks.

plants.name: Calochilus robertsonii
plants.form: Robust beard orchid with a dark green leaf, maroon at the base.
plants.flowers: 1-9 flowers. Widely spreading perianth segments, purple labellum hairs with the basal ones reduced to small purple calli, and 2 prominent dark purple eye spots at the base of the column wings.
plants.habitat: Heathy and grassy open eucalypt forest, teatree scrub and heathland on well drained sandy, loamy, clay and stoney soils. Widespread and common in lowland areas up to 350m, including several Bass Strait Islands, but is most abundant in the drier eastern, midland and south-eastern parts of the state.

plants.name: Calochlaena dubia
plants.form: Vigorously spreading terrestrial fern with yellow green foliage.
plants.habitat: Grows on upper slopes of fern gullies and in margins of wet eucalypt forest or in drainage areas in dry eucalypt forest. Frequently intermixed with bracken.
plants.notes: Very hardy; wide spreading

plants.name: Calorophus elongatus
plants.form: Perennial, scrambling over supporting vegetation.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers.
plants.habitat: Wet heaths and shrubberies, margins of rainforest and under light eucalypt cover, sea level to 400m.

plants.name: Calorophus erostris
plants.form: Perennial, similar to Calorophus elongatus.
plants.habitat: Wet heaths and shrubberies, riverbanks, sea level to 1100m.

plants.name: Calystegia sepium subsp. sepium
plants.form: Large perennial creeping herb with rhizomes and stolons, and slender, twining stems which climb up to 4m over supporting plants. Leaves 4-10cm long with sharp tip.
plants.flowers: Funnel-shaped flowers usually white, sometimes tinged with pink, which open during the day and close at night.
plants.habitat: Riverbanks and forest margins, especially in the Tamar in the north of the state.

plants.name: Calystegia soldanella
plants.form: Trailing or twining perennial herb with slender, far-spreading rhizomes. Stems branched, trailing and prostrate, up to 50cm long. Leaves are kidney or heart-shaped.
plants.flowers: Funnel-shaped white, pale pink or purplish flowers with yellow centres, 2.5-4cm long.
plants.habitat: Coastal sands in the north-east, granite soils and coastal grasslands which have been grazed.
plants.notes: Tolerant of high salt loads and dry conditions. Dispersed by ocean currents and found on coastlines around the world.

plants.name: Calytrix tetragona
plants.form: Erect, branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Showy heads, 5 white or pink petals, prominent stamens.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – turn bronze or green and release from plant as mature. Dry one seeded fruit, with a fine awn-like attachment with fine hairs.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet coastal heaths where it is often dense and wind pruned. Grows along some northern rivers. Likes well-drained soils in full sun or semi-shade but will tolerate periodic inundation. Tolerates extended dry periods.
plants.notes: Reputedly has high flammability. Useful in providing food for moths, butterflies and other insects. Bird attracting. The foliage provides good low refuge for small birds. Good front line coastal plant.

plants.name: Campynema lineare
plants.form: Slender lily with leaves clustered at the base of the stem.
plants.flowers: Flowers dull greenish-yellow or brown-purple, on a single, unbranched flower stem.
plants.fruit: Capsule – up to 2cm long; containing numerous pale red-brown seeds.
plants.habitat: Heaths and herbfields, cliffs, lake margins and cushion plant communities, 40-1000m altitude, in the north-west, Central Highlands, Mt. Field, south-west and west coast.
plants.notes: Difficult to grow – requires boggy alpine/cool conditions.

plants.name: Cardamine astoniae
plants.form: Perennial herb with stems that grow along the ground and root at the nodes, and erect, unbranched flowering stems.
plants.flowers: Flowers with all white or pink petals, 6-11mm long, are borne in a many-flowered flower head.

plants.name: Cardamine franklinensis
plants.form: Erect, perennial herb with a taproot.
plants.fruit: Capsule (siliqua) 2.5-3.5cm long; seeds are less than 1.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Sub-alpine areas.

plants.name: Cardamine gunnii
plants.form: Perennial edible herb with slender rhizomes. Leaf bases of rosette persistent for a season.
plants.flowers: White with oval petals, shortly clawed and borne in spikes which elongate in fruiting stage.
plants.fruit: Capsule (siliqua) 2-lobed, 2-3 cm long, narrow, with conspicuous veins and borne on spreading stalks.
plants.habitat: Common in moist places through a wide range of altitudes.

plants.name: Cardamine lilacina
plants.form: Perennial herb with basal rosette, leaves variable.
plants.flowers: White, pink, lilac or purple, in terminal groups, sepals purple with white margins, style > 1mm.
plants.habitat: Grassy and rocky places in eastern and central mountains.
plants.notes: Distinguished from Cardamine gunnii by the length of the style.

plants.name: Cardamine papillata
plants.form: Small herb which is covered with minute protuberances on the flower stalks and sometimes along the margins of the leaves that are borne on the aerial parts of the stems.

plants.name: Cardamine paucijuga
plants.form: Annual herb, sometimes hairy, with leafy flowering stems and basal rosette.
plants.flowers: In terminal groups about 3mm long, white or pink.
plants.habitat: Rocky places in the eastern mountains.
plants.notes: Leaves sometimes purple underneath.

plants.name: Cardamine tenuifolia
plants.form: Perennial herb with weak trailing stems, basal leaves Rarely seen.
plants.flowers: Petals white or lilac, 5-12mm long; 6 stamens.
plants.fruit: Capsule (siliqua) linear, 15-40mm long, erect to spreading. Seeds oval to oblong, compressed and without narrow wing.
plants.habitat: Found in swamps.

plants.name: Carex appressa
plants.form: Densely tufted, perennial sedge.
plants.flowers: Brown cylindrical spike up to 30cm long or sometimes dense up to 150cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – biconvex; golden brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in wet sclerophyll forest, ditches and wet places throughout the State.
plants.notes: Valuable in preventing creek bank erosion (at the bank/water interface) as the fibrous roots stabilise the soil. Also slows water flow in drainage lines. Frog habitat: provides protection for frogs and habitat for various insects. …

plants.name: Carex archeri
plants.form: Small, slender sedge with erect, wiry stems.
plants.flowers: A short spike at the end of the flowering stem.
plants.habitat: Local in sub-alpine heaths, Central Highlands, Ben Lomond, south-west and Mt. Field.

plants.name: Carex barbata
plants.form: Tufted sedge with ribbed stems, thick, felted roots and slender rhizomes.
plants.flowers: In spikes.
plants.habitat: In wet places, up to 1000m altitude, in the north-west, Midlands, east coast and Mt. Field.

plants.name: Carex bichenoviana
plants.form: Perennial sedge with creeping rhizome. Leaves erect, tend to curl when dry.
plants.flowers: In panicles of spikes.
plants.habitat: Occasional on the west coast and in the north-west.

plants.name: Carex breviculmis
plants.form: Tufted sedge, with narrow, outward-curving, grass-like leaves.
plants.flowers: Very small flower spikes.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, light to very dark brown, 1.5-2mm long.
plants.habitat: Damp grasslands and heaths, sea level to sub-alpine.

plants.name: Carex capillacea
plants.form: Slender sedge forming small, dense tufts.
plants.flowers: Solitary spikes at the end of the flowering stem.
plants.habitat: Known from four marshy habitats in the Central Highlands, 600-1400m altitude, and at Arm River flats in the north-west.

plants.name: Carex cataractae
plants.form: Loosely tufted sedge, with shining upper leaf surfaces.
plants.flowers: In flower spikes.
plants.habitat: Recorded from the west coast, Central Highlands, east coast and south-west.

plants.name: Carex cephalotes
plants.form: Densely tufted sedge with stout roots, and somewhat curved stems.
plants.flowers: In solitary spikes.
plants.habitat: One collection known, from Mt Eliza in the south-west, altitude 1250m.

plants.name: Carex chlorantha
plants.form: Perennial sedge with slender, creeping rhizome.
plants.flowers: In panicles.
plants.habitat: In woodlands and river flats prone to flooding in the Central Highlands, Midlands, Ben Lomond and the south-west.

plants.name: Carex curta
plants.form: Tufted sedge with pale or greyish-green leaves and woody, creeping rhizomes.
plants.flowers: In flower spikes.
plants.habitat: Occasional in sub-alpine areas of the Central Highlands.

plants.name: Carex fascicularis
plants.form: Large tufted sedge with thick, felted roots, and drooping stalked heads.
plants.flowers: Clustered into long drooping heads, the lower heads are female. Upper heads, tan, are male.
plants.habitat: Grows along rivers and open swampy ground. Tolerates temporary inundation.
plants.notes: Valuable in preventing creek bank erosion (at the bank/water interface) as the fibrous roots stabilise the soil. Also slows water flow in drainage lines. Frog habitat: provides protection for frogs and habitat for various insects. Rarely eaten by stock. May provide a harbour for rabbits. …

plants.name: Carex flaviformis
plants.form: Loosely tufted sedge with erect, smooth stems.
plants.flowers: In spikes.
plants.habitat: Frequent in alpine to sub-alpine habitats in the Central Highlands.

plants.name: Carex gaudichaudiana
plants.form: Tufted sedge with erect leaves, stems triangular in cross-section, and creeping rhizomes.
plants.flowers: In spikes.
plants.fruit: Nut – grey-brown, egg-shaped, 2-3mm long, in seed heads.
plants.habitat: On the banks of lakes, pools, streams and swamps, often forming large swards. Sea level to alpine.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Carex gunniana
plants.form: Tufted sedge with erect, smooth stems and thick roots.
plants.flowers: In spikes.
plants.habitat: Widespread in eucalypt forests, sandy heathlands and stream sides.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Carex hypandra
plants.form: Loosely tufted sedge with erect, smooth, ridged stems.
plants.flowers: In spikes.
plants.habitat: Collected from Cradle Mountain in the Central Highlands and the Mount Eliza plateau in the south-west.

plants.name: Carex inversa
plants.form: A floppy sedge with spreading rhizomes, forming grass-like mats.
plants.flowers: In flower spikes, 4-9mm long.
plants.habitat: Widespread in damp places, sometimes found as a weed in lawns.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Carex iynx
plants.form: Robust, tufted sedge with rough leaves and slender stems which droop when fruiting.
plants.flowers: Small and inconspicuous, tightly packed in spikes which tend to be either male or female.
plants.habitat: In rough grassland, and invading pastures.

plants.name: Carex longebrachiata
plants.form: Robust, perennial tussock-forming sedge with slender stems which droop at the tips.
plants.flowers: In panicles.
plants.habitat: In rough grassland, near watercourses and invading pastures.

plants.name: Carex polyantha
plants.form: Loosely tufted sedge with closely ribbed stems, triangular in cross-section.
plants.flowers: In spikes.
plants.habitat: On the banks of rivers, streams and seepage slopes, from sea level to sub-alpine areas.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Carex pumila
plants.form: Sedge with tufts arising from creeping rhizomes, able to grow through accumulating sand, stems triangular in cross-section.
plants.flowers: In spikes.
plants.habitat: On all Tasmanian coasts, and sometimes in inland sandy places, and on the edges of salt lagoons in the Midlands.

plants.name: Carex raleighii
plants.form: Slender sedge with thread-like, wiry, smooth stems.
plants.flowers: In a head of spikes.
plants.habitat: In wet alpine and sub-alpine grasslands on the Central Highlands and Ben Lomond, and at lower altitudes on the west coast.

plants.name: Carex tasmanica
plants.form: Tufted sedge with erect leaves and stout felted roots. Leaves typically curled at the apex.
plants.flowers: In spikes, female spikes densely flowered.
plants.habitat: In eucalypt forests on the east coast and in the Midlands. On hillsides and in grasslands and sandy places.

plants.name: Carex tereticaulis
plants.form: Stout, tufted sedge, with rigid but hollow stems.
plants.flowers: In panicles.
plants.habitat: Widespread, in ditches and very wet places on the east coast and in the Midlands.

plants.name: Carpha alpina
plants.form: Tufted sedge with slender, erect stems. Leaf tips tend to curl when drying.
plants.flowers: In clusters of spikes.
plants.fruit: Nut – pale to dark brown, 2.5-3.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Common on mountains of the west coast, Central Highlands, Ben Lomond, south-west, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Carpha curvata
plants.form: Tufted sedge, forming tussocks up to 40cm in diameter. The upper third of the leaves curl conspicuously when drying.
plants.flowers: In a panicle of clustered spikes.
plants.habitat: On mountains in the Central Highlands and south-west; at sea level at Bathurst Harbour.

plants.name: Carpha rodwayi
plants.form: Small, tufted, mat-forming sedge with erect, slender stems which are round in cross-section.
plants.flowers: In loose heads of clustered spikes.
plants.habitat: Mountains in the Central Highlands, south-west and Mt. Field. Forms dense cover on pool edges and in permanently wet areas.

plants.name: Carpobrotus rossii
plants.form: Fleshy perennial herb, stems to 1m long, triangular leaves.
plants.flowers: Light purple 4-6cm diam, solitary at branch ends. Many shiny, narrow petals 2cm long.
plants.fruit: Fleshy, fig-like, yellowish when ripe. Seeds small, edible.
plants.habitat: Widespread, common in coastal areas on rocky headlands and sand dunes, coastal cliffs and sand.
plants.notes: Bee attracting. Carpobrotus rossii can be distinguished from Disphyma crassifolium (round-leaved pigface) by D. crassifolium having smaller, less angular leaves, small capsules instead of fleshy fruits, smaller flowers.

plants.name: Cassinia aculeata subsp. aculeata
plants.form: Much-branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Florets 6-12, flower heads numerous in terminal clusters. Usually whitish but sometimes pale brown or pink especially in the bud stage.
plants.fruit: Achene – downy, pappus bristles very slender.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant often rapidly colonizing cleared land.
plants.notes: Useful for providing quick low-level shelter (up to 3m) in mixed species windbreaks while slow growing species are established. Bird attracting. May provide food for some parrot species. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Flowers may cause dermatitis in humans.

plants.name: Cassinia rugata
plants.form: Erect, slender, shrub; often densely multi-branched from the base.
plants.flowers: A hemispherical inflorescence, 3 to 12 cm in diameter, with 2 or more main branches, each supporting 20 to 300 flowerheads.
plants.fruit: Achenes – pale green to whitish, cylindrical.
plants.habitat: Known from only one site in Tasmania on privately owned remnant wetland.

plants.name: Cassinia trinerva
plants.form: Tall shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: White heads, numerous in dense clusters which spread past the leaves. Florets 3-8.
plants.habitat: Local at the margins of wet sclerophyll forest in the north-east of the state.
plants.notes: Useful for providing quick low-level shelter (up to 3m) in mixed species windbreaks while slow growing species are established. Bird attracting. May provide food for birds such as parrots.

plants.name: Cassytha glabella f. glabella
plants.form: Twining parasitic plant with smooth, slender stems; forms dense mats over undergrowth.
plants.flowers: About 3mm in diameter, 5-8 together. The flower enlarges and surrounds the developing fruit.
plants.fruit: Fleshy drupe is 5-6mm long and green when ripe. The drupe encloses one hard seed.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant, especially in coastal heath.
plants.notes: Requires a host plant to parasitise.

plants.name: Cassytha melantha
plants.form: Twining parasitic plant with tough stems. The plant, including flowers and fruit, becomes black when dried.
plants.flowers: 5-7mm in diameter, 3-10 together.
plants.fruit: Drupe is 7-10mm in diameter, fleshy, and dark greenish black. Drupe encloses one hard seed.
plants.habitat: Frequent in the north of the State.
plants.notes: Requires a host plant to parasitise.

plants.name: Cassytha pubescens
plants.form: Perennial twining parasitic plant, with stem thickness intermediate between C. glabella and C. melantha. Young stems and inflorescences are covered with hairs.
plants.flowers: 5mm in diameter, 3-10 together.
plants.fruit: Fleshy and hair-covered drupe is 5-6mm in diameter and encloses one hard seed. Drupe is green when ripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread in dry forests and woodlands.
plants.notes: Requires a host plant to parasitise.

plants.name: Caustis pentandra
plants.form: Perennial sedge with stems round in cross-section, leaves reduced to sheathing scales and a creeping rhizome.
plants.flowers: In spikelets.
plants.habitat: On coastal sands in the north-east and east coast.

plants.name: Celmisia asteliifolia
plants.form: Silver-blue tufted perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Daisy-like flower heads to 5cm in diameter. Disc florets yellow, ray florets white or Rarely pink.
plants.habitat: Widespread in alpine and sub-alpine situations where the soil is continuously moist.
plants.notes: Plants have been short-lived in cultivation possibly due to insufficient drainage. For best results a situation with partial to full sun in light to medium, very well drained soils is recommended. Suitable for container growing.

plants.name: Celmisia saxifraga
plants.form: Herb with numerous rosettes sprouting from branches or roots.
plants.flowers: Flower heads white, single, 2.5-3cm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Found in all types of vegetation except aquatic, but only at the highest altitudes.
plants.notes: Inhabits mountain slopes and depressions where it can be covered with snow for months at a time. It needs moist, well-drained soils in partial or full sun.

plants.name: Cenarrhenes nitida
plants.form: Spreading shrub or small tree. Leaves have a nauseating smell when crushed.
plants.flowers: White, on short spikes amongst leaves. Petals thick, waxy. Anthers with spring mechanism.
plants.fruit: Drupe – large, purple, spherical, 1.0–1.5 cm diameter.
plants.habitat: Local in rainforests of the Central Plateau and the south-west and west coasts. A small tree in rainforest on poor sites and understorey shrub in wet eucalypt forest. It also occurs in scrub and heath on poor soils in the wettest parts of the state, extending into the margin of the alpine zone.
plants.notes: Cultivation has proved very challenging. Requires well-composted soil in shade. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Centella cordifolia
plants.form: Perennial herb with creeping stems or rhizomes.
plants.flowers: Flowers very small, white to pink, or red, often in threes.
plants.habitat: Widespread; locally abundant in swamps and margins of slowly flowing streams.
plants.notes: Needs plenty of soil moisture.

plants.name: Centipeda cunninghamii
plants.form: Dwarf to small shrub with stems ascending.
plants.flowers: Flower heads greenish yellow, globular, 0.5-1cm across.
plants.habitat: Widespread, usually in inland areas along creek beds and places subject to periodic inundation.
plants.notes: A hardy shrub well suited to withstand hot situations.

plants.name: Centipeda elatinoides
plants.form: Prostrate or spreading annual herb (or short-lived perennial); aromatic.
plants.flowers: Flower heads yellowish to greenish/white.
plants.habitat: Local in hollows subject to flooding.
plants.notes: Semi aquatic. Grows in a variety of soil types and habitats. Could be useful in rockeries or as a colonizer of bare soils in inland regions.

plants.name: Centrolepis aristata
plants.form: A slender annual herb; the most robust of the Tasmanian species of Centrolepis. Forming only small tufts and very variable in size. A dwarf form has been given varietal status.
plants.habitat: Frequent in moist, sandy places; recorded from Furneaux, north-east and east coast.

plants.name: Centrolepis fascicularis
plants.form: A slender perennial herb, forming dense tufts or cushions.
plants.habitat: Frequent in wet, sandy and peaty ground from sea level to 800m. King Island, Furneaux, north-west, north-east, west coast, east coast and south-west.

plants.name: Centrolepis glabra
plants.form: A slender, glabrous annual herb, laxly tufted. Leaves radical.
plants.habitat: Recorded from the Central Highlands and from the Midlands, on muddy shores of lakes and submerged in the shallow water of lagoons.

plants.name: Centrolepis muscoides
plants.form: A very small perennial herb with slender, short, erect, branched rhizome, forming dense tufts.
plants.flowers: Stigmas crimson.
plants.habitat: Central Highlands and Ben Lomond in marshy sub-alpine ground and shores of lakes subject to fluctuations of water level.

photos.credit: Threatened Species Section DPIPWE – Natural Values Atlas

plants.name: Centrolepis pedderensis
plants.form: Perennial that forms tufts or cushions up to 15 to 20cm across
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – a compound structure of follicles; each follicle contains one seed.
plants.habitat: Grows at the margins of lakes and rivers in areas subject to seasonal inundation and drying.

plants.name: Centropappus brunonis
plants.form: Small tree or large shrub, branches marked by persistent scars of leaf bases.
plants.flowers: Clusters of daisy flowers. Twice as many disk as ray florets, which have broad yellow ligules.
plants.fruit: Achene without hairs; rigid and prominently barbed.
plants.habitat: Local on Mt. Dromedary and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington at around 800-1200m.

plants.name: Chamaescilla corymbosa var. corymbosa
plants.form: Perennial herbaceous plant with linear leaves and tuberous roots.
plants.flowers: 1-6 blue star shaped flowers. Anthers coil after flowering.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 3 lobes, up to 8mm long and 8mm wide. Seeds are black and smooth, about 2mm long.
plants.habitat: Damp areas, on sandy or peaty soils in heath or under light forest cover, from sea level to 200m altitude. North-west, north-east, Midlands and south-east.

plants.name: Cheilanthes austrotenuifolia
plants.form: Small fern; may reach 50cm but often much smaller. In all but very sheltered sites top growth collapses in summer.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in the eastern half of the state, from sea level to 300m but may be up to 680m. Grows in well drained and seasonally dry habitats in a thin soil layer over rock, in a rock-gravel matrix in dry sclerophyll forest or on the upper slopes of fern gullies. …
plants.notes: Prefers dolerite soils to granite.

plants.name: Cheilanthes distans
plants.form: Small fern with dense scales under pinnules and short, narrow, dark green fronds with widely spaced lower pinnae.
plants.habitat: Currently known from near Avoca, Royal George and the Douglas-Apsley National Park. It grows in shallow soil on exposed, north-facing rock ledges. Can be recognised by dense covering of scales under its pinnules and by short, narrow, dark green fronds.
plants.notes: One of the easiest species to grow. It requires a warm, well drained position such as in a sunny rockery. Resents shade and must not be overwatered.

plants.name: Cheilanthes sieberi subsp. sieberi
plants.form: Dwarf fern in spreading clumps, fronds very narrow, erect, bright green, no hairs.
plants.habitat: Uncommon and scattered throughout the eastern half of Tasmania, from exposed coastal rocks to dry inland sites below 450m but with one collection at 800m on the Central Highlands. …
plants.notes: One of the best ferns to grow, requiring a warm, well-drained position. Resents shade but will respond to water during dry periods. Poisonous to stock.

plants.name: Chiloglottis cornuta
plants.flowers: Flowers resemble the wide-open beak of a young bird begging to be fed. Flowers mainly green. Labellum green with dark reddish suffusions and green to dark red stalkless calli of variable size.
plants.habitat: Widespread from coastal to alpine and sub-alpine areas growing amongst forest litter, ferns and shrubs in deep shade.

plants.name: Chiloglottis grammata
plants.flowers: Small flowers, green-purplish. Widely spreading petals and lateral sepals projecting forward. Heart-shaped labellum with irregular ridges, shiny dark red swollen calli.
plants.habitat: Wetter areas, except west coast, up to 1200m altitude.

plants.name: Chiloglottis gunnii
plants.form: Tall bird orchid with 2 leaves 40-60mm long.
plants.flowers: Large green to purplish flower, held stiffly erect. A heart-shaped green to pinkish labellum with few short calli with dark shiny heads.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, near coastal to alpine and sub-alpine areas; grows amongst shrubs and ferns.

plants.name: Chiloglottis reflexa
plants.form: Paired green leaves, margins crinkled and often not fully developed at flowering. Often grow in extensive colonies.
plants.flowers: Pinkish, wasp-like, erect flower. Greenish-bronze labellum, horizontal, with the dorsal surface almost covered with dark reddish to shiny black calli.
plants.habitat: Widespread from coastal to alpine and sub-alpine areas.
plants.notes: Flowering stimulated by summer fires and disturbance.

plants.name: Chiloglottis trapeziformis
plants.form: Pair of leaves 50-80mm long.
plants.flowers: Greenish to brownish-purple bird orchid with a wide diamond-shaped, flat, upward-pointing labellum, small calli on the basal quarter of the labellum.

plants.name: Chiloglottis triceratops
plants.form: Small slender bird orchid with paired oval dark-green leaves.
plants.flowers: Bird orchid with a flat, heart-shaped labellum with three distinct column-like basal calli, longitudinal rows of small intermediate calli and a larger anvil-like distal gland at the apex.
plants.habitat: Widespread in sheltered, moist but well-drained coastal lowland scrub or heath in the east and north of Tasmania.

plants.name: Chiloglottis valida
plants.form: A larger, leatherish, bird orchid. A pair of elliptical dark-green leaves.
plants.flowers: Single, erect greenish-purple flower with shiny black calli. Large flat, mobile, heart-shaped labellum. Pollinated by male thynnine wasps that attempt to mate with the labellum.
plants.habitat: Grows in sheltered, mostly moist, coastal lowland areas, sometimes up to 800m altitude.

plants.name: Chordifex hookeri
plants.form: Rhizome, horizontal.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers.
plants.habitat: Heath and sedgeland, sandy or peaty soils, near sea level to about 1000m.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Chordifex monocephalus
plants.form: Rhizome, horizontal.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers.
plants.habitat: Heath and sedge land and low shrubberies, peaty and sandy soils, near sea level to about 1200m.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Chorizandra australis
plants.form: A stout perennial plant with bright green, erect, hollow stems. Resembles Juncus.
plants.flowers: In spherical flower heads, dark purplish-black, dense and bristly.
plants.habitat: In still or slowly running fresh water, from sea level to 850m altitude.
plants.notes: Grows well on clay, and very drought tolerant once established.

plants.name: Chorizandra enodis
plants.form: A stout perennial sedge with greyish-green, wiry stems. Resembles Juncus.
plants.flowers: In spherical flower heads, dark purplish-brown, dense and bristly.
plants.habitat: Recorded from the north-west, and from the north-east in George Town, in a damp sandy heath.
plants.notes: Grows well on clay, and very drought tolerant once established.

plants.name: Chrysocephalum apiculatum subsp. apiculatum
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.flowers: Yellow everlasting daisy with branched clusters of many small flower heads.
plants.fruit: Achene with a feathery pappus, bristles often yellow with a few long hairs at the tip.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent.

plants.name: Chrysocephalum baxteri
plants.form: Perennial herb with much-branched stems.
plants.flowers: Flower heads, papery white with yellow centres, 3cm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Known only from the islands of Bass Strait.
plants.notes: Grows in most soils in a sunny position. Cut back after flowering.

plants.name: Chrysocephalum semipapposum subsp. semipapposum
plants.form: Perennial herb with tough, woody, slender rhizomes.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow flower heads In dense clusters 3-9cm in diameter. Bracts golden yellow.
plants.fruit: Achene with slender yellow pappus bristles.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent.
plants.notes: Needs a sunny dry position. Cut back in winter to encourage new growth.

plants.name: Clematis aristata
plants.form: Small to medium vigorous climber.
plants.flowers: Creamy white, star-like and prolific. Male and female flowers on separate plants.
plants.fruit: Achene – seed heads are fluffy and plume-like.
plants.notes: Good trellis plant. Bird attracting. An important nesting site for many small birds and a source of nectar for nectar-feeding birds.

plants.name: Clematis clitorioides
plants.form: Dioecious, evergreen, woody climber.
plants.flowers: White flowers in axillary and terminal panicles.
plants.fruit: Achene – brown, ovate, compressed, 4–5 mm long.
plants.habitat: Widespread across Tasmania, found in dry or wet, lowland and highland forests and woodlands.

plants.name: Clematis decipiens
plants.form: Dioecious, evergreen, woody climber.
plants.flowers: Flowers in axillary and terminal dichasial panicles, unisexual. Tepals pale green to creamy white.
plants.fruit: Achene – light brown, compressed-ovoid, 4–6 mm long.
plants.habitat: Found on King Island, the Furneaux Group and sporadically along the north-eastern coast of Tasmania, in coastal forests, woodlands and scrub.

plants.name: Clematis gentianoides
plants.form: Small, erect, non-climbing perennial plant. Many short leafy stems close together.
plants.flowers: Flower has 4–8 white sepals to 6cm across. Solitary (usually) flower at end of branch.
plants.fruit: Achene – female flowers are followed by feathery seeds.
plants.habitat: Scattered widely especially in north and east on rocky hillsides.
plants.notes: The only non-climbing species of Clematis in Tasmania.

plants.name: Clematis microphylla
plants.form: Woody climber which scrambles through other plants, leaves usually twice divided.
plants.flowers: Greenish-cream, 2-4cm across.
plants.fruit: Achene – achenes flattened, wrinkled or warty with tail 4-6cm long.
plants.habitat: Common near the north coast.
plants.notes: A very useful climber or groundcover for coastal districts but is intolerant of bad drainage. Attracts butterflies. The leaves have been used to relieve skin irritations but can cause blistering with excessive use.

plants.name: Colobanthus affinis
plants.form: Densely tufted perennial herb, leaves linear, more or less limp and pointed, about 5cm long, not ending in a hair.
plants.flowers: Borne on stalks slightly longer than leaves. Small, no petals, white/cream sepals, usually 5.
plants.fruit: Capsule opening by as many valves as sepals. Seeds numerous.
plants.habitat: Recorded from Port Davey and the Hampshire Hills.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated but could be used amongst boulders or other low growing plants. Requires moist, well drained soils, rich in organic matter. Will tolerate full sun or partial shade. …

plants.name: Colobanthus apetalus var. apetalus
plants.form: Densely tufted small herb with leaves narrowly linear with sharp point which may finish in a fine hair, less than 0.5mm
plants.flowers: Single, at ends of stems as long as leaves. Sepals oval-shaped and pointed 2-4mm long.
plants.fruit: Capsule opening by as many valves as sepals. Seeds numerous.
plants.habitat: Widespread in a range of habitats, common on sandy coasts and on the Central Plateau. Occasional in grassy vegetation in the eastern mountains.
plants.notes: Suited to moist, well-drained soils in full sun or partial shade.

plants.name: Colobanthus curtisiae
plants.form: Densely tufted small herb, leaves narrowly linear with sharp point finishing in fine hair 1-2mm long.
plants.flowers: Single, ending stems about as long as leaves. Sepals narrow, triangular and pointed 4-4.5mm
plants.fruit: Capsule opening by valves as many as there are sepals. Seeds numerous.
plants.habitat: Recorded only once from the alpine zone in grassy heath at Ben Lomond at 1300m. Occasional in lowland grassland and grassy woodland.

plants.name: Colobanthus pulvinatus
plants.form: Dwarf cushion plant, forming a dense mat, 2-10cm diameter. Leaves to 0.5cm rigid, spreading, ending in a sharp point.
plants.flowers: Small, cream, solitary; no petals; sepals usually 5.
plants.fruit: Capsule opening by valves as many as there are sepals. Seeds numerous.
plants.habitat: Alpine habitats.
plants.notes: Not known in cultivation.

plants.name: Comesperma calymega
plants.form: Perennial undershrub with woody root-stock and erect rigid stems, almost glabrous.
plants.flowers: Small, in dense terminal racemes about 5cm long, usually blue, rarely pink or white.
plants.fruit: Capsule – wedge shaped, about 1cm long. Seeds hairy.
plants.habitat: Common in sandy heaths.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Will grow in most well drained soils, in dappled shade or partial sun. Will tolerate full sun if root area is protected. Will not withstand extended dry periods.

plants.name: Comesperma defoliatum
plants.form: Perennial undershrub with woody rhizome. Leaves few, stems erect.
plants.flowers: Small, in racemes similar to Comesperma calymega but wing sepals not longer than the outer ones.
plants.fruit: Capsule – narrow at the base. Seeds hairy.
plants.habitat: Found near Southport, Tasmania.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Most species prefer well drained soil, with dappled shade or partial sun.

plants.name: Comesperma ericinum
plants.form: Small shrub, leaves, crowded, to 1.5 cm long with strongly recurved margins and apex.
plants.flowers: Small, borne in short racemes, profuse, pink to purple.
plants.habitat: Local in sandy heaths near the east and north coasts.
plants.notes: Occurs naturally in a wide range of soil types, prefers well-drained soils, with dappled shade or partial sun. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Comesperma retusum
plants.form: Shrub with erect, slender, rather rigid branches.
plants.flowers: Bright pink/purple (rarely lavender coloured), 2 large sepals forming wings. Other parts small.
plants.fruit: Capsule is wedge-shaped. Seeds with a tuft of hairs.
plants.habitat: Widespread but infrequent in wet heaths and scrub from sea level to mountain plateaux, especially inland.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Comesperma volubile
plants.form: Perennial twining climber with hairless, furrowed stems.
plants.flowers: Small, blue or mauve in sprays, on stalks 2-4mm long. Posterior petals yellowish. Flowers sometimes white or pink.
plants.fruit: Capsule – a small purse-like capsule 10-14mm long. Seeds with a tuft of hairs.
plants.habitat: Abundant in heaths and dry forests.
plants.notes: A decorative twiner which scrambles through other vegetation. Prefers light shade or partial sun and needs root protection. Will grow in a wide range of soil types and can withstand light to moderate frosts and dry periods. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. …

plants.name: Conospermum hookeri
plants.form: Variable dwarf to small shrub, branches erect, slender. Leaves sometimes twisted.
plants.flowers: Flowers white to cream, tubular, 0.7cm long, in dense clusters on single or branched stems.
plants.habitat: Local near the coast in the east of the state. Grows in a wide range of soils.
plants.notes: Prefers well-drained position in partial sun but will tolerate dappled shade or full sun.

plants.name: Convolvulus angustissimus subsp. angustissimus
plants.form: Slender trailing/twining plant. Lower leaves arrowhead-shaped, upper leaves narrow and linear.
plants.flowers: Solitary, pink or white. Petals join to shape of funnel, 20mm diameter.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – 6-8mm, round. Seeds black/dark brown, hard, 4 per capsule.
plants.habitat: Common in dry, open and grassy places and roadside banks.
plants.notes: Needs well-drained, sunny situation. The roots are edible, but not particularly tasty.

plants.name: Coprosma hirtella
plants.form: Erect shrub. Leaves ovate 2-6cm long with a pointed tip and prominent central vein; thick, glossy and tough.
plants.flowers: Greenish flowers in small heads. Male and female on separate plants.
plants.fruit: Drupe – round, 2-seeded. Fruit turn from green to reddish-orange, occasionally chocolate brown, when ripe.
plants.habitat: Grows in open forest country often in small scattered colonies, on rocky hillsides and foothills of mountains.
plants.notes: Fire retardant. Bird attracting. The fruit are eaten by various birds and mammals. The foliage provides refuge for small birds. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Coprosma moorei
plants.form: Small prostrate shrub with much-branched stems, rooting at the nodes.
plants.flowers: Solitary, terminal on short branches, light yellowish-green, about 0.6cm across.
plants.habitat: Occasional in wet heath and bolster heath above 300m. Sometimes growing in sphagnum moss.
plants.notes: Useful as a rockery or container plant in cool positions. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Coprosma nitida
plants.form: Much-branched shrub, often erect.
plants.flowers: Solitary flowers with small petals. Male and female on different plants.
plants.fruit: Drupe – shiny, pale orange-red when ripe.
plants.habitat: Common throughout the state in alpine and sub-alpine eucalypt forests on slopes of mountains.
plants.notes: Grows on dolerite-derived clay. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Coprosma perpusilla subsp. perpusilla
plants.form: Prostrate mat-forming shrub rooting from its branches.
plants.flowers: Single at ends of branches, light greenish-yellow to pale orange-yellow.
plants.habitat: Occasional in heath and bog.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Coprosma pumila
plants.form: Matted or prostrate shrub rooting at the nodes.
plants.flowers: Solitary, terminal on short branches, greenish about 0.8cm long.
plants.habitat: Occurs above 500m. Occasional in bolster heath, heath and bog in the eastern mountains.
plants.notes: Must not be allowed to dry out. Best planted amongst rocks to give a cool root run. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Coprosma quadrifida
plants.form: Erect much-branched thorny shrub.
plants.flowers: Solitary on very short axillary stalks. Male and female flowers on separate bushes.
plants.fruit: Drupe – orange to red, very translucent and shining, stone breaking into 2 pyrenes.
plants.habitat: Widespread from sea level to around 800m.
plants.notes: Important understorey component. Bird attracting. Provides food and nest sites for several small bird species. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Coronidium scorpioides
plants.form: Perennial herb, branches often tufted.
plants.flowers: Yellow paper daisy alone on a stem arising from a rosette of pale leaves with loose hairs.
plants.fruit: Achene with pappus bristles slender, minutely hooked.
plants.habitat: Common at most altitudes but less so in the shady understorey of the denser forests. Particularly prominent after fires.
plants.notes: Flowering time depends on altitude – spring at lower altitudes, summer higher up.

plants.name: Correa alba var. alba
plants.form: Shrub, broad leaves; grey-green leathery. Many branches.
plants.flowers: 2-3 together on short stalks, ends of branches. 4 thick white petals (cup-shaped).
plants.fruit: Mericarp – pale lemon-green ripening to pale brown, 4 seeds per fruit. Seed 2-4 mm, brown, black or grey.
plants.habitat: Common in sandy soil on coasts. Sometimes grows in sand. Found on Furneaux Islands and east coast down to Triabunna.
