plants.notes: A good low wind break or hedge. Bird attracting (honeyeaters). The foliage was used by early settlers as a substitute for tea.

plants.name: Correa alba var. rotundifolia
plants.form: Shrub, leaves grey-green leathery. Many branches.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence 1–5-flowered, terminal on short branchlets; petals white.
plants.habitat: Restricted to south-eastern Tasmania (Tasman and Forestier Peninsulas, the South Arm area and Bruny Island).
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Correa backhouseana var. backhouseana
plants.form: Bushy upright or sometimes spreading shrub, branches and stems covered with rusty hairs.
plants.flowers: Tubular flowers to 2.5 cm long; terminal, 1-3 together, pale whitish-green.
plants.habitat: Coastal; on west and south coasts and islands of Bass Strait.
plants.notes: Excellent bird attracting plant.

plants.name: Correa lawrenciana var. ferruginea
plants.form: Slender shrub with leaves that are densely hairy on the abaxial surface.
plants.flowers: Terminal or axillary flowers, greenish yellow, 1-3 together on short stalks usually drooping.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent, from sea level to mountains; local in understorey of woodland and forest and more common higher up the mountain.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. An excellent plant for bird habitat; honeyeaters especially seek it for food and shelter. Withstands extended wet periods.

plants.name: Correa lawrenciana var. lawrenciana
plants.form: Slender shrub, the typical form, with glabrous leaves. Form from the east coast and Asbestos Range has reddish stems.
plants.flowers: Cream, green tubular, pendulous on short stalks, 3cm long.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent, from sea level to mountains; local in understorey of woodland and forest and more common higher up the mountain.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. An excellent plant for bird habitat; honeyeaters especially seek it for food and shelter. Withstands extended wet periods. Form from the east coast and Asbestos Range has reddish stems.

plants.name: Correa reflexa var. nummulariifolia
plants.form: Low, spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: 1-3 flowers at end of short branches; corolla yellow-green, cylindrical, 15–25 mm long.
plants.habitat: Confined to the Furneaux Group.
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Correa reflexa var. reflexa
plants.form: Prostrate to upright shrub. Leaves usually reflexed; slightly recurved margins.
plants.flowers: Tubular, 2-4cm long, tips reflexed. Colour varies; cream, green, pink/red. Tips may be contrasting.
plants.habitat: Occurs in a wide range of habitats from sandy heath to dry, rocky sites in open forest.
plants.notes: Requires part shade or sun. Tolerates some dryness and moist conditions. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Corunastylis archeri
plants.form: Single slender leaf 100-150mm sheathing stem, finishing just below inflorescence.
plants.flowers: Tiny dark greenish-red to purple flowers (2-15) have an insect-like appearance; oval, often recurved labellum with long hairs on the margin.
plants.habitat: Widespread and localised, occurring in many habitats from coastal scrub and heathland to open forest, often on the edge of poorly drained areas.

plants.name: Corunastylis brachystachya
plants.form: A very small midge orchid. Slender green leaf, 18-120 mm long with a reddish base ending well below the flower spike.
plants.flowers: 8-12 crowded, semi-nodding, shiny, green to brownish green with reddish petals and labellum; labellum narrow and turned-up with an irregular margins.
plants.habitat: Highly localised, grows in sandy soil in near-coastal heathland and heathy woodland to 200m elevation among low shrubs, boulders and rock plates.

plants.name: Corunastylis firthii
plants.form: A small slender midge orchid, single very slender leaf, 50-80 mm, ending below the flower spike.
plants.flowers: Pyramidal spike of up to 1-6 reddish nodding flowers with some greenish markings, red pointed labellum with irregular margins.
plants.habitat: Rarely seen in coastal scrub and heathland in freely draining sands in eastern Tasmania.

plants.name: Corunastylis nudiscapa
plants.form: Small midge orchid. Single slender green leaf with a maroon base, 60-80 mm long. The leaf projects up into and sometimes through the flowers.
plants.flowers: 5-25 brown to purplish nodding flowers, crowded in a dense terminal spike. Small white glands on the tepals. Narrow, fleshy toothed labellum with a callus extending three-quarters of the way to the apex.
plants.habitat: Only found at a few sites in south-east Tasmania, growing in open forests and woodlands dominated by Eucalyptus tenuiramis on mudstone.

plants.name: Corunastylis pumila
plants.flowers: A small green to yellowish midge orchid, with up to 25 poorly opening flowers, often with reddish suffusions on lateral sepals and labellum; single leaf finishing well below the inflorescence. A thick fleshy labellum with pointed apex.
plants.habitat: A few, small, widely separated populations from alpine and sub-alpine grasslands to lowland forest and heathlands, often on the margins of damper areas.

plants.name: Corunastylis tasmanica
plants.form: Robust midge orchid; slender green leaf with a maroon base finishing below the flower spike.
plants.flowers: 3-25 semi-nodding flowers, dark sometimes greenish, in a dense flower head. Lateral sepals with prominent whitish glands and a labellum with irregular margins and a sharply recurved, pointed apex.
plants.habitat: Locally common, growing in grassland, heathland and open forest in freely draining soil.
plants.notes: Growth may be promoted by burning and slashing.

plants.name: Corybas aconitiflorus
plants.form: A small ground-hugging helmet orchid. Heart-shaped leaf, dark green above, purple below.
plants.flowers: A single, semi-nodding, grey-green to greyish-pink flower, 20-25 mm, a hooded dorsal sepal almost enclosing the labellum and prominent spur-like appendages sheathing the stem at its base.
plants.habitat: Locally common in coastal and near-coastal lowland scrub on moist but well drained soils.
plants.notes: The only Tasmanian Corybas with a hooded dorsal sepal almost enclosing the flower.

plants.name: Corybas diemenicus
plants.form: A small, veined helmet orchid. Circular to heart-shaped leaf, bright green above, purple underneath.
plants.flowers: Single maroon, semi-nodding flower, 14-20 mm across, with an almost circular labellum with a flared, serrated margin enclosing a purple and white boss and a broad, partly translucent, dorsal sepal enclosing the labellum.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally common in moist areas from the coast to the foothills in eucalypt scrub and rainforest, often growing amongst moss and ferns. Flowers as late as December in sub-alpine areas. Can form quite large colonies.

plants.name: Corybas incurvus
plants.form: Small ground-hugging Corybas. Leaf heart-shaped to round, bright green on both surfaces.
plants.flowers: A single flower, 15 mm across with a translucent dorsal sepal with purplish blotches. Dorsal sepal caps an almost circular translucent labellum with a deep notch at the top and purplish suffusions. Has a conspicuous white boss and incurved serrated margins.
plants.habitat: Widespread in coastal woodland and heathland in damp, shady sites in the shelter of shrubs and bracken.

plants.name: Corybas unguiculatus
plants.form: A tiny dark maroon helmet orchid. Distinctive leaf, heart-shaped, light greyish-green with purple underside.
plants.flowers: Single erect flower, 10-16 mm across. Bulbous dark maroon dorsal sepal that covers the fused upper margin of the tubular labellum with only the apex and lower half visible. In the Arthur River area, several sites have multiflowered plants with translucent pink or lime green flowers.
plants.habitat: Locally common in coastal woodland and heathland, often around the base of trees or stumps.

plants.name: Cotula alpina
plants.form: Dwarf, stout, creeping perennial herb with fleshy roots and numerous rosettes.
plants.flowers: Yellow, single at ends of short stalks which elongate when in fruit.
plants.habitat: Local in alpine and sub-alpine grasslands, heaths, herbfields and sedgelands and also in wet grassland at lower altitudes.
plants.notes: A useful matting plant, tolerates a wide variety of moist soil types and shade to full sun.

plants.name: Cotula australis
plants.form: Spreading annual or perennial herb with stems covered in long soft hairs.
plants.flowers: White and yellow-green flower heads about 0.5cm in diameter. Stalks longer than leaves.
plants.habitat: Widespread in grassland and on roadsides, also growing in crevices in walls in Hobart.
plants.notes: Useful as a groundcover, especially in the shade where other plants will not grow. Can spread to become a nuisance.

plants.name: Cotula vulgaris var. australasica
plants.form: Small annual herb.
plants.flowers: Flower heads terminal, solitary and 3-5mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Local in wet or brackish swamps in the north and north-east and on the islands of Bass Strait.

plants.name: Craspedia glabrata
plants.form: Slender, tufted plant.
plants.flowers: Compound white flower heads 10-12mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Appears to be confined to areas of wet alpine and sub-alpine grassland.

plants.name: Craspedia glauca
plants.form: Perennial herb with narrow leaves some of which have loose covering of webby hairs.
plants.flowers: White or yellow flower heads about 1cm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Widespread in grassland and open eucalypt forest.
plants.notes: Requires moist well-drained soil and full sun.

plants.name: Craspedia gracilis
plants.form: Silver-grey rosette herb, flowering stem bearing some leaves.
plants.flowers: Single terminal flower heads, yellow, spherical and 1-2.5cm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Occasional in the eastern mountains in grassy vegetation.

plants.name: Craspedia macrocephala
plants.form: Perennial herb with stem and leaves densely covered with hairs.
plants.flowers: Flower heads white, solitary and spherical about 2.5cm in diameter; button-like.
plants.habitat: Frequent on mountain plateaux in all non-aquatic vegetation.

plants.name: Craspedia paludicola
plants.form: Green rosette herb with some leaves on the flowering stem.
plants.flowers: Clusters of spherical, terminal yellow flower heads 1.7-3cm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Occasional in wetlands in the eastern mountains. Also found on sandy flats growing in fresh water.

plants.name: Crassula closiana
plants.form: Annual herb with narrow, succulent leaves, 1-2cm long.

plants.name: Crassula decumbens var. decumbens
plants.form: Small succulent annual herb often reddish, stem sometimes creeping at base.
plants.flowers: Numerous, on stalks 4-10mm long. Petals pale pink about as long as sepals (2-3mm).
plants.fruit: Seed follicles – in fruiting stage, carpels about as long as the calyx with a short beak and 6-12 seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in damp hollows in sandy heaths, pastures and roadsides.

plants.name: Crassula exserta
plants.form: Succulent annual herb with erect stem, branched from the base or simple.
plants.flowers: Small, in dense clusters along nearly the whole stem on stalks equal in length to the sepals.
plants.habitat: Recorded from Flinders Island.

plants.name: Crassula helmsii
plants.form: Aquatic or marsh plant with slender stems creeping or floating, rooting at nodes.
plants.flowers: White to pale pink, solitary in upper leaf axil, 0.3-0.4cm across.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent on the margins of swampy places.
plants.notes: A perennial succulent which spreads fairly rapidly. Usually found growing in or alongside fresh water and roots in mud. Occasionally grown as an aquatic in ponds or dams or as a bog plant.

plants.name: Crassula moschata
plants.form: Mat-forming, succulent herb with trailing main stems which root at the nodes, and erect lateral stems. Leaves are spoon-shaped to lance-shaped, reddish at the base, and about 3mm long and 1-1.5mm wide.
plants.flowers: Flowers have white petals and pink sepals, and occur singly in the upper leaf axils, on stalks up to 2cm long.
plants.fruit: Seed follicles containing 4 seeds, 0.8mm long, roughly oval with a base or tip which seems to have been cut straight across.
plants.habitat: Littoral zone on coastal beach rock stacks, on humic sandy soils on rocky shores, and on thin peaty soil on beach pebbles, often near fresh water pools and runoff.

plants.name: Crassula peduncularis
plants.form: Succulent annual herb, stems very slender, ascending.
plants.flowers: Solitary, axillary, often only 1 to a pair of leaves, on slender stalks which elongate at fruiting.
plants.habitat: Local in wet places but readily overlooked. Recorded from Mt. Direction near Hobart.

plants.name: Crassula sieberiana
plants.form: An erect succulent annual herb. Becomes much-branched and tufted after flowering.
plants.flowers: Pink, about 0.4cm across and with 4 petals, borne in dense clusters along the stem.
plants.habitat: Very abundant throughout the State on rocks, gravel and other dry places.
plants.notes: A tiny annual sometimes grown as a rockery plant. If planted in gravelly soil in a sunny position it can be induced to re-establish itself from seed each year.

plants.name: Cryptandra alpina
plants.form: Small, much-branched undershrub with wiry branches and leaves 1.5-3mm long.
plants.flowers: White flowers are usually solitary and at the end of the lateral branches.
plants.habitat: Central Plateau and Western Tiers, above 750m altitude.

plants.name: Cryptandra amara
plants.form: Small, wiry shrub with rigid branches often ending in a fine spine. Young branches are covered in tiny star-shaped hairs. Leaves are thin and blunt, 2-6mm long.
plants.flowers: Solitary or in clusters of 2-3, the oldest flowers are at the base and the youngest towards the top of the stem.
plants.habitat: Grazed dolerite paddocks, rocky dry sclerophyll forests, heathy woodlands along roadsides, dry, north-facing dolerite outcrops and on rock plates near rivers. Midlands, north and east coast.

plants.name: Cryptandra exilis
plants.form: Small, low-growing shrub with tiny flat leaves.
plants.flowers: Small and white, in clusters of 2-6 together at the ends of branches, resembling epacrid flowers.
plants.habitat: Tasman Peninsular and other areas near the east coast.

plants.name: Cryptostylis subulata
plants.form: A tall duck-billed orchid. Small groups of green lanceolate leaves.
plants.flowers: 3-20 green to yellow-green flowers, only a few open at a time. Large projecting labellum, dark-brown at the apex, rolled at the edges, forming a partial tube.
plants.habitat: Localised on coastal moorland and heathland on damper, poorly drained soils and at the edge of swamps.

plants.name: Cullen microcephalum
plants.form: Perennial herb, stems straggling or ascending and woody rhizome.
plants.flowers: Pea, small with petals purplish-pink to white and almost stalkless in dense spikes.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oval, blackish, hairless and ridged or wrinkled.
plants.habitat: Local on the west coast and the north-west coast at Woolnorth.

plants.name: Cuscuta tasmanica
plants.form: Parasitic herb with yellow twining stems, leaves reduced to small scales.
plants.flowers: 5 petalled flowers, clustered 2-5 together on stalks which are stouter than the stem.
plants.habitat: On plants on landward margins of salt and brackish marshes.

plants.name: Cyanothamnus anemonifolius subsp. variabilis
plants.form: Erect shrub, variable in leaf size. Leaves are long stalked, sticky and very glandular.
plants.flowers: In stalked clusters, often 3 clusters on a stalk and each cluster up to 3 pink and white flowers.
plants.habitat: Local in the south on dry hillsides and near the north coast.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Cyanothamnus nanus var. hyssopifolius
plants.form: Weakly erect or spreading undershrub. Leaves simple.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence 1–7-flowered; 4 petals pink or white crowded along stems at end of branches.
plants.habitat: Occurs in eastern and northern Tasmania. Found in heath, woodland and forest on a variety of substrates.
plants.notes: Hardy, requiring moisture and partial shade.

plants.name: Cyanothamnus nanus var. nanus
plants.form: Small plant with woody underground stem and several thin prostrate branches. Leaves pinnate.
plants.flowers: Small flowers in axils, 4 sepals, 4 pink petals twice as long as sepals, 8 stamens finely hairy.
plants.habitat: Found in heath and open woodland usually on sandy or rocky substrates. Local near the north coast.
plants.notes: Needs a well-drained situation with some shade. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Cyathea australis subsp. australis
plants.form: Trunk to 40cm in diameter, fibrous at base with roughened frond bases on upper half. Large crown of mid-green triangular fronds to 3.5m long.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in moderate to high rainfall areas in the north and east Tasmania. Sparsely occurring on the west coast. Requires more light than Dicksonia antarctica. The two species frequently grow together but Cyathea australis usually occurs on higher, drier slopes. Tolerates boggy soils.
plants.notes: Very hardy

plants.name: Cyathea cunninghamii
plants.form: Trunk tall and slender, to 10cm diameter. Fibrous at base, woody above.
plants.habitat: Rare species with only scattered populations in Tasmania within 3km of the coast. Typically grows in deep sheltered fern gullies beside creeks.
plants.notes: Very particular in its requirements. Suitable for growing in large container.

plants.name: Cyathea x marcescens
plants.form: Trunk up to 35cm diameter, fibrous at base often has persistent dead fronds in a skirt.
plants.habitat: Very rare in Tasmania known from near-coastal fern gullies in the south-east, north-east, central north and King Island. It is a natural hybrid of the Endangered Cyathea cunninghamii and the more widespread Cyathea australis, and will only be present where these two species co-occur. …
plants.notes: Relatively untried in cultivation because of its rarity but requires conditions similar to those for other species. It can grow quite vigorously.

plants.name: Cyathodes glauca
plants.form: Open woody shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: White tubular flowers in clusters among the leaves at the ends of branches.
plants.fruit: Drupe – red, pink or purple (rarely white), rounded and somewhat flattened.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant on wet hillsides and mountain foothills, reaching an altitude of 1100m. Usually a straggling shrub but sometimes (on the west coast) a small tree up to 10m high.
plants.notes: Bee attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Cyathodes platystoma
plants.form: Tall shrub with brown branchlets, and leaves 36-63mm long, with pointed tips and raised veins, arranged in whorls.
plants.flowers: Floral tube is short, broad and U-shaped, with long, dense hairs near the throat.
plants.habitat: Wet forest on the Tasman and Forester Peninsulas, also Bruny Island.
plants.notes: Described in 1996.

plants.name: Cyathodes straminea
plants.form: Shrub, branches tending to rise in false whorls and spreading widely.
plants.flowers: White, bell-shaped with strong cheesy smell, clustered in leaves at the end of branches.
plants.habitat: Frequent on the dolerite mountains of the northern and eastern parts of the State often growing amongst boulders.

plants.name: Cycnogeton alcockiae
plants.form: Rhizome
plants.habitat: Fresh or brackish water in pools, swamps an margins of streams, near sea level to 750m.
plants.notes: Aquatic plant.

plants.name: Cycnogeton procerum
plants.form: Extremely variable perennial, tufted or from a stout rhizome.
plants.flowers: Slender form, flowers not densely clustered. Robust form, flowers dense.
plants.habitat: Slender form, shallow water or exposed mud in fresh or brackish situations or damp areas in coastal sands, sea level to 800m. Robust from, usually aquatic in fresh water up to 1m in depth, occasionally on exposed mud, sea level to 1000m.
plants.notes: Aquatic plant. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Cycnogeton rheophilum
plants.notes: Aquatic plant.

plants.name: Cymbonotus preissianus
plants.form: Dwarf perennial rosette herb.
plants.flowers: Yellow flower heads about 1cm in diameter on stalks shorter than leaves.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent on roadsides and in sparse vegetation on dry hillsides and paddocks.
plants.notes: Will grow in a wide range of soils and climatic conditions. Prefers soils rich in humus but will not survive in permanently wet sites. Used by early settlers as an ointment to treat wounds. Leaves were combined with lard.

plants.name: Cynoglossum australe
plants.form: Perennial herb with erect flowering stems, covered in hairs. Rough-textured leaves in a basal rosette; leaves on the stem getting progressively smaller towards the top.
plants.flowers: Petals round, usually blue, Rarely white, in clusters on erect stems.
plants.habitat: On the landward margins of coastal sand dunes, and grasslands and dry places throughout the State.

plants.name: Cyperus gunnii
plants.form: Tufted sedge with erect, shining stems, triangular in cross-section.
plants.flowers: In umbels on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – seed heads turn brown when seed is ripe.
plants.habitat: In marshy places in the Midlands and on the east coast.

plants.name: Cyperus lucidus
plants.form: Robust tufted sedge with erect stems, shiny dark green leaves and woody rootstock.
plants.flowers: Bright reddish-brown, in umbels on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – seed heads turn brown when seed is ripe.
plants.habitat: Wetlands, marshes and other wet areas on King Island, Furneaux, north-west, north-east, Midlands and east coast.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Cyphanthera tasmanica
plants.form: Shrub with grey-green, blunt-tipped leaves, 1-4cm long. The stems and leaves are covered with minute hairs, which give them a sandpaper texture and yellowish appearance.
plants.flowers: Creamy flowers with prominent purple stripes, occurring in groups of 1-3 towards the ends of the branches.
plants.fruit: Capsule – reddish-brown; usually 4 reddish-brown seeds about 2.5mm long.
plants.habitat: In gullies and on hillsides, on the east coast.
plants.notes: Usually present after fire, when it appears in large numbers and lives for about 10 years.

plants.name: Cyrtostylis reniformis
plants.form: A small slender colony-forming orchid. Leaves in close contact with the ground, heart-shaped to oval, grey-green, paler and crystalline underneath.
plants.flowers: 1-4 pinkish-brown flowers with narrow petals and sepals; a prominent paddle-like protruding pinkish-brown labellum; raised central callus with two conical glands with dark central spots at the base.
plants.habitat: Common in heathy and grassy forest to 400m altitude.

plants.name: Cystopteris tasmanica
plants.form: Fronds delicate, brittle, thin-textured, pale green, once-divided.
plants.habitat: Uncommon highland species. Usually occurs at about 1000m but also found on the Huon River near Scotts Peak. Confined to very sheltered rock ledges, crevices or boulder grottos, often close to running water. …
plants.notes: A tiny fern, very difficult to grow and resents disturbance. Needs cool, moist, humid conditions. Best grown in a bottle, aquarium or terrarium.

plants.name: Damasonium minus
plants.form: Annual herb, leaves long-petioled with sheathing bases
plants.flowers: White or pale pink.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – dry, between 4-6 mm long with 2 seeds .
plants.habitat: Swamps and dams; uncommon; found on the east coast.
plants.notes: Annual aquatic herb.

plants.name: Dampiera stricta
plants.form: Slightly woody undershrub.
plants.flowers: Pale to bright blue, sometimes white, backs of petals covered with dense felt of brown hairs.
plants.fruit: Nut or drupe – 2-3mm long each containing one seed. Fruit is dry when mature.
plants.habitat: Frequent on sandy soils near east and north-east coasts, and in Asbestos Range. In cultivation most aspects are satisfactory.
plants.notes: Attracts butterflies.

plants.name: Daucus glochidiatus
plants.form: Annual herb
plants.flowers: Flowers 1.5 mm diameter with crimson petals.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent, especially in dry places, including coastal dunes.
plants.notes: Treat as an annual.

plants.name: Daviesia latifolia
plants.form: Open woody shrub.
plants.flowers: Common pea flower with numerous small brown and yellow flowers.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – flat, triangular, to 10mm. Seed pods become light brown and brittle when ripe. Seed turns from green to black and drops very soon after maturity. Each pod contains 1 seed.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent, especially on banks at roadsides. Prefers semi-shade but will tolerate full sun. Adaptable to most soils.
plants.notes: Useful in providing low cover (up to 3m) in mixed species windbreaks and for screening. Bird attracting. Useful for honey production and flowers provide excellent nectar for insects and birds. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits. …

plants.name: Daviesia sejugata
plants.form: Widely spreading shrub with dull dark green, very thick, somewhat fleshy phyllodes which are wrinkled when dry. Branchlets are spiny and have strong ridges.
plants.flowers: Yellow, with deep lobes, borne in 3+ flowered-umbels, 1 or 2 umbels per leaf axil.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – seeds are orange-brown to tan with black mottling, ellipsoid and 2.5-3mm long. The aril is about 1.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Sandy habitats in Eastern Tasmania and King Island.
plants.notes: Closely related to Daviesia ulicifolia, but a more rigid, robust and prickly plant with broader leaves.

plants.name: Daviesia ulicifolia subsp. ruscifolia
plants.form: Open, prickly shrub.

plants.name: Daviesia ulicifolia subsp. ulicifolia
plants.form: Rigid, much-branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flower with petals light-yellow or deep reddish-orange, purplish at the base.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – triangular, flat, about 10mm long. Seed pods turn brown and become brittle when ripe. Each pod usually contains one seed which turns from green to black on maturity.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in a range of lowland habitats.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. The prickly foliage provides good refuge sites for small birds and has a richer flower colour than the other Daviesias. Susceptible to browsing by hares and rabbits.

plants.name: Deschampsia cespitosa
plants.form: Very variable perennial forming large tussocks.
plants.flowers: Spikelets green purplish, anthers yellow or purple.
plants.habitat: Damp to wet situations, fresh or brackish water, margins of saltmarsh, from sea level to over 1500m on the west coast, south-west, east coast, north-east, north-west, Midlands, Ben Lomond and Central Highlands.

plants.name: Deschampsia gracillima
plants.form: Densely tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Golden Brown
plants.habitat: Maxwell Ridge and Moonlight Ridge near Mt La Perouse at about 1000m.

plants.name: Desmodium gunnii
plants.form: Perennial herb with woody rootstock and slender branches, sometimes prostrate.
plants.flowers: Small pea flowers, arranged singly or in pairs on terminal, unbranched stems. Petals blue or lilac 5-6mm long.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – flattened, lightly hairy, constricted into 2-6 one-seeded parts. Seed with hard coat.
plants.habitat: Found on the north-west coast.

plants.name: Deyeuxia apsleyensis
plants.form: Loosely tufted erect perennial.
plants.flowers: Purplish
plants.habitat: East of Apsley River above Apsley Gorge, in Eucalyptus amygdalina/Eucalyptus viminalis forest in undulating low hills.

plants.name: Deyeuxia brachyathera
plants.form: Erect, stout, glabrous perennial.
plants.flowers: Spikelets green or purplish.
plants.habitat: Recorded only from the Central Highlands and Ben Lomond area, 400-1435m altitude.

plants.name: Deyeuxia carinata
plants.form: Erect or decumbent glabrous perennial.
plants.flowers: Green or purplish.
plants.habitat: Stream banks, seepage areas, cliff ledges, moorland above 1000m, Central Highlands, west coast, Mt Field, kunanyi/Mt Wellington.

plants.name: Deyeuxia contracta
plants.form: Very variable erect or ascending perennial.
plants.flowers: Green or purplish.
plants.habitat: Under light eucalypt cover and on the margins of wet sclerophyll forest from sea level to about 400m, north-west, east coast, west coast, south-west.

plants.name: Deyeuxia decipiens
plants.form: Erect, tufted, glabrous perennial.
plants.flowers: Panicle open, branches naked for half their length.
plants.habitat: Under light forest cover in the Bicheno area, east coast.

plants.name: Deyeuxia densa
plants.form: Erect or geniculate perennial.
plants.flowers: Panicle moderately dense, 2-11cm long.
plants.habitat: Open to lightly shaded situations, heaths, sedgelands, streambanks, Furneaux Group, east coast, south-west, west coast, Central Highlands, sea level to 750m.

plants.name: Deyeuxia frigida
plants.form: Erect or geniculate and ascending perennial.
plants.flowers: Green or purplish.
plants.habitat: Under light forest or open areas in denser eucalypt forest, 400-1000m altitude, Ben Lomond, Central Highlands, east coast and kunanyi/Mt Wellington.

plants.name: Deyeuxia gunniana
plants.form: Slender tufted erect or ascending glabrous perennial.
plants.flowers: Green or purplish.
plants.habitat: Wet situations, creek and river banks, margins of moor and bog, sea level to 850m; north-west, west coast, Central Highlands, Ben Lomond, south-west.

plants.name: Deyeuxia innominata
plants.form: Erect loosely or occasionally somewhat densely tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Purplish or pale green.
plants.habitat: 1000-1300m altitude, Central Highlands, Ben Lomond, Mt Field, kunanyi/Mt Wellington, south-west and 550m and above east coast.

plants.name: Deyeuxia minor
plants.form: Glabrous tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Spikelets green.
plants.habitat: Under light eucalypt cover or margins of wet sclerophyll forest, south-west and east coast.

plants.name: Deyeuxia monticola
plants.form: Erect tufted or occasionally decumbent perennial.
plants.flowers: Panicle 2-20cm, contracted and often dense.
plants.habitat: Open and usually well drained situations, occasionally also in wet sclerophyll forest, all regions of the state from sea level on the east coast to over 1400m in the Central Highlands.

plants.name: Deyeuxia quadriseta
plants.form: Extremely variable tufted, subglabrous perennial.
plants.flowers: Spikelets green or purplish.
plants.habitat: All regions of the state from sea level to 1200m in a variety of open or lightly shaded situations.

plants.name: Deyeuxia rodwayi
plants.form: Slender, erect or ascending perennial.
plants.flowers: Spikelets green or tinged purple.
plants.habitat: Wet sclerophyll forest, dry sclerophyll forest exposed to sea mists, sub-alpine areas, 200-750m altitude, east coast, Ben Lomond, south-west, west coast, kunanyi/Mt Wellington, Mt Field.

plants.name: Deyeuxia scaberula
plants.form: Erect, rather robust, tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Larger spikelets than similar Deyeuxia contracta.
plants.habitat: East coast and kunanyi/Mt Wellington, wet sclerophyll forest.

plants.name: Dianella amoena
plants.form: Tufted, mat-forming perennial; slightly fleshy and much-branched underground stems (rhizomes).
plants.flowers: Sweetly scented flowers are on slender stems 20–90 cm high, arranged in a slender panicle.
plants.fruit: Berry – round, off-white to dark-blue, about 5 mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Reserved in the Township Lagoon Nature Reserve, Jordan Nature Reserve and Rosny Hill Nature Recreation Area; also on three private properties in areas covered by a conservation covenant.
plants.notes: Bird attracting

plants.name: Dianella brevicaulis
plants.form: Tufted plant with long narrow leaves, with the edges often rolled back.
plants.flowers: Flowers bright blue, stamens with black or dark brown anthers and swollen yellow filaments. Flower spikes are buried with stems shorter than the leaves.
plants.fruit: Berry – pale blue containing shiny, black seeds.
plants.habitat: Rocky shorelines and open woodland on the north-east and east coasts.
plants.notes: Bird attracting

plants.name: Dianella revoluta var. revoluta
plants.form: Tufted perennial spread by rhizomes. Clumps can be large.
plants.flowers: Flowers blue-purple in open clusters on stems longer than the dark green strap-like leaves. Bright yellow filaments.
plants.fruit: Berry – blue-purple containing many black seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread; prefers damp to dry conditions. Coast up to 400m altitude.
plants.notes: Suitable for growing under trees. Will survive dry conditions. Bird attracting

plants.name: Dianella tasmanica
plants.form: Tufted plant forming dense clumps and tussocks.
plants.flowers: Blue lilies with 6 prominent yellow stamens in the middle.
plants.fruit: Berry – blue-purple, oval-shaped containing black, shiny seed. Fleshy fruits turn soft when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common especially in wetter areas on rocky hillsides, sea level to mountain foothills.
plants.notes: Plants spread by stout rhizomes and may be invasive. Divided plants can either be planted directly into their final growing position or potted up and grown on for a year. Remove half of the leaf area to reduce transpiration and water loss and aid establishment. Bird attracting. …

plants.name: Dichelachne crinita
plants.form: Slender, tufted perennial grass with tall, smooth stems and finely ribbed leaf blades, 6mm wide.
plants.flowers: Very dense, fluffy, pale green flower heads, up to 25cm long by 3cm wide.
plants.habitat: Largely coastal, in open situations or under light woodland and heath, from sea level to 550m altitude.
plants.notes: Fast-growing grass, tolerates a wide range of conditions and is an important food source for grazing animals.

plants.name: Dichelachne inaequiglumis
plants.form: Tufted perennial grass with smooth stems and leaf blades up to 15cm long, the upper surface with prominent ribs.
plants.flowers: Floppy flower heads up to 25cm long, with green or purplish flowers. The glumes (leaf-like structures in the flower head, immediately below the flowers) are unequal.
plants.habitat: To 880m altitude in the Central Highlands, east coast and west coast.

plants.name: Dichelachne micrantha
plants.form: Loosely tufted perennial grass with flat, slender (1-2.5mm wide) leaves which taper to a point.
plants.flowers: In erect flower heads, 2.5 to 10.5cm long.
plants.habitat: Usually in dry situations, including rock slopes, dry banks and roadsides, to 800m altitude.

plants.name: Dichelachne montana
plants.form: Perennial, leaf blade 6.5-31cm long, 2-5mm wide, stems 50-110 high.
plants.flowers: Panicle 3.5-17cm.
plants.habitat: Stoney places

plants.name: Dichelachne parva
plants.form: Perennial, stems erect or kneed. 2 noded, 15-80cm tall. Leaves mainly basal with blades 4-20 long, 1-2.5 wide.
plants.flowers: Oval panicle, 3-28cm long, 1-2cm wide.
plants.habitat: Tolerates better soils than Dichelachne montana.

plants.name: Dichelachne rara
plants.form: Stems and nodes smooth, variable tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Flower heads range from 6cm long with few flowers, to dense, 25cm long flower heads.
plants.habitat: Usually in dry situations on heath margins or under light forest cover, from sea level to 870m altitude.

plants.name: Dichelachne sieberiana
plants.form: Tufted perennial, stems and nodes hairy and rough to touch.
plants.flowers: Flowerheads range from 6cm long with few flowers, to dense, 25cm long flowerheads.

plants.name: Dichondra repens
plants.form: Slender-stemmed perennial herb with prostrate, kidney shaped leaves 3cm wide, smooth or slightly hairy.
plants.flowers: Solitary flowers develop in leaf axils, small, greenish and inconspicuous.
plants.fruit: Capsule usually contains a single seed.
plants.habitat: Coastal sand and cliffs to alpine and sub-alpine grassland.
plants.notes: Plant at 30cm intervals. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Dichosciadium ranunculaceum var. tasmanicum
plants.form: Perennial herb, has 5-7 lobes on leaves.
plants.flowers: Umbels have 6-12 flowers.
plants.notes: Difficult to grow, prefers high elevation sub-alpine areas.

plants.name: Dicksonia antarctica
plants.form: Large tree fern, trunk to 1m diameter, densely covered with brown fibrous roots. Large crown of dark green fronds to 4m long.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant from sheltered gullies in dry sclerophyll to rainforest, ranging from sea level to sub-alpine forest. Mostly absent above 900m e.g. Central Plateau and low rainfall areas.
plants.notes: Suitable for growing in large containers. Young plants are very slow-growing for the first 2-3 years. Produces copious spores (800 million per plant annually). Early to re-colonise in disturbed soils. Its trunk is the host for at least 30 other plants. Moderate flammability. …

plants.name: Dillwynia cinerascens
plants.form: Slender shrub, trailing or erect.
plants.flowers: Pea 3-8 together in terminal clusters. Petals orange with dark red, keel blunt, purplish red.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – turn brittle and brown at maturity. Each pod contains one or two seeds which become hard and turn from green to dark brown when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in dry heaths and grassy places.
plants.notes: Hardy. Prefers well drained soil and some sun.

plants.name: Dillwynia glaberrima
plants.form: Shrub with slender arching branches.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow pea flowers with red markings, flowers arranged in short terminal heads.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – short, rounded, turn brittle at maturity. Each pod contains only one or two seeds which become hard and turn from green to dark brown when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in wet heaths both coastal and inland.
plants.notes: In cultivation requires good drainage, preferably a sandy soil, mulching and about half shade. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Dillwynia sericea
plants.form: Erect shrub with stiff, lightly haired branches.
plants.flowers: Pea, crowded in long sprays, orange/apricot/red tonings with blunt keel which is often greenish yellow.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – small, sparsely hairy, turn brittle at maturity. Each pod contains only one or two seeds which become hard and turn from green to dark brown when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in dry open habitats.
plants.notes: Requires well drained soil and part shade to full sun.

plants.name: Diplarrena latifolia
plants.form: Tufted perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Iris-like flowers on long flat stems.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – oblong, found at the ends of the old flower stems, rarely more than 4-lobes to each. Flattened seeds are red-brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Found in heath, herbfields and sub-alpine shrubberies from near sea level to about 1000m in Central Highlands, south-west and west coast.
plants.notes: Needs constant moisture, well-drained soil and full sun. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Diplarrena moraea
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.flowers: White and yellow with purple lines on tall stalks.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – 3-lobed, cylindrical, found at the end of old flower stems. Capsule contains numerous flattened seeds, red-brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread in sandy, peaty or rocky places. Common in a wide range of situations, coastal dunes and scrub, heaths, rocky banks, under light forest cover and on the margins of wet sclerophyll forest, sea level to about 1000m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Low flammability. Has been identified as being used in traditional Palawa basket weaving.

plants.name: Diplaspis cordifolia
plants.form: Perennial herb with erect, stalked, heart-shaped leaves forming a rosette.
plants.flowers: Flower heads of more than 20 flowers per umbel, yellowish green, about 2 cm across.
plants.habitat: In peaty soils amongst rocks above 900m altitude in western mountains and on peaty heaths at sea level in the west and south-west.
plants.notes: Prefers high elevation areas.

plants.name: Diplaspis hydrocotyle
plants.form: A small perennial herb with stalked, heart-shaped leaves, up to 10cm long, forming a rosette.
plants.flowers: Small yellowish green flower heads with 12-20 flowers per umbel, on stems to 4 cm long.
plants.habitat: Frequent in wet ground on mountains and at the margins of lakes or tarns.
plants.notes: Prefers high elevation areas at the snow line.

plants.name: Diplazium australe
plants.form: Large, soft, fleshy. Rootstock forms a woody trunk in old plants. Fronds triangular.
plants.habitat: Found in north and north-western Tasmania sometimes locally abundant but with only scattered occurrences elsewhere. Grows in deep, fertile soils below 300m. Typically occurs in dark, sheltered sites but colonies in more exposed sites have been observed frosted and frondless.

plants.name: Dipodium roseum
plants.form: A distinctive large, leafless pink hyacinth orchid. The only representative of it genus in Tasmania.
plants.flowers: 15- 50 pale pink finely spotted flowers, recurved tips on the perianth segments. Striped labellum covered in dense pink hairs in the centre.
plants.habitat: Heathy open forest and woodland on well-drained sandy soils, loams and clays, usually in rather bare spots. Locally quite common in lowland areas up to 400m in south-eastern, eastern and northern Tasmania including islands off the Furneaux Group. …
plants.notes: Most habitats are dry and fires occur fairly frequently.

plants.name: Discaria pubescens
plants.form: Thorny shrub with green branches, covered with small white hairs. The smaller branches are reduced to solid 2.5-4cm long spines. Leaves are 10cm long, flat and wedge-shaped, with serrated edges and a blunt tip.
plants.flowers: Flowers are small and cream, and borne in the leaf axils underneath the spiky branches.
plants.habitat: Grassy banks and roadsides, sandy or gravelly soil and clefts amongst fractured dolerite rocks and flood channels, on the Central Plateau and near Launceston.

plants.name: Diselma archeri
plants.form: Grey-green shrub, branches curving downwards at the ends. Branchlets with foliage appear square in cross section.
plants.fruit: Cone – male and female cones on separate plants. Female have 2 pairs of scales, only upper pair fertile. Ripe seeds, 2 per cone, longer than scales which become hard and brownish-purple in colour.
plants.habitat: Found mainly in the central and western mountains but also occurring on unburnt sections of the Central Plateau and as a small tree (to 6m) in rainforest.
plants.notes: Withstands frost and snow and does best in moist, well drained soils in a cool location. Relatively slow growing and has been in cultivation for many years.

plants.name: Disphyma crassifolium subsp. clavellatum
plants.form: Prostrate, spreading plant, with succulent leaves which are circular or triangular in cross-section and stems up to 2m long.
plants.flowers: Purple to pink with long, narrow petals, solitary, 3cm in diameter.
plants.fruit: Fleshy red capsules which become hard and dry when mature.
plants.habitat: Saline flats, saltmarshes and coastal areas in rocky spray zones.
plants.notes: Low maintenance plant which can form extensive mats if planted at 30cm intervals. Grows in sunny frost-free situations, and is tolerant of salt spray. Requires good drainage. Leaves are juicy and edible, can be used in salads. Good for soil stabilisation. …

plants.name: Distichlis distichophylla
plants.form: Branched creeping grass, with rhizomes more than 1m long, and narrow leaf blades up to 5cm long. Old leaf sheaths are persistent.
plants.flowers: Flower heads are 2.5-5cm long, and terminal on upright leafy stems. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants. Flowers in spring, or in response to rain.
plants.habitat: Coasts and estuaries around the state, and salt lagoons in the Midlands.
plants.notes: Useful for soil conservation in coastal areas due to binding properties. Considered to be of little pasture value.

plants.name: Diuris chryseopsis
plants.form: Moth orchid. Spring flowering. Erect, linear, grass-like leaves 50-150 mm long.
plants.flowers: 1-4 nodding lemon-yellow flowers with brown streaking on spade-like labellum; 13-40 mm across and narrow oval petals.
plants.habitat: Common in coastal grasslands in the north and east of Tasmania as well as in the Midlands; found in places that are seasonally wet in winter.

plants.name: Diuris lanceolata
plants.form: Larger golden moth with 2-4 erect, linear, grass-like leaves 50-180 mm long.
plants.flowers: 1-3 semi-nodding orange-yellow flowers with brown markings 25-40 mm across. Narrow spade-like, yellow labellum with a prominent yellow hairy callus.
plants.habitat: Highly localised and rare. Occurs in the north-west of Tasmania in coastal scrub and windswept coastal grassland and heathland among dwarfed shrubs and sedges, sometimes on rocky outcrops.

plants.name: Diuris monticola
plants.habitat: Occurs in the north-west in coastal scrub and windswept coastal grassland and heathland, among dwarfed shrubs and sedges, on moist to well-drained sandy and clay loam, sometimes on rocky outcrops.

plants.name: Diuris orientis
plants.form: A common donkey orchid with 1-3 erect, folded leaves 100-300mm long.
plants.flowers: 1-6 yellow flowers with pink, brown or purple suffusions, 30-50 mm across. Large oval petal with yellow external stripe. Lateral sepals narrow and flared at distal end.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally common in a variety of habitats from the coast to lower alpine and sub-alpine areas. Often found in clumps.

plants.name: Diuris pardina
plants.form: A donkey orchid, blotched with brown spots; 2-3 folded leaves 150-300mm long.
plants.flowers: 2-10 pale yellow, heavily blotched flowers, 20-25 mm across. Lateral sepals 12-16 mm, deflexed, recurved and crossed. Broad lateral lobes on the labellum.
plants.habitat: Common on the east coast, growing in woodlands, often in rocky locations.

plants.name: Diuris sulphurea
plants.form: Sulphur-yellow tiger orchid; tall robust double-tail. 1-3 folded leaves, 200-500mm long. Forms vegetatively produced colonies.
plants.flowers: 1-7 bright yellow flowers with dark-brown markings. Dorsal sepal with 2 dark blotches at base. Long straight to curved and touching lateral sepals. The labellum midlobe is small with large lateral lobes and a single callus.
plants.habitat: Widely distributed in a variety of coastal to montane habitats in sandy, loam, clay and gravel soils.

plants.name: Dockrillia striolata
plants.form: A clumping, epiphytic, rock-dwelling orchid with wiry stem; long tubular, fleshy leaf 50-150mm long.
plants.flowers: Short racemes with 1-3 yellowish flowers streaked with brown and white, particularly prominent on the outside of the perianth segments; flowers downward hanging and fragrant.
plants.habitat: Epiphytic, growing on isolated rocks, most commonly grano-diorite and granite, often in river gorges, from the Furneaux group of Islands south down the Tasmanian east coast to Freycinet Peninsula. Most colonies are found on east-facing sites directly exposed to moisture laden sea breezes.
plants.notes: Dockrilla roots spread widely over the rock surfaces and in crevices. As they are not insulated by soil, the plants are very vulnerable to all but low intensity ground fires.

plants.name: Dodonaea filiformis
plants.form: Small, erect, much-branched shrub.
plants.flowers: In small terminal groups; male and female on different plants.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – small, reddish-brown, usually 3-winged. Seed is black and firm when ripe.
plants.habitat: Usually found on well-drained slopes and river banks.

plants.name: Dodonaea viscosa subsp. spatulata
plants.form: Dense upright shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Small, in terminal clusters; dioecious.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – usually 3-winged; turn from red to tan-brown and become brittle as seed ripens. Seed is black and firm when ripe.
plants.notes: Good screen or shelter plant. The flowers attract moths, butterflies and other insects. Bee attracting. Bird attracting. Foliage provides refuge for small birds, with the fruits providing forage for some. Kangaroos and wallabies browse the foliage. High flammability. …

plants.name: Donatia novae-zelandiae
plants.form: Densely tufted, perennial plant with erect, closely packed stems which form hard, compact mounds, 1m or more in diameter.
plants.flowers: Solitary, 5-6mm wide and long.
plants.habitat: Mountain summits, on wet screes and exposed places with snow lie for several months of the year. Often grows together with other cushion plants.
plants.notes: Difficult to maintain in cultivation, requiring constantly moist cool growing conditions.

plants.name: Dracophyllum milliganii
plants.form: A woody plant with main axis erect and often unbranched. Distinguishing features – a dense tuft of leaves which taper to a fine point, often curved or almost coiled at the end.
plants.flowers: White, crowded on the red branched flowering stem.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet places in mountain gullies and on exposed slopes reaching altitudes of about 1200m.
plants.notes: Rare in cultivation. Require a well-composted soil and plenty of moisture but reasonable drainage. A cool location should be found but some sunlight is necessary. May be difficult to grow in warm coastal areas.

plants.name: Dracophyllum minimum
plants.form: Hard, compact, mounding, densely branched cushion plant.
plants.flowers: White; open widely with five anthers clearly visible in the throat.
plants.fruit: Capsule – at first semi-succulent and crimson but becoming hard and dry when mature.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant at altitudes above about 1200m in places where snow lies for several months of the year on mountains of the Central Plateau and west.
plants.notes: Hard to grow at lower altitudes. It is worth trying in a rockery but it must have a peaty soil, ample moisture and good light.

plants.name: Drosera arcturi
plants.form: Perennial insectivorous herb with long, fibrous roots and leaves in a basal rosette.
plants.flowers: Solitary flowers with white petals about 1cm long.
plants.habitat: Frequent in sub-alpine moors and bogs.
plants.notes: Seedlings are susceptible to weed competition.

plants.name: Drosera auriculata
plants.form: Slender insectivorous plant. Stem leaves covered with sticky hairs.
plants.flowers: Terminal, few, petals pale pink, twice as long as sepals and spreading widely.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant on dry hillsides and heaths. Requires lime-free infertile soil.
plants.notes: Dies back to ground level in summer.

plants.name: Drosera binata
plants.form: Perennial herb with fibrous roots and underground runners. Leaves forked once or twice.
plants.flowers: Main flower stalk long, bearing clusters of white sweetly scented flowers, 2cm across.
plants.habitat: Occasional in bogs and soaks in wet heaths, sea level to alpine and sub-alpine.

plants.name: Drosera glanduligera
plants.form: Ground-hugging, insectivorous rosette herb, with leaves which vary in colour from green to yellow or bright red. Leaves 3cm long, with glandular hairs.
plants.flowers: 8mm in diameter, orange or scarlet with blackish centres, on multiple stems. Up to 20 flowers per stem.
plants.habitat: Local on Flinders Island.
plants.notes: A winter growing annual which dies after flowering. Seedlings are susceptible to weed competition.

plants.name: Drosera gunniana
plants.form: Tuberous rosette herb with roundish leaves, about 3mm in diameter
plants.flowers: Unopened flower buds and calyx of open flowers are hairy. Petals usually white, and up to 1.3cm in diameter, usually twice as long as sepals, on terminal flowers. Flowering stem is erect and narrow.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant in grassy places and pastures.
plants.notes: Keep moist but not wet, and allow to dry out in summer. Seedlings are susceptible to weed competition. Similar in appearance to Drosera auriculata, which can be distinguished by its smooth unopened flower buds and calyx. Thought to be poisonous to livestock.

plants.name: Drosera macrantha subsp. planchonii
plants.form: Slender, single stemmed, trailing or weakly climbing plant growing from tuber.
plants.flowers: Several in terminal clusters, white with hairy sepals and 5 stamens.
plants.habitat: Common in coastal areas. Carnivorous in habit.
plants.notes: The tiny seedlings may be susceptible to weed competition.

plants.name: Drosera peltata
plants.form: Tuberous rosette herb with roundish leaves, about 3mm in diameter
plants.flowers: Unopened flower buds and calyx of open flowers are hairy. Petals usually white, and up to 1.3cm in diameter, usually twice as long as sepals, on terminal flowers. Flowering stem is erect and narrow.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant in grassy places and pastures.
plants.notes: Keep moist but not wet, and allow to dry out in summer. Seedlings are susceptible to weed competition. Similar in appearance to Drosera auriculata, which can be distinguished by its smooth unopened flower buds and calyx. Thought to be poisonous to livestock.

plants.name: Drosera pygmaea
plants.form: Tiny, flat basal rosette herb measuring 1-1.5cm in diameter. Numerous red leaves with glandular hairs on the upper surface, 1-2mm in diameter.
plants.flowers: Solitary, with four petals.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in peaty heaths from sea level to about 1200m above sea level.
plants.notes: Self pollinates, and is one of the easiest sundews to grow.

plants.name: Drosera spatulata var. spatulata
plants.form: Herb with basal rosette of 1.5-3cm diameter and red, spoon-shaped leaves 1-2cm long.
plants.flowers: Flower stems up to 15cm long, flowers 1cm in diameter with white or pink petals.
plants.habitat: Occasional in wet heaths.
plants.notes: Seedlings are susceptible to weed competition.

plants.name: Drymophila cyanocarpa
plants.form: Herbaceous perennial that spreads by rhizomes. Simple bare stem , sometimes branched, arising from tubers then bending over.
plants.flowers: White, 1.5cm diameter, shortly stalked in the axils of the leaves, facing downwards.
plants.fruit: Berry – heart-shaped, succulent, turquoise blue or paler, to 16mm. Hang on the plant for a long time. Seeds 8-10 shining, brown.
plants.habitat: Widely distributed in damp shady places in forests.

plants.name: Dryopoa dives
plants.form: Tall, erect, robust and tufted perennial, with flat, linear leaves which taper to a fine point. The stems are smooth, round in cross-section and hollow.
plants.flowers: Flower heads in a pyramid shape, 20-50cm long, and containing plump green and purple spikelets.
plants.habitat: Recorded only from the Snug Plains area.

plants.name: Echinopogon ovatus
plants.form: Erect or kneed rhizomatous annual or short lived perennial.
plants.flowers: Flower erect, oval oblong, 0.8-5cm long, 1-2.5cm diameter, green purplish.
plants.habitat: Widespread in light woodland in lowland areas up to 900m.

plants.name: Einadia nutans subsp. nutans
plants.form: Prostrate or scrambling, multi-branched climber to 1m across, with grey-green arrowhead-shaped leaves to 3cm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers are inconspicuous and green, and borne in terminal flower spikes arising from the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Red berry-like fruit, soft when ripe containing one black, shiny seed.
plants.habitat: Dry places, including forests and woodlands, especially near the coast.
plants.notes: Very hardy in most situations, and tolerates very dry conditions. Thrives in well-drained soil.

plants.name: Elaeocarpus reticulatus
plants.form: Shrub or tree, leaves shortly stalked, elliptical-oblong, glabrous, margins serrate.
plants.flowers: Usually white, sometimes pink, in loose racemes shorter than the leaves.
plants.habitat: Occurs on King and Flinders Islands. Found in many different habitats.
plants.notes: Once established plants are quite hardy to dryness and will tolerate moderate coastal exposure. May be grown in a variety of positions from full shade to full sun. Bird attracting. High flammability.

plants.name: Elatine gratioloides
plants.form: Submerged, hairless annual herb with opposite leaves and creeping stems, 30cm long.
plants.flowers: Single small flowers with greenish sepals and pink petals about 1mm long.
plants.fruit: Capsule – produces 12-50 cylindrical or curved seeds.
plants.habitat: Fairly common in marshes and the edges of still fresh waster in central and northern areas of the state.
plants.notes: Annual aquatic herb. Self-seeds in good conditions. Requires sun or part shade, and is useful for disguising concrete pool edges. Suitable for poorly drained areas.

plants.name: Eleocharis acuta
plants.form: Perennial sedge with tufted, needle-like stems and a woody rhizome.
plants.flowers: In cylindrical spikes.
plants.fruit: Nut – egg-shaped, 1.5mm long, turning from yellowish-brown to dark brown when mature. Seed heads dry and turn brown when seed is ripe.
plants.habitat: Riparian vegetation along slowly flowing streams, wetlands and shallow water. King Island, north-east, west coast, Central Highlands, Midlands, east coast and south-west.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Provides habitat for many birds and other animals.

plants.name: Eleocharis gracilis
plants.form: Perennial sedge with slender stems (less than 0.5mm wide) and a woody rhizome.
plants.flowers: 5-15 flowers in an oval spikelet.
plants.fruit: Nut – 1.25mm long, light to dark brown. Seed heads dry and turn brown when seed is ripe.
plants.habitat: In swamps in the north-east, west coast, Central Highlands, Midlands, east coast and south-west.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Provides habitat for many birds and other animals.

plants.name: Eleocharis pusilla
plants.form: Small, densely tufted perennial sedge with erect stems and slender rhizomes.
plants.flowers: Spikelets with a few flowers.
plants.fruit: Nut – pale, 1mm long. Seed heads dry and turn brown when seed is ripe.
plants.habitat: On stream and lake banks, and in swampy ground, on the west coast, Central Highlands, Midlands and east coast.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Provides habitat for many birds and other animals.

plants.name: Eleocharis sphacelata
plants.form: Tall perennial sedge with erect, jointed, hollow stems and a stout woody rhizome.
plants.flowers: In cylindrical spikes, 3-6cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – 2.5mm long and straw-coloured. Seed heads dry and turn brown when seed is ripe.
plants.habitat: Riparian vegetation and wetlands, in slowly flowing streams and shallow water. King Island, north-east, west coast, Central Highlands, Midlands, east coast and south-west.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Provides habitat for many birds and other animals. Used for basket weaving (contemporary).

plants.name: Empodisma minus
plants.form: Rhizome, short, stout, erect.
plants.flowers: Female spikelets
plants.habitat: Heath and sedgelands, sub-alpine shrubberies, sphagnum bogs, buttongrass plains, near sea level to over 1400m.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Epacris acuminata
plants.form: An erect bushy shrub.
plants.flowers: Few, in axils of upper leaves. White, tubular with oblong, rounded lobes shorter than tube.
plants.habitat: Occasional from sea level to about 900m. On rocky river banks, shrubberies, flood zones. Wet dolerite soil.

plants.name: Epacris apsleyensis
plants.form: An erect sparsely branched shrub.
plants.flowers: White, bell shaped, anthers are enclosed within the tube.
plants.habitat: The Apsley river area. Dry dolerite rocky outcrops.

plants.name: Epacris barbata
plants.form: A shrub, usually branched near the base with long erect branches.
plants.flowers: Large white flowers about 1cm in diameter. Floral bracts and sepals tinged red, covered with silky hairs.
plants.habitat: Found only in the vicinity of Freycinet Peninsula.

plants.name: Epacris corymbiflora
plants.form: Small shrub with spreading branches.
plants.flowers: Narrow, white, tubular with brown, shining bracts and sepals. In corymbs on short stalks.
plants.habitat: Local in wet peaty heaths near the west and south-west coasts and in the Rasselas Valley.
plants.notes: Outstanding dwarf species. Requires moist, light to medium soils, rich in organic matter and prefers dappled shade. A good container plant. Bird attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Epacris curtisiae
plants.form: A shrub with one to several erect and slender stems.
plants.flowers: The white flowers are solitary and arranged in short, leafy heads at the ends of the top branches.
plants.habitat: Grows on buttongrass moorland between 150m and 400m, also in shrubby heathland/sedgeland.

plants.name: Epacris exserta
plants.form: Much-branched, erect shrub.
plants.flowers: White, tubular, rather large with short spikes of flowers on main and many lateral branches.
plants.habitat: Local in north on banks of several rivers including the South Esk.
plants.notes: Has had limited cultivation but plants appear to grow well. It requires moist, well drained soil with dappled shade and partial sun. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Epacris glabella
plants.form: Open shrub with erect slender branches.
plants.flowers: White, solitary in the leaf axils and scattered along the upper parts of branches.
plants.habitat: Heathy scrub on clay or serpentine.

plants.name: Epacris grandis
plants.form: Erect shrub
plants.flowers: White, bell-shaped, larger in floral parts than Epacris limbata and with hairy bracts.
plants.habitat: Found on dolerite cliff edges, dry sclerophyll forest and in river deposits on clay.

plants.name: Epacris graniticola
plants.form: Erect multi-stemmed shrub.
plants.flowers: White, solitary in the leaf axils, clustered at the ends of branches.

plants.name: Epacris gunnii
plants.form: Rigid shrub with a few slender erect branches. Leaves heart-shaped, sharply pointed.
plants.flowers: White, wide bell-shaped, along upper parts of branches in conspicuous spikes.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet heaths from sea level to mountain plateaux at about 1000m.

plants.name: Epacris heteronema var. heteronema
plants.form: Stout, much-branched shrub sometimes (on west coast) a small tree.
plants.flowers: White, tubular, anthers scarcely reaching top of tube, in leafy heads at ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in wet heaths in the west and south-west.

plants.name: Epacris impressa
plants.form: Erect, straggly, small shrub.
plants.flowers: Red, pink or white tubular.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – opens by 5 lines, seeds numerous.
plants.habitat: Widespread and very abundant, sea level to 800m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Bee attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Epacris lanuginosa
plants.form: Shrub, often branched near the base with slender erect stems, often much larger (west coast).
plants.flowers: White, bracts and sepals straw-coloured or brown, papery.
plants.habitat: Widespread, abundant in wet heaths, sea level to 1000m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Epacris limbata
plants.form: Erect shrub with long slender stems.
plants.flowers: White, bell-shaped with short style. Bracts, sepals translucent, streaked pink, in crowded heads. Epacris limbata occurs in the same general area as Epacris lanuginosa and tasmanica but its long dense flower heads and heart-shaped leaves with thin translucent margins easily distinguish it.
plants.habitat: Margins of marshes on the east coast where sedgy eucalyptus woodlands grade into forests usually of Eucalyptus amygdalina and/or tenuiramis.

plants.name: Epacris marginata
plants.form: A stout, rigid, much-branched shrub with the young branches slightly hairy.
plants.flowers: White, tubular, very shortly stalked, clustered below the tips of branches, sweet-scented.
plants.habitat: Local on the Tasman Peninsula at Eaglehawk Neck, Cash’s Lookout and Mt. Brown.
plants.notes: Should be suited to moist, well-drained, light to medium soils. Withstands limited coastal exposure. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Epacris moscaliana
plants.form: An erect much-branched shrub.
plants.flowers: White, tubular, solitary, and scattered along the upper parts of the branches in the leaf axils.

plants.name: Epacris myrtifolia
plants.form: Stout, erect, bushy shrub.
plants.flowers: White 5mm long, solitary in leaf axils, crowded near branch ends in dense showy heads.
plants.habitat: Local near the coasts in the south, Recherche Bay and Tasman Peninsula.

plants.name: Epacris navicularis
plants.form: Much branched shrub recognisable by its tiny leaves closely appressed to each other.
plants.flowers: White, solitary in leaf axils towards ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Found in a few very exposed situations in the south-western mountains. Most common in bolster heath in mountain saddles.

plants.name: Epacris obtusifolia
plants.form: Shrub with slender, erect branches, sometimes hairy.
plants.flowers: White or cream in spikes at ends of slender often unbranched stems 30cm-1m.
plants.habitat: Damp heaths and wet places.

plants.name: Epacris paludosa
plants.form: Small, much-branched shrub , leaves with short wide stalks.
plants.flowers: Corolla tube white, bracts and sepals egg-shaped and with fine hairs along margins.
plants.habitat: Local at the summit of Strzelecki Peak, Flinders Island.

plants.name: Epacris petrophila
plants.form: Erect, sparingly branched shrub with leaves closely appressed to the stems.
plants.flowers: White bell-shaped, in the axils of uppermost leaves and with narrow triangular lobes.
plants.habitat: Local at altitudes of about 1000m on the Western Tiers and in alpine and sub-alpine shrubby grassland near Arthur’s Lake.

plants.name: Epacris serpyllifolia
plants.form: Stout, bushy shrub prostrate when growing in exposed alpine and sub-alpine situations.
plants.flowers: White, bell-shaped, solitary but crowded in short, dense, terminal heads.
plants.habitat: Widespread in alpine and sub-alpine heaths and bogs throughout the mountains of the state.

plants.name: Epacris stuartii
plants.form: Small shrub, leaves very shortly stalked, blades flat, rounded, entire margin, lower surface 1-3 ribbed.
plants.flowers: White, forming loose clusters along the upper parts of the branches.
plants.habitat: Known only from type material collected at Southport in the south. Found on top of steep seaward slope in shallow loam on dolerite.

plants.name: Epacris tasmanica
plants.form: Shrub with few branches.
plants.flowers: White; floral tube hidden in hard bracts but 5 showy petals surround stamens and style.
plants.habitat: Abundant in several localities in the east and south-east. Found in eucalypt woodland with grassy understorey on dolerite, top of sea cliffs and on rocky river banks and open muddy sites.

plants.name: Epacris virgata
plants.form: Small white heath (shrub), few slender upright branches.
plants.flowers: White tubular flowers 6mm across; solitary in numerous axils.
plants.habitat: Damp foothills. Local in northern Tasmania on Asbestos Hills.

plants.name: Epilobium billardiereanum subsp. billardiereanum
plants.form: Perennial layering herb.
plants.flowers: Mauve /pink, notched petals on a long ovary at the end of short stalk.

plants.name: Epilobium billardiereanum subsp. cinereum
plants.form: Perennial layering herb.

plants.name: Epilobium billardiereanum subsp. Intermedium
plants.form: Perennial layering herb.

plants.name: Epilobium curtisiae
plants.form: Slender perennial herb, often branched from the base, with elliptical, blunt-tipped leaves.
plants.flowers: Flowers are pale purplish-pink, 6-7mm long and solitary in the upper leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Capsule – downy, 1-1.5cm long; contains smooth, golden-brown seeds with a narrow, thin and translucent wing.
plants.habitat: Marshy places in alpine and sub-alpine grasslands such as the Middlesex Plains, and in soaks on river flats in the North, including the Meander River, south-west of Deloraine.
plants.notes: Not widely grown.

plants.name: Epilobium gunnianum
plants.form: Herb with a woody, usually unbranched stem, and mostly opposite leaves with small teeth on the margins.
plants.flowers: Flowers are purplish-pink, 12-14mm long with a 2mm long notch in the apex of each petal. Flowers are solitary, and borne in the axils of the upper leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule 4-6cm long. Seeds have lateral wings.
plants.habitat: Mountains above 1000m altitude.
plants.notes: Seeds freely so has weed potential.

plants.name: Epilobium hirtigerum
plants.form: Perennial herb with stems prostrate and woody at the base, then erect, greyish-green or purple and shaggy in the upper part.
plants.flowers: Flowers are cream or purplish, with a notch in each petal, and 1cm in diameter. Flowers are solitary, and borne in the axils of the upper leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule – hairy, 5-7cm long. Seeds are egg-shaped.
plants.habitat: Lowland habitats, and often colonising disturbed ground, e.g. roadside quarries.

plants.name: Epilobium pallidiflorum
plants.form: Perennial herb, often with purplish, hard, hollow stems, which are prostate and bear roots on the lower parts, and are erect with dense short hairs on the upper parts. Leaves are generally opposite, long, thin and stalkless.
plants.flowers: Flowers are white or rose pink, and have a notch at the end which is about 3mm long. Flowers are solitary and are borne in the leaf axils on the upper part of the stem.
plants.fruit: Capsule – hairy, 5-6cm long; contains egg-shaped seeds with one side flattened. Unlike most other Epilobium species, the seeds do not have a plume of hairs.
plants.habitat: Wet places, especially in the north and north-west.

plants.name: Epilobium perpusillum
plants.form: Small herb with creeping stems, and opposite, somewhat crowded leaves with rounded tips, 4-7mm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers are white with a notch in the petals, solitary and borne in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 2.5cm long, on a stalk 2.5-5cm long.
plants.habitat: On the banks of the Franklin and Picton Rivers, West Coast.

plants.name: Epilobium sarmentaceum
plants.form: Perennial herb with somewhat floppy stems which often droop at the tip, becoming upright at the mature flower and fruiting stages. Leaves are pale green, lanceolate and mostly opposite, 1.5-2cm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers are pale lilac or rose-pink, and solitary in the axils of the upper leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule – hairy when young and smooth later; contains seeds with lateral wings.
plants.habitat: Moist places on mountains, including crevices between rocks, above 600m altitude.

plants.name: Epilobium tasmanicum
plants.form: Small herb with creeping stems 2-8cm long, and opposite, thick, shining, somewhat crowded leaves, 8-10mm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers are pink with a notch in the apex of each petal, and occur in pairs in the axils of the upper leaves.
plants.habitat: Wet places on mountain plateaux.
plants.notes: Not widely grown.

plants.name: Epilobium willisii
plants.form: Herb with spreading stems and erect leaves with 2-5 teeth on the margins, arranged oppositely.
plants.flowers: Flowers are pink, and occur in pairs in the upper leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Capsule – seeds are pale-rimmed and unusual because they don’t have a plume of hairs, unlike most other Epilobium species. Epilobium species produces vast amounts of seed.
plants.habitat: Wet alpine and sub-alpine herbfields around the central mountains, and bare places around the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Eriochilus cucullatus
plants.form: Summer and autumn flowering orchid with a thin, wispy, scape. Oval dark green ground-hugging leaf develops fully after flowering.
plants.flowers: Small flowers that have a pair of enlarged white or pink lateral sepals, tiny thin petals, and a sharply recurved hairy labellum closely embracing the column. Bristles red-white.
plants.habitat: Common in a range of habitats from heathy open eucalypt forest to heathland and buttongrass moorland on well drained as well as poorly drained soils, from coast to sub-alpine areas.
plants.notes: The flowers produce nectar that gathers in the base of the labellum.

plants.name: Eryngium ovinum
plants.form: Annual herb, extremely prickly, with erect, rigid, much-branched stems.
plants.flowers: Heads of blue/purplish flowers, with long prickly bracts, develop a metallic blue colour.
plants.habitat: Widespread, usually inland, often in colonies.
plants.notes: Flowering stems are often dried for use in floral arrangements.

plants.name: Eryngium vesiculosum
plants.form: Perennial herb (prostrate) with spiny-toothed leaves to 15cm long.
plants.flowers: Prickly blue flower heads 1 cm in diameter, surrounded by spines to 2 cm.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant in sandy flats near the sea.
plants.notes: Good for coastal and saline areas.

plants.name: Eucalyptus amygdalina
plants.form: Small trees with mallee habit or tall tree. Leaves: Juvenile – narrow, dull green. Adult narrow (8-10 mm), green to sub-glaucous. Bark: Rough, fibrous, usually dark grey and often charred.
plants.flowers: Umbel with 11-20 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – cup-shaped; disc is more or less level.
plants.notes: Tolerates shallow and poor acid soils. Bee attracting. Timber is durable in the ground and is used for fence posts. High flammability. Makes good firewood; easily split.

plants.name: Eucalyptus archeri
plants.form: Small tree, stunted and shrubby in exposed situations. Leaves: Juvenile – round with indented apex, heart-shaped base, dull green to glaucous. Adult – lanceolate, green and glossy. Concolorous. Bark: Smooth olive green when new fading to grey/cream.
plants.flowers: 3-flowered umbels.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – cylindrical with sunken valves.
plants.habitat: Occurs on well-drained rocky sites near the margins of dolerite plateaux, and is known only from the north-east of the Central Plateau and Ben Lomond.
plants.notes: Very little known about the horticulture of this species, but it would be reasonable to expect its requirements to be similar to the closely related Cider Gum, Eucalyptus gunnii.

plants.name: Eucalyptus barberi
plants.form: Shrubby mallee or sometimes a small tree. Leaves: Juvenile – elliptical with marked oil glands on a short petiole. Adult – lanceolate, green and glossy. Concolorous. Bark: Smooth copper to light grey, sheds in ribbons.
plants.flowers: 7-flowered umbels.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – cup-shaped to cylindrical with a narrow disc slightly sunken; usually 3 valves.
plants.habitat: Forms small stands in well-drained rocky situations in the east of the State. Confined to shallow soils on dolerite rock outcrops.
plants.notes: Graceful and very hardy. Being a mallee type tree it makes an excellent low windbreak. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Eucalyptus brookeriana
plants.form: Shrub to tall tree. Leaves: Juvenile – petiolate and ovate with round-toothed margins, glossy, dark green with obvious oil dots. Adult – ovate to lanceolate, glossy, dark green, thin and undulate(wavy). Discolorous. Bark: Rough at the base but flaking to reveal dark grey, green or orange patches.
plants.flowers: 7-flowered umbels.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – bell-shaped with a level disc and exserted valves.
plants.habitat: Occurs in stands on higher ground on upper slopes of gullies and watersheds.
plants.notes: Fast growing and with a dense, bright green canopy of leaves held at the ends of the branches. Branching almost from ground level this tree makes an excellent tall hedge screen or wind-break.

plants.name: Eucalyptus coccifera
plants.form: A stunted shrub or a tree. Leaves: Juvenile – round with a small point and blue glaucousness that cannot be removed. Adult – oblong to lanceolate, green to glaucous with crimson hooked tip. Bark: Smooth, white, streaked with tan/orange or grey.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 3, 5 or 9 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – usually more than 7, but is 3s on kunanyi/ Mt Wellington; cup-shaped with a wide flat disc, often glaucous.
plants.habitat: Forms pure stands on rocky dolerite soils on exposed sites and mixed woodland below 1100m.
plants.notes: Trees grown from seed collected from trees on dolerite talus may be quite drought tolerant. Makes a delightful specimen when open grown. Colourful smooth bark. Bee attracting.

plants.name: Eucalyptus cordata subsp. cordata
plants.form: Straggly shrub or small tree. Leaves: Juvenile and adult leaves are the same. Round to heart-shaped with toothed margins, stem-clasping and very glaucous. Bark: Smooth, grey over pale grey with shedding orange ribbons.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 3 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – cup-shaped, glaucous, with sunken disc.
plants.habitat: Local in the south and south-east from sea level to about 800m. In scrub and forest on poorly drained ground, usually on dolerite hills. Isolated small stands in wet eucalypt forest.
plants.notes: The dense silvery canopy extends almost to ground level. Ideal for screen or windbreak. Unfortunately very susceptible to leaf-eating insects.

plants.name: Eucalyptus cordata subsp. quadrangulosa
plants.form: Medium to tall tree. Leaves: Juvenile – usually orbicular, 45-90mm long by 40-65mm wide, dull grey-green. Adult only occasionally produced in taller trees. Bark: Mostly smooth.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 3 flowers, white
plants.habitat: Clay to loam soils in hilly terrain.
plants.notes: Requires moderately fertile soil with reliable rainfall. Not drought tolerant.

plants.name: Eucalyptus dalrympleana subsp. lutruwita
plants.form: Large tree. Leaves: Juvenile – ovate to heart-shaped, dull green to glaucous blue. Adult – lanceolate, glossy green 80-220mm long, 10-35mm wide. Concolorous. Bark: Smooth, cream/white, streaked with grey, shedding in strips.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 3 buds diamond shaped with long, conical operculum, white.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules with a raised disc, valves protruding.
plants.habitat: Grows mainly from 400-1000m above sea level in central and eastern Tasmania.
plants.notes: Requires moderately fertile soil with reliable rainfall.

plants.name: Eucalyptus globulus subsp. globulus
plants.form: Small to tall tree. Leaves: Juvenile – oblong with stem-clasping, heart-shaped base, glaucous blue with red margin. Adult-sickle-shaped (falcate), long (around 30cm) green and glossy. Concolorous. Bark: Rough at the base, but peeling in red-brown ribbons to reveal a smooth copper/grey trunk.
plants.flowers: Large, usually solitary. Rarely 3 flowered on the West Coast. Usually white; very rarely pale pink Tasman Peninsula.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – large, greater than 15mm, rough and warty with four ribs.
plants.habitat: Reaches its maximum development in well-drained soil in sheltered valleys.
plants.notes: Frost hardiness depends on provenance. Even seedlings from cold areas will be frost susceptible when young. Useful for control of erosion and to provide soil stabilization. Provides dense shade. Bee attracting. Bird attracting. …

plants.name: Eucalyptus globulus subsp. pseudoglobulus
plants.form: Medium to large tree. Leaves: Juvenile – sessile, arranged in opposite pairs, elliptic to egg-shaped, the lower surface covered by a white, waxy bloom, 33–100 mm long and 20–60 mm wide. …
plants.flowers: Umbels of 3, creamy white.
