plants.fruit: Woody capsules – conical, 6–8 mm long and 9–12 mm wide with the valves protruding slightly above rim level.
plants.habitat: Only known population is on Rodondo Island 10km south of Wilsons Promontory (within state boundary of Tasmania).

plants.name: Eucalyptus gunnii subsp. divaricata
plants.form: Small to medium woodland tree, often with obvious forked branches, and small, rounded, bluish-green, stalk less leaves which occur in opposite pairs along the stem. Leaves: Juvenile – round with an indented apex and a heart-shaped base, glaucous blue. …
plants.flowers: Flowers are stalk less, in clusters of 3 and are borne in the axils.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – cylindrical with a sunken disc; capsule glaucous, 7-9mm long.
plants.habitat: Restricted to poorly drained frost hollows in open woodland around the Great Lake region, Central Plateau over 800m asl.
plants.notes: Highly frost tolerant.

plants.name: Eucalyptus gunnii subsp. gunnii
plants.form: Small to medium woodland tree, often with obvious forked branches, and small, rounded, bluish-green, stalkless leaves which occur in opposite pairs along the stem. Leaves: Juvenile – round with an indented apex and a heart-shaped base, glaucous blue. Adult – lanceolate to ovate, green to glaucous. …
plants.flowers: Flowers are stalkless, in clusters of 3 and are borne in the axils.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – slightly bent at the tip like a hook with waxy bloom; capsule glaucous, 7-9mm long.
plants.habitat: Restricted to poorly drained frost hollows in open woodland around the Great Lake region, Central Plateau over 800m above sea level.
plants.notes: Highly frost tolerant.

plants.name: Eucalyptus johnstonii
plants.form: Tree. Leaves: Juvenile – round with a toothed margin, green and glossy. Adult – lanceolate with a toothed margin, dark green, glossy and leathery. Concolorous. Bark: Smooth, grey streaked orange-red or yellow-green when new.
plants.flowers: Umbels 3-flowered.
plants.fruit: Wood capsules – bell-shaped, green to brown, ribbed, with protruding valves.
plants.habitat: A tall tree in wet sclerophyll forest and a small tree in dry sclerophyll forest on acid sandstone in areas of high rainfall.
plants.notes: Deep green, glossy leaves and smooth yellow bark characterise this beautiful tree suited to damp acidic soils in larger gardens.

plants.name: Eucalyptus morrisbyi
plants.form: Small tree. Leaves: Juvenile – round with a toothed margin, an indented apex and a heart-shaped base, glaucous blue. Adult – ovate to lanceolate and glaucous.
plants.flowers: Umbels 3-flowered.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – cylindrical with a sunken disc, a central rib and very glaucous.
plants.habitat: In two localities near South Arm and Risdon from sea level to about 150m.
plants.notes: A candidate for the rarest of eucalypts. Two natural occurrences, one stand at Calverts Hill, South Arm; a few trees near Geilston Bay. Easily grown and an attractive specimen tree. Flowers profusely.

plants.name: Eucalyptus nebulosa
plants.form: Small tree. Leaves: Juvenile – arranged in opposite pairs, greyish blue colour, concolorous, 24–45 mm long and 15–25 mm wide on a petiole up to 2 mm long. …
plants.flowers: Umbels 7-11 creamy white flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – hemispherical and more or less top-shaped.
plants.habitat: Mostly in the Pieman River Catchment.

plants.name: Eucalyptus nitida
plants.form: From tall tree to a multi-stemmed shrub. Leaves: Juvenile – broadest near the middle. Adult – narrow to lanceolate green and leathery. Bark: Rough, fibrous and usually dark grey but smooth on the branches.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 7-23 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – cup-shaped, disc is nearly level.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in the west of the State and on the islands of the Furneaux Group. Grows on poor siliceous soils from sea level to about 400m. Frost tolerance depends on provenance.
plants.notes: Widespread tree or mallee in south, south-west and north-west of State. Tolerates poor, acid wet soils and exposure. Bee attracting.

plants.name: Eucalyptus obliqua
plants.form: Tall straight tree with a dense crown. Leaves: Juvenile – asymmetrical, stalked, ovate, oblique, tapering suddenly to pointy tip, green, to 190mm long. Adult – asymmetrical, lanceolate, oblique, dark green to 130mm long, glossy and leathery. Concolorous.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 7-16 flowers, profuse, white-cream.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – barrel-shaped, with a sunken disc.
plants.habitat: Grows on deep soils with good drainage from sea level to about 600m. Is absent from poorly drained sites, dry sites and highly infertile soils. Generally frost and drought resistant, but this is strongly related to provenance.
plants.notes: Useful in providing high-level shelter (up to 50m) in windbreaks. Its dense foliage provides useful shade. Bee attracting. Large quantities of cream-coloured pollen is yielded producing a mild flavoured honey. Bird attracting. …

plants.name: Eucalyptus ovata var. ovata
plants.form: A straggling tree or a tall tree. Leaves: Juvenile – petiolate, ovate and dull green or sub-glaucous. Adult – ovate to lanceolate, leathery, glossy and undulating. Concolorous. Bark: Rough and scaly at the base; smooth, grey/copper above.
plants.flowers: Umbels usually with 7 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – trumpet-shaped with a level disc and 3 valves.
plants.habitat: Widespread in woodlands and forests on swampy ground. Frequent on coastal sandy heaths and sometimes forms pure stands on badly drained soils; occasional on well drained soils in mixed eucalypt forest.
plants.notes: Useful for planting in wet areas and to provide dense shade. Also as a second line planting for coastal conditions. Bee attracting. Produces valuable hardwood timber, which is also good for firewood.

plants.name: Eucalyptus pauciflora subsp. pauciflora
plants.form: Trees sometimes with long pendulous branches, and rounded crown. Leaves: Juvenile – petiolate, ovate, thick, leathery and dull blue-green. Adult – lanceolate, glossy green and leathery with marked longitudinal veins. Concolorous.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 5-15 creamy-white flowers. Flowers prolifically.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – pear-shaped or hemispherical, top flat and opening by 3 or 4 pores.
plants.habitat: Widespread in the east, north and Midlands in rain shadow areas, but also coastal and on the southern edge of the Central Plateau in well-drained situations. Tolerates long periods of heavy snow but may not tolerate drought, depending on provenance.
plants.notes: Trees are useful in providing medium-level shelter (up to 20m) in mixed species windbreaks. Is also useful in second line plantings in coastal conditions. Valued in highland areas for assisting in erosion control and for intercepting drifting snow. Bird attracting. …

plants.name: Eucalyptus perriniana subsp. perriniana
plants.form: Small tree with mallee habit or with single trunk. Leaves: Juvenile – fused across the base, very glaucous, and always present on the tree. Adult – lanceolate, very glaucous but rare. Bark: Smooth, grey to salmon pink; small trunks are often glaucous with circular leaf scars.
plants.flowers: 3 flowered umbels commonly formed in the axils of juvenile leaves.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules are deeply cup-shaped, small, 5-6mm across with sunken disc and raised rim, very glaucous.
plants.habitat: Local near Tunnack and Strickland at 300-600m. In natural stands on poor mudstone soils in ill-drained situations this species seldom attains tree height or develops adult leaves.
plants.notes: Often grown as an ornamental tree or for its foliage. Requires regular light lopping if ornamental juvenile foliage is to be maintained.

plants.name: Eucalyptus pulchella
plants.form: Graceful tree usually with a short trunk. Leaves: Juvenile – narrow, linear. Adult – linear, narrow (8mm), pale green to sub-glaucous. Bark: Smooth, cream streaked with grey.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 9-20 flowers massed stamens, no obvious petals. Mainly in late spring.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – small, pear-shaped with a more or less level disc.
plants.habitat: Endemic to the lowlands of south-east Tasmania (100-500m asl) where it grows as a spreading tree on the upper, north-west facing slopes of dolerite-capped hills, in grassy or heathy open forests.
plants.notes: Useful for planting in shady areas. An extremely ornamental tree with pleasing fine foliage and usually neat and compact form. Bird attracting. Bee attracting. High flammability.

plants.name: Eucalyptus radiata subsp. radiata
plants.form: Medium to large tree with straight trunk and dense crown. Leaves: Juvenile – broadest near the rounded base. Adult – narrow to narrow lanceolate, green to sub glaucous. Concolorous. Bark: Rough and fibrous, even on smaller branches.
plants.flowers: Stalks carrying two umbels with a total of 9-11 or more white-cream flowers. Prolific.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – cup or pear-shaped, very small (4-6mm), disc level.
plants.habitat: Local on well-drained slopes of river valleys in the north and north-west of the state. Tolerates some snow. Fast growing but grows poorly on sandy or poorly-drained soils.
plants.notes: Useful for providing medium to high-level shelter (up to 30m) in mixed species windbreaks. Suitable species for the production of high grade eucalypt oil. Bird attracting. The flowers provide food (pollen) for various insects, mammals and birds. Insect-eating birds are also attracted. …

plants.name: Eucalyptus regnans
plants.form: Tree with a shaft-like trunk which, in mature tees, is buttressed at the base. Leaves: Juvenile – asymmetrical and petiolate. Adult – lanceolate, asymmetrical, glossy green. Bark: Smooth, streaked grey sheds in long strips often caught in branches.
plants.flowers: Often 2 umbels together in an axil, each with 7-16 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – funnel-shaped with a level disc, relatively thin walls and usually 3 small valves.
plants.habitat: Found on well-drained sites with moderate fertility and high rainfall, usually in sheltered valleys in the south and Central Plateau but not on the west coast.
plants.notes: Fast growing. The tallest known flowering plant in the world. Bee attracting. An important source of timber marketed as ‘Tasmanian Oak’; also used extensively as a raw material for newsprint pulp. Also suitable for firewood. Will not coppice after damage by fire or after felling.

plants.name: Eucalyptus risdonii
plants.form: Small open widely-branched tree, or tall untidy shrub. Leaves: Juvenile – fused across the base, very glaucous, and always present on the tree. Adult – lanceolate, very glaucous but rare. Bark: Smooth, glaucous on small stems with circular leaf scars but streaked light/dark grey on larger trunks.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 5-15 small stalked cream flowers. Flowers irregularly, commonly in axils of juvenile leaves.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – cup-shaped, top level, 6-10mm long by 6-9mm wide with a white-ish bloom.
plants.habitat: Occurs on dry mudstone slopes, local at Risdon and Grass Tree Hill from sea level to 150m.
plants.notes: An ornamental small tree despite its usually informal or untidy appearance. Attractive silvery juvenile foliage is long persistent and is maintained by regular lopping as the tree matures.

plants.name: Eucalyptus rodwayi
plants.form: Tree with compact crown. Leaves: Juvenile – petiolate, narrow elliptical, dark green. Adult – narrow to lanceolate, glossy dark green. Bark: Rough, fibrous including branches.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 7 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – very small, approx. 4mm diameter, funnel-shaped with a slightly raised disc and 3 valves.
plants.habitat: Forms forests and woodlands around the margins of swampy flats with a typical understorey of tussock grassland. Most abundant on the lower parts of the Central Plateau. Grows in grassy frost hollows in woodlands and open forests.
plants.notes: Very adaptable and useful free for harsh conditions. Tolerates heavy frost and waterlogged soils for some time.

plants.name: Eucalyptus rubida subsp. rubida
plants.form: Tree with straight, largely bark-free trunk. Leaves: Juvenile – round with a red margin, heart-shaped base and very glaucous blue. Adult – lanceolate, dusty blue-green. Bark: Scaly at the base but smooth white, flaking to reveal blotched reds and pinks.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 3 flowers – white.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules with a slightly raised disc.
plants.habitat: Typically dominates grassy forest and woodland on poor mudstone soils in exposed situations and in the rain shadow of mountains.
plants.notes: Useful for providing medium to high level shelter (up to 30m) in mixed species windbreaks on moderately fertile hills. Bird attracting. The trees form branch hollows that provide excellent habitat for many birds and mammals. Rosellas are attracted to the capsules and seed. …

plants.name: Eucalyptus sieberi
plants.form: Tree. Leaves: Juvenile – ovate, blue-green to glaucous. Adult – sickle-shaped, leathery, grey-green and glossy with marked semi-longitudinal veins.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 5-15 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – pear-shaped with a level disc and 3 valves.
plants.habitat: Local in the north-east from sea level to about 600m. Usually found on steep slopes with gravelly soils. Often forms pure stands with almost totally absent understorey.
plants.notes: May be quite ornamental, with dark hard deeply furrowed bark on trunk; bark on branches smooth and chalky white; young twigs reddish. Not suitable for suburban gardens due to mature size. Bee attracting. Produces valuable hardwood.

plants.name: Eucalyptus subcrenulata
plants.form: Tall straight tree at lower altitudes; small and contorted in sub-alpine habitats. Leaves: Juvenile – round with a toothed margin, green and glossy, on a square stem. Adult – lanceolate to ovate, a toothed margin, dark green, glossy and leathery. …
plants.flowers: Umbels with 3 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – bell-shaped, ribbed, green to brown, with protruding valves.
plants.habitat: Extends from sub-alpine woodlands to lower alpine and sub-alpine wet sclerophyll forests, and in the west is often found as a tall tree over rainforest.
plants.notes: Tree form is very similar to Eucalyptus johnstonii. The smooth trunk is very ornamental especially when wet, almost glows with beautiful shades of yellow, bronze and greenish-orange. Bee attracting.

plants.name: Eucalyptus tasmaniensis
plants.form: Tree, often one or two of the branches stout and spreading then bent upwards. Leaves: Juvenile – asymmetrical, elliptical, blue-grey. Adult – asymmetrical, blue-green. Bark: Reddish-brown, fibrous at the base but smooth, cream/grey on the branches and upper trunk.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 7-15+ flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – top-shaped with a sunken disc and 4 valves.
plants.habitat: A major dominant of tall eucalypt forest on the more fertile mountain and plateaux soils.
plants.notes: An ornamental tree with contrasting smooth/stringy bark and grey pendulous leaves. The size of the tree renders it suitable only for large properties. Bee attracting. An important source of timber, marketed as ‘Tasmanian Oak’. Also good for firewood.

plants.name: Eucalyptus tenuiramis
plants.form: Trees sometimes with pendulous branches. Leaves: Juvenile – fused across the base (except on the Tasman Peninsula), very glaucous. Adult – lanceolate with a hooked tip and very glaucous. Bark: Smooth and steaked light and dark grey.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 7-23 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – top-shaped, glaucous or green with white speckling.
plants.habitat: Occurs mostly on mudstone, uncommon on sandstone, dolerite and granite. Abundant in the south and south-east from sea level to about 500m.
plants.notes: Some forms are very ornamental with a graceful open crown; thin branches pendulous to ground level almost like a weeping willow. The leaves are silvery. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Eucalyptus urnigera
plants.form: Tree. Leaves: Juvenile – are rounded with a heart-shaped base, a toothed margin, glaucous or green. Adult – lanceolate to ovate, green and glossy or slightly glaucous. Bark: Smooth and streaked grey; green and orange when new.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 3 flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – distinctly urn-shaped with a deeply sunken disc.
plants.habitat: Found in sub-alpine forests and woodlands on dolerite mountains.
plants.notes: Provides dense shade. An ornamental species, very colourful bark and quaintly shaped characteristic capsules.

plants.name: Eucalyptus vernicosa
plants.form: Small shrub of mallee habit. Leaves: Juvenile and adult leaves are very similar. Very small (2.5mm long), round to ovate with a small point on the apex, sessile to shortly petiolate, green, glossy and leathery. Bark: Smooth and streaked grey, green and orange when new.
plants.flowers: Sometimes solitary, or in umbels of 3.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – cup-shaped, green to brown, with a sunken disc.
plants.habitat: Restricted to the south-western part of the State. Almost exclusively a plant of mountains and ridges, often in peaty soils.
plants.notes: Makes an excellent rockery specimen shrub.

plants.name: Eucalyptus viminalis subsp. viminalis
plants.form: Tall tree. Leaves: Juvenile – lanceolate and dull green. Adult – lanceolate, green and glossy. Bark: Smooth, cream/white, streaked with grey.
plants.flowers: Umbels of 3 flowers, white. Does not always flower prolifically.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules with a raised disc with protruding valves
plants.habitat: Grows on moist, well-drained alluvial soils near watercourses, but also grows on drier sites at higher altitudes. Tolerates snow and some flooding. Drought tolerance depends on provenance.
plants.notes: Provides good high-level shelter (up to 50m) and shade in mixed species windbreaks. Good for second-line planting in coastal conditions. Useful in controlling underground seepage and stabilising landslip areas. Bird attracting. …

plants.name: Eucalyptus viminalis subsp. x hentyensis
plants.form: Large tree. Leaves: Variable depending on parent cross (E. viminalis, E. ovata). Bark: Variable between parent crosses (E. viminalis, E. ovata).
plants.flowers: Flowers are white.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules – but variable between parent crosses (E. viminalis, E. ovata).

plants.name: Eucalyptus willisii
plants.form: Tree or sometimes a mallee. Leaves: Juvenile – opposite, lanceolate 65-90mm long by 20-30mm wide. Adult – lanceolate 60-160mm long by 8-24mm wide, dull and slightly blue-green. Bark: Rough throughout the tree.
plants.flowers: Umbels 11-20 flowers – white.
plants.fruit: Woody capsules cup-shaped to hemispherical, 4-6mm long, 4-6mm wide, disc slightly raised.

plants.name: Euchiton involucratus
plants.form: Annual herb with stems 6-40cm long and slender tap root.
plants.flowers: About 4mm long, crowded into globular compound heads, very short stalks with long woolly hairs.
plants.habitat: Occasional but widespread.

plants.name: Euchiton japonicus
plants.form: Perennial herb with short rootstock with stolons arising from it. Stem, white/silvery.
plants.flowers: Several flowers, crowded in heads.
plants.habitat: Occasional in grassy vegetation on the eastern mountains, more common at lower altitudes.

plants.name: Euchiton traversii
plants.form: White rosette herb forming patches, with rosettes connected by stolons.
plants.flowers: Solitary, on short stalk (longer during fruiting), surrounded by long, narrow hairy leaves.
plants.habitat: On eastern and central mountains in open places in wet heath and alpine sedgeland. Local in alpine and sub-alpine grassland and on mountain plateaux.

plants.name: Euchiton umbricola
plants.form: Perennial rosette herb with stems 5-15cm; persistent root-stock from which numerous stolons arise.
plants.flowers: Spherical clusters with 1-3 narrow leaves at right angles to the stem below.
plants.habitat: Occasional on cliffs in eastern and central mountains. Sometimes local on mountain plateaux, usually in the shelter of boulders. Also found in sub-alpine grassland.

plants.name: Eucryphia lucida
plants.form: Tall shrub or tree with an open, spreading crown.
plants.flowers: Large, white, 4 petals, very numerous long stamens with purple anthers fading to grey.
plants.habitat: Confined to areas with high rainfall and low fire frequency in rainforests of the west, centre and south.
plants.notes: Bee attracting. This tree is the source of nectar for leatherwood honey. In cultivation prefers well-composted soil and plenty of shade.

plants.name: Eucryphia milliganii subsp. milliganii
plants.form: Dwarf to small, spreading shrub. Leaves oblong with sparse short, soft hair.
plants.flowers: Fragrant, white flowers, 2-3 cm across, solitary in upper axils.
plants.habitat: Occurs in western and south-western Tasmania, usually north of 43°S. Found in high rainfall alpine shrubbery and rainforest on mountain plateaux usually above 800 m.
plants.notes: Bee attracting.

plants.name: Eucryphia milliganii subsp. pubescens
plants.form: Dwarf to small, spreading shrub. Leaves oval, densely covered with short, soft hair.
plants.flowers: Flowers large, showy, perfumed, solitary in axils of upper leaves.
plants.habitat: Occurs in south-western Tasmania, usually south of 43°S. Found in high rainfall alpine shrubbery and rainforest over a wide range of altitudes.

plants.name: Euphrasia amphisysepala
plants.form: Short-lived perennial herb.
plants.flowers: At ends of branches, up to 15 flowers. Scented, with creamy white petals, sometimes with a pink-purple tinge, particularly on the back of the hood. The petals can have purple stripes extending from the flower throat.
plants.fruit: Capsule – seeds are small and whitish, and disperse when ripe.
plants.habitat: Restricted to coastal dolerite cliff faces on the Tasman Peninsula, in Tasman National Park.
plants.notes: Euphrasia are semi-parasitic, and although they can survive without their hosts, they do not thrive.

plants.name: Euphrasia collina subsp. collina
plants.form: Small perennial semi-parasitic herb with erect red flower stems.
plants.flowers: White to mauve with purple throat.
plants.habitat: Widespread in a variety of habitats: sandy/peaty heaths, rocky hillsides, alpine grasslands in the east.

plants.name: Euphrasia fragosa
plants.form: Short-lived perennial herb with up to 10 slender branches.
plants.flowers: Flowers terminal on branches, up to 10 pairs. Flowers have mauve petals, fading to white in the throat, with marked deep purple lines and a yellow spot below the anthers.
plants.habitat: Occurs in heathy, grassy or sedgy open woodland or on forest edges in the Southport area and on South Bruny Island.
plants.notes: Euphrasia are semi-parasitic, and although they can survive without their hosts, they do not thrive.

plants.name: Euphrasia gibbsiae subsp. gibbsiae
plants.form: Perennial herb with a single erect stem, branching above ground.
plants.flowers: White with prominent striations in terminal clusters. Hood of 2 fused petals; skirt of 3 fused petals.
plants.habitat: Mostly in Central Highlands and west and south.
plants.notes: Semi-parasitic.

photos.credit: Threatened Species Section DPIPWE – Natural Values Atlas
Threatened Species Section DPIPWE – Natural Values Atlas

plants.name: Euphrasia hookeri
plants.form: Erect herb
plants.flowers: In dense terminal spike; white with mauve markings, yellow in mouth and throat, red-purple on each lobe.
plants.fruit: Capsule – small whitish seed released when ripe.
plants.habitat: In bolster heath, heath and coniferous heath in wet places in the western and central mountains, generally occurring at altitudes of 700-1300 m.
plants.notes: This euphrasia is easily distinguished from other species by its deeply lobed leaves.

plants.name: Euphrasia phragmostoma
plants.form: Semi-parasitic perennial herb; many branches, new growth ascending from previous year’s procumbent growth.
plants.flowers: Up to about 15 densely arranged cream-white flowers per raceme.
plants.fruit: Capsule – small whitish seed released when ripe.
plants.habitat: Usually occurs on exposed high coastal cliffs or in low scrub in a few locations on the Tasman Peninsula.

plants.name: Euphrasia scabra
plants.form: Annual herb; stem erect, branches ascending.
plants.flowers: Up to 50 densely arranged yellow flowers per raceme; sometimes with 3 red-brown striations.
plants.fruit: Capsule – small whitish seed released when ripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread and occasionally frequent near coasts and on dry hillsides; from sea-level to about 1500m.

plants.name: Euphrasia semipicta
plants.form: Semi-parasitic perennial herb; few branches, ascending to erect.
plants.flowers: Up to 24 densely arranged flowers per raceme; white to mauve, with yellow patch on lower side of mouth; 3 red-purple to indigo striations except on upper lip which is unmarked.
plants.fruit: Capsule – small whitish seed released when ripe.
plants.habitat: Confined to isolated locations in south-east Tasmania where it occurs in coastal heath on sandstone or deep sand.

plants.name: Euphrasia striata
plants.form: Semi-parasitic herb with stems prostrate at first, then vertical.
plants.flowers: Up to 22 flowers on terminal spikes; white or lilac, with purple or crimson striations and yellow patches lower side and in throat.
plants.fruit: Capsule – small whitish seed released when ripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread in coniferous heath and heath. Frequent on mountain plateaux and summits and in alpine and sub-alpine grassland. Also at sea level in the south-west of the State.

plants.name: Eurychorda complanata
plants.form: Rhizome short, erect, much branched.
plants.flowers: Spikelets, blackish purple, pearl grey.
plants.habitat: All regions except King Island and kukanyi/Mt Wellington, coastal heaths, grass-sedgelands, margins of lagoons, alpine heath and scrub, sandy and peaty soils, near sea level to 1100m.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Euryomyrtus parviflora
plants.form: Prostrate shrub, much branched and spreading.
plants.flowers: Axillary, solitary with white petals sometimes tinged pink; 1.5 – 2.5mm diameter.
plants.habitat: Common in heaths and under light forest, in the east and north of the state; from sea level to about 250m elevation.

plants.name: Euryomyrtus ramosissima
plants.form: Small, slender, erect or prostrate shrub with long spreading branches.
plants.flowers: Numerous, white or pinkish or white blotched with pink, 10 stamens, variable in size 8-15mm.
plants.fruit: Capsule – small and cup-like turn from green to pale brown when ripe and open to release seed by 2-3 valves. Fruits are not persistent.
plants.habitat: Sandy heathlands and woodlands throughout the State. Also locally abundant on rocky river banks.

plants.name: Eutaxia microphylla
plants.form: Prostrate trailing shrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, solitary or paired in leaf axils, shortly stalked, yellow and red (sometimes all yellow).
plants.fruit: Seed pod – long-stalked and sometimes downy. Turns light brown when mature. Ripe seed is black.
plants.habitat: Local in the north-east and on Flinders Island.
plants.notes: Will tolerate full shade but prefers dappled. Will also tolerate a wide range of soils and is hardy to most frosts. Likes sandy loams or heavy clay loams which are subject to waterlogging but will withstand dry periods. Useful for soil erosion control of small areas.

plants.name: Ewartia catipes
plants.form: Perennial herb forming loose mats with many branches decumbent or ascending.
plants.flowers: Flower heads daisy-like, about 0.5cm across, white ray-florets, white to crimson/rusty brown centre.
plants.fruit: Achene with downy hairs and pappus bristles slightly thickened towards the tip. Sometimes free, sometimes joined and falling in small groups.
plants.habitat: Local in exposed places on mountains of the west and of the Central Plateau. Also found in the eastern mountains.
plants.notes: Has been grown in the ground or as a container plant with limited success. Needs plenty of sunshine and very well drained soils. If grown in shade plants can suffer dieback.

plants.name: Ewartia meredithiae
plants.form: Much-branched mat-forming plant with rosette of small leaves and adventitious roots.
plants.flowers: Heads white and papery, close to leaves early in season, stems lengthening as seeds ripen.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet exposed places in the central and western mountains, in bolster heath mixed with other cushion plants.
plants.notes: Not well known in cultivation. Does not like to dry out but must have excellent drainage and plenty of sunshine. From seed, plants may not grow true to their mountain form.

plants.name: Ewartia planchonii
plants.form: Creeping herb with leaves overlapping and white woolly hairs on both surfaces.
plants.flowers: Flower heads small, brownish, solitary, with stems longer than leaves during flowering.
plants.habitat: Occasional in high altitude heaths, most common in the central mountains.
plants.notes: Needs excellent drainage and abundant sunshine.

plants.name: Exocarpos cupressiformis
plants.form: Small pine-like tree; brown-ridged bark; dense fine yellow-green branches.
plants.flowers: Insignificant cream flowers; clustered on short stems towards ends of branches.
plants.fruit: Nut – ripe fruit base is fleshy, red and edible; nut sits on top. Green nut has thin outer shell (contains 1 seed).
plants.habitat: Common. Widespread in light forests. Often in dry rocky sites in eucalyptus woodlands in the east.
plants.notes: Parasite on roots of nearby plants; requires host species for successful growth. Tolerates shallow soils. High flammability. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Exocarpos humifusus
plants.form: Prostrate trailing shrub; yellow-green leaves reduced to triangular scales 0.5 mm long,
plants.flowers: Groups of 2-6 greenish-yellow flowers in axils of branches.
plants.fruit: Nut – seed is contained in hard nuts that become greenish black on maturity.
plants.habitat: Widespread in all types of alpine heath.
plants.notes: The plant uses stems for photosynthesis. It is parasitic on the roots of other plants, hence requires a host plant for successful growth.

plants.name: Exocarpos nanus
plants.form: Prostrate dwarf shrub with many spreading branches; leaves reduced to minute triangular scales.
plants.flowers: Minute yellow-green flowers, sometimes with red, in axillary clusters of 2-4 together.
plants.fruit: Nut – seed is contained in hard nuts that become green to red-brown on maturity, attached to a succulent bright red elongated stalk to about 0.5 cm long; often profuse.
plants.habitat: Occasional in tussock grassland and grassy heaths. In wet places on the mountains of the north and north-east.
plants.notes: Some growers recommend seedlings be planted out where Casuarinaceae, Fabaceae, Myrtaceae or Proteaceae family are growing.

plants.name: Exocarpos strictus
plants.form: Large, upright or spreading shrub with many vertical branches; leaves reduced to minute scales.
plants.flowers: Flowers small or minute, in small axillary clusters of 2-4 together.
plants.fruit: Nut – seed is contained in hard nuts that become green to purplish-black on maturity, attached to a succulent whitish to pale-purplish stalk.
plants.habitat: Found on a wide variety of climatic and soil conditions, including in wet forests, on the coast, sub-alpine and inland regions. Also is widespread but occasional in dry heath.
plants.notes: Some growers recommend seedlings be planted out where Casuarinaceae, Fabaceae, Myrtaceae or Proteaceae family are growing.

plants.name: Exocarpos syrticola
plants.form: Erect or spreading small shrub.
plants.flowers: Flowers small or minute, in small axillary clusters of 2-4 together.
plants.fruit: Nut – seed is contained in hard nuts that become green to purplish-black on maturity, attached to a succulent pink stalk.
plants.habitat: Occasional on coasts in the north and south-west and on the islands of Bass Strait.

plants.name: Festuca plebeia
plants.form: Very variable, tufted grass. In dry, open habitats, the leaves are grey-green and rarely longer than 10cm; in damper and shaded sites, the leaves are soft, bright green and up to 20cm long. Stems are smooth and round in cross-section.
plants.flowers: Flower heads up to 20cm long with greenish or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Rocky areas under light eucalypt cover, 800-1200m above sea level, in the Central Highlands, Midlands, Ben Lomond, east coast, south-west and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

photos.credit: Queensland Herbarium Sharp 43 and Simon by D. Sharp CC BY
Queensland Herbarium Sharp 103 and Simon by D. Sharp CC BY

plants.name: Ficinia nodosa
plants.form: Tufted sedge with dense erect green stems, cylindrical in cross-section.
plants.flowers: Reddish-brown, globular flower-head formed just below stem apex.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, oval, shiny dark brown to black; contained in bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: Common on sandy coasts, or near permanent water.
plants.notes: Very hardy, useful near ponds (frog habitat), and for binding sandy soil in coastal environments. Tolerant of salt spray. Needs little attention once established. Prefers full sun.

plants.name: Forstera bellidifolia
plants.form: Dainty, perennial rosette herb.
plants.flowers: White, usually single, at the end of a thin, erect stalk 6-12 cm tall.
plants.fruit: Capsule – ovoid, 5–6 mm long, unilocular, but with a partial septum at the base.
plants.habitat: In deciduous, coniferous, and bolster heath and alpine sedgeland in western and some central mountains.
plants.notes: Moist, very well-drained acidic soil is required; plants should not be allowed to dry out. Addition of organic matter, such as peat moss, to the soil should be beneficial in helping to retain moisture. …

plants.name: Frankenia pauciflora var. gunnii
plants.form: Small much-branched undershrub, prostrate or ascending, almost hairless.
plants.flowers: Terminal leafy clusters, without stalks, in forks of branches 5-6 petals, pink or white.
plants.fruit: Capsule – opening by valves. One brown seed per capsule with a pappus-like attachment to 2mm.
plants.habitat: In salt ground on the north coast and islands of Bass Strait.

plants.name: Gahnia filum
plants.form: Densely tufted sedge with long, in rolled leaves with fine wavy tips.
plants.flowers: Many clustered flowers in a dense, bristly flower head up to 60cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – triangular and rusty-brown when mature, 5-6mm long.
plants.habitat: In saline or brackish habitats; coastal creek and river edges, saltmarshes and flats near sea level, and up to 200m altitude inland where saline.
plants.notes: Requires moist, sandy soil in a sunny position. This species is common in the wetland flats at Lauderdale and Pittwater in the south-east, and helps provide habitat for migratory birds. …

plants.name: Gahnia grandis
plants.form: Very large tussocky sedge.
plants.flowers: Heads bright brown when young, blackish in fruit.
plants.fruit: Nut – bright red, hanging from the heads by long black filaments.
plants.habitat: Common in wet or poorly drained situations, sea level to mountains. Margins of forest and marsh, road cuttings and ditches, buttongrass heaths. All regions except Midlands and north-east.
plants.notes: Bee attracting. Bird attracting. Relies on birds, including the currawong, to germinate its seed. Provides good frog habitat and bandicoot habitat. High flammability. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Used in traditional Palawa basket weaving.

plants.name: Gahnia microstachya
plants.form: Densely tufted perennial sedge with persistent old leaf-sheaths.
plants.flowers: Many clustered flowers in a dense, bristly flower head 15-50cm long.
plants.habitat: On the east coast, in open woodland, often between granite boulders or on granitic sands, to 450m altitude.

plants.name: Gahnia radula
plants.form: Loosely tufted sedge with hollow stems, round in cross-section.
plants.flowers: Many clustered flowers in a dense, bristly, black flower head up to 60cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – white to brown, egg-shaped, 2mm long.
plants.habitat: In coastal areas, including sandy heaths, coastal scrub and woodland, and the edges of swamps.
plants.notes: Attracts butterflies, including the Endangered Chaostola skipper (Antipodia chaostola leucophaea), the flame skipper (Hesperilla idothea) and Donnysa skipper (Hesperilla donnysa), which lay their eggs on the leaves and feed on the pollen. …

plants.name: Gahnia rodwayi
plants.form: The smallest saw-sedge; a perennial plant with grass-like, flat, smooth leaves. The stem is always shorter than the leaves.
plants.flowers: Many clustered flowers in a dense, bristly flower head 4-13cm long.
plants.habitat: On the east coast, in open dry sclerophyll woodland in heathy/grassy-sedgy understoreys, and near the coast.

plants.name: Gahnia sieberiana
plants.form: Perennial sedge with hollow stems, triangular in cross-section.
plants.flowers: Many clustered flowers in a dense, bristly honey-brown flower head which blackens with age, 25-90cm long.
plants.habitat: In damp places, including the edges of swamps, wet heaths, roadside ditches and coastal areas in the north-west, Midlands and north-east.

plants.name: Gahnia trifida
plants.form: Densely clustered sedge with persistent remains of old leaf sheaths at the base.
plants.flowers: Many clustered flowers in a dense, bristly flower head up to 85cm long.
plants.habitat: Coastal; on margins of marshes and mudflats, on cliffs and among boulders.
plants.notes: A host plant of the Chrysotricha skipper butterfly (Hesperilla chrysotricha), also known as the golden haired sedge-skipper. The butterflies twist the leaves together in a spiral to form a shelter.

plants.name: Gaimardia amblyphylla
plants.form: Loosely tufted perennial herb with slightly rounded or square leaf tips, forming small fan-shaped groups from the base of the plant.
plants.flowers: Flowers in spikes on the end of the flowering stems, which are slightly longer than the leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule – golden yellow with dark tips, 0.8mm long, egg-shaped; dehiscent.
plants.habitat: In sandy marshy areas in the south-west, often in buttongrass heathland.
plants.notes: Requires alpine boggy conditions.

plants.name: Gaimardia fitzgeraldii
plants.form: Perennial, much-branched herb with erect, slender stems and leaves with needle like tips and densely woolly bases, forming soft cushions 10-60cm in diameter.
plants.flowers: On flowering stems which are longer than the leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule – seeds bright brown with a dark rounded base and pointed tip, 1mm long.
plants.habitat: Wet sub-alpine swamps on the west coast and Mt. Field.
plants.notes: Requires alpine boggy conditions.

plants.name: Gaimardia setacea
plants.form: Much-branched, densely tufted perennial herb with erect, slender stems and stiff leaves with needle-like tips, forming a compact cushion.
plants.flowers: Flowers on stems longer than the leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule – seeds pale yellow with a dark upper end, pointed either end.
plants.habitat: Sub-alpine bogs on the west coast and Mt. Field.
plants.notes: Requires alpine boggy conditions.

plants.name: Galium australe
plants.form: Slender perennial herb with straggling stems 20-60cm long which sometimes root at the base.
plants.flowers: Very small in 1-5 flowered clusters along length of stem and also sometimes on lateral shoots.
plants.fruit: 2 lobed mericarp – densely covered with stiff hooked hairs.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in a variety of habitat, dry pastures and hillsides, coastal dunes and heaths, and occasionally epiphytic on trunks of tree ferns in fern gullies.

plants.name: Galium ciliare subsp. ciliare
plants.form: Small perennial herb with slender rhizome. Stems quadrangular, sparingly branched.
plants.flowers: Very small, with yellow petals in 3-flowered clusters in axils of two opposite leaves of whorl.
plants.fruit: 2 lobed mericarp – dry, about 2-5mm broad, smooth or sometimes with scattered bumps.
plants.habitat: Frequent in dry pastures, particularly in the midlands and north of the state. Generally found growing in basaltic soils.
plants.notes: Will withstand slightly exposed situations but prefers a semi-shaded position.

plants.name: Galium gaudichaudii subsp. parviflorum
plants.form: Slender perennial herb with overground parts downy (almost glabrous).
plants.flowers: Petals white, very small, 1-2 in axils of leaves, or terminal or in 3-flowered clusters along stem.
plants.fruit: 2 lobed mericarp – dry, about 2-5mm broad, smooth or sometimes with scattered bumps.
plants.habitat: Occasional but widespread in open sclerophyll forests and dry places. Grows in a wide range of soil types including those derived from slate, shale, limestone and sandstone.
plants.notes: Often treated as a weed. Will grow in many situations but prefers dappled shade or partial sun.

plants.name: Gastrodia procera
plants.form: Robust, tall leafless orchid with a brown scape.
plants.flowers: 5-70 tubular, horizontal to semi-nodding flowers, to 25mm long, on a crowded raceme. Flowers cinnamon-brown and warty on exterior, crystalline white within. Labellum whitish-yellow with orange margins. Flowers only lightly scented.
plants.habitat: Tall, shrubby or grassy open eucalypt forest, often in clearings and on disturbed road margins, in well-drained loams and clays rich in humus, often in deep accumulated litter. Widespread but localised and common, favouring higher rainfall areas up to 600m.
plants.notes: Fires do not occur frequently in the habitats of this species, but flowering is enhanced by summer fires.

plants.name: Gastrodia sesamoides
plants.form: Slender leafless orchid with a brown scape.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence apex strongly hooked in bud. Relatively few (3-25) pendant-like uncrowded flowers to 20mm long. Flowers greyish-white externally, crystalline white internally. Labellum whitish with orange margins. Flowers with a strong cinnamon-like fragrance. Self-pollinating.
plants.habitat: Tall open eucalypt forest, heathy open forest and shrubby woodland, teatree scrub and heathland on moderately to well-drained sandy and clay soils. …
plants.notes: Favours fire prone habitats and flowering is strongly promoted by summer fires.

plants.name: Gaultheria depressa
plants.form: Low, spreading shrub, branchlets with long bristles, obvious reddish bristles tipping the teeth of the leaf margins.
plants.flowers: Solitary, in the axils of the uppermost leaves. Flower tube about 2.5mm long, with short lobes.
plants.fruit: Capsule surrounded by a fleshy calyx, red or sometimes white.
plants.habitat: Amongst rocks on mountain plateaux.

plants.name: Gaultheria hispida
plants.form: Erect and spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: White urn-shaped clusters at the ends of the branches.
plants.fruit: Capsule surrounded by a fleshy calyx, white or sometimes pinkish. Capsule contains fine seed.
plants.habitat: Grows in a wide range of situations, sea level in west to alpine and sub-alpine.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Gaultheria lanceolata
plants.form: Small shrub with erect stems, bristly branchlets and lance-shaped, leathery leaves with serrated margins, 12-22mm long. The young leaves are covered with tiny, soft hairs; the older leaves are hairless and shiny.
plants.flowers: Solitary, in the axils of the upper leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule surrounded by a fleshy calyx, red, about 8mm wide.
plants.habitat: Mountains of the Central Plateau and the west of the State.

plants.name: Gaultheria tasmanica
plants.form: Small prostrate shrub, 15-30cm diameter, forming dense mats with wiry stems and yellow-green leaves which are narrow, shiny and hairless.
plants.flowers: White, almost round, with five joined, pointed petals.
plants.fruit: Capsule surrounded by a fleshy calyx, red or yellowish-white, 1cm across. Capsule contains seed.
plants.habitat: Mostly limited to mountains in the north.

plants.name: Gentianella brevisepala
plants.form: Small, erect herb with a rosette of oval to lance-shaped leaves.
plants.flowers: Small, 1-1.5mm in diameter. The flowers are 5-petalled with thin blue or purple lines on the inside of the petals, and borne on stems arising from the centre of the foliage.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, in alpine herbfield or sub-alpine heath on the Central Plateau. Also occurs in buttongrass moorland in the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated, but would be suitable for growing in containers, particularly in moist but well-drained soils, with high organic matter.

plants.name: Gentianella demissa
plants.form: One of the smallest snow gentians, a herb with a rosette of oval to lance-shaped leaves; stem leaves are small and less than 1cm long.
plants.flowers: The flowers are 5-petalled with thin blue or purple lines on the inside of the petals, and borne on stems arising from the centre of the foliage. Flowering stems are less than 5cm tall.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, in alpine and sub-alpine areas in the south of the State, including treeless vegetation in the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated, but would be suitable for growing in containers, particularly in moist but well-drained soils, with high organic matter.

plants.name: Gentianella diemensis subsp. diemensis
plants.form: Small herb with a rosette of oval to lance-shaped leaves with wide stalks. Stems are often purple-green to nearly black.
plants.flowers: Small. The flowers are white, 5-petalled and cup-shaped, with thin blue or purple lines on the inside of the petals, and borne on stems arising from the centre of the foliage.
plants.habitat: Found widely in Tasmanian alpine to sub-alpine areas, including grasslands, and also on hills at lower altitudes.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated, but would be suitable for growing in containers, particularly in moist but well-drained soils, with high organic matter.

plants.name: Gentianella diemensis subsp. plantaginea
plants.form: Small herb with a rosette of oval to lance-shaped leaves with wide stalks. Stems are often purple-green to nearly black.
plants.flowers: Small. The flowers are white, 5-petalled and cup-shaped, with thin blue or purple lines on the inside of the petals, and borne on stems arising from the centre of the foliage.
plants.habitat: Found in Tasmanian alpine to sub-alpine areas, including grasslands, and also on hills at lower altitudes.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated, but would be suitable for growing in containers, particularly in moist but well-drained soils, with high organic matter.

plants.name: Gentianella eichleri
plants.form: Small herb with a rosette of oval to lance-shaped leaves.
plants.flowers: Small. The flowers are white and 5-petalled, with thin blue or purple lines on the inside of the petals, and borne on stems arising from the centre of the foliage.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, in short alpine herbfield or alpine/sub-alpine heath on the Central Plateau, and treeless vegetation in the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated, but would be suitable for growing in containers, particularly in moist but well-drained soils, with high organic matter.

plants.name: Gentianella gunniana
plants.form: Small, erect herb with a rosette of oval to lance-shaped leaves.
plants.flowers: Small. The flowers are white and 5-petalled, with thin blue or purple lines on the inside of the petals, and borne on stems arising from the centre of the foliage. Dies after flowering.
plants.habitat: It is found on well drained soils widely in grassland and open forests in eastern Tasmania.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated, but would be suitable for growing in containers, particularly in moist but well-drained soils, with high organic matter.

plants.name: Gentianella pleurogynoides subsp. milliganii
plants.form: Small herb with a rosette of oval to lance-shaped leaves. The basal leaves are 10-40mm long, and the stem leaves are 12-25mm long.
plants.flowers: Small. The flowers are white and 5-petalled, with thin blue or purple lines on the inside of the petals, and borne on stems arising from the centre of the foliage.
plants.habitat: Sub-alpine to alpine areas of eastern Tasmania.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated, but would be suitable for growing in containers, particularly in moist but well-drained soils, with high organic matter.

plants.name: Gentianella pleurogynoides subsp. pleurogynoides
plants.form: Small herb with a rosette of oval to lance-shaped leaves. The basal leaves are 10-40mm long, and the stem leaves are 12-25mm long.
plants.flowers: Small. The flowers are white and 5-petalled, with thin blue or purple lines on the inside of the petals, and borne on stems arising from the centre of the foliage.
plants.habitat: Sub-alpine to alpine areas of eastern Tasmania, including alpine/subalpine treeless vegetation in the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated, but would be suitable for growing in containers, particularly in moist but well-drained soils, with high organic matter.

plants.name: Gentianella polysperes
plants.form: Small, erect herb with a rosette of oval to lance-shaped leaves.
plants.flowers: Small. The flowers are white and 5-petalled, with thin blue or purple lines on the inside of the petals, and borne on stems arising from the centre of the foliage. Dies after flowering.
plants.habitat: Open forests, and sometimes grasslands, in high altitude areas.
plants.notes: Not often cultivated, but would be suitable for growing in containers, particularly in moist but well-drained soils, with high organic matter.

plants.name: Geococcus pusillus
plants.form: Small annual herb, usually stemless. Leaves 3-8cm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers on very short radical stalks, petals white, oval, shorter than sepals.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oblong 5-12 mm long with horny valves and prominent midrib. Seeds 3-5, brown.
plants.habitat: Recorded from coastal areas on Mile and Mt. Chappell islands in the Furneaux Group, Bass Strait.

plants.name: Geranium brevicaule
plants.form: Perennial herb with stout rootstock, leaves arranged in a basal rosette.
plants.flowers: Solitary red flowers on densely hairy flower stalks.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – long, slender; containing 4-5 dark brown or black seeds.
plants.habitat: Occasional in mountain grasslands and herbfields.
plants.notes: The roots of cranesbill plants are high in tannins; in Victoria, these were traditionally used to treat diarrhoea.

plants.name: Geranium potentilloides var. potentilloides
plants.form: Perennial herb with short, thick stem bearing a rosette of leaves. Leafy stems have short, silky hairs and lobed leaves. Spreading to 1m.
plants.flowers: Small, single flowers with creamy-pink petals.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – long, slender; containing 4-5 dark brown or black seeds.
plants.habitat: Mountains above 900m altitude.
plants.notes: The roots of cranesbill plants are high in tannins; in Victoria, these were traditionally used to treat diarrhoea.

plants.name: Geranium retrorsum
plants.form: Perennial herb with flowering stems spreading to about 50 cm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers solitary or paired, petals bright pink to purplish.
plants.habitat: Uncommon – occurring in widely separated low-land areas in the south-east, north-east and Midlands localities.

plants.name: Geranium solanderi
plants.form: Perennial herb with a swollen taproot, and hairs on the branches and stems. Flowering stems spreading to 30–60 cm long.
plants.flowers: Single or paired, with pale pink petals.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – long, slender; containing 4-5 dark brown or black seeds.
plants.habitat: Common in open country, especially in low woodlands.
plants.notes: The roots of cranesbill plants are high in tannins; in Victoria, these were traditionally used to treat diarrhoea.

plants.name: Geum talbotianum
plants.form: Perennial rosette herb with thick rootstock and broad, dark, kidney-shaped leaves which are covered on both sides with stiff short hairs.
plants.flowers: Single large white flowers (5 cm diameter) with yellow centres on end of stalk, up to 60 cm high.
plants.habitat: Confined to southern-most mountains, in shaded rocky places at high altitude and on wet slopes.
plants.notes: Difficult to grow. Requires high altitude, well drained but moist conditions. This plant is not successful in open gardens, however it may be grown in containers.

plants.name: Gleichenia abscida
plants.form: Fern with slender rootstock, fronds 30-60cm long, scattered, pinnae to 4cm long, pinnules bright green, dull beneath, margins revolute.
plants.habitat: Uncommon and restricted to high rainfall as in the south and south-west of the State. Typically a plant of semi-sheltered situations under sub-alpine scrub.
plants.notes: Experience in cultivation is limited and plants have proved sensitive to disturbance and difficult to maintain.

plants.name: Gleichenia alpina
plants.form: Fern forming extensive colonies, with numerous, intertwined fronds, 20-50cm long, branched 1-3 times.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread on exposed alpine plateaux and bogs.
plants.notes: Plants are tricky to grow and resent disturbance.

plants.name: Gleichenia dicarpa
plants.form: Fern forming tangled colonies; fronds 100-400cm long, erect, wiry, branching many times. Pinnules with strongly revolute margins.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in badly drained, permanently wet soils of heathland, buttongrass plains and edges of watercourses. Has a high light requirement.
plants.notes: Sunny situations are favoured.

plants.name: Gleichenia microphylla
plants.form: Fern forming tangled colonies; fronds,100-300cm long, wiry, branching many times, dark green to yellowish; pinnules triangular, flat.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in permanently wet soils of heathland, edges of watercourses and dry sclerophyll forest. This species and Gleichenia dicarpa frequently grow together. Tolerates salt laden winds in coastal situations.
plants.notes: Sunny situations are favoured.

plants.name: Glossodia major
plants.form: Wax lip with a single, long, oblong to elliptical, dark-green leaf, hairy on both surfaces.
plants.flowers: 1-2 mauve to purple flowers (occasionally white); labellum white at the base and purple-tipped with yellow basal calli.
plants.habitat: Heathy and grassy open eucalypt forest, woodland, shrubland and heathland, usually on well-drained sandy soils and gravelly loams. Widely distributed and often abundant in the east and north-east, including Bass Strait Islands, including lowland areas up to 400m.
plants.notes: Found in habitats where fires occur very frequently. Flowering increases significantly after fires and flowers tend to be larger. The flowers increase noticeably in size during the first few days after opening. There are localised populations with a high percentage of white flowers.

plants.name: Glossostigma elatinoides
plants.form: A small aquatic herb, much-branched, prostrate, ascending at the tips, forming dense patches 5-10cm diameter.
plants.flowers: Flowers solitary, in axils; corolla white, stamens 4, shorter than corolla, stigma large, bearded.
plants.habitat: On the banks of streams in the north of the State, may be more or less submerged in shallow water.
plants.notes: Aquatic plant.

plants.name: Glyceria australis
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial grass with flat or folded leaves, up to 20cm long and 4mm wide, which taper gradually to the tip. Stems are rather weak, erect and smooth.
plants.flowers: Flower heads are erect or nodding, bearing few spikelets.
plants.habitat: Widespread in freshwater lagoons, drains, low-lying areas and along creeks and rivers, from sea level to 750m altitude. North-west, east coast, Midlands and Central Highlands.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Plants provide important habitat.

plants.name: Glycine clandestina
plants.form: Small, slender, open climber. Perennial herb with woody rootstock.
plants.flowers: Pale lavender to purple small pea flowers, 8-20 in clusters on short stems.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – downy, straight, 15-25mm long. Turns almost black when mature. Ripe seed is red- brown.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in heaths near the east and north coasts and on the Central Plateau up to an altitude of about 900m.
plants.notes: Natural regeneration is from seed and suckers, particularly following fire. Useful addition to mixed-species windbreaks to add diversity and interest and attract wildlife. Bee attracting: the flowers provide a food source (nectar and pollen) for native insects, including bees and wasps. …

plants.name: Glycine latrobeana
plants.form: Perennial herb with woody rootstock and short stems.
plants.flowers: 8-20 pea flowers in clusters usually crowded near ends of stalks. Similar to Glycine clandestina.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – downy, straight, 15-25mm long. Turns almost black when mature. Ripe seed is red -brown.
plants.habitat: Rare in pastures in the north-west of the State.
plants.notes: Requires semi-shaded site with well-drained soil. Once established can withstand extended dry periods. Plants generally prefer some root protection.

plants.name: Glycine microphylla
plants.form: Small, perennial herb with twining prostrate stems which are cloaked in short, backward-curving brown hairs.
plants.flowers: White, pink or purplish pea flowers, to 6mm long, borne on long stalks from the leaf axils, in clusters of 8-20.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – short with hairs, 15-25mm long. Pods become almost black and seeds turn red-brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Dry sclerophyll forest and woodland in the north-east.
plants.notes: Appears very similar to Glycine clandestina and Glycine latrobeana; differs in leaf shape and stipule shape.

plants.name: Gnaphalium indutum subsp. indutum
plants.form: Slender herb, white with stems 2- 6cm and with dense cottony hairs. Often much-branched at base.
plants.flowers: Flower heads numerous in terminal clusters with yellowish bracts. Clusters loose or dense.
plants.fruit: Achene with pappus bristles free, falling separately.
plants.habitat: Local on coastal cliffs and sandy places in the east, north-east and north-west of the State.

plants.name: Gompholobium ecostatum
plants.form: Small erect or trailing shrub, branches with short spreading hairs.
plants.flowers: Pea flower, all petals with inner surfaces apricot to red, outer surfaces almost black.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – elliptical, about 8mm long, without hairs. Seeds numerous.
plants.habitat: Recorded only from Flinders Island. Wet, sandy heathland.

plants.name: Gompholobium huegelii
plants.form: A slender pea with woody base and spreading or ascending branches.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, solitary or two together, usually creamy yellow, shaded black on the outside.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – fat oval, containing numerous small seeds which are dropped on maturity.
plants.habitat: This form is common in sandy heathland and light forest but a form with bright yellow flowers and blue-green leaves also occurs in sandy heaths and in gravel ironstone soils. Tolerates most frosts and extended dry periods.
plants.notes: Useful for recharge control plantings in conjunction with trees in hilly areas. Often short lived in cultivation. Seems to require very good drainage and protection from other plants.

plants.name: Gonocarpus humilis
plants.form: Similar to G. teucrioides in appearance, but has small bracts beneath the flowers.
plants.flowers: Solitary, on short, thread-like stalks.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, smooth, and often brown, silvery-grey or reddish when mature. Only 1 seed usually matures.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in moist, shady places.

plants.name: Gonocarpus micranthus subsp. micranthus
plants.form: Prostrate creeping perennial herb, with opposite, serrated leaves.
plants.flowers: Reddish flowers, very tiny.
plants.fruit: Nut – 8 edged, very small, grey to reddish.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in damp places at all altitudes, from sandy heaths at sea level to sub-alpine moors.
plants.notes: Requires damp soil; tolerates shade. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Gonocarpus montanus
plants.form: Small prostrate perennial herb with tough, slender stems and opposite leaves, 4-12mm long. Young stems are rectangular.
plants.flowers: Red small inconspicuous in terminal spikes.
plants.fruit: Nut – silvery with 8 ribs. Only 1 seed usually matures.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in alpine areas.
plants.notes: Requires well drained moist soil and some sun.

plants.name: Gonocarpus serpyllifolius
plants.form: Small perennial herb with wiry, rough, short-haired stems and opposite leaves, 4-12mm long.
plants.flowers: Solitary
plants.fruit: Nut – small, smooth, and dark reddish brown with a metallic sheen when mature. Only 1 seed usually matures.
plants.habitat: Alpine regions, especially on the Central Plateau.

plants.name: Gonocarpus tetragynus
plants.form: Perennial, much-branched, more or less rough-feeling herb with stems 15-50cm long, and toothed, lance-shaped leaves.
plants.flowers: Green to red, solitary in the leaf axils; 1-3mm across.
plants.fruit: Nut – 1.5mm long and grey, with scattered short hairs. Only 1 seed usually matures.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in dry, stony places.
plants.notes: Not widely grown.

plants.name: Gonocarpus teucrioides
plants.form: Perennial herb, rough to touch, with short, spreading hairs. Stems are erect or sometimes prostrate; leaves are opposite and serrated, 8-15mm long.
plants.flowers: Pink/red, solitary, on short, thread-like stalks.
plants.fruit: Nut – 1.5mm long, grey, with 4 prominent ribs. Only 1 seed usually matures.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant, especially in wet, shaded places.
plants.notes: Not widely grown.

plants.name: Goodenia elongata
plants.form: Dwarf perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Solitary yellow flowers, to 2.5 cm across, on slender axillary stalks.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent in marshy places.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Goodenia geniculata
plants.form: Dwarf perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Solitary yellow flowers, 2.5 cm across on bent stalks.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – opens by two bifid valves, obovoid, about 10 mm long. Seeds are yellow-brown, about 3.5 mm long, flat, elliptic and pointed, with a vestigial wing.
plants.habitat: Rocky Cape and probably local elsewhere in the north-west of Tas.
plants.notes: Can form large colonies by suckering.

plants.name: Goodenia humilis
plants.form: Dwarf, tufting perennial herb which suckers from a slender branched rhizome.
plants.flowers: Flowers of 1.5 cm across are yellow, sometimes solitary, and profuse.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – 3–4 mm long, ovoid. Seeds yellow-brown, pitted, wing vestigial.
plants.habitat: Sandy flats near the coast in the north and on the Central Plateau at altitudes of about 800m.

plants.name: Goodenia lanata
plants.form: Spreading, carpet forming perennial herb with a slender tap-root.
plants.flowers: Yellow irregular flowers, 2 cm across, with 5 winged petals.
plants.fruit: Paper capsule – 6-7 mm long, ovoid-cylindric. Seeds yellowish, surface rough, wing vestigial.
plants.habitat: Common in dry heathlands and woodlands. Abundant in dry pastures and on open hillsides. Colonises open ground after fire or disturbance.

plants.name: Goodenia montana
plants.form: Perennial herb with stout rootstock and many leaves in a rosette at the base.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – turn from green to tan and become brittle when mature. Each fruit contains several disc-shaped seeds.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent, sometimes forming large patches, in wet ground on the Central Plateau.

plants.name: Goodenia ovata
plants.form: Erect or spreading shrub or undershrub.
plants.flowers: Yellow
plants.fruit: Paper capsule – usually opens by 2 valves. Seeds flat, with a border or wing.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant on roadsides and in open forests. Also often found on wetter sites.
plants.notes: Very useful for permanently wet soils.

plants.name: Goodenia paradoxa
plants.form: Perennial herb with rosette of softly woolly leaves to 20 cm long.
plants.flowers: Yellow; the corolla is 15-30 mm long, pale yellow and winged with a conspicuous spur at the base of the tube.
plants.fruit: Capsule – compressed; containing several flat seeds 3-5 mm in diameter, with winged margins.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent, mainly in dry pastures.

plants.name: Goodenia radicans
plants.form: Small herb with yellowish stem running along or sometimes under the ground.
plants.flowers: Solitary, fan-shaped with 5 petals almost white on inside, dull red or purplish-grey outside.
plants.fruit: Capsule – about 6mm long, succulent. Seeds flattened, brown with a thick irregular white border.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant on the landward margins of saltmarshes, also inland on margins of streams and lakes and on ground subject to flooding.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Goodia lotifolia
plants.form: Small to medium open shrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, bright yellow with red-brown throat.

plants.name: Gratiola nana
plants.form: Perennial herb with stems creeping, branches intertangled; procumbent or tips ascending.
plants.flowers: Flowers pale pink, veins sometimes deeper in colour; solitary, axillary on short stems.
plants.fruit: Capsule – seeds are numerous, small, reticulate.
plants.habitat: Local in swampy ground, from sea level to mountain plateaux.

plants.name: Gratiola peruviana
plants.form: Creeping perennial herb; stems somewhat fleshy, rooting at lower nodes, then erect or ascending.
plants.flowers: Solitary tubular flowers, pale pink, 1 cm long.
plants.fruit: Capsule – seeds are numerous, small, reticulate.
plants.habitat: Local on river flats, in marshes and wet ditches.
plants.notes: A hardy plant for wet places or shallow water. Prefers some shade. Also grows well in indoor terrarium.

plants.name: Gratiola pubescens
plants.form: Erect to procumbent perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Single in the leaf axils on stalks 1 to 2.5 mm long; corolla is white or pinkish-purple and the tube yellow.
plants.habitat: Most commonly in permanently or seasonally damp to swampy ground and wetland margins.

plants.name: Grevillea australis
plants.form: Very variable shrub. Branches erect, spreading or procumbent, often prostrate.
plants.flowers: White, in small heads in leaf axils and at the end of short shoots.
plants.habitat: Widespread but occasional in alpine shrubberies, shrubby sub-alpine heaths, open forests and riparian scrub; mostly on soils derived from sandstones or dolerite, from sea-level to about 1000m.
plants.notes: Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability. Flowering and seeding times according to specimens examined at the Tasmanian Herbarium by Alan Gray.

plants.name: Gunnera cordifolia
plants.form: Fleshy, stoloniferous herb which often forms large patches that consist of rosettes.
plants.flowers: Small, unisexual, crowded on spikes, usually on separate leafless stalks.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant near streams and in swampy places. Most common in alpine and sub-alpine zone, Rare at low altitudes in wet grassy places in the central and eastern mountains.
plants.notes: Suited to cultivation in containers or a bog garden. Requires constant moisture, an acidic friable soil and full sun. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Gymnoschoenus sphaerocephalus
plants.form: Densely tufted perennial sedge forming large tussocks. Stems are round in cross-section.
plants.flowers: Dense, spherical flower head on the end of the flowering stems. Flowers are yellow-brown.
plants.fruit: Nut – shiny, pale red-brown, slightly wrinkled, 2.5 mm long.
plants.habitat: Sedgelands, heaths and on low nutrient soils, such as peat on quartzite gravel, with high rainfall. Sea level to 900m.
plants.notes: Fire tolerant. Frog habitat. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Flower stalks are used by contemporary basket weavers.

plants.name: Gynatrix pulchella
plants.form: Medium to tall tree-like shrub. Separate male and female plants.
plants.flowers: The small white flowers are highly perfumed, on axillary stalks.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – tan brown at maturity. The seed firms and turns red-brown at maturity.
plants.habitat: Common in the north of Tasmania.
plants.notes: These plants naturalize readily in disturbed areas, however they may be short-lived in cultivation. In the 19th century, the bark was regarded as producing a good quality yarn.

plants.name: Gyrostemon thesioides
plants.form: Undershrub with a hard, woody stem and many erect branches. Short-lived (less than 10 years).
plants.flowers: Very small, solitary in the upper leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 2mm long and 4mm wide, deeply ribbed, and occur only on female plants. Seeds are kidney-shaped and reddish-brown with a white aril, 2mm long.
plants.habitat: Allocasuarina forest in the north and east, and on Bass Strait islands. Sites include Cataract Gorge, Douglas-Apsley National Park, Sleepy Bay and Orford.

plants.name: Hackelia latifolia
plants.form: Perennial herb with branched, straggling stems 100cm long or more, and egg-shaped leaves.
plants.flowers: Small, solitary, with rounded petals, on thread-like stalks.
plants.fruit: 4 nutlets, 3.5mm long, densely covered with small barbed spines.
plants.habitat: Damp, shaded places in the north-west of the State.

plants.name: Hackelia suaveolens
plants.form: Perennial herb covered with short, stiff hairs, with a rough-textured basal rosette of leaves and a stout rootstock.
plants.flowers: White or cream flowers in loose, branched flower heads, usually with a strong, sweet scent.
plants.fruit: 4 nutlets, each 6mm long, egg-shaped and densely covered with small barbed spines.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in grasslands, woodlands and dry forest, on dry or well-drained soil in lowland areas.

plants.name: Haemodorum distichophyllum
plants.form: Perennial rhizomatous herb; rigid and tufted, with hard, erect dark bluish-green leaves 5-9 cm long which are bright red at the base.
plants.flowers: 7-8 red, green, and black flowers together at the end of the stem.
plants.habitat: Grows in heath and buttongrass plains of the west and south-west.
plants.notes: Requires full sun, but do not allow to dry out.

plants.name: Hakea decurrens subsp. physocarpa
plants.form: Monoecious shrub; open, woody, prickly.
plants.flowers: Inflorescences 4–8-flowered; cream to pink spider-like flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody seed follicle – ovate, 2.5–3.5 cm long; valves thick, woody. Seed and wing blackish-brown, 15–20 mm long, wing extending only down one side of seed.
plants.habitat: Furneaux Group – coastal sandy heaths, open shrubberies and woodlands, from sea level to about 300m.

plants.name: Hakea decurrens subsp. platytaenia
plants.form: Monoecious shrub; open, woody, prickly.
plants.flowers: Inflorescences 4–8-flowered; cream to pink spider-like flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody seed follicle – ovate, 2.5–3.5 cm long; valves thick, woody. Seed and wing blackish-brown, 15–20 mm long, wing extending only down one side of seed.
plants.habitat: Furneaux Group – coastal sandy heaths, open shrubberies and woodlands, from sea level to about 300m.

plants.name: Hakea epiglottis subsp. epiglottis
plants.form: Erect shrub, often well-branched.
plants.flowers: White through to bright yellow clusters in the bases of the needles.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – woody with a beak which is curved upwards. Seed has terminal wing, slightly sickle-shaped. Two seeds per fruit.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent, especially in peaty heaths, from sea level to about 1000m. Dry rocky sites near the east coast. Damp heaths up to 1000m elsewhere.
plants.notes: Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability. The species varies in floral presentation – in some areas it has miniscule flowers but dense flowering forms can be found. Some are very fragrant. …

plants.name: Hakea epiglottis subsp. milliganii
plants.form: Erect shrub, often well-branched.
plants.flowers: White through to bright yellow clusters in the bases of the needles.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – woody with a beak which is curved upwards. Seed has terminal wing, slightly sickle-shaped. Two seeds per fruit.
plants.habitat: Scattered in the west of the state and represented by a very limited number of collections.
plants.notes: The species is sometimes bisexual, sometimes unisexual, so fruit will not be found on every plant. Bird attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Hakea lissosperma
plants.form: Shrub or small tree with many stout branches.
plants.flowers: White/cream clustered in leaf axils on stalks 4-6mm long.
plants.fruit: Seed follicles – brownish-purple, hard woody, warty with small beak. Seeds winged, usually two per fruit.
plants.habitat: Widespread, especially on mountains to 1200m and to sea level in areas of high rainfall.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Provides protection for native birds and animals and nectar for birds. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Hakea megadenia
plants.form: Erect shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Cream-white spider-like.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – small with large, membranous wing.
plants.habitat: Found on the Furneaux Islands and on the east coast as far south as Tasman Peninsula. Grows in riverside shrubbery or dry open forest, low altitude and coastal on the mainland but at higher altitudes on the islands.
plants.notes: Closely related to Hakea epiglottis. Chiefly distinguished by different flowering times and growth habit. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Hakea microcarpa
plants.form: Small rigid woody shrub.
plants.flowers: Creamy-white spider-like, prolific.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – ovoid at right angle to stem, 1–1.2 cm long; valves semi-woody when dry. Seed and wing brown, 6–10 mm long, wing extending partly along one side of seed.
plants.habitat: In wet areas along stream banks and near bogs in rocky situations, in heath and woodland. Locally frequent in open situations on the banks of streams and in alpine and sub-alpine scrub. Does not adapt to stagnant conditions. Tolerates heavy frost and drought.
plants.notes: Useful for planting in wet areas with other species for drainage control. Provides low-level cover (up to 2m) in mixed species plantings for shade and shelter, particularly on damp sites. Bird attracting. The foliage provides refuge for small birds. The flowers provide food for native insects. …

plants.name: Hakea nodosa
plants.form: A bushy shrub with slender branches.
plants.flowers: Tiny, yellow, claw-like; crowded along upper branchlets, tube 2-3mm long splitting into 4 lobes.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – brown, woody, with rough warty surface and small beak; contains 2 winged seed.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in the north-east and on Flinders, Cape Barren and Clarke islands.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Hakea teretifolia subsp. hirsuta
plants.form: Erect, much-branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Spider-like, creamy white, clustered in leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – woody, elongated, dagger-shaped opening to free 2 winged seeds with crests.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent especially in coastal heaths.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Foliage provides protection for small birds and flowers provide nectar. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability and spiny foliage.

plants.name: Hakea ulicina
plants.form: Branched shrub.
plants.flowers: White, tiny, spider-like, in clusters.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – cone shaped 12-18mm long with a short beak which is usually straight. Seed, black with a terminal wing.
plants.habitat: Islands of Bass Strait.
plants.notes: Soil tolerance and time to planting out data are for the Vic. form (Les Payne). Bird attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Halophila australis
plants.form: Submerged, smooth perennial herb with a slender, creeping stem and paired leaves.
plants.flowers: Male flowers are found among the leaf axils of the prostrate stem, females on erect branches up to 15cm long.
plants.habitat: At and below the low water level of spring tides. Collected on the east coast, Barnes Bay, Coles Bay and George Town in the north-east.

plants.name: Haloragis aspera
plants.form: Dwarf, perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Very small green to red flowers, singly or 2 together, borne in terminal or axillary heads.
plants.habitat: Widespread; common in forest and heathland, growing in a wide variety of soil types.
plants.notes: Useful as pioneer plants for colonizing areas which have been disturbed, however it may become a pest as it is difficult to eradicate due to its deep root system.

plants.name: Haloragis heterophylla
plants.form: Perennial herb with erect or ascending stems, much-branched at the base.
plants.flowers: Flowers insignificant, red, 1-4 together in axils toward top of stalk.
plants.habitat: Widespread; common in forest and heathland, growing in a wide variety of soil types.

plants.name: Haloragis myriocarpa
plants.form: Perennial herb with erect, cylindrical leaves, about 45mm long and 1mm wide.
plants.flowers: Flowers are red and 1mm wide, and have green, triangular bracts, or leaflike structures.
plants.fruit: Nut – 1.5mm long, with 8 ribs or narrow wings.
plants.habitat: Heathland on King Island, Clarke Island and the central east coast, including Friendly Beaches.

plants.name: Hardenbergia violacea
plants.form: Slender stems, wiry and rigid, trailing over low growing plants.
plants.flowers: Purple, sprays of massed pea flowers along branches.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – turn dark brown and become brittle. The ripe seed are hard and grey.
plants.habitat: Occurs in a diverse range of soil types and habitats from near sea-level to high mountains. Tolerates frost and extended dry periods.
plants.notes: Bee attracting. Flowers provide food (nectar and pollen) for various insects including native moths and butterflies, and native bees and wasps. Plants provide refuge for reptiles and various insects. Grows well in most acidic to slightly alkaline soils. …

plants.name: Hedycarya angustifolia
plants.form: Small tree
plants.flowers: Small, insignificant green flowers, 0.5-0.6 cm across.
plants.habitat: Widely distributed and common, particularly in rainforests and cool shady gullies and near water.
plants.notes: Good background plant, or shelter plant for ferns. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Helichrysum leucopsideum
plants.form: Perennial herb, stems sometimes woody at the base and much-branched forming a shrub.
plants.flowers: Solitary at ends of branches, 2-3 woolly leaves at base, sepals shining white or tinged pink.
plants.habitat: Grows in a wide range of habitats, coastal heaths, forest and woodlands.
plants.notes: Plants are not long-lived and should be treated as biennials. Grows well in sunny or semi-shaded positions and adapts to most free-draining soils. Useful for many situations including borders, underplanting of taller shrubs or trees, rockeries and containers. …

plants.name: Helichrysum luteoalbum
plants.form: Annual or short-lived perennial herb, densely hairy, may have faint sweet smell.
