plants.flowers: Flower heads about 4mm in diameter, shining pale golden or brownish-yellow, in dense clusters.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in pastures and dry rocky places and along roadsides.

plants.name: Helichrysum pumilum var. pumilum
plants.form: Small perennial herb with narrow leaves. Stems short, silky/hairy. Flower stalks up to 10cm.
plants.flowers: White everlasting , solitary, 1.5-2cm across outer bracts purple-red or brown, inner-white.
plants.fruit: Achene with pappus bristles minutely rough with thickened tips.
plants.habitat: In mountain herbfields reaching down to the coast in the south-west and west.
plants.notes: Grows in peaty soils from sea level to mountain sides. Requires plenty of organic material and moist soils. Tolerates some shade but prefers sunshine. Highly suitable for rockeries, containers and beside pathways.

plants.name: Hemarthria uncinata var. uncinata
plants.form: Stiffly erect perennial grass, forming dense mats.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence 4-8cm long, 2-3mm broad, falling into two spikelets at the nodes.
plants.habitat: Widespread, in wet soils.
plants.notes: While not particularly ornamental, this plant should be useful for erosion control. Bird attracting. It provides good habitat for wildlife and birds.

plants.name: Hemichroa pentandra
plants.form: Small, trailing herb with woody stems; new growth is hairy.
plants.flowers: Pink or white flowers about 0.5 cm across.
plants.habitat: Wet, saline areas, e.g. coastal swamps or lowlands subject to inundation.
plants.notes: Saline tolerant.

plants.name: Herpolirion novae-zelandiae
plants.form: Rhizomatous creeping herb, forming spreading clumps.
plants.flowers: Attractive lily flowers, about 2 cm across, white to lilac or blue, always at ground level.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – seeds are black and shiny, usually 1 or 2 per loculus.
plants.habitat: Alpine and sub-alpine areas in moist to wet grass and heath.
plants.notes: Winter chilling apparently necessary for successful flowering. Best success in cultivation is with container-grown plants in cooler temperatures, with the base of the container submerged in water.

plants.name: Heterozostera nigricaulis
plants.form: Submerged rhizomatous perennial seagrass with erect stems.
plants.notes: Sea grass.

plants.name: Heterozostera tasmanica
plants.form: Perennial seagrass with creeping rhizomes, forming extensive beds. Leaves 10-25cm long and 1-2mm wide, with 3 nerves.
plants.flowers: In spathes, large leaf-like structures enclosing the flowers.
plants.fruit: Seeds are chestnut-brown and shining, 1.75-3mm long.
plants.habitat: Coastal sands or mud below the low tide level, in the north-west, north-east, east coast and south-west.
plants.notes: Sea grass

plants.name: Hibbertia acicularis
plants.form: Dwarf prickly shrub with needle-like leaves; may be erect or sprawling.
plants.flowers: Yellow, solitary on slender stalks 1-2 cm long; size extremely variable, 0.8-1.5 cm across.
plants.fruit: Seed follicles – seeds brown and shiny with jagged aril.
plants.habitat: Common in sandy heaths.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Hibbertia appressa
plants.form: Scrambling shrub with wiry stems.
plants.flowers: Similar to Hibbertia empetrifolia, but has hairs which are pressed close to the sepals (appressed).

plants.name: Hibbertia empetrifolia subsp. empetrifolia
plants.form: Shrub, trailing or climbing by intertwining branches; young stems reddish and roughened.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow, 1 cm across, on slender stalks to 1.5 cm long; 4-5 deeply notched petals.
plants.habitat: Widespread from sea level to 750m; common in sandy heaths near coasts. In coastal scrub it usually adopts a trailing habit; in high rainfall forests it is a vigorous climber, forming tangled clumps.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Hibbertia ericifolia subsp. ericifolia
plants.form: A small prostrate shrub with a spreading habit.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow flowers, to 3 cm diameter.
plants.habitat: Sandy flats in the midlands and north of Tasmania.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Hibbertia hirsuta
plants.form: Much branched shrub, often prostrate, with wiry stems.
plants.flowers: Solitary yellow flowers to 1.2 cm across; sessile.
plants.habitat: Widespread, growing on slopes in open forests.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Hibbertia hirticalyx
plants.form: Erect shrub with long straggling branches. May climb over other plants.
plants.flowers: 1-1.5cm across, petals yellow, stamens grouped at one side of the hairy ovary.
plants.habitat: Known in a few isolated patches in north and north-east Tasmania and the Furneaux Islands but may be more widespread. Will grow in most soils and aspects.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi, otherwise hardy.

plants.name: Hibbertia mathinnicola
plants.form: Erect, dwarf shrub. Leaves linear, 1 x 0.1 cm, flattened and bristled. Young growth with grey hairs. Similar to Hibbertia riparia but distinguished by pointed leaves and acute bracts on flowers.
plants.flowers: Yellow, 1.5 cm across, sessile with numerous acute bracts.
plants.notes: Probable requirements are for filtered or partial sun in well-drained soil. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Hibbertia procumbens
plants.form: Prostrate, woody plant.
plants.flowers: Large, to 2.5cm across, golden yellow with five petals.
plants.habitat: Abundant in heaths, sea level to mountain plateaux.
plants.notes: The flowers provide food for many insects including moths, butterflies and native wasps. Also bee attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Hibbertia prostrata
plants.form: Prostrate shrub with erect or sprawling branches.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow to 2 cm across, terminal on short branches; several per flowering stem.
plants.fruit: Seed follicles – seed is brown, shining, and globular; 1.5 mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Common in coastal areas and light forests slightly inland.
plants.notes: Good drainage essential as species is sensitive to root rotting fungi (Phytophthora cinnamomi). Tends to be short-lived in cultivation.

plants.name: Hibbertia riparia
plants.form: Erect or spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow, 1-2cm diameter, petals deeply notched. Borne on ends of short branches.
plants.habitat: Abundant in many places in eastern parts of Tasmania in a range of lowland habitats, often in sunny positions and often growing on banks of streams.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Hibbertia rufa
plants.form: Small, woody shrub with procumbent or trailing habit.
plants.flowers: Yellow, solitary flowers to 1.5 cm across on reddish brown wiry stems.
plants.habitat: Only occurs in a single collection from eastern Tasmania.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Hibbertia sericea var. sericea
plants.form: Small shrub, usually erect, sometimes spreading.
plants.flowers: Yellow flowers to 2-3 cm across.
plants.fruit: Seed follicles – shiny, brown globular shaped seeds, 1 mm diameter.
plants.habitat: Dunes and coastal heath in the north of Tasmania.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Root rotting fungi are a major source of loss. Good drainage is essential as grey mould can cause foliage damage in shady or stagnant conditions.

plants.name: Hibbertia virgata
plants.form: Small, erect shrub with light coloured or reddish branches; young growth has short, curly, or cobwebby hairs.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow flowers are to 2.5 cm across with 2 or 3 brown bracts prominent.
plants.habitat: Local in north-east of Tasmania.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Should not be allowed to dry out.

plants.name: Hierochloe fraseri
plants.form: Loose tufting perennial grass; narrow, linear leaves strongly in-rolled near their base, tapering to a long point, strongly scented.
plants.flowers: Panicles up to 9 cm long.
plants.habitat: Widespread. Common in herb and grass fields and in wet, peaty swamps at fairly high altitudes, in open sunny sites.

plants.name: Hierochloe rariflora
plants.form: Tufted perennial grass; aromatic.
plants.flowers: Sweetly fragrant panicles 4-13 cm long.
plants.habitat: From coastal to mountainous regions, in open forests and along riverbanks, up to 400 m altitude.

plants.name: Hierochloe redolens
plants.form: Loose tufting perennial grass; leaves flat & linear, tapering to a long, in-rolled point. strongly scented.
plants.flowers: Panicles up to 20 cm long.
plants.habitat: Occasional in a wide variety of vegetation types; occurs in wet, peaty swamps at fairly high altitudes.

plants.name: Histiopteris incisa
plants.form: Fern rootstock, wiry, with reddish hairs; fronds, 50-200cm long, 2-4 times pinnate, pale green, soft, hairless, lowest pinnae at angle resembling bat’s wing.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant throughout the State; broadly absent from areas of low rainfall and less common in exposed alpine situations. It is an opportunistic species, colonising disturbed sites on the margins of, or in, wet forest. …
plants.notes: This species is not popular because it can easily spread and smother other plants. It is an attractive fern for large gardens, or in a large container. Requires well-drained loamy soil and mulching.

plants.name: Hiya distans
plants.form: Slender fern; rootstock: long-creeping with dark brown hairs; fronds narrow-ovate 2-3 times pinnate, dark green, harsh to touch.
plants.habitat: Very rare in Tasmania. Known only from the north-west and King Island in Tasmania. Occurs in moist, badly drained soils or on rotting logs in teatree and Melaleuca scrub or on margins of swampland. Tolerates light to moderate frosts. Recognise by bipinnate fronds with well-spaced pinnules.
plants.notes: Grows readily in a shady position and is not invasive. Grows best in loamy soil or where they can grow onto a rotting tree fern log. Also a successful container plant.

plants.name: Hookerochloa hookeriana
plants.form: Tussock-forming perennial grass.
plants.flowers: An open panicle with spikelets of 2-4-5 florets clearly separated.
plants.habitat: Occurs in lowlands in northern Tasmania in damp low-lying grasslands. Also on dry hillsides under light eucalypt forest, Central Highlands, Ben Lomond and east coast from near seal level to about 800m altitude.

plants.name: Hovea corrickiae
plants.form: Small shrub or slender tree with alternate, 3-4cm long, glossy green leaves, the undersides of which are densely covered in yellow-white to rust hairs.
plants.flowers: White pea flowers, on long stalks arising from the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – turn from green to black at maturity. Seeds are dark brown and kidney-shaped and occur 2 to a pod.
plants.habitat: Rocky sites, riparian areas with wet sclerophyll understorey shrubs and open forest in the north-east.

plants.name: Hovea heterophylla
plants.form: Small, woody shrub, slender branches, spreading to erect; long narrow leaves 3cm.
plants.flowers: Blue-mauve pea flowers, 8mm across in leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – round/egg-shaped hairy pod 1cm long, with 2 seeds. Pods turn from green to black at maturity and seeds turn from cream to dark grey when ripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread in dry grassland and stony places.

plants.name: Hovea magnibractea
plants.form: Spreading shrub with tough, wiry stems; branchlets densely covered in rusty hairs.
plants.flowers: Violet blue pea flowers, in leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oval, inflated, with rust coloured fine hairs. Pods turn from green to black and seeds turn from cream to dark grey when ripe.
plants.habitat: Very occasional in low alpine heath.

plants.name: Hovea montana
plants.form: Small to medium shrub with densely hairy branchlets, ascending to erect.
plants.flowers: Conspicuous bluish purple, pea-shaped with white at base, 0.8 cm across, on axillary stalks to 5 cm.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – turn from green to black at maturity. Seeds turn from cream to dark grey when ripe.
plants.habitat: Grows in sandy soils amongst rocky outcrops.

plants.name: Hovea tasmanica
plants.form: Spindly, erect shrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers deep mauve and arranged together in groups of 2 or 3.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – approximately 10 mm long, covered with pale hairs.
plants.habitat: Dry, rocky ridges or slopes (mostly dolerite) in forest and riverine scrub.

plants.name: Huperzia australiana
plants.form: Fern ally with stems erect or hanging, sometimes branching, leaves in a spiral. Possesses bulbils but lacks strobili.
plants.habitat: Grows in areas above 1000m in shallow soil over rock in the protection of boulders or on semi-exposed ledges. Appears to be resistant to competition and almost invariably occurs amongst grasses, herbs or low shrubs.
plants.notes: Possesses gemmae (vegetative buds or bulbils) which appear as small outgrowths circling the stems in groups at regular intervals. These may drop off and develop into mature plants if conditions are suitable. The viability of using this as a means of cultivation is not known.

plants.name: Hyalosperma demissum
plants.form: Dwarf, much-branched annual herb.
plants.flowers: Flower heads solitary, terminal surrounded by 4-5 of the uppermost leaves. Hermaphrodite.
plants.habitat: Occasional and local in dry sandy places.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle callicarpa
plants.form: A small prostrate annual herb with erect or ascending stems 2-8 cm high.
plants.flowers: 6-12 minute white to purple flowers in each umbel.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – dry, indehiscent; 1mm long, black when ripe.
plants.habitat: Local in open and dry places; roadbanks.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle capillaris
plants.form: Small prostrate annual herb with wiry stems, branched from the base and erect or ascending.
plants.flowers: 3-6 minute flowers per umbel, on very short stalks.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – dry, indehiscent; 1mm long, black when ripe.
plants.habitat: In hollows and on sandy cliff tops in the north-east.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle comocarpa
plants.form: Annual herb with deeply divided, mostly hairless leaves, on hairy stalks. It has yellow or white outgrowths at the base of the leaf stalks. Usually branches from the base and spreads along the ground.
plants.flowers: 10-20 flowers in a flat-topped head.
plants.fruit: Mericarp – oval shaped, slightly flattened and with a wrinkly or ridged surface. It is 2mm long, and has a row of thin dry hairs, up to 1mm long, at the tip.
plants.habitat: Recorded only once on Flinders Island, on shallow soil on a ridge crest with other forbs, shrubs and Eucalyptus nitida.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle foveolata
plants.form: Erect herb with deeply divided leaves, each with 3-5 leaflets. Each leaflet is 3-toothed.
plants.fruit: Mericarp – oval shaped, slightly flattened and with a wrinkly or ridged surface. It is 2mm long, and has a row of thin dry hairs, up to 1mm long, at the tip.
plants.habitat: Woodland on sandy or loamy soils.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle hirta
plants.form: Perennial herb with creeping stems mainly above ground.
plants.flowers: Flower heads 1-2 cm across, greenish, on long hairy stalks, giving off a strong offensive odour.
plants.fruit: Mericarp – about 2.5 mm broad in two sections, each with a blunt dorsal rib.
plants.habitat: Local in open grassland on the Queen’s Domain, Hobart.
plants.notes: Excellent groundcover for shaded positions and erosion control on shady banks, however it may be invasive in home gardens and its strong odour also makes it unattractive for most garden settings.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle laxiflora
plants.form: Perennial, rhizomatous herb with erect or ascending flowering branches to 15 cm high. Highly odiferous. Rounded leaves with scalloped margins.
plants.flowers: Flower heads 1-2 cm across, greenish, on long hairy stalks, giving off a strong offensive odour.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – dry, indehiscent; 1mm long, black when ripe.
plants.habitat: Open grassland and in woodlands and forests.
plants.notes: Excellent groundcover for shaded positions and erosion control on shady banks, however it may be invasive in home gardens and its strong odour also makes it unattractive for most garden settings.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle muscosa
plants.form: Small perennial mat herb with rhizomes or creeping stems.
plants.flowers: Inflorescences are simple terminal heads with 3-4 insignificant flowers.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet places in montane heath and on banks of streams.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle pterocarpa
plants.form: Perennial herb with creeping stems.
plants.flowers: Inflorescences are terminal heads with up to 20 insignificant flowers.
plants.habitat: In the north and west of the state, occasional along banks of streams.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides
plants.form: Small perennial mat herb with almost- round leaves with scalloped margins and creeping stems.
plants.flowers: Inflorescences are simple terminal heads with 3-7 insignificant flowers.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in wet forests and becoming common in poorly drained lawns.

plants.name: Hydrocotyle tripartita
plants.form: Small, slender, perennial herb. The leaves resemble Italian parsley. They are almost circular but are divided into three leaflets, which are often lobed. Leaves are glossy and 4-20mm wide.
plants.flowers: Insignificant.
plants.habitat: Swamps, soaks and riparian areas.
plants.notes: May be a suitable lawn alternative in moist areas.

plants.name: Hymenophyllum applanatum
plants.form: Small filmy fern in clumps; fronds, 5-20cm long, rusty coloured on thin, wiry stems, stellate hairs.
plants.habitat: Restricted to high rainfall areas of the west and south. Seems to be epiphytic on Athrotaxis selaginoides from 680m to 1080m and Athrotaxis cupressoides from 950m to 1120m. Also found at lower altitudes. It is also lithophytic on quartzitic or schistose rocks. …
plants.notes: Epiphytic, Lithophytic. Difficult to maintain in cultivation – dies out easily. Requires cool humid conditions with some air movement. Best in a terrarium or very humid fernery.

plants.name: Hymenophyllum australe
plants.form: Fern with long, creeping, thread-like rootstock: fronds, 6-15cm long, 1-3 times pinnate, semi-erect, dark green, crinkled, veins conspicuous.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in rainforest, wet sclerophyll forest and fern gullies from sea level to 650m. It occupies sites near ground level, soil, rock, mossy logs and the bases of trees and Dicksonia. Occasionally on more exposed, wet rock-faces with Hymenophyllum rarum.

plants.name: Hymenophyllum cupressiforme
plants.form: Fern; rootstock, creeping, thread-like, much-branched; fronds bipinnate, 4-9cm long, dark green, crowded; indusium tubular.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant from sea level to sub-alpine shrubberies. Common on outermost limbs of tall rainforest trees and in seasonally dry sites or upper slopes of gullies where fronds may shrivel during dry periods.
plants.notes: Also suitable for bottle, terrarium or aquarium culture.

plants.name: Hymenophyllum flabellatum
plants.form: Epiphytic fern; rootstock long, creeping, wiry; fronds, 10-20cm long, pendulous, pale green, tri-pinnate; indusium 2-lipped.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in rainforest, wet sclerophyll forest and fern gullies from sea level to 650m. Prefers overhanging or vertical substrates; the first filmy fern to colonise root buttresses, logs and stumps in disturbed forests.
plants.notes: Best grown on a slab of tree-fern fibre in a bottle, terrarium or aquarium. Dries out very quickly if removed from a constantly damp habitat.

plants.name: Hymenophyllum marginatum
plants.form: Tiny epiphytic or lithophytic fern, with long creeping, thread-like rootstock; fronds, 1-3cm long, light green with black, wavy margins.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in the west and south of the State with scattered records from the east coast. Occurs on rocks, logs and a range of tree species. Grows in rainforest but also in high sheltered granite ledges and crevices where its fronds shrivel in summer.
plants.notes: Can be grown on a slab of tree-fern fibre in a bottle or terrarium.

plants.name: Hymenophyllum peltatum
plants.form: Lithophytic or epiphytic fern with much-branched, creeping, wiry rootstock; fronds, 4-12cm long, 1-2 times pinnate, semi-erect, dark green.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant from near sea level. Grows in soil, on rock, and on the limbs and trunks of a range of tree species. In alpine regions, often in boulder grottos near running water.

plants.name: Hymenophyllum rarum
plants.form: Rootstock much-branched, creeping thread-like; fronds, 5-15cm long, pinnate, light green, pendulous, narrow, indusium 2-lipped.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant from sea level to sub-alpine areas. Terrestrial on logs and rocks, or epiphytic on trees and Dicksonia. Will tolerate excessively shaded situations where fronds are long and slender with little segmentation.
plants.notes: Can be grown on a slab of tree-fern fibre in a terrarium.

plants.name: Hypericum gramineum
plants.form: Slender, hairless, perennial herb; stems erect and rigid.
plants.flowers: Yellow, solitary, 1.5cm across, 5 petals.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule and seed turn from green to red-brown on maturity.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common in pastures and grassy places.
plants.notes: Grows in most soils and conditions.

plants.name: Hypericum japonicum
plants.form: Prostrate; perennial, mat-forming herb, to 60 cm in diameter.
plants.flowers: Tiny yellow to orange flowers, less than 1 cm across, usually single, on short stalks.
plants.habitat: Damp places from sea level to about 1000m elevation.
plants.notes: Not widely grown. Needs damp, shaded position near water’s edge.

plants.name: Hypolaena fastigiata
plants.form: Small perennial rhizomatous herb with erect, faintly grooved stems covered in white scales.
plants.flowers: Male spikelets numerous, reddish brown on slender whitish stalks; female spikelets few, terminal, solitary and erect.
plants.habitat: Widely distributed, particularly in sandy, moist soils.

plants.name: Hypolepis amaurorachis
plants.form: Slender fern, rootstock covered with reddish brown hairs; fronds narrow-ovate, 2-3 times pinnate, bright green, soft.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, scattered locations across most of Tasmania from near sea level to at least 850m. Prefers cool, moist gullies where it often grows on rocks close to water, singly or in small colonies.
plants.notes: An excellent fern for a cool, shady position. Forms small clumps but is not invasive. Grows best in loamy soils. Also a successful container plant, including hanging baskets.

plants.name: Hypolepis glandulifera
plants.form: Coarse textured fern; rootstock with soft, reddish brown hairs; fronds 80-270cm long, broadly ovate, 2-4 times pinnate, dull green.
plants.habitat: Absent from most of Tasmania but locally abundant along the central north and east coasts. Grows in alluvial flats and on the higher slopes of gullies. Often occurs with Hypolepis rugosula.
plants.notes: Grows in extensive colonies in shady situations and also in full sun where clumps are extremely dense. Best suited to large gardens or where it can spread. Fronds are sticky in shady situations but much less so if grown in full sun.

plants.name: Hypolepis muelleri
plants.form: Coarse fern, rootstock with reddish-brown hairs; fronds 50-130cm long, ovate to broadly ovate, 2-4 times pinnate, dark green, leathery, harsh.
plants.habitat: Occurs along watercourses, swampy areas or deep, rich, alluvial soils below 120 m elevation in northern Tasmania (including King and Flinders islands). Has also been recorded from forest dominated by Acacia melanoxylon, Melaleuca or Eucalyptus species. Appears similar to bracken fern.
plants.notes: Adapts readily to cultivation but needs to be kept in check.

plants.name: Hypolepis rugosula
plants.form: Coarse fern, rootstock with dense reddish hairs; fronds 50-200mm long, broadly ovate, dull green, 2-4 times pinnate, coarse, stipes chestnut.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant everywhere except low rainfall and alpine regions. Freely colonises disturbed sites; an early coloniser.
plants.notes: Most suitable for large gardens or sites where it can spread without detriment to other plants.

plants.name: Hypoxis hygrometrica var. hygrometrica
plants.form: Small herbaceous perennial with underground corms and dark-green, folded linear leaves.
plants.flowers: Solitary bright yellow to golden yellow flowers 2 cm across, on stems up to 20 cm long.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – long, ellipsoidal, open at maturity to release the dark brown seed through a horizontal split.
plants.habitat: Widespread in a variety of forest habitats and coastal heaths.
plants.notes: Protect from snails and slugs.

plants.name: Imperata cylindrica
plants.form: Perennial grass with long, thick rhizomes, and smooth stems, either erect or bent abruptly. Leaves are flat or slightly in rolled, and finely ribbed on both surfaces.
plants.flowers: Flower head dense, silky and cylindrical, up to 20cm long. When flowering, the stigmas are purple or brownish, and the yellow anthers are prominent.
plants.habitat: Coastal sands in the north-west, north-east and east coast.

plants.name: Indigofera australis subsp. australis
plants.form: Erect undershrub or shrub.
plants.flowers: Clusters of small pink-lilac pea flowers, occasionally white.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – narrow, brown, with 5-10 seeds. Seeds are grey-brown at maturity.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant. In sandy heaths and on hillsides in areas of light or moderate rainfall. Tolerates moderately heavy frosts and extended wet periods. Adapts to most acidic soils that are well-drained. Hardiness depends on provenance.
plants.notes: Useful for providing low-level shelter (up to 2m) in windbreaks. Bee attracting. Flowers provide food (pollen and nectar) for many native insects, including bees and wasps. The foliage is very palatable to sheep and wallabies, although it is reputedly toxic when flowering. …

plants.name: Isachne globosa
plants.form: Perennial, often aquatic, rhizomatous or tufted. Stems herbaceous.
plants.flowers: Open panicle.
plants.habitat: East coast

photos.credit: Queensland Herbarium, D. Sharp CC BY

plants.name: Isoetes drummondii subsp. drummondii
plants.form: Very small annual fern ally with rootstock corm-like, three-lobed; leaves 3-20cm long, thin, grass-like, sporangia not veiled.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, occurs in scattered locations on the Central Plateau, eastern highlands and in the Midlands. Grows as a semi-aquatic of damp soils amongst grasses in waterlogged pastures and waterways of the Midlands. Also occurs on the seasonally inundated shores of lakes and lagoons.
plants.notes: Top growth desiccates when soil substrate dries out and re-shoots as water rises. Distinguished from other members of the species by its habitat, spreading habit and excessively swollen leaf bases and deciduous nature. Can be grown as a perennial in a container of sand covered with water.

plants.name: Isoetes elatior
plants.form: Aquatic fern ally; rootstock 3-lobed; leaves, up to 60cm long, thin, grasslike; sporangia not veiled.
plants.habitat: Known only from some rivers on the east coast of Tasmania. Typically occurs with its roots in a gravel/silt substrate in moderate to swiftly flowing water with all parts submerged throughout the year. In calmer water grows in mud or silt, often with Isoetes muelleri.
plants.notes: Isoetes eliator is the largest of the Australian species of Isoetes. Makes an attractive aquatic for a pond or cold water aquarium.

plants.name: Isoetes gunnii
plants.form: Tall stout aquatic fern ally; which forms a tussock of hollow leaves, undivided and circular in cross-section; rootstock 3-lobed.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in highland tarns, natural lakes and rivers at a variety of elevations. Plants which occur in rocky or gravelly substrate in flowing water or shallow margins of lakes may form clumps only a few centimetres in height. At greater depths, in mud, leaves may reach 38cm.
plants.notes: Can be grown as an aquarium plant in cold water.

plants.name: Isoetes humilior
plants.form: Aquatic fern ally; which forms a tussock of hollow leaves, 5-8 cm long, undivided and circular in cross-section; rootstock 2-lobed.
plants.habitat: Occurs in slow moving sections of running water and also in still waters on the Central Plateau and in Cradle Mt./Lake St. Clair Nat Pk; frequently occurs with Isoetes gunnii growing together in communal clumps. Isoetes humilior is smaller in all parts and has a veil covering the sporangia.
plants.notes: Usually grows submerged in permanent water.

plants.name: Isoetes jarmaniae
plants.form: Small, aquatic fern ally with stout, backward-curving leaves, less than 6cm long.
plants.habitat: Flat alkaline pans in the lowlands of the south-west.
plants.notes: Propagate through spores that are dispersed by water or animals.

plants.name: Isoetes muelleri
plants.form: Aquatic fern ally.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in lowland rivers and highland lakes and are fully submerged for most of the year but commonly exposed with low water levels in summer. Deeper running waters of the lowlands support larger plants while masses of dwarfed plants occur in some natural or man-made waters.
plants.notes: Appears to be the hardiest member of the genus in Tasmania. Morphologically very diverse and has been found growing with all other named Isoetes species in Tasmania as well as with the uncommon aquatic fern Pilularia novae-hollandiae.

plants.name: Isoetopsis graminifolia
plants.form: Small, densely tufted herb almost without stem.
plants.flowers: Heads without stalks, crowded at the bases of leaves, florets 12-20.
plants.fruit: Achene – inverted cone-shaped with long hairs, pappus with 8-10 scales.
plants.habitat: Collected from Queen’s Domain, Hobart. Possibly still in this and in other open and grassy places.

plants.name: Isolepis alpina
plants.form: Small and densely tufted perennial sedge with stiff stems.
plants.flowers: Flowers in heads of spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, purplish-grey, 1.4-1.7mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: In sub-alpine moors and tarns, in the Central Highlands, Ben Lomond and Mt. Field. Also at lower altitudes on the west coast.

plants.name: Isolepis aucklandica
plants.form: Small perennial sedge with slender stems, forming dense tufts.
plants.flowers: Flowers in heads of spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, smooth and shiny, pale purplish-grey, 1-1.5mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: In wet places in alpine and sub-alpine areas on the west coast, Central Highlands, east coast, south-west and Mt. Field.

plants.name: Isolepis cernua
plants.form: Highly variable, densely tufted perennial sedge.
plants.flowers: At the end of flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, reddish-brown to dark grey when ripe, 0.75-1mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: On damp ground near the coast, including wet sands and brackish estuary banks on King Island, Furneaux, north-west, north-east, west coast, east coast and south-west.

plants.name: Isolepis crassiuscula
plants.form: Aquatic plants have branched stems which root at the nodes. Land plants are tufted with erect stems.
plants.flowers: A single spikelet on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, 1.5-2.25mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads. Nuts are dark purplish-brown when fresh, turning whitish-grey when dry.
plants.habitat: Grows in wet mud or under water, in swampy areas, shallow pools and lakes in alpine and sub-alpine habitats. Found on Ben Lomond, east coast, south-west, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Isolepis fluitans
plants.form: Slender perennial with branched stems floating at the surface or submerged. Land plants form compact tufts.
plants.flowers: A single spikelet on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, 1.4-1.7mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads. Nuts are pale brown when fresh and whitish-grey when dry.
plants.habitat: Forms dense mats in still or flowing fresh or brackish water.

plants.name: Isolepis habra
plants.form: Slender perennial sedge with erect, threadlike, rather soft stems, forming dense tufts.
plants.flowers: Egg-shaped, solitary spikelet, 2.5-3.5mm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – triangular and pale-coloured, 1-1.5mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: Very wet mountain and riparian habitats on kunanyi/Mt. Wellington; near sea level in the south-west.

plants.name: Isolepis hookeriana
plants.form: Slender, tufted, annual sedge with fibrous roots.
plants.flowers: In spikelets, 2.5-3.5mm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, 1.2-1.5mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads. Nuts are dark brown to black.
plants.habitat: Wet sandy places in the Midlands and east coast, also in the Central Highlands.

plants.name: Isolepis inundata
plants.form: Tufted perennial sedge with firm, slender stems, sometimes up to 1mm in diameter.
plants.flowers: In heads of spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nut – shining, oval, 0.8-1.1mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: In wet places throughout the State.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Isolepis limbata
plants.form: Tufted perennial sedge with threadlike stems and leaves.
plants.flowers: Usually in solitary spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, 1mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads. Nuts are deep purple or brownish purple, with numerous purple dots or streaks.
plants.habitat: Very wet places, such as stream banks, in the north-west, Central Highlands, south-west, and Russell Falls at Mt. Field.

plants.name: Isolepis marginata
plants.form: Small annual sedge with erect stems forming rigid tufts.
plants.flowers: In heads of spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, 0.8-1mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: On very shallow soils of coastal rocks and wet sand, also on rough pasture hummocks and cleared forests inland.

plants.name: Isolepis montivaga
plants.form: Small tufted perennial sedge.
plants.flowers: A head of spikelets containing many flowers.
plants.fruit: Nut – smooth, shining and oval; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: In wet ground or more or less submerged; in and on the edges of tarns in alpine and sub-alpine habitats, in peaty heaths and very wet places at lower altitudes.

plants.name: Isolepis platycarpa
plants.form: Small, densely tufted sedge with bristly stems.
plants.flowers: In spikelets on the end of flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, 0.75mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads. Nuts are dark brown to black when mature.
plants.habitat: In wet depressions between dunes and on rocks on the coast, and on riverbanks.

plants.name: Isolepis producta
plants.form: Very slender aquatic perennial sedge with floating or submerged stems, forming dense mats.
plants.flowers: In single spikelets on the end of flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval-shaped, pale brown, 1.5mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: In fresh or brackish water in the Furneaux, north-east, west coast, Central Highlands, Midlands and south-west.

plants.name: Isolepis stellata
plants.form: Small tufted annual sedge with erect, bristly stems, 2-9cm long.
plants.flowers: Seed heads of 3-8 spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nuts – oval, 0.75mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads. Nuts are dark brown to black.
plants.habitat: Edges of swamps, saltmarshes, roadside soaks and wetlands in the north-east and north-west.

plants.name: Isolepis subtilissima
plants.form: Small perennial sedge with erect, threadlike stems and leaves.
plants.flowers: Borne in a solitary spikelet.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, 0.9mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: Wet alpine and sub-alpine habitats in the Central Highlands, south-west, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington; also recorded from Maria Island.

plants.name: Isolepis tasmanica
plants.form: Very slender perennial with bristly stems.
plants.flowers: In heads of spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nut – shining, smooth and oval, 1.2-1.5mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: Rarely collected; the type collection was from fern gullies in the north-west, also recorded from the Central Highlands.

plants.name: Isolepis wakefieldiana
plants.form: Densely tufted annual sedge with slender, spreading stems.
plants.flowers: A head of spikelets on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – oval, shining, 1mm long; contained in dense, bristly seed heads.
plants.habitat: Very damp places, including the South Esk River Gorge in Launceston and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Isophysis tasmanica
plants.form: Tufted perennial herb; flat, erect leaves form fans at base of flowering stems; woody rhizomes.
plants.flowers: Large (6 cm diameter) single terminal flowers are dark purple, occasionally yellow.
plants.fruit: Capsule – numerous light brown seeds, 2 mm long.
plants.habitat: Alpine sedgeland and heath in western mountains.

plants.name: Isopogon ceratophyllus
plants.form: Dwarf to small shrub with thick woody rootstock, forming dense prickly tufts.
plants.flowers: Flower heads terminal, yellow flowers in spherical cones to 1.5-2cm in diameter, without hairs except for hairy tuft at tip.
plants.fruit: Nut – seed is enclosed in small round cones which turn from green to brown as seeds mature.
plants.habitat: Found on well-drained acidic, sandy or loamy soils in dry heathlands around the Furneaux Group. Occasionally found on sandy clays which may be subject to extreme wetness.
plants.notes: Best in dappled shade but will tolerate full sun. Very susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Isotoma fluviatilis subsp. australis
plants.form: Small creeping prostrate perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Solitary, irregular shape, on erect stems. Petals blue or white, lower petals with darker blue or purple blotch near mouth of tube.
plants.habitat: Local in swampy ground and river flats in the Midlands and north of the state.

plants.name: Juncus amabilis
plants.form: Rhizomatous perennial forming dense clumps.
plants.flowers: Slender erect branches with clusters of flowers.
plants.habitat: Local in Midlands and north-east, not in the wettest areas.

plants.name: Juncus antarcticus
plants.form: A small densely tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Terminal head of 2-5 flowers.
plants.habitat: Local but widespread on wet places on mountains of the Central Highlands to 1220m.

plants.name: Juncus astreptus
plants.form: Rhizomatous perennial forming tight clumps.
plants.flowers: Small clusters, brownish-green.
plants.habitat: Common in damp pastures and disturbed places.

plants.name: Juncus australis
plants.form: Rhizomatous perennial with creeping rhizome forming loose clumps.
plants.flowers: Flowers clustered at tips, greenish-brown.
plants.habitat: Tolerates cold winters but not in wettest parts.

plants.name: Juncus bassianus
plants.form: Rhizomatous perennial forming large clumps.
plants.habitat: Frequent in wet places.

plants.name: Juncus bufonius
plants.form: Slender annual very variable in size and habit.
plants.flowers: Flowers solitary and distant, chestnut-brown.
plants.habitat: Frequent in all regions especially in damp areas at low altitudes e.g. wet fields, roadsides and margins of ponds.

plants.name: Juncus caespiticius
plants.form: A perennial forming soft tufts.
plants.flowers: Dark brown, chestnut-brown.
plants.habitat: Occasional in swampy places.

plants.name: Juncus curtisiae
plants.form: A small perennial with slender branched rhizome forming mats.
plants.flowers: Greenish and reddish-brown.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in very wet places from sea level to 1300m. Also grows between and through cushion plants.

plants.name: Juncus falcatus subsp. falcatus
plants.form: A perennial with long, spreading, rather slender but tough, branched rhizomes.
plants.flowers: Pale brown, greenish, dark chestnut brown, mauve.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet alpine and sub-alpine habitats.

plants.name: Juncus filicaulis
plants.form: A slender rhizomatous perennial forming small tufts.
plants.flowers: Green, reddish-brown, red-brown.
plants.habitat: Local in King Island, Midlands and in alpine and sub-alpine grasslands of the Central Highlands.

plants.name: Juncus fockei
plants.form: Loosely clustered rush resembling Juncus holoschoenus.
plants.flowers: Green, chestnut-brown.
plants.habitat: Known from one locality in the north-east.

plants.name: Juncus gregiflorus
plants.form: A rhizomatous perennial forming tight clumps.
plants.flowers: Greenish-brown, pale brown, light brown.
plants.habitat: Rare as a component of closed communities in moist situations e.g. areas of seepage.

plants.name: Juncus holoschoenus
plants.form: A loosely tufted perennial with a short rhizome.
plants.flowers: Green with chestnut-brown.
plants.habitat: Frequent in wet places.

plants.name: Juncus pallidus
plants.form: Large rush, usually tall and stout.
plants.flowers: Pale, very numerous in loose clusters on stiff stalks.
plants.fruit: Capsule – numerous small capsules contained in open, branched seed heads. Capsules dry and turn brown as they mature. Seed is dust-like.
plants.habitat: Wet places, ponds and ditches, usually lowland or sandy soil. Withstands seasonal dryness.
plants.notes: The tussocks provide habitat around pools and waterways, for small animals including birds, fish and crustaceans; important frog habitat. Bird attracting. The seed probably provides food for birds including finches, pigeons and parrots. Used in traditional Palawa basket weaving. …

plants.name: Juncus pauciflorus
plants.form: A rhizomatous perennial forming moderate sized clumps.
plants.flowers: Greenish-brown or reddish.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent especially in moist shaded areas.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Juncus planifolius
plants.form: A tufted rush very variable in size and inflorescence.
plants.flowers: Dark chestnut-brown to black, centre green or pale brown, sides dark brown.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common throughout the state especially in wet, disturbed ground e.g. roadsides and drainage ditches from sea level to about 900m.

plants.name: Juncus prismatocarpus
plants.form: A loosely tufted perennial with a short rootstock.
plants.flowers: Greenish brown or reddish, straw or rust-coloured.
plants.habitat: Occasional in swampy places.

plants.name: Juncus procerus
plants.form: Tall robust, rhizomatous perennial forming large clumps.
plants.flowers: Flowers loosely clustered at end of branches, green with central reddish-purple streak.
plants.habitat: Frequent, often growing with Juncus pallidus.

plants.name: Juncus ratkowskyanus
plants.form: Small perennial with a slender branching rhizome, forming mats that may be dense and hard.
plants.flowers: Greenish or straw coloured to reddish-brown, brownish.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet places with altitudes 750-1300m.

plants.name: Juncus revolutus
plants.form: Small perennial with long slender rhizomes.
plants.flowers: Pale green with narrow reddish-brown membranous margins.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in marshes and wet places near the sea.

plants.name: Juncus sandwithii
plants.form: Small perennial having a slender, much branched rhizome.
plants.flowers: Pale green, straw coloured or reddish, golden or chestnut brown.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet places from sea level to 915m.

plants.name: Juncus sarophorus
plants.form: Tall rhizomatous perennial forming dense clumps.
plants.flowers: Straw coloured to pale golden, dull reddish-purple.
plants.habitat: Widespread throughout the state and locally abundant in very wet places.

plants.name: Juncus subsecundus
plants.form: A rhizomatous perennial forming small clumps.
plants.flowers: Straw coloured or greenish, pale brown.
plants.habitat: From sea level to alpine and sub-alpine regions.

plants.name: Juncus vaginatus
plants.form: A tall rhizomatous perennial forming large clumps.
plants.flowers: Pale green
plants.habitat: Local and uncommon in the north-east, west coast and east coast, the plants scattered near margins of streams or in permanently wet soakage areas of marshes.

plants.name: Kelleria dieffenbachii
plants.form: Dwarf herb forming loose mats or soft cushions to 30cm diameter.
plants.flowers: White, unisexual or bisexual, 2-7 in terminal cluster.
plants.habitat: Occurs in northern and western Tasmania, in dry to moist well drained soils in sheltered locations as well as in fairly open alpine tussock grassland.
plants.notes: Rarely cultivated. Requires high altitude cool conditions, light to medium soils rich in organic matter, semi-shade or partial sun and tolerates frosts and snowfalls. Carpeting, self-layering species.

plants.name: Kennedia prostrata
plants.form: Prostrate, spreading to 1m.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers red or, rarely, almost black. Solitary or two together.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – long brown pod which turns brittle at seed maturity; small black seeds.
plants.habitat: Colonises bare ground after fire or disturbance. Frost tolerance depends on material source.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Koori use: stems were used for string.

plants.name: Kunzea ambigua
plants.form: Shrub with long arching branches. Teatree like.
plants.flowers: White fluffy bottlebrush-like heads, honey scented.
plants.habitat: Granitic country of the east and north-east and Bass Strait Islands. Coastal heaths and wet scrub areas. Sandy heathlands.
plants.notes: Grows fairly quickly into a large shrub. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis aemula
plants.form: Erect tufted annual grass
plants.flowers: Numerous spreading open-flowering panicles, to 5mm long, purplish at maturity .
plants.habitat: Occurs in open situations or under light woodland. Occasional in grassy vegetation in the eastern and central mountains. When growing in coastal sands is often less than 15cm high.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis billardierei subsp. billardierei
plants.form: Erect or kneed annual of coastal areas.
plants.flowers: 30cm panicle flowerhead, wide spreading from being enclosed at the base.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis collicola
plants.form: Erect or bent tufted annual grass, leaf blades flat 4-6mm wide.
plants.flowers: Panicle few-flowered spreading widely in maturity, spikelets about 4mm long.
plants.habitat: Differs from Lachnagrostis billardierei subsp. tenuiseta in that it occurs inland at 800-1050m altitude. Found in the Central Highlands and south-west.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis filiformis
plants.form: Annual, occasionally perennial, grass with flat or folded leaves, finely tapering and with large, intricate panicles.
plants.flowers: Loose panicle with spreading branches. Spikelets touch each other – only occurs in lachnogrostis.
plants.habitat: Occasional in grassy vegetation in the eastern mountains. Widespread in a variety of usually damp situations from sea level to about 1200m. Plants from coastal sands and from highland situations are often less than 15cm high.

photos.credit: Queensland Herbarium, D. Sharp CC BY

plants.name: Lachnagrostis lacunarum
plants.form: Aquatic grass, rooting at nodes, leaves flat 2.5mm wide.
plants.flowers: Panicle spreading widely in maturity, less than 12 cm long. Spikelets 2.5-4mm long.
plants.habitat: Found in aquatic vegetation in the central mountains.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis morrisii
plants.form: Erect annual grass, leaves flat up to 17cm long, 4mm wide.
plants.flowers: Panicle to 12cm, spikelets green or purple- tinged, flowering glume shining with fine awn.
plants.habitat: Found in damp areas on margins of forest from 200m to 1200m altitude in the Midlands, Central Highlands, east coast, south-west and Mt. Field.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis robusta
plants.form: Erect or bent annual grass, leaf blades narrow, in rolled and smooth on the side away from the axis.
plants.flowers: Panicles spreading in maturity, bracts with very rough keels.
plants.habitat: Found on the east coast.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis rudis subsp. nana
plants.form: Either erect, or bent sharply, annual grass.
plants.flowers: Panicles up to 25cm long. Ultimate branchlets with 1 to several pale green or purple spikelets.
plants.habitat: Found in coastal habitats. Plants growing in beach sands are usually less than 15cm high.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis rudis subsp. rudis
plants.form: Either erect, or bent sharply, annual grass.
plants.flowers: Panicles up to 25cm long. Ultimate branchlets with 1 to several pale green or purple spikelets.
plants.habitat: Found in coastal habitats. Plants growing in beach sands are usually less than 15cm high.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis semibarbata var. filifolia
plants.form: Erect or bent annual grass, leaf blades narrow, almost filiform.
plants.flowers: Panicle fewer flowered than Lachnagrostis billardierei, bracts smooth on the sides.
plants.habitat: Coastal areas of north-west, north-east and east coast.

plants.name: Lachnagrostis semibarbata var. semibarbata
plants.form: Erect or bent annual grass, leaf blades narrow, almost filiform.
plants.flowers: Panicle fewer flowered than Lachnagrostis billardierei, bracts smooth on the sides.
plants.habitat: Coastal areas of north-west, north-east and east coast.

plants.name: Lagarostrobos franklinii
plants.form: Tall tree with spreading or drooping branches with a dense pyramidal crown.
plants.fruit: Cone – male cones inconspicuous; female very small and loose with 6-10 well-spaced seed-bearing scales about 4mm across, each with a single seed.
plants.habitat: Rainforest in south-west Tasmania, along rivers, on swampy ground and fringing lakes, sea level to 850m and from the Pieman River to western edge of the Central Plateau and middle reaches of the Huon River. Usually a cypress-like tree but may be reduced to shrub form on rock outcrops along rivers.
plants.notes: Prefers constantly moist (well drained) humus rich soils which do not become too dry in summer and a cool root run.

plants.name: Lagenophora gunniana
plants.form: Perennial herb with short stout rootstock. Basal leaves green above/purple below.
plants.flowers: Solitary, white to blue, about 1.2cm across.
plants.fruit: Achene with curved beak at apex.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in woodland and forest, most prevalent in moist gullies and near water.
plants.notes: Does best in moist free draining soils with a semi-shaded position. May also be grown in rock gardens or containers.

plants.name: Lasiopetalum baueri
plants.form: Small shrub; younger leaves and branches are densely covered in white or rusty-red star-shaped hairs.
plants.flowers: Flowers covered with hairs, minute pink or white petals, red stamens form star in centre.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – splits into 4 segments each containing one brownish seed 2-3mm long.
plants.habitat: Very local distribution in three widely separated areas in the north. Pink form at Rocky Cape, white form above Bakers Beach.
plants.notes: Withstands exposed coastal position and salt-laden winds.

plants.name: Lasiopetalum discolor
plants.form: Small to medium shrub with hairy young growth; many branches ascending to erect.
plants.flowers: 7-19 tiny flowers crowded onto each pendant head.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – splits into 4 segments each containing one brownish seed 2-3mm long.
plants.habitat: Coastal communities of the north-west coast and Bass Strait Islands, where soil is often highly alkaline.

plants.name: Lasiopetalum macrophyllum
plants.form: Tall perennial shrub with red/brown new growth.
plants.flowers: In crowded clusters, very small petals and having rust-coloured hairs.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – splits into 4 segments each containing one brownish seed.
plants.habitat: Local on coasts in the north-west and east and on the islands of Bass Strait.
plants.notes: Vigorous in garden conditions, grows to 2m x 3m. Tolerates salt-laden winds.

plants.name: Lasiopetalum micranthum
plants.form: Dwarf spreading shrub; rusty hairs on young growth; prostrate to ascending branches also hairy.
plants.flowers: Few small flowers on short stalks.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – splits into 4 segments each containing one seed.
plants.habitat: Local in the central eastern coastal region of the State, extending inland slightly. It grows in poor, dry soil under eucalypts.
plants.notes: Requires full sun. Withstands dry periods.

plants.name: Lastreopsis acuminata
plants.form: Fern with rhizome, tufted with brown scales; fronds, up to 90cm long, arching on stipes as long as frond dark green, shiny, usually bipinnatifid.
plants.habitat: Uncommon but locally abundant across northern Tasmania, scattered and coastal elsewhere. Grows typically in dark sheltered conditions beside running water; terrestrial or lithophytic; from sea level to 200m (rarely 400m).

plants.name: Lastreopsis hispida
plants.form: Fern with fronds, up to 90cm long, erect, finely divided, dark green, thin but harsh, tri-pinnate or quadri-pinnate, ult. segments narrow, pointed.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in Tasmania, occurring in rainforest in the west and north-west. Grows in dark, moist sheltered habitats close to running water. Occurs from sea-level to 200m (rarely 300m). Grows on gravelly soil or on rocks and logs, occasionally as an epiphyte on Dicksonia.
plants.notes: This species is distinguished by its long-creeping rhizome, the dense long brown bristles covering the stipes and the finely divided frond with the narrow ultimate segments.

plants.name: Lawrencia spicata
plants.form: Stout perennial herb, stem erect, almost woody at base and purplish in colour, simple or sparingly branched.
plants.flowers: Greenish-yellow, stalkless, hermaphrodite, 5-petalled and forming a dense, terminal spike.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – separate into 1-seeded carpels, angular and pointed at the apex.
plants.habitat: Common in saltmarshes.

plants.name: Laxmannia orientalis
plants.form: Stilt-rooted herb, may be erect, tufted, or mat-forming.
plants.flowers: In 2-7 flowered clusters; outer bracts brown, with one inner bract subtending each flower.
plants.habitat: Sea-level to 200m altitude.
plants.notes: Requires sandy soils which are moisture retentive.

plants.name: Leiocarpa supina
plants.form: Spreading, aromatic, perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Heads 1.5-2.5cm across, yellow or white, solitary on slender stems and terminal.
plants.fruit: Achene without hairs; pappus bristles slender.
plants.habitat: Local in the islands of the Hogan Group and possibly other islands in Bass Strait. Found mainly on sandy soils amongst granitic rocks or limestone, fairly common on cliffs.
plants.notes: Needs excellent drainage and prefers plenty of sunshine but tolerates some shade. Hardy to light frosts and extended dry periods.

plants.name: Leionema bilobum subsp. truncatum
plants.form: Small, erect shrub.
plants.flowers: White or pinkish flowers in small clusters.
plants.habitat: Occurring in heath or woodlands on well-drained soils such as those derived from granite.
plants.notes: Attracts butterflies.

plants.name: Leionema montanum
plants.form: Much branched, spreading shrub; decumbent or prostrate.
plants.flowers: Solitary flowers in axils of upper leaves; white or pinkish petals, may be crimson-tipped.
plants.habitat: Well-drained alpine heath of north and eastern mountains and on the Western Tiers.

photos.credit: K and D Storey – Natural Values Atlas

plants.name: Leionema oldfieldii
plants.form: Erect, much branched shrub.
plants.flowers: White or pink flowers, in groups, at end of branches.
plants.habitat: Local in lower altitude heath in northern central and western mountains and on mountains in the south.

plants.name: Lemna disperma
plants.form: Small plant with green or purple-tinged, egg-shaped or round leaves, floating on the water surface.
plants.flowers: Flowers produced in either of the side pouches.
plants.fruit: Each fruit is a sac, open at a narrow tip, and containing 1-7 seeds.
plants.habitat: Common in lagoons, dams, marshes, still stream pools, lowland areas and fresh or brackish water in the north-west, Midlands, north-east, east and west coasts.

plants.name: Lemna trisulca
plants.form: Small plant floating submerged except when flowering, attached in chain-like groups. Leaves are oblong and green or brownish.
plants.flowers: 1 female and 2 male flowers are produced in one of the side pouches.
plants.fruit: Each fruit is a sac, open at a narrow tip, and containing 1-7 seeds.
plants.habitat: Pools, lakes and marshes, from sea level to 600m on King Island, north-west, east coast and west coast.

plants.name: Lepidium desvauxii
plants.form: Annual or short-lived perennial herb with stems sparsely hairy, almost glabrous.
plants.flowers: Minute, petals sometimes present, stamens 2, sepals elliptical.
plants.fruit: Capsule (silicula) with apex very shortly notched. Seeds orange-brown and densely blistered.
plants.habitat: Widespread, often a roadside weed, locally abundant near coasts.
plants.notes: Needs freely draining soil and sunshine. Some species of Lepidium were steamed on hot stones by Aboriginal people on the mainland and eaten as a green vegetable but research is lacking in this use or use as a herb or seasoning.

plants.name: Lepidium flexicaule
plants.form: Perennial herb forming weak underground stems. The leaves are 4cm long and wider towards the tip, with scalloped or indented margins. Juvenile leaves are succulent.
plants.flowers: White, arranged on stalks which become shorter towards the top of the stem.
plants.fruit: Oval capsule with a narrow wing. Seeds are 1.5-2mm long.
plants.habitat: Largely coastal, inhabits very shallow soil in rock crevices in the south-west and Bruny Island. Most common near bird rookeries.
plants.notes: May succumb to white rust disease if grown near other brassicas.

plants.name: Lepidium foliosum
plants.form: Perennial herb with branches widely divergent.
plants.flowers: Sepals and petals about 1.5mm long with 6 stamens.
plants.fruit: Capsule (silicula) 1 seed suspended in each loculus.
plants.habitat: Local on sea coasts.
plants.notes: Needs freely draining soil and sunshine. Some species of Lepidium were steamed on hot stones by Aboriginal people on the mainland and eaten as a green vegetable but research is lacking in this use or use as a herb or seasoning.

plants.name: Lepidium hyssopifolium
plants.form: Perennial herb with short, fine hairs and variable leaves.
plants.flowers: In elongating spikes, petals reduced or absent; with 2 stamens and sepals 0.75mm long.
plants.fruit: Capsule (silicula) oval to narrowly elliptical, sometimes hairy and with slight wings in upper half forming a small notch at the apex. Seeds 1.5mm long.
plants.notes: Will grow in most freely draining soils with a sunny or semi-shaded aspect.

plants.name: Lepidium pseudotasmanicum
plants.form: Annual or biennial herb with pinnate basal leaves.
plants.flowers: Borne in an elongating spike, petals reduced or absent; with 2 stamens and sepals 0.5-1mm.
plants.fruit: Capsule (silicula) elliptical, 2.5-3mm long, with wing slight in upper half, forming a narrow notch. Seeds 1.2-1.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Found in the south-east and also on the north coast of the State.

plants.name: Lepidosperma concavum
plants.form: Common sedge with branched creeping rhizome and erect fans of leaves, 20-60cm long.
plants.flowers: Flower heads dense with several narrow clusters of greyish brown spikelets; bracts blunt.
plants.fruit: Nut – pale coloured, about 1.5mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Sands, sandy heaths, wet sandy peat in coastal and near coastal areas, near sea level to about 350m, King Island, north-west, Furneaux, east coast and west coast.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Leaves used for weaving (contemporary).

plants.name: Lepidosperma curtisiae
plants.form: Tufted perennial sedge with erect leaves; stems always shorter and narrower than leaves.
plants.flowers: Flowers in spikelets, 5-6mm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – 2.5-3.5mm long; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: In open, dry Eucalyptus, Allocasuarina and Callitris woodlands, from sea level to 300m altitude, in the north-east, Midlands and east coast.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma elatius
plants.form: Loosely tufted perennial sedge with leaves up to 3.5m long, with a deeply sunken vein.
plants.flowers: Compact heads of brown flowers at the top of the stem, 16-80cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, grey-green when ripe, 2.5-3.25mm long; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: On creek banks, swamp and lagoon edges and seepage areas, from sea level to 500m altitude.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Its long, soft leaves are used for weaving (contemporary).

plants.name: Lepidosperma ensiforme
plants.form: Perennial sedge with leaves up to 1.4m long.
plants.flowers: Compact heads of brown flowers at the top of the stem, 15-80cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, reddish-brown when ripe; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: In swamps, ditches, coastal riparian scrub, shrubby heath and in shrubbery under light forest cover, from sea level to 500m altitude.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma filiforme
plants.form: Slender, perennial sedge with erect, densely clustered stems, round in cross section (up to 1mm in diameter).
plants.flowers: A spike with 1-7 flowers, up to 5cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, egg-shaped, greenish to buff, mottled brown; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Grass, sedgelands and wet heathlands, on edges of lakes, creeks and estuaries, on peaty and sandy soils, from sea level to 1100m altitude, statewide.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma forsythii
plants.form: Perennial sedge with stems much longer than leaves and orange brown rhizomes.
plants.flowers: 3-7 flowers in a spike.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, 4.5mm long; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Wet heath and sedgeland, in areas near the coast, up to 220m altitude in the north-east and east coast.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma gladiatum
plants.form: Robust sedge with flattened stems and sword-like leaves, 2cm wide, 1m or more long and all in one plane.
plants.flowers: Compact heads of brown flowers at the top of the stem, 15cm long by 6cm wide. Spikelets in dense clusters, change from pale red to black over time.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, pale to dark brown, 2-4mm long; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Coastal sands around the State.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Its leaves are used for weaving (contemporary), contributing interesting colour. Flower heads are also used in dried flower arrangements.

plants.name: Lepidosperma globosum
plants.form: Tufted perennial with erect leaves, 1-3mm wide.
plants.flowers: In a flower head 3.5-8cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, 3mm long; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: On the east coast, on river, creek and swamp edges, damp areas in dry sclerophyll woodlands and near the coast, to 300m altitude.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma gunnii
plants.form: Perennial sedge with leaves up to 35cm long, about the same length as the stems (55cm) in larger plants, and shining, blackish rhizomes.
plants.flowers: A flower head 1.5-8cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, 3-3.5mm long, changing from pale green to brown when ripe; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Open eucalypt woodland and sedgelands from sea level to 400m altitude, on the east coast, Central Highlands and Midlands.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma inops
plants.form: Perennial sedge forming dense clumps or mounds, leaves arranged in two opposite rows in the same plane, like a fan.
plants.flowers: In spikes up to 8cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, 2.5-3.25mm long, shining and dark brown when ripe; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: In open, dry situations, and sometimes in damp and shaded situations, on rocky hillsides, and from light lowland eucalypt forest to open areas up to 1200m altitude.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma laterale
plants.form: Variable perennial sedge with long, narrow, slightly curved leaves, up to 70cm long.
plants.flowers: In panicles, 4-25cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, 3mm long, changing from pale yellowish-green to pale brown when ripe; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Heaths, shrubberies and open woodland, stream edges, and moist or dryish sites from sea level to 750m altitude.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma longitudinale
plants.form: Loosely tufted perennial sedge growing from a spreading rhizome.
plants.flowers: In reddish-brown flower heads.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, shiny, wrinkled and pale greenish-brown; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Damp situations: swamps, river edges, wet scrubs and wet heaths, from sea level to 400m altitude.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma neesii
plants.form: Perennial sedge with leaves mostly shorter than stems, and a short rhizome.
plants.flowers: In an erect dark brown or blackish flower head, 4-5cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, greyish brown; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Shallow quartzitic soils on the Furneaux Islands.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma oldfieldii
plants.form: Densely tufted perennial sedge; leaves and stems with sunken midveins.
plants.flowers: In a flower head 15-35cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, 3mm long; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Damp areas in dry sclerophyll forest, and edges of wet sclerophyll forest, from sea level to 300m altitude on the east coast and south-west.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma tortuosum
plants.form: Slender, tufted sedge with spirally twisted leaves and wavy stems.
plants.flowers: 2-5 flowers in a spike.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, 3-3.5mm long and greenish; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Open eucalypt woodland in the north-east and east coast, from sea level to 460m altitude.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lepidosperma viscidum
plants.form: Perennial sedge with leaves overlapping at the base in two opposite rows, and glossy leaf margins.
plants.flowers: In a linear flower head, 8-17cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, changing from greenish-white to pale brown when ripe; contained in dry seed heads.
plants.habitat: Only known from a few sites near the coast in open, rocky situations, in the Midlands and east coast.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Leptecophylla abietina
plants.form: Erect, much-branched shrub, leaves 15mm narrow thick hard-pointed, large pink berries.
plants.flowers: White, tubular, solitary, clustered near end of branch.
plants.fruit: Drupe – round, pink and fleshy about 12mm across.
plants.habitat: Local but dominant on areas of exposed rocky coasts in west, south-west, south, and neighbouring southern islands.

plants.name: Leptecophylla divaricata
plants.form: An erect, much-branched shrub. Prickly, narrow leaves are striped white under.
plants.flowers: Small, cream with short stalk and functionally unisexual.
plants.fruit: Drupe – colour varies from pale-pink to red, about 8mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Dry, rocky sites in woodlands, usually within 40km of the south-eastern coast.
plants.notes: Not commonly cultivated. Requires a well-composted soil and heavy shade.

plants.name: Leptecophylla oxycedrus
plants.form: Compact woody shrub.
plants.flowers: White, tubular
plants.fruit: Drupe – red or pink, spherical, slightly flattened, 6–10 mm diameter.
plants.habitat: Coastal and Bass Strait Islands.
plants.notes: Not commonly cultivated. Requires a well drained soil. Tolerates extended dry periods.

plants.name: Leptecophylla parvifolia
plants.form: Erect, compact woody shrub.
plants.flowers: White, tubular, axillary near top of new growth; male and female on different plants.
plants.fruit: Drupe – red to pink, or Rarely white to greenish-grey, spherical, 5–9 mm diameter.
plants.notes: Bee attracting.

plants.name: Leptecophylla pendulosa
plants.form: Diffuse or compact shrub.
plants.flowers: White, tubular flowers; male and female on different plants.
plants.habitat: Lowland and sub-alpine habitats in the eastern highlands, including Ben Lomond.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Leptecophylla pogonocalyx subsp. decipiens
plants.form: Compact or tall shrub.
plants.flowers: White, corolla tube equal to or shorter than the calyx.

plants.name: Leptecophylla pogonocalyx subsp. pogonocalyx
plants.form: Small dense shrub.
plants.flowers: Numerous small cream bell-shaped flowers in the leaf axils; male and female on different plants.
plants.fruit: Drupe – pink or red (Rarely white), 6-8mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent on rocky slopes of hills and mountains.
plants.notes: Plants are slow to grow on to planting out size.

plants.name: Leptinella filicula
plants.form: Very small creeping herb, stout and fleshy.
plants.flowers: Daisy flower about 6mm in diameter without rays but with minute greenish-yellow tube florets.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds small with short wings and no pappus.
plants.habitat: Frequent on mountain summits and in rainforests at lower altitudes.

plants.name: Leptinella longipes
plants.form: Perennial herb with creeping hairless stems and erect leaves.
plants.flowers: Flower heads solitary, terminal on stems about as long as the leaves. Florets greenish-yellow.
plants.fruit: Achene – angled with thick spongy wings but with fewer hairs than Leptinella reptans.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in brackish and saline swamps.

plants.name: Leptinella reptans
plants.form: Perennial herb with creeping stems which have soft scattered hairs. Leaves erect.
plants.flowers: Heads solitary, terminal on slender stems, about as long as the leaves. Florets greenish/yellow.
plants.fruit: Achene with thickened spongy margins, somewhat flattened.
plants.habitat: Landward margins of saltmarshes, wet ground in a variety of localities, including alpine and sub-alpine grassland.

plants.name: Leptocarpus tenax
plants.form: Rhizome, shortly creeping.
plants.flowers: Female spikelets
plants.habitat: Heath and sedgeland and under light eucalypt forest, predominantly in coastal areas, sea level to 800m.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Leptoceras menziesii
plants.form: Colony forming orchid with a bright green, hairless, ovate-lanceolate ground-hugging leaf; wiry scape.
plants.flowers: Up to 3 small perfumed flowers that have prominent paired white lateral sepals, hooded red dorsal sepal and erect dark red petals resembling ears.
plants.habitat: Heathland and heathy open eucalypt forest on well-drained peaty and sandy soils. Locally fairly common in low and coastal areas mostly in the north, including King Is. and the Furneaux Group.

plants.name: Leptomeria drupacea
plants.form: Broom-like shrub with angular branches, often slender, leafless at flowering time.
plants.flowers: Cream, very small (under 3mm across) and numerous in spikes on the twiggy branches.
plants.fruit: Drupe – greenish, white or red, 5-8mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Occasional but widespread, more frequent in the north than in the south of the state. Sea level to at least 500m in heathland and dry open scrub forest.

plants.name: Leptomeria glomerata
plants.form: Small shrub with rigid, coarse branches; leaves reduced to tiny scales.
plants.flowers: White or pinkish, 3mm in diameter, hermaphrodite. Sometimes arranged in a spike, sometimes in clusters.
plants.habitat: Occasional near the coast in the south and west, and in peaty moors on the Central Plateau.
plants.notes: Plants are semi-parasitic, but will grow without a host, as long as they are planted out within a year. Host plants include eucalypts, acacias and native grasses.

plants.name: Leptorhynchos elongatus
plants.form: Dwarf perennial herb with woody tap-root, stems ascending/erect.
plants.flowers: Creamy white to pale yellow button-like, often profuse and with prominent stalks.
plants.habitat: Local near the Macquarie River in the Midlands.
plants.notes: Will grow in a wide range of soils and conditions but usually occurs naturally on sandy or sandy loam soils. Prefers a sunny position but will tolerate some shade.

plants.name: Leptorhynchos nitidulus
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender woody rhizomes, aerial stems arising in tufts.
plants.flowers: Pale yellow button-like to 2cm across, terminal, solitary, usually on upright stems.
plants.fruit: Achene – shortly beaked. Pappus bristles many, finely toothed.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent often growing in sandy or loam soils in open woodland and heath.
plants.notes: Should cope with sunny or semi-shaded sites in soils which are free draining. Should be hardy to moderate frosts.

plants.name: Leptorhynchos squamatus subsp. squamatus
plants.form: Perennial herb usually in clumps.
plants.flowers: Solitary yellow daisy flower heads on wiry stems to 20cm.
plants.fruit: Achene – tapering to a short neck; seeds black, seed heads turn white.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant from dry sandy and stoney places at sea level to alpine and sub-alpine grasslands.
plants.notes: Occurs in a variety of soils and climatic conditions. Adapts to most well-drained soils and tolerates full sunshine, dappled shade or semi-shade.

plants.name: Leptospermum glaucescens
plants.form: Shrub or small tree. Very variable in size and form. In west and south-west a tree to 18m.
plants.flowers: White with red centre, solitary with 5 petals.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – succulent, dark red or purple, drying to leathery. Persistent on plant for only 1 or 2 seasons.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in wet peaty heaths. Most common in lowland heath in shrub form. Widespread in scrub and forest understories in the west. Does not occur on poorly drained sites or at high altitudes.
plants.notes: Good wind break and screen plant. Bird attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Leptospermum grandiflorum
plants.form: Shrub, much-branched and spreading.
plants.flowers: Solitary, white petals, red sepals. Large flowers to 18mm wide.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – somewhat wrinkled, 1.2cm in diameter, opening into 5 valves.
plants.habitat: Occasional in the east of the State. Locally plentiful on granite rocks at an altitude of about 300m on the Freycinet Peninsula. Common by cool mountain watercourses on rocky terrain.
plants.notes: Provides useful low-level shelter in mixed species windbreaks (up to 4m). Useful in gully plantings for soil erosion control, as the roots help stabilise the soil. Bird attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Leptospermum laevigatum
plants.form: Tall shrub or small tree with spreading branches.
plants.flowers: Solitary in the axils, about 2cm in diameter.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – persistent with 8-10 longitudinal furrows, opening by 8-10 valves.
plants.habitat: Local in sandy heaths near the north-east and north-west coasts and in the islands of Bass Strait. Most common on coastal sand dunes rich in lime.
plants.notes: Its dense growth makes it useful as a windbreak or hedge. Bird attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Leptospermum lanigerum
plants.form: Erect, dense tall shrub or small tree. More typically a shrub than a tree.
plants.flowers: Creamy-white, solitary, about 1.8cm in diameter.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – button-shaped grey-brown when ripe, with defined valves at the top. Seeds are tiny, brownish “slivers” 1mm x 2mm.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant. Very hardy. Wide range of soil from acidic to strongly alkaline. Occurs in both poorly-drained and well-drained sites on moderately fertile soils in areas of high rainfall.
plants.notes: Useful for providing low-level shelter (up to 6m) in mixed species windbreaks. Also useful in gully erosion control as the fibrous roots help stabilise the soil, and the branches can produce roots when they are in contact with moist soil. Bird attracting. …

plants.name: Leptospermum nitidum
plants.form: Rigid shrub, erect and much- branched, leaves light shining green.
plants.flowers: White with green centres, to 1.5cm in diameter. Petals sometimes flat, sometimes frilled.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – deep cup-shaped when mature, nearly 1cm in diameter, scaly, and opening into 5 valves. Sepals are retained for some time around rim of fruit.
plants.habitat: Common on buttongrass plains extending into forests and scrub fringing the plains. Locally abundant in wet heaths from sea level in the south-west and west to sub-alpine on the Central Plateau. At Cradle Mountain it grows on flat areas and slopes, in alluvial soils or on glacial till. …
plants.notes: Flowers on this species are good to spectacular, sometimes petals are flat, sometimes frilled. Bird attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Leptospermum riparium
plants.form: Upright, dense well-formed shrub.
plants.flowers: Prolific, large, white with 5 round petals. At the base of the petals is a ring of short stamens.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – rounded, often have five prominent lobes on top. Each capsule contains many viable seed.
plants.habitat: Only known from a few rivers near the west coast (including the Arthur River) and the Huon River in the south-east. Restricted to river edges in areas of rainforest.
plants.notes: Despite its natural habitat being riparian, in the garden it copes well with dry conditions. Withstands winter wet, summer dry, low lying position or occasional inundation. Could be used as a hedge and highly recommended for general garden use. Bird attracting. …

plants.name: Leptospermum rupestre
plants.form: Small shrub with woody stems spreading over boulders or sometimes a bushy shrub.
plants.flowers: Five round white petals arising from a disc, with a large number of stamens.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – rounded, present throughout the year.
plants.habitat: Abundant on the dolerite mountains of the north and east. Has survived severe frosts.
plants.notes: Moderately slow growing. Bird attracting. Resistant to wildlife browsing due to its unpalatability.

plants.name: Leptospermum scoparium
plants.form: Medium to tall shrub.
plants.flowers: White, perfumed, solitary on leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – convex top and 5 cells.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in a variety of habitats, from sea level to about 1000m.
plants.notes: Prefers full sun, will tolerate periods of dryness. Bird attracting. Bee attracting. High flammability.

plants.name: Lepyrodia muelleri
plants.form: Dioecious or monoecious, rhizomes creeping.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers.
plants.habitat: Usually in wet sedgelands, sea level to 300m.

plants.name: Leucophyta brownii
