plants.form: Shrub, rigid and spreading, wiry interlacing branches form silvery mounds.
plants.flowers: Terminal clusters, many tiny white heads with 2-3 florets.
plants.habitat: Common, particularly in the north on coastal dunes, cliffs and headlands.
plants.notes: Well adapted to a range of well drained soils, including those that are alkaline. Needs abundant sunshine, tolerates frost and drought but dislikes warm to hot conditions. Especially suitable for coastal planting. Overwatering can cause death.

plants.name: Leucopogon affinis
plants.form: Erect shrub
plants.flowers: White, pink-tipped, bearded, borne in solitary spikes, often crowded at ends of branches.
plants.fruit: Drupe – ellipsoid, about 3 mm long, green at first, orange-red when ripe.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained in cultivation. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Can be grown in full shade, part shade or full sun.

plants.name: Leucopogon australis
plants.form: Shrub with erect non-hairy branches.
plants.flowers: White, with a strong sweet scent in solitary spikes crowded at the ends of branches .
plants.fruit: Drupe – spherical, somewhat flattened, fleshy and amber-yellow in colour.
plants.habitat: Local in sandy coastal heaths in the east and north.
plants.notes: Most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run which can be provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Further experimental work is necessary.

plants.name: Leucopogon collinus
plants.form: Small shrub, variable in habit, from much-branched, erect, to prostrate.
plants.flowers: White, in many flowered spikes with bearded petals.
plants.fruit: Drupes – small, succulent and fleshy. Turn from green to translucent white.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in heaths and dry places from sea level to alpine and sub-alpine.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Leucopogon oreophilus
plants.form: Prostrate; diffuse mat-forming shrub with branches 10-20cm long.
plants.habitat: Prostrate form is common on nutrient-poor ground on mountains in the west.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained in cultivation. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial.

plants.name: Leucopogon parviflorus
plants.form: Much-branches shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: White, in numerous straight, close spikes covered densely with white hairs. Buds pinkish.
plants.fruit: Drupe – cream, waxy. Turn from green to translucent white when ripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant on sandy coasts.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained in cultivation. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Leucopogon pilifer
plants.form: Dwarf shrub, prostrate to decumbent, with numerous, slender branches, young growth with long hairs.
plants.flowers: Few, white, not showy, about 2cm long.
plants.habitat: Sub-alpine areas on damp heaths beside streams, on the Central Plateau.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained in cultivation. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial.

plants.name: Leucopogon virgatus var. brevifolius
plants.form: Small, erect or spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: White (pink in bud), in 3 to 4-flowered spikes at the ends of the branches. Leaves 2–7 mm long, ovate, not pungent.
plants.fruit: Drupe – small, spherical, 2 mm diameter, almost dry, greenish-black.

plants.name: Leucopogon virgatus var. virgatus
plants.form: Small shrub with slender, wiry branches, non-hairy, erect or spreading.
plants.flowers: White, in short dense spikes, crowded at ends of branches. Sepals have prominent central vein. Leaves mostly > 7mm, lanceolate, pungent.
plants.fruit: Drupe – small spherical greenish-black, almost dry.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in poor dry soils.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained in cultivation. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial.

plants.name: Libertia pulchella var. pulchella
plants.form: Perennial herb with prominently ribbed leaves forming flattened fans.
plants.flowers: Pair or cluster of white flowers at end of flowering stem.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – 3-winged brown capsule, 3-4.5 mm diameter; contains several dark brown seeds.
plants.habitat: Damp shady places from sea level to 1100m.
plants.notes: Needs moist, shady position.

plants.name: Libertia pulchella var. pygmaea
plants.form: Sub-alpine tiny plant.

plants.name: Lilaeopsis novae-zelandiae
plants.form: Semi-aquatic plant.

plants.name: Lilaeopsis polyantha
plants.form: Rhizomatous perennial herb; submerged or emergent aquatic or bog plant growing in dense colonies.
plants.flowers: Umbels of 1-8 deep red to white flowers. Leaves 1-10cm long.
plants.habitat: Forms dense colonies in shallow water and wet mud close to water.
plants.notes: Leaves are eaten by water birds and probably fish.

plants.name: Limonium australe var. australe
plants.form: Robust rosette herb with a strong root, wide leaves up to 6cm long.
plants.flowers: Many small yellow flowers produced on 50cm tall flowering stems. Papery white or pink calyxes persist after flowering.
plants.habitat: Occurs on the seaward edge of saltmarshes.
plants.notes: Suitable for rockeries and container planting. Needs full sun and constant moisture.

plants.name: Limonium australe var. baudinii
plants.form: Glabrous short-lived perennial herb with a stout, erect, woody rootstock.
plants.flowers: Flowering stems are erect, much-branched with panicles that bear numerous spikelets. White to pink calyx, petal’s small lobes oblong and yellow.
plants.fruit: Capsule – dehiscent 5-angled capsule with a solitary brown seed 3 to 3.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Saltmarsh near small brackish streams.

plants.name: Limosella australis
plants.form: Herb, with slender rhizomes or runners.
plants.flowers: Small, solitary, and axillary.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – globular, containing numerous seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant on the margins of streams and in low-lying areas subject to flooding.

plants.name: Lindsaea linearis
plants.form: Fern with fronds to 25cm, erect, pale. Distinguishing features: the black or dark-brown axes of the lamina (broad part of the leaf), the narrow fertile fronds with screw-like pinnae. Sterile fronds shorter, broader.
plants.habitat: Common from coastal regions in Tasmania. Grows on buttongrass plains, heathland, dry sclerophyll forest and on high ground in Melaleuca or Leptospermum swamps.
plants.notes: Very difficult to establish or keep growing.

plants.name: Lindsaea trichomanoides
plants.form: Fern with fronds, 5-25cm long, usually bipinnate in the lower part, on wiry, shiny reddish stipes; rhizome short-creeping; pinnae oval or obovate.
plants.habitat: A rare rainforest species of western and southern Tasmania. Terrestrial; found in dark, moist and sheltered situations; also on rotting logs and as a low epiphyte on Nothofagus cunninghamii and Lagarostrobos franklinii.
plants.notes: Difficult to grow.

plants.name: Linum marginale
plants.form: Slender, upright herb, branched in upper parts; leave stalkless, linear or narrow lance-shaped, hairless.
plants.flowers: Blue or white in loose terminal collection.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – tan-brown when mature with usually 7-10 seeds.
plants.habitat: Most common on grassy vegetation in eastern mountains.

plants.name: Liparophyllum exaltatum
plants.form: A swamp plant with thick root; length of leaf stalk depends on depth of water.
plants.flowers: Yellow, 2-3 cm across in branched clusters held above the water.
plants.fruit: Capsule – oblong, opening at the summit into 4 valves.
plants.habitat: Common in swamps and on river flats, sea level to Central Plateau.
plants.notes: Aquatic plant.

plants.name: Liparophyllum exiguum
plants.form: Small perennial herb, has runners in wet mud, but floating and tangled when aquatic.
plants.flowers: Single pale-yellow flowers.
plants.habitat: Occasional in short alpine herbfield and aquatic vegetation in the eastern mountains, saltmarshes at Southport, lagoons at the mouth of the Pieman River, and in marshy ground at Huonville. Found in shallow fresh or brackish water and constantly wet mud.
plants.notes: Aquatic plant.

plants.name: Liparophyllum gunnii
plants.form: Small perennial herb with thick, fleshy leaves which are almost clustered in rosettes, and 12-25mm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers are solitary and white, with a slightly hairy inner surface, and borne on stout stalks.
plants.fruit: Fleshy capsule – succulent and nearly spherical, 5-6mm in diameter. Contains numerous yellow seeds, 1.2mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Margins of mountain lakes and tarns, often spreading throughout small pools, sometimes partially submerged.
plants.notes: Aquatic plant.

plants.name: Lissanthe strigosa subsp. subulata
plants.form: Small shrub, much-branched. Often forms a low-growing thicket.
plants.flowers: In clusters of 1-4 crowded at ends of branches; white, striped pink with pinkish sepals.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in dry places, usually in the understorey of woodlands.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out.

plants.name: Lobelia anceps
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender rhizomes and aerial stems, ascending or erect, angled and narrowly winged.
plants.flowers: Pale blue or lilac, solitary, on slender stems shorter than leaves. Flowers most of year.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent in salt and brackish marshes and in wet coastal heaths.
plants.notes: Prefers full sun in a damp location and may become invasive. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Lobelia gibbosa
plants.form: Glabrous annual herb with erect flowering stems and few erect, often reddish, somewhat succulent branches from base.
plants.flowers: Deep blue or bluish-purple, corolla variable in size. Anther lobes purple with hair tuft at apex.
plants.fruit: Capsule with the upper side swollen. Seeds small.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent especially on sandy heaths but also on wet moors from sea level to about 1000m.

plants.name: Lobelia irrigua
plants.form: Slender perennial herb resembling Lobelia pratioides but hairless in all parts. Stems leafy, a few cm long.
plants.flowers: Short stems or without stems, in axils with very small corolla 2-3mm long.
plants.habitat: Occasional in brackish marshes.

plants.name: Lobelia pedunculata
plants.form: Prostrate ground covering perennial herb with much-branched stems, and ascending leafy, flowering branches forming tangled patches.
plants.flowers: Solitary in axils on stems much longer than leaves; unisexual; size variable; pale blue.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent on the margins of rivers and lakes and in wet places.
plants.notes: Attractive ground cover. Useful for around a water feature where it may grow into the water. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Lobelia pratioides
plants.form: Slender perennial herb; stems creeping, with erect or ascending leafy flowering branches.
plants.flowers: Pale blue or lilac in axils on stems about as long as, or longer than leaves. Unisexual.
plants.habitat: Occasional on the margins of rivers and in wet places in the Midlands and north of the state.

plants.name: Lobelia rhombifolia
plants.form: Glabrous annual herb with erect branches arising from slender, fleshy white, branched rootstock.
plants.flowers: Solitary, terminal; lobes bright blue, tube and throat of corolla pale greenish-yellow.
plants.habitat: Local in a variety of locations near the east coast.

plants.name: Lobelia surrepens
plants.form: Hairless perennial herb with slender leafy stems, creeping or prostrate.
plants.flowers: Corolla pale blue or almost white, tube slightly longer than sepals, lobes narrow at base.
plants.habitat: In short alpine herbfield and wet grassland in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Lomandra longifolia
plants.form: Tussocky plant
plants.flowers: Small, crowded into spikes, yellowish or straw-coloured. Male and female on different plants.
plants.fruit: 3-parted capsule. Stems have globose capsules in spikes.
plants.habitat: Very common and widespread especially in dry stony or rocky places, under light forest cover, coastal shrubberies, heaths and dunes from sea level to about 750m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Flowers provide food and foliage provides refuge for insects. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Used in traditional Palawa basket weaving. Also used in contemporary basket weaving.

plants.name: Lomandra nana
plants.form: Tufted, with narrow, curved leaves, 5-20cm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers almost at ground level in very small clusters.
plants.fruit: 3-parted capsule. Stems have egg-shaped capsules in spikes, which turn brown when ripe, and contain 2-3 hard, cream, orange, brown or reddish seeds.
plants.habitat: Dry banks and hillsides, open situations or under light forest cover to 300m, in the Midlands and on the east coast.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Lomatia polymorpha
plants.form: Erect to spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: Large, creamy-white in heavy heads. Very sweet-scented.
plants.fruit: Woody seed follicle – stalked follicle opening into a wide, oval-shaped flat plate revealing winged seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent on mountains from about 400m-1000m and at sea level on the west coast and in the south. Grows as an understorey shrub in high altitude forest.
plants.notes: Requires moist well-drained soil. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Lomatia tasmanica
plants.form: Mid to tall slender shrub, branches often few, erect, young growth hairy.
plants.flowers: Dull crimson in terminal racemes.
plants.habitat: Known only from the southern end of the Bathurst Range in the south-west at altitudes from sea level to about 280m.
plants.notes: A distinctive and attractive plant rarely cultivated and difficult to maintain for more than a few years. May do well as a container plant in ferneries.

plants.name: Lomatia tinctoria
plants.form: Small shrub
plants.flowers: White or cream in loose spikes, pleasant scent.
plants.fruit: Woody seed follicle – woody fruits are guitar-shaped. Seeds are winged.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent, especially in poor soil, from sea level to about 900m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Lordhowea velleioides
plants.form: Short-lived perennial herb, stems erect, finely striate and sparingly branched.
plants.flowers: Flower heads in large terminal clusters, often numerous about 2.5cm in diameter, florets yellow.
plants.fruit: Achene – ribbed; pappus-bristles fine and silky.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent in moist places on hills, especially after fires.

plants.name: Lotus australis
plants.form: Perennial, sometimes shrubby at base, erect or ascending.
plants.flowers: Pea, petals white to purple-red, often creamy pink, keel shorter, darker, usually 3-8 together.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – straight, 3-5 cm long, brown when mature, contains up to 15 dark brown, hard seeds. Valves twist spirally at maturity.
plants.habitat: Local on sandy coasts. Resistant to salt spray.
plants.notes: Often short-lived in cultivation, 3-4 years being the normal life span.

plants.name: Luzula acutifolia subsp. acutifolia
plants.form: Densely tufted perennial forming small cushions.
plants.flowers: Cone-shaped or oval spike, single head or often with 1-3 clusters at base, papery bracts.
plants.habitat: Widespread on the Central Highlands and on mountains of the west coast and Ben Lomond.

plants.name: Luzula atrata
plants.form: Loosely tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Stems stiffly erect at maturity, 7-12cm tall. Cone-shaped or globular spike with light brown bracts.
plants.fruit: Nut – dark brown to blackish with small, raised protuberances towards the tip. Seeds black.
plants.habitat: Local on the Cradle Mountain plateau of the Central Highlands.

plants.name: Luzula australasica subsp. australasica
plants.form: Sturdy, loosely tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: A terminal head of clustered spikelets with cream, triangular bracts.
plants.fruit: Nut – reddish-brown. Seeds black with small white ‘outgrowth’.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent on mountains of the Central Highlands, Ben Lomond, south-west, Mount Field and kunanyi/Mt Wellington.

plants.name: Luzula densiflora
plants.form: A loosely tufted perennial, with erect flowering stems.
plants.flowers: Flowers in dense, elongated terminal clusters, with light brown floral bracts.
plants.fruit: Nut – reddish-brown. Seeds black with small white ‘outgrowth’.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet grassy places and hollows in sandy heaths from sea level to sub-alpine altitudes.

plants.name: Luzula flaccida
plants.form: A loosely tufted perennial variable in form of flowers and size of parts.
plants.flowers: Either above leaves with clusters about 5mm in diameter or below leaves in 1-3 heads about 10mm in diameter.
plants.fruit: Nut – cream or pale greenish sometimes with red-brown margins. Seeds black about 1mm long with white ‘outgrowth’.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent among grass in moist open places from sea level to sub-alpine altitudes.

plants.name: Luzula meridionalis
plants.form: A loosely tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Umbels with 1-10 spreading branches of uneven length carrying flowers in small clusters.
plants.fruit: Nut – chestnut brown, shining. Seeds black with white or cream “outgrowth”.
plants.habitat: Widespread in open forests and grasslands from sea level to sub-alpine habitats in the north-east, Midlands, east coast and south-west regions.

plants.name: Luzula modesta
plants.form: A tufted perennial forming long slender stolons at or just below surface or ground.
plants.flowers: 1-8 flowers in a single narrow-oblong spike or in 2-3 adjacent groups.
plants.fruit: Nut – pale yellowish-brown with margins of the valves darker. Seeds about 1mm long, dark purplish-brown to black.
plants.habitat: Local in damp sub-alpine habitats, in areas of seepage often growing with mosses in the Central Highlands and at Ben Lomond.

plants.name: Luzula novae-cambriae
plants.form: A loosely tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Flowering stems usually longer than leaves with terminal umbels of 2-7 short branches.
plants.fruit: Nut – dark brown, shining, often paler below. Seeds black.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet alpine to sub-alpine habitats in the north-east, west coast, Central Highlands, Ben Lomond, south-west and Mount Field regions.

plants.name: Luzula poimena
plants.form: A tufted perennial with a short, stout rhizome.
plants.flowers: Pyramidal head of densely packed flower spikes sometimes with short spike below head.
plants.fruit: Nut – light yellowish-brown, usually reddish-brown at the apex, when mature. Seeds dark reddish-brown with the outermost layer of the wall very thin and translucent.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet alpine and sub-alpine habitats in the Central Highlands and south-west.

plants.name: Lycopodiella diffusa
plants.form: Prostrate fern ally, stems often tinged reddish brown to black.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in the west and south of the State where it is a terrestrial species of permanently wet and badly drained soils.

plants.name: Lycopodiella lateralis
plants.form: Fern ally with weak upright stems needing support when growing amongst grasses or below shrubs.
plants.habitat: In exposed situations becomes discoloured and has tightly compacted growth making it difficult to distinguish from Lycopodiella diffusa. Common and widespread in Tasmania especially in the west and south.

plants.name: Lycopodiella serpentina
plants.form: Fern ally with brittle pale-green, long-creeping stems that root at regular intervals and large erect stroboli.
plants.habitat: Extremely rare on mainland Tasmania and known only from a few disjunct locations. Several known populations on King Island and Cape Barren Island.

plants.name: Lycopodium deuterodensum
plants.form: Fern ally with long creeping rhizomes and erect aerial stems. Sterile leaves narrowly triangular; fertile leaves in erect cone-like spikes.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in lowland Tasmania in well-drained sites in heathland or dry sclerophyll forest. Also colonises road cuttings where it grows with its rhizomes exposed.
plants.notes: An attractive and distinct species with large upright stems resembling a small conifer. This species has not yet been successfully cultivated with collected plants dying quickly.

plants.name: Lycopodium fastigiatum
plants.form: Upright, bushy and much-branched fern ally with underground rhizomes; leaves overlapping, shaped like narrow lance.
plants.habitat: Terrestrial species. Abundant alpine or sub-alpine species found in moist, well-drained high plateaux or sunny clearings in highland forest; may occur at much lower altitudes in shady situations, particularly in disturbed areas. In extreme exposure leaves are tinged orange.

plants.name: Lycopodium scariosum
plants.form: Fern ally with wiry, prostrate main stems, rooting at intervals; leaves in two rows, in a flat plane.
plants.habitat: Terrestrial, common in alpine areas of Tasmania, around 1000m or above except on the west coast where it is found lower down. Grows in moist well-drained soils of stony plateaux and in low shrubberies.

plants.name: Lycopus australis
plants.form: Perennial herb with erect rigid stems.
plants.flowers: Small, white, four-lobed flowers, arranged in dense clusters in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Nut – 1.5 mm long with a smooth outer surface.
plants.habitat: Occasional but widespread in moist shaded places.

plants.name: Lyperanthus suaveolens
plants.form: Erect linear-lanceolate, greyish-green leaf; stout dark scape.
plants.flowers: Strongly perfumed and 2-8 red-brown flowers that have widely spreading sepals and petals, a hooded dorsal sepal and a prominent yellow tipped labellum.
plants.habitat: Heathy and sedgy open eucalypt forest and woodland, sedgeland, heathland and grassland on poorly drained to well-drained sandy and peaty soils, often in dense vegetation. Locally fairly common in coastal and near coastal lowland areas from north-eastern to south-eastern Tas. …
plants.notes: Flowering is not stimulated by fires.

plants.name: Lythrum hyssopifolia
plants.form: Slender, erect annual herb with alternate leaves about 2cm long.
plants.flowers: Small, white to pinkish-mauve flowers, 5mm in diameter, which are borne in the leaf axils along the length of the stem. Alternate leaves and solitary flowers distinguish it from L. salicaria.
plants.habitat: Open vegetation prone to flooding, including roadside ditches.
plants.notes: Often self-sows in open ground. Requires constant moisture.

plants.name: Lythrum salicaria
plants.form: Erect perennial herb with a stout aerial stem, and lance-shaped, opposite, stalkless leaves.
plants.flowers: Flowers are tubular, deep pink to purple with 5 or 6 petals, and borne in spikes.
plants.habitat: Swamps, streambanks and rivers in the north and north-east, and between gaps in Melaleuca ericifolia forest.
plants.notes: Often self-sows in open ground. Requires constant moisture. Can reproduce vegetatively and may be bird dispersed. An easy garden plant which thrives in any soil, and forms a bushy and well-shaped clump. Cut back to ground level in winter.

plants.name: Machaerina acuta
plants.form: Perennial sedge with flattened stems, leaves often spirally twisted and blackened towards the tip.
plants.flowers: Flower head 2-5cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – barrel-shaped, blackish and shining, 2-2.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Coastal areas on sandy and peaty soils, in heaths and sedgelands.
plants.notes: Reasonably drought tolerant once established. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Machaerina arthrophylla
plants.form: Highly variable perennial sedge, with leaves wider than stems and rhizomes up to 25cm long.
plants.flowers: In flower heads 7-45cm long.
plants.habitat: Lagoons, marshes, streams and wet heaths, to 1150m altitude.
plants.notes: Reasonably drought tolerant once established. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Machaerina articulata
plants.form: Perennial sedge with hollow stems which are divided internally by partitions. The upper leaves have a soft hollow blade which can be up to 120 cm long.
plants.flowers: In loosely clustered flower heads 30-40cm long, containing many red-brown spikelets of flowers.
plants.fruit: Nut – spindle-shaped and triangular in cross-section, 3mm long.
plants.habitat: Along rivers on the north-east coast.
plants.notes: Reasonably drought tolerant once established. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Machaerina gunnii
plants.form: Perennial sedge with round, reed-like, crowded shoots, leaves sometimes spirally twisted, stems leafless and hollow.
plants.flowers: Flower head is 2.5-24 cm long and made up of spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nut – either broad spindle shaped or almost spherical with a rounded tip, 2.5-3.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Marshes, wet moors, creek and river banks throughout the State, to 750m altitude.
plants.notes: Reasonably drought tolerant once established. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Machaerina juncea
plants.form: Perennial sedge with creeping rhizome, shoots arising in clusters, stems pale green with white lines.
plants.flowers: Red-brown flower head up to 6cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – dark red-brown and shining, 3mm long.
plants.habitat: All coasts, estuaries and sandy and peaty soils, buttongrass moorlands, heaths and coastal scrub, dunes, and creek and marsh edges to 250m altitude.
plants.notes: Reasonably drought tolerant once established. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Machaerina rubiginosa
plants.form: Perennial sedge with hollow stems, both stems and leaves 80cm long.
plants.flowers: In flower heads up to 40cm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – orange, smooth and shining when mature, 3mm long.
plants.habitat: Recorded from a marsh in the Tamar Valley and a creek near Gladstone.
plants.notes: Reasonably drought tolerant once established. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Machaerina tetragona
plants.form: Perennial sedge with leaves and culms square-shaped in cross section, and a spreading rhizome.
plants.flowers: In red-brown, 2-20cm long flower heads.
plants.habitat: Damp heath and sedgelands, marshes and the edges of creeks and lakes, to 500m altitude.
plants.notes: Reasonably drought tolerant once established. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Malva preissiana
plants.form: Short-lived perennial shrub with hairy young growth and branches.
plants.flowers: White to lilac flowers to 6 cm in diameter, in clusters in leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – turns light brown and becomes papery at maturity. Contains numerous seeds which are dark brown and hard when mature.
plants.habitat: Generally more prevalent in areas subject to flooding or where the soil has been disturbed.

plants.name: Mazus pumilio
plants.form: Small perennial prostrate herb with green rosettes arising from rhizomes, leaves 1.5-7.5cm long.
plants.flowers: Purple (rarely white), 1.5cm long, with two white protuberances at the opening of the floral tube. Flowers are held above the leaves on slender stalks.
plants.habitat: Frequent in lowland swampy ground and coastal sites.
plants.notes: Prefers a damp situation with some sun, and is ideal for pool edges. Plant at 50cm intervals. Spreads rapidly by layering. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Meionectes brownii
plants.form: Aquatic or semi-aquatic perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Flowers are insignificant, greenish with red petals, with up to 11 per head in upper axils.
plants.habitat: Near the coast and in freshwater pools and permanently wet sites where there is ample sunshine, in the south-west, west, and north coasts.

plants.name: Melaleuca armillaris subsp. armillaris
plants.form: Rounded, spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: White or rarely, pink, bottle-brush type flowers.
plants.notes: Excellent windbreak, resistant to salt spray. Hardy plant. Bird attracting. Susceptible to browsing by possums and wallabies.

plants.name: Melaleuca ericifolia
plants.form: Tall shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Creamy white in spikes.
plants.habitat: Withstands severe coastal conditions and is moderately frost hardy. Occurs as a dominant of forest and scrub in poorly drained areas with moderately fertile soil. It also extends as an understorey species in eucalypt forest.
plants.notes: Recommended for wet areas and as a second-line windbreak in coastal conditions. Will take salt exposure but needs protection of front-line plants. Slightly frost tender when young. Will accept most soils and aspects. Good for shady areas. Bird attracting. Bee attracting. …

plants.name: Melaleuca gibbosa
plants.form: Shrub with branches often slender and spreading.
plants.flowers: Mauve, in small dense oblong spikes. Flowers sparsely throughout the year, mainly spring.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – in cylindrical spikes. The branches continue to grow so that old fruits encircle the stem. Seeds are very fine, like short hairs.
plants.habitat: Wet, peaty ground in east, north-east and north-west. Grows vigorously in exposed spots such as Cape Bruny and Hurricane Heath.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Susceptible to browsing by possums and wallabies.

plants.name: Melaleuca pallida
plants.form: Stiffly erect dense shrub.
plants.flowers: Spikes 4-8cm long of pale yellow flowers.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule 3.9-6.6 mm long; retained on plant for years.
plants.habitat: Widespread along streams, on hillsides in wet areas.
plants.notes: Useful in shelter belts. Flowers provide food for nectar-eating mammals. Bee attracting as well as attracting other insects. Bird attracting (insect-eating birds). Good for direct seeding if sufficient moisture available. Susceptible to browsing by possums and wallabies.

plants.name: Melaleuca pustulata
plants.form: Glabrous much-branched shrub with spreading crown.
plants.flowers: Yellow, few together in terminal heads about l cm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Local near the east coast as at Oyster Bay and up to 20km inland.
plants.notes: Melaleuca pustulata has pustule-like protuberances on its leaves which distinguish it from Melaleuca ericifolia. Bird attracting. Susceptible to browsing by possums and wallabies.

plants.name: Melaleuca squamea
plants.form: Small to medium erect shrub.
plants.flowers: Usually pink-purple less commonly white or yellow, terminal spherical clusters, no stalks.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule 3.5-7.0 mm long; persistent for several years.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet heaths, sea level to approximately 1500m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by possums and wallabies.

plants.name: Melaleuca squarrosa
plants.form: An erect shrub.
plants.flowers: Small bottlebrush-like flowers which are usually pale yellow.
plants.habitat: Common in shallow gullies and damp areas in heathlands and forests. Widespread and abundant in damp sandy soil.
plants.notes: A good street tree and screen and hedging plant. Will shoot back from a woody root stock after coppicing. Bird attracting. Bee attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Susceptible to browsing by possums and wallabies.

plants.name: Melaleuca virens
plants.form: Erect or spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: Flower spikes pale yellow or greenish yellow.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – turn from green to grey brown and develop distinct valves when mature. Very fine seed which has very high viability. Seed usually persistent.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet places, especially in alpine and sub-alpine habitats.
plants.notes: Valued in environmental plantings (e.g. bird attracting, bee attracting, wildlife habitat, providing valuable cover and food, erosion control and as components of windbreaks to enhance agricultural productivity), and amenity plantings. Adapts to dry situations. …

plants.name: Melicytus angustifolius subsp. angustifolius
plants.form: Spreading to procumbent shrub. Branches bearing slender, pliant spines.
plants.flowers: Flowers cream, usually mauve in the distal half.
plants.habitat: Rare plant of estuarine habitat in northern Tasmania.
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Melicytus angustifolius subsp. divaricatus
plants.form: Rigid, erect to spreading to procumbent shrub.
plants.flowers: Flowers cream, usually mauve in the distal half.
plants.habitat: Widespread species usually found in dry areas under light forest or woodland or along river banks.
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Mentha australis
plants.form: Perennial herb; erect or ascending stems branch at 30-60 cm high.
plants.flowers: Numerous white flowers in axillary false whorls.
plants.habitat: Local in marshes in northern and central districts.
plants.notes: Vigorous, can be invasive in moist locations. Strong peppermint aroma.

plants.name: Mentha diemenica var. diemenica
plants.form: Suckering perennial herb, forming a dense ground cover, with highly aromatic leaves.
plants.flowers: Flowers are small, usually lilac or pale mauve.
plants.habitat: Occasional but widespread from sea level to alpine and sub-alpine grassland.
plants.notes: Can be used to flavour drinks. Can withstand occasional foot traffic, however needs a moist situation. It may become invasive in favourable conditions. It may defoliate in dry or very cold conditions.

plants.name: Micrantheum hexandrum
plants.form: Hardy, densely growing shrub with slender erect branches.
plants.flowers: Small, numerous, male and female on different plants. Yellowish or cream.
plants.fruit: Capsule – ovoid, glabrous, 5–8 mm long. Seed cylindrical, 3.5–4.0 mm long, light reddish brown, glossy.
plants.habitat: Common on river banks, along water courses and in gullies in east and north.
plants.notes: A hardy, densely growing shrub.

plants.name: Micrantheum serpentinum
plants.form: Heath-like, much-branched woody shrub, with leathery leaves in groups of 2-5 which half-encircle the stems.
plants.flowers: Solitary or in small clusters, in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Capsule – oval-shaped and yellow-brownish, with purplish-black protrusions from the top.
plants.habitat: Heathy shrubland, moist shady gullies and creek banks on serpentine soils in the west of the State.

plants.name: Microcachrys tetragona
plants.form: Spreading shrub with some erect branchlets. Branchlets appear square in cross section.
plants.fruit: Cone – Male cones – small, terminal, ovoid. Female cones – terminal with 20-28 fertile scales. Ripe seed embedded in the bract scale which becomes fleshy and scarlet in colour.
plants.habitat: Frequent in sub-alpine habitats, exposed ridges and wet moors on mountains of the Central Plateau, west and south-west at about 1000-1300m.

plants.name: Microlaena stipoides var. stipoides
plants.form: Tufted perennial grass with underground stems. Leaves have long, coarse hairs and a prominent midrib on the lower surface, and a few scattered hairs on the upper surface.
plants.flowers: In compact flower heads up to 20cm long, at the end of long drooping flowering stems.
plants.habitat: Widespread in a wide range of open habitats, from sea level to 700m altitude.
plants.notes: Beware of planting this grass in the garden, as without mowing/grazing, it grows lanky, spreads by stolons throughout other plants and self-seeds. It is recognised as a useful species for a regularly mown lawn or pasture feed.

plants.name: Microlaena tasmanica var. subalpina
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial. Leaves whitish upper surface, dark on lower surface. Damp shaded situations.
plants.flowers: Loosely pyramidal flowerheads to 25cm long.
plants.habitat: Central Highlands, south-west, west coast; sea level to 960m.

plants.name: Microlaena tasmanica var. tasmanica
plants.form: Leaves 2-25 cm long.
plants.flowers: Compact flowerheads.
plants.habitat: Highland areas to 1160m altitude, in the Central Highlands, south-west and west coast.

plants.name: Microseris lanceolata
plants.form: Perennial herb with fleshy edible tubers.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow daisy-like, solitary on long stalks. Flower head and bud droop downward.
plants.fruit: Achene – 8-10mm long with a hard, swollen base. Seeds with 14-24 pappus of flattened scales.
plants.habitat: Widespread and occasional in grasslands and open places from sea level to mountain plateaux.
plants.notes: Very susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Microsorum pustulatum subsp. pustulatum
plants.form: Male fronds upright, strap-like; female fronds shaped like a kangaroo’s paw. Fronds variable in size (5-50cm) and shape, from simple up to 8 pairs of lateral lobes.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant from sea level to at least 850m within boulder grottos on low mountain summits. Grows on rocks or logs and is epiphytic on Dicksonia and a range of tree species in rainforest, wet sclerophyll, fern gullies and sheltered sites in dry sclerophyll forest. …

plants.name: Microtis arenaria
plants.form: A robust, green to yellowish-green onion orchid; green to greenish-yellow tubular leaf 300-600mm long.
plants.flowers: 10-60 pale green to yellowish green, densely crowded flowers with recurved lateral sepals and a dorsal sepal that is prominently turned up at the tip. A long rectangular labellum, constricted in the middle and noticeably notched at the apex.
plants.habitat: Found in damper spots in coastal heathland, grassland and woodland.

plants.name: Microtis parviflora
plants.form: A slender, green onion orchid; leaf 200-500mm long.
plants.flowers: Up to 80 tiny, crowded flowers. Dorsal sepal up to 3mm with only a very slight upturn at the apex. Small, triangular to round labellum with smooth or only slightly ruffled margin.
plants.habitat: Widely distributed in coastal grassland, heathland and sedgeland on poor to moderately drained soils. Often colonises disturbed sites and is common in gardens that have been mulched.

plants.name: Microtis unifolia
plants.form: Robust, green onion orchid with a single tubular, green leaf, 100-400mm long.
plants.flowers: A robust green to greenish-yellow onion orchid with up to 100 crowded flowers, a short, oblong labellum with undulating margins, two dark-green, mounded basal calli.
plants.habitat: Common in disturbed grassy environments, such as roadsides and lawns.

plants.name: Milligania densiflora
plants.form: Tufted, rhizomatous herb; leaves to 55cm long and 5cm wide, flowering stems 30-50cm high.
plants.flowers: Flowers white, sometimes tinged red on the tube and at the throat, rarely pink all over.
plants.habitat: Prefers damp situations, boggy heaths. Central Highlands, south-west and west coast, 700-1500m altitude.

plants.name: Milligania johnstonii
plants.form: Mat-forming rhizomatous herb.
plants.flowers: Conspicuous white flowers, about 1cm across.
plants.habitat: Sea-level to 1000m altitude in the south-west.

plants.name: Milligania lindoniana
plants.form: Rhizomatous herb, forms dense mats; leaves to 20cm long and 2.4cm wide.
plants.flowers: Flowers white, with dark red centre, on erect stems up to 40cm high.
plants.habitat: Alpine sedgeland in central and western mountains and also in short alpine herbfields associated with snow patches and bolster heath. 1250 – 1450 m altitude.

plants.name: Milligania longifolia
plants.form: Perennial herb with creeping rhizomes and long narrow leaves up to 125 cm long and 2.5 cm wide.
plants.flowers: Numerous white or cream flowers with greenish centres, to about 1cm long.
plants.habitat: Rocky cliffs on quartzite or limestone along the Gordon and Franklin rivers in the south-west at low altitudes and along the Vale River in the Central Highlands at 700m altitude.

plants.name: Milligania stylosa
plants.form: Perennial, rhizomatous herb with leaves to 50cm long and up to 3.5cm wide.
plants.flowers: Profuse, conspicuous white flowers with greenish centres, to about 1.3cm across.
plants.habitat: In exposed, rocky areas and cliff ledges where there is seepage. At altitudes of 900-1200m in southern and western regions.

plants.name: Millotia muelleri
plants.form: Small annual herb, densely hairy with stems terete, slender and wiry.
plants.flowers: Florets all hermaphrodite, tubular and one end 4-5 toothed. Outer florets curving over bracts.
plants.fruit: Achene – cylindrical, tapering to slender beak.
plants.notes: Rare annual.

plants.name: Millotia tenuifolia var. tenuifolia
plants.form: Slender annual herb, often branched at base and white with soft woolly hairs.
plants.flowers: Yellow on terminal stalks to about 0.5cm across.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in dry places. Occurs in a wide range of habitats and soils.
plants.notes: Should do best in free draining soils with a warm sunny or semi-shaded aspect.

plants.name: Mitrasacme pilosa var. pilosa
plants.form: Small, slender prostrate perennial herb with coarse, stiff hairs and stems 3-30cm long.
plants.flowers: Small, white with four petals, terminal and in the axils of the upper leaves. The inner surface of the tube is hairy.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in a range of habitats, often in sandy places or in heaths. Sea level to about 830m.
plants.notes: Not widely grown

plants.name: Mitrasacme pilosa var. stuartii
plants.form: Low-growing, tufted perennial herb forming clumps to 20 cm diameter.
plants.flowers: Flowers white on long slender stalks.
plants.notes: Not widely grown

plants.name: Mitrasacme serpyllifolia
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender, creeping, much-branched stems, forming sparse, short mats.
plants.flowers: Solitary, white and about 4mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: On mountains near the west coast, and grassy plains in the north-west, about 670m above sea level.

plants.name: Monotoca elliptica
plants.form: Tall shrub, much-branched or sometimes a small tree.
plants.flowers: White, often profuse.
plants.fruit: Drupe – oval, orange-red, fleshy, about 4mm long.
plants.habitat: Local on coasts in the north and east. Common component of coastal forest, heathland and dunes. Drought tolerant.

plants.name: Monotoca empetrifolia
plants.form: Small shrub with spreading, almost prostrate branches, densely foliaged.
plants.flowers: 2-3 together in short spikes.
plants.habitat: Widespread in alpine heath in the eastern and central mountains above 900m and often associated with rocky sites.
plants.notes: Infrequently cultivated. Should do well in a well-drained position and makes a good container plant or bonsai.

plants.name: Monotoca glauca
plants.form: A densely branched shrub or small tree with slender branches.
plants.flowers: Small, cream, solitary in axillary spikes. Trees often unisexual. Flowers sweetly fragrant.
plants.fruit: Drupe – greenish when mature, only about 2mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Common understorey shrub at edges of wet forest and in previously logged areas.
plants.notes: An ideal hedging plant. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Monotoca linifolia subsp. algida
plants.form: Erect, woody shrub, usually compact, or small tree.
plants.flowers: Flowers with 5 petals. Smaller, shorter leaves than Monotoca linifolia subsp. linifolia.
plants.fruit: Drupe – red to pink or purple, ovoid to spherical.

plants.name: Monotoca linifolia subsp. linifolia
plants.form: Tall shrub.
plants.flowers: Flower has 4 petals.

plants.name: Monotoca scoparia
plants.form: Much-branched with compact growth habit, dwarf to medium shrub. Has blackish bark and leaves end in a prickly point.
plants.flowers: Sometimes solitary but often 2-4 crowded in very short spike. Creamy white sweetly fragrant.
plants.fruit: Drupe – oval, dull yellowish in colour.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in sandy coastal heaths in the north-west and east. Withstands extended dry periods.
plants.notes: Takes many years to reach maximum height. Good for background planting. A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out.

plants.name: Monotoca submutica var. autumnalis
plants.form: Erect and dense shrub.
plants.flowers: 1-4 flowers in the leaf axils of the upper branches.
plants.fruit: Drupe – yellow to orange or red, ovoid, 2-4mm long.
plants.notes: Not widely cultivated. Should do best in well drained, moist soil with some sun.

plants.name: Monotoca submutica var. submutica
plants.form: Much branched compact shrub.
plants.flowers: tubular with 5 white petals, at ends of branches
plants.fruit: Drupe – spherical, green becoming orange-red as it matures.
plants.notes: Not widely cultivated. Should do best in well drained, moist soil with some sun.

plants.name: Montia australasica
plants.form: Prostrate perennial with creeping stems which root at nodes.
plants.flowers: 1-6 fragrant, white or pale pink flowers, 1.5-2 cm across on terminal cymes on stalks 3.5 cm long.
plants.habitat: Widely distributed, occurring at most altitudes; common in swamps.
plants.notes: Has the capacity to be dormant during dry periods and regrow when conditions are suitable. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Montia fontana subsp. chondrosperma
plants.form: Small annual to perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Small, terminal white flowers on stalks.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – 3 valves. Contains 3 black seeds.
plants.habitat: Common in wet places.

plants.name: Montitega dealbata
plants.form: Prostrate with slender woody branches forming a dense mat 15-40cm in diameter.
plants.flowers: White, tube longer than sepals. Flowers solitary in leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Drupe – red, spherical, about 5mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Widespread as dominant in mat heath on the summit of mountains and subordinate in other types of heath .
plants.notes: In cultivation they require a well-composted soil and heavy shade. In less favourable conditions growth is extremely slow.

plants.name: Muehlenbeckia adpressa
plants.form: Climber with stems twining, leaves crowded, alternate, glabrous, may have reddish tonings, margins usually crinkled, apex pointed .
plants.flowers: Cream to green, 2-5 per cluster, in axillary spikes to about 8cm long. Flowers most of the year.
plants.fruit: Nut – small, ovoid, black or dark red-brown, 3-angled, glabrous. Nuts are enclosed in a small cone-shaped structure to 5mm long.
plants.habitat: Occurs mainly on the coast and is often very prominent but may also be found further inland.
plants.notes: Tolerates sunshine but does best in semi-shade. Copes well with salt spray and strong winds and is a useful screening climber.

plants.name: Muehlenbeckia axillaris
plants.form: Dwarf, often matted shrub or climber with branches red-brown to blackish, prostrate to ascending, crowded or may be sparse.
plants.flowers: Very small, greenish in axillary or terminal clusters (few-flowered).
plants.fruit: Nut – long, shining, black. Nuts are enclosed in a small cone-shaped structure to 5mm long.
plants.habitat: Occasional in alpine and deciduous heath at low altitude in eastern and central mountains especially in rocky places. Will tolerate short dry periods.
plants.notes: Useful for massed plantings, capable of forming an impenetrable barrier.

plants.name: Muehlenbeckia gunnii
plants.form: Perennial twining plant with woody stems, often climbing over trees.
plants.flowers: Pale yellow 8-9mm across in straight leafy spikes several centimetres long.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet forests, along roadsides and in fern gullies; may be a nuisance blanketing other vegetation. Resistant to salt.
plants.notes: Can be used as a ground cover.

plants.name: Myoporum insulare
plants.form: Tall woody shrub or small tree. Leaves thick, elliptical and pointed, slightly toothed towards tips, 3-9cm long.
plants.flowers: Small, 5-petalled flowers, white spotted with purple, 7mm wide and occurring in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Drupe – purple to black, succulent, about 8mm wide.
plants.habitat: Common on sandy coasts.
plants.notes: Suitable as a hedge or screening plant, especially in sandy soil and other well-drained positions, resistant to salt spray. Tolerates salt winds and dry conditions. The fruits are salty-sweet and edible.

plants.name: Myoporum parvifolium
plants.form: Small prostrate shrub with trailing, reddish stems 60-100cm long, and thick, more or less succulent leaves.
plants.flowers: Star-shaped white, pink or pale lilac flowers with purple spots, solitary or 2-3 together.
plants.habitat: Restricted to gahnia sedgeland at Long Point and roadside allocasuarina forest near West End, Flinders Island.
plants.notes: Prefers well-drained position. Bee attracting.

plants.name: Myosotis australis subsp. australis
plants.form: Annual herb with stiff, bristle-like hairs on the upper part of the stem, and leaves in a basal rosette. Leaves on the lower parts of the stem are alternate.
plants.flowers: Flowers yellow or white, with rounded petals, in clusters on the end of the main stem and on the ends of the axillary branches.
plants.fruit: Nutlets are dark brown and 1.5mm long.
plants.habitat: Widespread, from coastal sand dunes to mountains at 1000m altitude.

plants.name: Myosotis exarrhena
plants.form: Perennial herb with long hairs, erect stems and a stout rootstock.
plants.flowers: Sweet-scented, white or pale blue flowers, in flower heads on the ends of stems.
plants.fruit: Nutlets are dark brown and 2mm long.
plants.habitat: Widespread but local, from sea level to mountains at 870m altitude.

plants.name: Myosurus australis
plants.form: Short-lived annual herb with a rosette of rather fleshy narrow linear leaves up to 10 cm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers solitary, terminal, very small and greenish-yellow.
plants.fruit: 100 to 300 dry, leathery achenes at the top of the flower stem in a dense slender spike up to 4 cm long.
plants.habitat: Found at 2 sites, in the Southern Midlands (400m) and in the Central Plateau (925m).

plants.name: Myriophyllum amphibium
plants.form: Small reddish perennial herb with creeping stems.
plants.flowers: Solitary. Male flowers with narrow pink petals, females with bright red stigmas and no petals.
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – tiny, egg-shaped, about 1mm long, split into 2-4 segments when mature. Seed may be difficult to find.
plants.habitat: Local in freshwater and tidal river estuaries, particularly in the south-west.

plants.name: Myriophyllum austropygmaeum
plants.form: Mat forming perennial alpine or sub-alpine plant of marshes.
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – splits into 2-4 segments when mature. Seed may be difficult to find.

plants.name: Myriophyllum integrifolium
plants.form: Very small perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Solitary, in leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – splits into 2-4 segments when mature. Seed may be difficult to find.
plants.habitat: Rare, in swamps and wet sites in pastures in the north of the state.

plants.name: Myriophyllum muelleri
plants.form: Slender, glabrous aquatic herb; stems up to 60cm long.
plants.flowers: Solitary; male and female flowers on the same plant.
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – splits into 2-4 segments when mature. Seed may be difficult to find.
plants.habitat: In or on edges of brackish or freshwater pools and lagoons, in the far north-east and Bass Strait Islands.

plants.name: Myriophyllum salsugineum
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – splits into 2-4 segments when mature. Seed may be difficult to find.

plants.name: Myriophyllum simulans
plants.form: Aquatic or terrestrial plant which roots at the nodes.
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – splits into 2-4 segments when mature. Seed may be difficult to find.
plants.notes: Hardy plant with attractive foliage, forms mats on wet soils and also grows as an aquatic.

plants.name: Myriophyllum variifolium
plants.fruit: Fruitlet – splits into 2-4 segments when mature. Seed may be difficult to find.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Nablonium calyceroides
plants.form: Small perennial with basal rosette of leaves, white underneath.
plants.flowers: White daisy on stout erect stem 4-8cm long, outer bracts greenish, papery margins.
plants.habitat: Wet flats behind dunes, margins of lagoons, on Bass Strait islands and a few localities on the west coast.

plants.name: Nematolepis squamea subsp. retusa
plants.form: Small to tall shrub.
plants.flowers: Flowers white-cream; solitary or in 2–5-flowered inflorescence.
plants.habitat: Mainly in north-east Tasmania and the Central Plateau where it is found in eucalyptus forest, riverine areas and exposed, rocky slopes.

plants.name: Nematolepis squamea subsp. squamea
plants.form: Tall shrub or small tree, with branches without glands.
plants.flowers: White-cream petals, prominent stamens in axillary clusters; 5-20 flowers per flower head.
plants.habitat: Common in damp eucalyptus forests and woodlands, rainforest, tall and low heath.
plants.notes: Bee attracting. Grows to 12m in the north-west of the State, and was used for timber for telegraph poles.

plants.name: Nertera granadensis
plants.form: Prostrate perennial herb forming patches from 6-40cm in diameter.
plants.flowers: Minute with calyx absent or scarcely visible, corolla about 2mm long, lobes shorter than tube.
plants.fruit: Drupe – red, ovoid, about 4mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Rare in short alpine herbfield throughout the state.
plants.notes: Useful for cool shaded spots around pools or amongst ferns.

plants.name: Netrostylis capillaris
plants.form: Tufted perennial sedge with wiry stems.
plants.flowers: Spikelets of flowers, 4-6mm long.
plants.habitat: Marsh and stream margins, ditches, wet heaths and shrubberies, and buttongrass plains, from sea level to 850m altitude.

plants.name: Notelaea ligustrina
plants.form: Tall shrub or sturdy tree.
plants.flowers: Tiny white or green 4-petalled flowers in much-branched clusters in axils.
plants.fruit: Drupe – olive-shaped, 1cm x 8mm, green at first, becoming yellow or pink and then dark purple. Not often seen.
plants.habitat: Widespread along river banks and on moist shady hillsides. Also found in rocky gullies.
plants.notes: An adaptable, slow-growing plant. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Nothofagus cunninghamii
plants.form: Tree or sometimes a dense shrub.
plants.flowers: On new growth. Male: solitary stalked, hanging stamens; Female: unstalked in threes in axils.
plants.fruit: Nutlet – 4mm in diameter, with a central small flat seed and two winged seeds (both germinable).
plants.habitat: Dominates rainforest throughout most of the state. It also occurs as an understorey tree in tall eucalypt forest and extends as a shrub into the sub-alpine and alpine zones.
plants.notes: Slow growing in cultivation. Will stand full sun but prefers shade. The timber, pinkish-brown in colour, takes a fine polish and is valued for cabinet work, joinery, floor-boards and the heels of shoes.

plants.name: Nothofagus gunnii
plants.form: Medium shrub or small tree; leaves small and deeply indented on the upper surface.
plants.flowers: Small, creamy green unisexual flowers.
plants.habitat: Altitudes from 900-1250 m.
plants.notes: Leaves are light green in spring and summer and turn golden-brown to reddish before falling in autumn. Tasmania’s only winter-deciduous tree. Popular with bonsai enthusiasts. Very slow-growing; highly fire-susceptible and reluctant to regenerate after fire.

plants.name: Notogrammitis angustifolia subsp. nothofageti
plants.form: Small fern with pendulous, linear fronds, 3-13cm long; lithophytic or epiphytic on tree species e.g. Nothofagus cunninghamii, Olearia argophylla and others.
plants.habitat: In Australia it is known only in Tasmania, where it is uncommon.

plants.name: Notogrammitis billardierei
plants.form: Small fern fronds, 6-15cm long, growing on tree trunks, tree-ferns, and mossy boulders. Rootstock erect to short-creeping.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common, extending to high altitudes. Grows on mossy logs and rocks or is epiphytic on Dicksonia trunks and the lower branches and trunks of trees. One of the first non-terrestrial ferns to re-establish after fire or logging.
plants.notes: Grows on vertical branches or tree trunks.

plants.name: Notogrammitis crassior
plants.form: Small fern, fronds 1-3.5cm long, with rootstock creeping, much-branched.
plants.habitat: Grows on mossy rocks, protected beneath large boulders or on semi-exposed rock ledges and crevices. Occurs on exposed, doleritic high mountain summits in Tasmania.
plants.notes: Grows on mossy rocks.

plants.name: Notogrammitis garrettii
plants.form: Small fern, similar to Notogrammitis crassior but with larger fronds and without the creeping rhizome.
plants.habitat: Possibly restricted to alpine and sub-alpine sandstone in the extreme south-east of the State. Grows from sheltered rock ledges with other Notogrammitis species or as the sole species on extremely exposed sites.

plants.name: Notogrammitis gunnii
plants.form: Small fern with long creeping rhizome. Also has black stipes and hairs on sori.
plants.habitat: On rock outcrops in alpine areas. Most closely resembles Notogrammitis crassior but differs because of its black stipes and the presence of soral hairs.

plants.name: Notogrammitis heterophylla
plants.form: Fronds, 10-30cm long, weeping, leathery, broad, dull, lobed, winged, broadest towards middle.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in lowland areas of moderate to high rainfall. Grows on logs, rocks or as an epiphyte on a range of tree species. Most abundant in near-coastal gullies and scrub.
plants.notes: Epiphytic. Has proven very difficult to keep growing and has been tried with a range of treatments in various conditions.

plants.name: Notogrammitis pseudociliata
plants.form: Small fern; rootstock erect to creeping, fronds, 2-10cm long, matt, pale-green and densely hairy often with irregular margins.
plants.habitat: Common in lowland forests of the north-west but localised elsewhere, growing as an epiphyte in rainforest on Eucryphia lucida and Atherosperma moschatum.
plants.notes: Epiphytic

plants.name: Odixia achlaena
plants.form: Small shrub with many spreading/ascending branches and sticky yellow young growth.
plants.flowers: Daisy like flower heads, white, in terminal heads, profuse and very conspicuous.
plants.habitat: Known only from a limited area near the coast in north-east Tasmania.
plants.notes: Adapts to a range of moderate to well drained soils and semi-shaded aspect. Flowers are long lasting.

plants.name: Odixia angusta
plants.form: Small to medium shrub with branches spreading/ascending and young growth yellow.
plants.flowers: White, short-stalked daisy like flowers profuse and very conspicuous in rounded heads.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in coastal heaths at Eaglehawk Neck and Coles Bay.
plants.notes: Adapts to a wide range of well-drained soils and a sunny or semi-shaded site.

plants.name: Olearia algida
plants.form: Small much-branched woody shrub; dense hairy new growth.
plants.flowers: Flower heads stalkless, florets white.
plants.habitat: Common in alpine heath, grasslands and alpine sedgeland in the eastern mountains, especially in disturbed areas.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia archeri
plants.form: Medium shrub with bronze or pinkish young growth.
plants.flowers: Flower-heads white, daisy like about 3cm across in crowded terminal clusters, disc florets yellow.
plants.habitat: Occurs from sea level to about 650m on the east coast. Favours shady sites on hillsides or stony slopes and acidic soils.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia argophylla
plants.form: Tree with trunk often branched shortly above the base, crown spreading.
plants.flowers: Daisy type, 1cm across with a few white rays, cream centres. Very numerous in large heads.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds with long straight pappus bristles.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in wet eucalypt forests and in fern gullies from sea level to moderate altitudes.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Bee attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Moderate flammability. Timber, when large enough, was formerly esteemed for cabinet making, inlays etc. Burrs often occur on the trunks near the base and these may be cut into figured veneers.

plants.name: Olearia axillaris
plants.form: Shrub with slender, erect branches.
plants.flowers: Flower heads solitary, florets white.
plants.habitat: Local on coastal sand dunes in the north-east of the State; also on the islands of Bass Strait.
plants.notes: Plants are suitable for semi-arid and temperate regions and are fast growing in acidic or slightly alkaline soils. They make excellent soil-binders and form effective windbreaks. They tolerate salt spray, moderate frosts and extended dry periods. Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia ciliata
plants.form: Small shrub, branched from the base.
plants.flowers: Heads 2-2.5cm in diameter. solitary on wiry stalks 8-14cm long. Florets white or purplish-blue.
plants.habitat: Local in sandy heaths especially near the east and south-east coasts. Tolerates heavy frosts and extended dry periods.
plants.notes: Will grow in alkaline or acidic soils, prefer semi-shade but will grow in full sun. Flowers winter/spring, also sporadically at other times. Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia ericoides
plants.form: Sticky shrub with slender branches.
plants.flowers: Flower heads solitary. Florets often bluish, sometimes white, about 24 to a head.
plants.habitat: Occasional on dry hillsides in the south and south-east. Tolerates most frosts and limited dry periods.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia erubescens
plants.form: Shrub with stout straight branches.
plants.flowers: Flower heads on slender stalks, 3-5 together. Florets 12-15 pale pinkish-purple, or white.
plants.fruit: Achene – hairless pappus bristles 7-8mm long, pinkish brown.
plants.habitat: Widespread but local from sea level to the Central Plateau. Tolerates most frosts and lengthy dry periods.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Flowering times often sporadic. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia floribunda
plants.form: Shrub with slender branches.
plants.flowers: Flower heads numerous, solitary, without stalks. Florets white 6-10.
plants.fruit: Achene without hairs or slightly downy.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent especially along banks of rivers and drainage channels.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia glandulosa
plants.form: Shrub with slender, erect branches.
plants.flowers: Small stalked white daisy flowers in flat topped tufts at the ends of branches.
plants.fruit: Achene with a feathery attachment called a pappus.
plants.habitat: Found in soaks and wet places, lowland to alpine and sub-alpine.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia glutinosa
plants.form: Much-branched shrub, glutinous but apparently without hair.
plants.flowers: Flower heads stalked, florets white 16-24.
plants.habitat: Occasional on the north and west coasts.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia hookeri
plants.form: A slender, sticky shrub, apparently hairless (but with tiny glandular hairs).
plants.flowers: Flower heads usually solitary without stalks. Florets usually bluish-purple 20-30.
plants.fruit: Achene, hairy, pappus in young flowers purplish at the tips, light brown when dry.
plants.habitat: Occasional in the east and south-east near Hobart.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia ledifolia
plants.form: Densely branched small shrub, with stout branches.
plants.flowers: Large white daisies with yellow disc florets. Outside bracts covered with rusty brown hairs.
plants.fruit: Achene – pappus with straight rust-coloured hairs.
plants.habitat: Mountain shrubberies and among boulders on mountain plateaux.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia lepidophylla
plants.form: Much-branched shrub with branches covered with dense fine white hairs.
plants.flowers: Flower heads stalkless, solitary. Florets white 6-12.
plants.habitat: Near coasts and sometimes on sand dunes, also on dry hills along the estuary of the River Derwent.
plants.notes: Adapts to acidic or slightly alkaline soils in a semi-shaded or sunny position. Tolerates extended dry periods. Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia lirata
plants.form: Small to large open shrub.
plants.flowers: Numerous white daisies with 12-15 ray florets.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent on the margins of wet eucalypt forest and in wet gullies.
plants.notes: An excellent shrub for native gardens. Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia myrsinoides
plants.form: Much branched shrub with downy young shoots.
plants.flowers: Flower heads stalked, 1-3 together. Florets white or pinkish-purple 4-8, honey-scented.
plants.fruit: Achene without hairs, pappus-bristles cream or frequently pinkish-brown.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent throughout the State from sea level to the Central Plateau.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia obcordata
plants.form: Much-branched straggly shrub.
plants.flowers: Flower heads without stalks. Florets white, usually 10-15.
plants.fruit: Achene without hairs, pappus about 7mm long.
plants.habitat: Occasional in alpine and sub-alpine shrubberies at altitudes of 900-1000m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Olearia could be susceptible to mealy bug. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia persoonioides
plants.form: Shrub often straggly when growing in rainforest.
plants.flowers: 12-16 florets, ends of main/short side branches. Daisy-like, few white petals and yellow centre.
plants.habitat: Mostly in high-altitude rainforest and shrubberies in the south and west and on the Western Tiers.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Olearia could be susceptible to mealy bug. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia phlogopappa subsp. angustifolia
plants.form: Medium shrub with greyish toothed leaves.
plants.flowers: Usually white, daisies in large terminal clusters from side branches; 10-14 florets. Small grey-green toothed leaves. Aromatic.
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Olearia phlogopappa subsp. gunniana
plants.form: Medium shrub with greyish toothed leaves.
plants.flowers: Usually white, daisies in large terminal clusters from side branches; 10-14 florets. Small grey-green toothed leaves. Aromatic.
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Olearia phlogopappa subsp. insularis
plants.form: Medium shrub with greyish toothed leaves.
plants.flowers: Usually white, daisies in large terminal clusters from side branches; 10-14 florets. Small grey-green toothed leaves. Aromatic.
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Olearia phlogopappa subsp. phlogopappa
plants.form: Small upright shrub with greyish foliage.
plants.flowers: Usually white, sometimes pink or blue, daisies in large terminal clusters from side branches; 10-14 florets. Small grey-green toothed leaves. Aromatic.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common from coast to mountain.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia phlogopappa subsp. salicina
plants.form: Medium shrub with greyish toothed leaves.
plants.flowers: Usually white, daisies in large terminal clusters from side branches; 10-14 florets. Small grey-green toothed leaves. Aromatic.
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Olearia phlogopappa subsp. subrepanda
plants.form: Medium shrub with greyish toothed leaves.
plants.flowers: Usually white, daisies in large terminal clusters from side branches; 10-14 florets. Small grey-green toothed leaves. Aromatic.
plants.notes: Bird attracting.

plants.name: Olearia pinifolia
plants.form: Rigid shrub with stout branches sometimes branched only above and like a small tree.
plants.flowers: Flower heads often numerous, each solitary. Florets white, 18-24.
plants.fruit: Achene without hairs; pappus white sometimes drying pinkish-purple.
plants.habitat: Frequent in alpine and sub-alpine and sub-alpine shrubberies at altitudes between about 800m and 1200m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Olearia could be susceptible to mealy bug. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia ramulosa
plants.form: Shrub, variable in habit.
plants.flowers: Small, white florets, numerous. Occasionally blue.
plants.habitat: Widespread behind dunes, in wet places in heaths and woodlands, and on hillsides in moderate rainfall areas.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. May be susceptible to mealy bug. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia rugosa subsp. intermedia
plants.flowers: Small, white florets

plants.name: Olearia stellulata
plants.form: Variable, woody shrub. Slender, upright branches covered with microscopic hairs.
plants.flowers: Numerous daisy-like flower heads towards end of branches; white, occasionally blue.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant, in shrubby understorey of wet eucalypt forests especially in the south. Roadside near Fern Tree.
plants.notes: Leaves aromatic when crushed. Bird attracting. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia tasmanica
plants.form: Bushy shrub
plants.flowers: Flower heads solitary, stalked. Florets white about 15.
plants.habitat: Occasional in sub-alpine shrubberies at altitudes above about 1000m and at lower altitudes near the west and south-west coasts.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. May be susceptible to mealy bug. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Olearia viscosa
plants.form: Much-branched shrub, young shoots often sticky.
plants.flowers: Flower heads small, numerous in clusters with shorter stalks at top. Florets 4-6 creamish-white.
plants.fruit: Achene mainly hairless, but often downy below the pappus.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet sclerophyll forests and on the lower slopes of mountains.
plants.notes: Prefers well-drained acidic soils which retain moisture and a semi-shaded site. Bird attracting. May be susceptible to mealy bug. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Opercularia ovata
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender rhizome. Has strong foetid smell when bruised.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 2-valved, formed from 2-7 adjacent flowers to make compound. Seeds broadly oval, outer surface smooth, inner surface with 2 prominent ribs and usually a narrow ridge between.
plants.habitat: Occasional in open country in the north of the state.

plants.name: Opercularia varia
plants.form: Dwarf perennial herb, with an unpleasant smell.
plants.flowers: 2-7 small purplish flowers form a semi-globular head.

plants.name: Ophioglossum lusitanicum subsp. coriaceum
plants.form: Terrestrial, rootstock knobby with fleshy roots; sterile fronds narrow-elliptical widest towards middle; fertile pinnae up to 15cm tall.
plants.habitat: Uncommon from scattered coastal localities and the Central Highlands up to at least 1190m. Favours sites with little competition. May grow in thin, mossy soil layers over rock platforms and along margins of coastal and highland lagoons. Will also grow exposed to salt spray.

plants.name: Oreobolus acutifolius
plants.form: Perennial sedge, forming dense tufts or cushions from ascending rhizomes.
plants.flowers: Single flower on stalk.
plants.habitat: Occurs at high elevations in sphagnum bogs and wet seepages, and in open patches in heath in the central and western mountains.
plants.notes: Require high altitude, boggy sites to grow.

plants.name: Oreobolus distichus
plants.form: Dwarf perennial sedge which forms dense tufts or mats from ascending rhizomes.
plants.flowers: Flowering stems about 5 cm long.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in wet moors and floors and margins of tarns.
plants.notes: Require high altitude, boggy sites to grow.

plants.name: Oreobolus oligocephalus
plants.form: Tufted perennial sedge with stiff leaves, forming mounds of crowded rosettes. The rosettes sometimes decay in the centre, leaving ‘fairy rings’.
plants.flowers: Spikes on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.habitat: On mountains at about 1200m altitude on poorly drained, exposed ridges, and in bogs at lower altitudes on the west coast, Central Highlands, Ben Lomond and the south-west.
plants.notes: Require high altitude, boggy sites to grow.

plants.name: Oreobolus oxycarpus subsp. brownii
plants.form: Small, densely tufted perennial sedge with leaves arranged in spirals.
plants.flowers: Solitary spikelets on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – pale brown or grey, sometimes spotted with black and sometimes all purplish-black; 1.8-2.5mm long.
plants.habitat: In wet sub-alpine areas at 1200m altitude, and in buttongrass moors at 750m altitude. north-west, west coast, Central Highlands, east coast, south-west, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.
plants.notes: Require high altitude, boggy sites to grow.

plants.name: Oreobolus pumilio subsp. pumilio
plants.form: Tufted sedge with spirally arranged leaves, forming dense mats.
plants.flowers: Solitary spikelets on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.habitat: On open rocky places and swampy moors, on mountains of the west coast, Central Highlands, Ben Lomond, south-west, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.
plants.notes: Require high altitude, boggy sites to grow.

plants.name: Oreomyrrhis argentea
plants.form: Perennial rosette herb with a stout taproot, silvery-white all over with a dense covering of silky hairs. Leaf blades 2.5-8cm long, and 0.8-2cm wide, divided into leaflets.
plants.flowers: Flower stems stout and erect, bearing 15-25 flowers on stalks which form 4-5mm long, egg-shaped fruit.
plants.habitat: Occasional in alpine and sub-alpine grassland on the Central Plateau.
plants.notes: High elevation plant. From the same family as parsley, fennel, dill, coriander, cumin and caraway. Good for growing in spaces between native grass and sedge tussocks. Edible – can be added to stir-fries.

plants.name: Oreomyrrhis ciliata
plants.form: Perennial herb with a slender taproot and lobed leaves arranged in a rosette.
plants.flowers: 5-25 flowers with erect white petals, and brownish-crimson anthers.
plants.habitat: Local on mountains on the northern and western Central Plateau, in damp places or growing on cushion plants.
plants.notes: High elevation plant which likes wet conditions. From the same family as parsley, fennel, dill, coriander, cumin and caraway.

plants.name: Oreomyrrhis eriopoda
plants.form: Perennial rosette herb with a taproot. Leaves 2.5-20cm long, and 1-3cm wide.
plants.flowers: 12-35 flowers with hairy stalks produced on erect, stout flower stems. Petals white and less than 1mm long, anthers crimson.
plants.habitat: Widespread from coastal heaths to alpine and sub-alpine grassland.
plants.notes: From the same family as parsley, fennel, dill, coriander, cumin and caraway. Has a thick taproot which can be eaten like parsnip. Edible – the aromatic leaves and seeds may be used for flavouring food.

plants.name: Oreomyrrhis gunnii
plants.form: Perennial herb with a slender taproot and lobed leaves arranged in a basal rosette. Leaves 1-9cm long and 0.5-3cm wide, and divided into leaflets with scattered spreading hairs.
plants.flowers: 10-25 flowers producing fruit which is broadest in the middle and 4-5mm long.
plants.habitat: Known only from the type collection from limestone cliffs of the Gordon River, Macquarie Harbour.
plants.notes: Cliff growing species.

plants.name: Oreomyrrhis sessiliflora
plants.form: Perennial herb with a stout taproot, leaves 1-9cm long and 0.5-3cm wide, leaflets lobed or divided. Leaves arranged in a basal rosette or sometimes erect, leafy branches.
plants.flowers: 10-20 flowers.
plants.notes: High elevation plant. Characteristic smell, similar to carrot. From the same family as parsley, fennel, dill, coriander, cumin and caraway. Good for growing in spaces between native grass and sedge tussocks. Can be added to stir-fries.

plants.name: Orites acicularis
plants.form: Yellow-green small shrub with many erect/ascending branches sometimes spreading.
plants.flowers: Creamy-white, sometimes with pinkish tips, in pairs in spikes, sweetly scented. Style reddish.
plants.fruit: Woody seed follicle – oblong and flattened with a short straight beak, thin but hard, light brown and hairless. Seed surrounded by a wing which is wider at each end.
plants.habitat: Abundant and widespread on mountain plateaux, in all except aquatic or short alpine vegetation.
plants.notes: Valuable as a traffic control plant because of its highly prickly nature. Good background planting. Sunny or semi-shaded aspect is suitable. Hardy to most frosts and snowfalls.

plants.name: Orites diversifolius
plants.form: An erect, rigid, slightly branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Candles of small cream flowers near the ends of branches, strongly honey scented.
plants.fruit: Woody seed follicle – boat shaped in loose clusters at the ends of branches. Seed has a large wing.
plants.habitat: Found in sub-alpine situations in the south and west. When growing on clay, the clay will be dolerite-derived.
plants.notes: Difficult to grow in lowland situations. Leaf size varies; in rainforest it can be twice as large as the form found on kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Orites milliganii
plants.form: Dense, upright, much-branched shrub. Leaves with sharply pointed coarse teeth.
plants.flowers: White, glabrous, sweetly perfumed, profuse and conspicuous. In pairs in terminal spikes.
plants.fruit: Woody seed follicle – a woody, boat-shaped follicle.
plants.habitat: Local at altitudes above 1200m on mountains near the west coast.
plants.notes: Very prickly and may have application for foot traffic control. Plants best suited to a semi-shaded aspect with well-drained soils which are moist for most of the year. Hardy to most frosts and snowfalls. Has been found to be difficult to establish in cultivation.

plants.name: Orites revolutus
plants.form: Much-branched, erect or spreading shrub. In the open, sprawls over ground or rocks.
plants.flowers: Creamy-white, grouped into short candles.
plants.fruit: Woody seed follicle – short, blunt, covered with dense brown hair. Seed has a large terminal wing.
plants.habitat: Abundant and widespread on mountain plateaux. Extends down into sub-alpine woodland as a larger shrub.
plants.notes: Would make an interesting garden plant with its distinct leaves and mass flowering.

plants.name: Ornduffia reniformis
plants.form: Robust, aquatic or semi-aquatic herb, with kidney-shaped leaves about 6-8cm long borne on fleshy stalks. Stolons up to 2m long.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow, 2.5-4cm in diameter, on erect branched stems.
plants.habitat: Grows in freshwater lagoons and marshes, as a terrestrial in damp soils or as an aquatic in water up to 60cm deep.
