plants.notes: Aquatic plant. When water dries up, the plant may collapse but will regrow from the root. Good in poorly drained areas, such as ponds or pond edges. Frog habitat.

plants.name: Ornduffia umbricola var. umbricola
plants.form: A tufted perennial or sometimes annual, without stolons.
plants.flowers: Yellow flower with 5 lobes.
plants.habitat: Found in damp, boggy areas, shallow fresh water pools and the edges of slowly flowing streams.
plants.notes: Aquatic plant.

plants.name: Orthoceras strictum
plants.form: Plant with rigid flowering stem and grass like leaves.
plants.flowers: Green-grey or yellow-brown orchid with dark markings. Upper sepal forms a hood.
plants.habitat: Not common, usually found in wet heaths, often inland e.g. Trial Harbour Road, near Serpentine Quarry, Renison Bell on the west coast.

plants.name: Oschatzia saxifraga
plants.form: Small, hairless, perennial herb, with a rosette of lobed leaves about 8mm long growing from the root.
plants.flowers: Flower stalks erect and bearing 1-6 flowers of about 5mm diameter, with white or pink-tinged petals.
plants.habitat: Occasional in wet peaty heaths in the west and south-west.

plants.name: Ourisia integrifolia
plants.form: Small, smooth perennial herb with short, prostrate branches stems and opposite, rounded, somewhat thick leaves.
plants.flowers: 1 or 2 flowers, white or pale bluish-purple, 10-16mm in diameter, borne on erect flowering stems.
plants.habitat: Moist, shaded places on mountains, in the north and east. Sometimes between rocks beside creeks.

plants.name: Oxalis exilis
plants.flowers: Yellow
plants.habitat: Reasonably common in dry environments.

plants.name: Oxalis magellanica
plants.form: Creeping rhizomatous herb with clover-like leaves.
plants.flowers: Large and white, delicate petals have veins radiating outwards.
plants.fruit: Capsule – brown seeds are ejected explosively from the cylindrical capsule.
plants.habitat: Wet and shady places, especially at high altitude.

plants.name: Oxalis perennans
plants.form: Small perennial herb with thick spreading stems.
plants.flowers: Single, 5 golden yellow petals.
plants.habitat: Widespread in a range of soils and habitats.
plants.notes: Mostly treated as a weed species because of its spreading habit.

plants.name: Oxalis radicosa
plants.form: Annual or perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Petals yellow, 7–12 mm long.
plants.fruit: Capsule 6-20 mm long, cylindric, erect, hairy.

plants.name: Oxalis rubens
plants.form: Small, herbaceous perennial.
plants.flowers: Petals yellow, 7–10 mm long.
plants.fruit: Capsule – cylindric, often slightly expanded in the middle portion, 12–24 mm long, densely hairy.

plants.name: Oxylobium arborescens
plants.form: An erect shrub with slightly hairy branches.
plants.flowers: Bright orange-yellow pea flowers at the ends of short side branches. Distinguished from Oxylobium ellipticum by its longer leaves and axillary position of flowers. Oxylobium ellipticum has terminal flower heads.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – 7-8mm long, rounded, grey-brown with long silky hairs.
plants.habitat: Usually found in scrubby situations in the west of the State in locations of high rainfall.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Oxylobium ellipticum
plants.form: Spreading, much-branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow pea flowers in dense terminal clusters.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – 7-8mm long, rounded, grey-brown with long silky hairs.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent, especially in the south, from sea level to 1000m.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Oxylobium oxylobioides
plants.form: Erect, spreading shrub, with stems covered by soft downy hairs, and narrow, oval-shaped, 2-10mm long leaves which are arranged in opposite pairs.
plants.flowers: Flowers are orange-yellow with red markings, on silky stalks which are up to 4mm long. The oldest flowers occur at the base of the flower head.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – brown, 8-10mm long, covered with soft downy hair and has pointed tips. Seeds are 2-4mm long.
plants.habitat: Below and directly above sandstone cliffs. Only known from one population in the Heathy Hills Nature Reserve near Elderslie, in the south-east.
plants.notes: Oxylobium oxylobioides has internal wall partitions in the pods, which distinguishes it from Oxylobium ellipticum.

plants.name: Ozothamnus antennaria
plants.form: Small to medium shrub with branches erect and sticky, hairy young growth.
plants.flowers: In terminal clusters, profuse. Flower heads about 0.2cm across, buff-cream in colour.
plants.habitat: Inhabits hills and slopes from 150m to 920m.
plants.notes: Tolerates freely draining, acidic or alkaline soils with high organic content. Will not tolerate extended periods of frost and snow and prefers a semi-shaded site.

plants.name: Ozothamnus argophyllus
plants.form: Small to medium shrub with few erect branches.
plants.flowers: Flower heads about 0.4cm across, white, fragrant, daisy-like, in clusters.
plants.habitat: Local in the islands of Bass Strait.
plants.notes: Prefers partial or filtered sun.

plants.name: Ozothamnus cinereus
plants.form: Small to medium, bushy shrub with erect or decumbent branches. Aromatic.
plants.flowers: Flower heads about 0.4cm across, cream to yellowish, crowded in elongated heads.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent on coastal sand dunes. Tolerates light to moderate frosts.
plants.notes: Has very useful sand-binding properties. Useful shrub for coastal gardens and may be grown in heavier soils inland but is then susceptible to root-rotting fungi. Tolerates salt-laden winds and calcareous soils.

plants.name: Ozothamnus costatifructus
plants.form: Small to medium shrub with branches ascending to erect and whitish-hairy young growth.
plants.flowers: Profuse in flower heads about 0.7cm across, creamy white with buff bracts.
plants.habitat: Local near the coasts in southern and eastern Tasmania.
plants.notes: Dislikes extended dry periods and prefers some shade.

plants.name: Ozothamnus ericifolius
plants.form: Small to medium shrub with erect branches often assuming a column-like shape.
plants.flowers: Profuse in dense terminal clusters, heads about 0.5cm across, ray florets white, bracts buff.
plants.habitat: Local in alpine and sub-alpine heaths on the Central Plateau. Found in alpine heath at lower altitudes in the eastern mountains.
plants.notes: Plants are tolerant of open sites but need to have adequate moisture.

plants.name: Ozothamnus ferrugineus
plants.form: Shrub or small tree; open, woody and aromatic.
plants.flowers: White in large clusters at ends of main and lateral branches. About 6 florets to each flower head.
plants.habitat: Moist gullies and along creeks, wet margins of forest.
plants.notes: Adaptable to a wide range of soils and positions.

plants.name: Ozothamnus floribundus
plants.form: Slender, columnar shrub producing many flowers.
plants.flowers: The florets are arranged in terminal clusters of 4 to 5 .
plants.fruit: Achene – covered in tiny protrusions, and the bristles of the pappus are barbed with club-shaped ends.
plants.habitat: Known only from a single location in lowland south-east Tasmania in shrubby, heathy Eucalyptus obliqua dry sclerophyll forest.

plants.name: Ozothamnus gunnii
plants.form: Small shrub with ascending to erect branches and woolly-hairy young growth.
plants.flowers: Flower heads about 0.5cm across cream and pale brown in terminal clusters.
plants.habitat: On Flinders Island and north-east coast.
plants.notes: Useful for providing quick growth while slower growing plants develop.

plants.name: Ozothamnus hookeri
plants.form: Dwarf to small shrub with branchlets covered densely with white hairs.
plants.flowers: Flower heads yellowish/cream/green about 0.2cm across, stalkless in dense clusters.
plants.habitat: Frequent on mountains at altitudes from about 900m. Tolerates moderately heavy frosts and snowfalls.
plants.notes: Suitable for use among rocks or in containers.

plants.name: Ozothamnus ledifolius
plants.form: Dwarf to small shrub with sticky, bright yellow young growth. Aromatic.
plants.flowers: Flower heads about 0.5cm across, in crowded clusters, ray florets white, bracts yellow/brown.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant on mountains above abut 800m.
plants.notes: Prefers an open or semi-shaded site.

plants.name: Ozothamnus lycopodioides
plants.form: Dwarf shrub, with spreading branches, young growth sticky, leaf scars prominent.
plants.flowers: Flower heads to about 0.5cm across, profuse and conspicuous, white with buff/brown bracts.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent along the rocky slopes bordering the Prosser River and elsewhere near the east coast.
plants.notes: Adapts well to most soil types with good drainage but plants are sometimes difficult to maintain.

plants.name: Ozothamnus obcordatus
plants.form: Dwarf to small shrub with slender or spreading branches from near base.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow flower heads about 0.5cm across in dense almost flat clusters.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant on dry hills. Tolerates light to moderate frosts.
plants.notes: Plants will tolerate full sun to partial sun or shade.

plants.name: Ozothamnus purpurascens
plants.form: Much branched shrub.

plants.name: Ozothamnus reflexus
plants.form: Neat columnar shrub with dense aromatic foliage.
plants.flowers: Dense clusters at ends of branches, buds purplish-pink, flower head white, 8-10 florets.
plants.fruit: Achene with pappus bristles with minute barbs.
plants.habitat: Common on dry open hillsides in the south from sea level to about 250m. Widespread and occasional throughout the State.
plants.notes: Full to part sun.

plants.name: Ozothamnus reticulatus
plants.form: Sturdy shrub, spreading branches, leaves dark green, long, narrow, shiny, 3-6cm.
plants.flowers: Almost round, white heads 5-7mm across.
plants.fruit: Achene – large creamy white seed heads, many small seeds within each head. Seed has fluffy white attachment.
plants.habitat: Local on coastal cliff-faces and rocks, rocky parts of sandy coasts. Less common in north of Tasmania.

plants.name: Ozothamnus rodwayi var. kingii
plants.form: Compact small rounded shrub with silvery-greyish foliage.

plants.name: Ozothamnus rodwayi var. oreophilus
plants.form: Compact shrub with dark green leaves.

plants.name: Ozothamnus rodwayi var. rodwayi
plants.form: Compact small rounded shrub.
plants.flowers: Profuse clusters of white daisy flowers with distinct brown hairy bracts.
plants.habitat: Common on exposed alpine to sub-alpine heathlands.

plants.name: Ozothamnus rosmarinifolius
plants.form: Small to medium shrub with ascending to erect branches and woolly white bark.
plants.flowers: Flower heads about 0.2cm across, inner bracts small, white; outer bracts pink to reddish.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in wet peaty heaths. Hardy to light or moderate frosts.
plants.notes: Soils need to be well-drained even though plants tolerate extended wet periods. Adapts to open, sunny or semi-shaded sites.

plants.name: Ozothamnus scutellifolius
plants.form: Shrub, many branches. Tiny dark green leaves closely pressed to stems.
plants.flowers: Heads 3-5 together at end of branch; yellowish white with brownish outer, 4mm long.
plants.fruit: Achene – seed heads large, creamy and white.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent on dry hillsides.
plants.notes: “Now that Ozothamnus has been divided from Helichrysums we are calling Ozothamnus ‘Bush Everlasting’ as Helichrysums were always known as ‘Everlastings’ ” – Will Fletcher.

plants.name: Ozothamnus thyrsoideus
plants.form: Shrub with slender, spreading branches.
plants.flowers: Heads numerous, small, 6-8 florets outer bracts brown, inner bracts white-tipped papery.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds with pappus of fine bristles with thickened tips.
plants.habitat: Common as regrowth shrub in burnt or logged areas of medium high rainfall and margins of wet eucalypt forest from sea level to alpine and sub-alpine.
plants.notes: Plant may be highly perfumed and may self seed.

plants.name: Ozothamnus x expansifolius
plants.form: Small shrub with stout erect branches.
plants.flowers: Very short-stalked, 6-30 in compact terminal clusters, cream/white or reddish-brown.
plants.habitat: Inhabits mountain slopes and heaths at altitudes of 900-1200m. Tolerates snowfalls.
plants.notes: Adaptable to semi-shaded or sunny sites.

plants.name: Pachycladon radicatus
plants.form: Herb with thick brown branches (almost woody), usually spreading.
plants.flowers: Spatula shaped leaves along flowering stems, flowers white, in terminal cluster.
plants.fruit: Capsule (siliqua) narrowly oval on stalks about 1cm long; opening by valves with seeds in 2 rows in each part.
plants.habitat: In crevices of rock on mountains at about 1200m.
plants.notes: Requires moist, well-drained soils, will grow in full sun or partial shade but must have shelter to provide a cool root run.

plants.name: Pandorea pandorana
plants.form: Hairless, fast-growing, climbing shrub with twining branchlets. Leaves are opposite with a glossy upper surface, 5-20cm long and variable in shape and size.
plants.flowers: 2cm long funnel-shaped cream or white flowers with broad lobes, streaked with red in the throat, and often with purple or crimson spots at the base of the larger lobes. The throat is bearded inside.
plants.fruit: Capsule – pod-like, 4-7cm long, containing flat seeds surrounded by a broad, transparent wing. Capsule turns from green to yellow and mottled with brown, and release the winged, red-brown seed at maturity.
plants.habitat: Damp gullies and wet sclerophyll forest on Flinders Island.
plants.notes: Extremely vigorous, and often found scrambling through large trees. Prefers well-composted soil, good for features or screens, for fences and trellises.

plants.name: Pappochroma bellidioides
plants.form: Perennial herbs with leaves spatula shaped.
plants.flowers: Flower heads white to purple, terminal on erect flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Achenes – flattened with pappus of capillary bristles.
plants.habitat: Found in grassland and heath in the eastern mountains.
plants.notes: This genus has not been generally cultivated apart from Pappochroma stellatum.

plants.name: Pappochroma gunnii
plants.form: Rosette herb with wedge-shaped leaves, serrated near the ends.
plants.flowers: White to purple, terminal flower heads.
plants.fruit: Achenes – flattened with pappus of capillary bristles.
plants.habitat: Found in grassland and heath in the central and eastern mountains.
plants.notes: This genus has not been generally cultivated apart from Pappochroma stellatum.

plants.name: Pappochroma pappocromum
plants.form: Prostrate rosette herb, flowering stalk longer than spatula-shaped leaves with wavy margins.
plants.flowers: Flower heads terminal, white to purple.
plants.fruit: Achenes – flattened with pappus of capillary bristles.
plants.habitat: Widespread in most types of non-aquatic alpine and sub-alpine vegetation.
plants.notes: This genus has not been generally cultivated apart from Pappochroma stellatum.

plants.name: Pappochroma stellatum
plants.form: Prostrate yellowish-green rosette herb with flowers amongst leaves or stalks exceeding leaves.
plants.flowers: Daisy-like, purple and white.
plants.fruit: Achenes – flattened with pappus of capillary bristles.
plants.habitat: Common on sub-alpine herbfields. Most common in the central and western mountains.
plants.notes: In cultivation it will need moist but well drained, acid to neutral soils with plenty of organic matter and a sunny situation.

plants.name: Pappochroma tasmanicum
plants.form: Bright green rosette herb with erect flowering stem longer than leaves.
plants.flowers: Flower heads white to purple and terminal.
plants.fruit: Achenes – flattened with pappus of capillary bristles.
plants.habitat: Grassland, heath and bog mainly in eastern and central mountains.
plants.notes: This genus has not been generally cultivated apart from Pappochroma stellatum.

plants.name: Paracaleana minor
plants.form: Small duck orchid. Very slender plant with flowering stem erect and wiry. Reddish-brown leaf, often withered at flowering, 50-120mm long.
plants.flowers: Small, 1- 7 greenish-brown flowers. Duckbill-shaped labellum green with black calli, attached to the base of the column by a broad, sensitive strap. The reddish column and its wings make the ‘body’ of the duck.
plants.habitat: Occasional but widespread in damp coastal heaths.
plants.notes: The labelllum at top of flower is covered with dark red raised glands and attached by a narrow flexible strap which acts as a hinge enabling the ‘head’ to swing down when an insect alights on the flower. Pollination is effected as the insect struggles out of the body cavity.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum alpinum
plants.form: A small leek orchid, a single tubular leaf, 80-200 mm with a whitish base.
plants.flowers: 3-14 shiny greenish-brown flowers, labellum shiny whitish-green, sharply recurved at the apex with a shiny, thick, greenish callus extending almost to the labellum apex.
plants.habitat: Locally common in alpine and sub-alpine sedgelands, moorlands and buttongrass, often growing in association with Tasmanian cushion plant, Abrotanella forsteroides, in damp soils.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum amoenum
plants.form: A short, slender, white-lipped leek orchid, a single dark-green tubular leaf, purplish at the base, 120-300mm long.
plants.flowers: 4-12 widely-spreading, greenish-white flowers with purplish suffusions. Lateral sepals at least partly fused. White triangular labellum, covered with minute papillae, a wavy margin and a yellowish-green callus, notched at the apex.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, restricted to alpine and sub-alpine sedgelands and moorlands on Snug Tiers and kunanyi/Mt Wellington in the south of the state.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum apoxychilum
plants.form: Medium, white-lipped leek orchid with a dark-green to greenish-brown stem, a single dark-green tubular leaf, purplish at the base.
plants.flowers: 8-20 flowers, light green with narrow white petals with purplish midland, lateral sepals widely spread. Long, tapered white labellum with crisped margins often recurved through the lateral sepals. Scented.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in coastal and near-coastal heathland and further inland in open eucalypt forest.
plants.notes: Flowering may be enhanced by summer fires.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum concinnum
plants.form: Green-brown leek orchid. Single dark-green, tubular leaf, purplish at the base, 150-300mm long.
plants.flowers: 10-20 brownish-green flowers on a moderately crowded spike, lateral sepals free but often held closely together. Labellum reddish-green, long and recurved with margin often pinched in towards the centre with a broad, fleshy callus extending nearly to the labellum apex. Fragrant.
plants.habitat: Common in moderately drained soils and peat in coastal and near-coastal heathlands, sedgelands and open forest in the south-east.
plants.notes: A variable species, particularly in size. Responds well to summer fires with plants often being much more robust (up to 800 mm) for the following couple of seasons.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum crebriflorum
plants.form: A slender green-brown leek orchid, single dark-green leaf, base purplish, often withered at flowering.
plants.flowers: 6-25 greenish-pink to brown flowers, widely opening flowers on a crowded spike. Lateral sepals free, dorsal sepal typically reflexed and twisted, petals upswept. Labellum recurved and sharply tapered towards the apex. Mildly fragrant.
plants.habitat: Confined to several areas of native grassland in Tasmania’s north-west, mostly on private land.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum favonium
plants.form: A short, slender leek orchid with a single, tubular, dark-green leaf, purplish at the base, 120-280mm long.
plants.flowers: 5-15 small green-pink to brown flowers with a distinctive purplish, abruptly recurved and crisped labellum with a thick, shiny, green callus. Slightly scented.
plants.habitat: Known only from the heathlands and sedgelands around Arthur River in north-west Tasmania.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum incorrectum
plants.form: Slender, greenish to reddish-brown leek orchid with a single tubular, green leaf, purple at the base and the apex often dried off or missing at flowering.
plants.flowers: 10-20 widely-gaping green-brown flowers, protruding ovaries. Pale green labellum with pinkish-brown margins that is abruptly recurved in the middle, often projecting back through the lateral sepals; prominent, shiny-green, fleshy callus.
plants.habitat: Restricted to several sites in the Tasmanian Midlands where it occurs in relatively damp native grassland and grassy eucalypt and banksia woodland on sandy loam.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum incurvum
plants.form: A medium to large white-lipped leek orchid with a single, tubular bright green leaf, purplish at the base, 160-350 mm long.
plants.flowers: 5-40 brownish-green flowers with white and purplish petals curving inwards, white labellum, sharply recurved in the distal half but rarely projecting through the greenish lateral sepals.
plants.habitat: Locally common in moister alpine and sub-alpine grasslands, sedgelands and moorlands, particularly in seasons following fire.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum limnetes
plants.form: A slender green-brown leek orchid, a single, green leaf, base purplish, 20-35 mm long, usually partly withered at flowering.
plants.flowers: 15-35 widely opening flowers, pale green with pink suffusions, on a crowded spike. Green to mauve labellum, recurved at right-angles in the middle. A darker callus extends almost to the apex. Scented.
plants.habitat: Only found at one site near Port Sorell on marshy ground.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum lindleyanum
plants.form: A slender, bright-green leek orchid with a single tubular leaf to 350 mm.
plants.flowers: 12-50 green to yellowish flowers in a loose, uncrowded spike. A white to pinkish labellum, margins highly crisped and a greenish-yellow callus. Highly scented.
plants.habitat: Uncommon and localised to coastal sedgeland, heathland and open eucalypt scrub.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum milfordense
plants.form: A robust white-lipped leek orchid, single, tubular, dark-green leaf, purplish at the base.
plants.flowers: 8-20 greenish-brown and white flowers held in a loose spike, lateral sepals free. Blunt, white labellum with heavily crisped margins, sharply recurved near the middle and projecting through the lateral sepals with a short, yellowish-green callus.
plants.habitat: Only on one site on private land near Cambridge, southern Tasmania, where it grows in sandy sedgeland.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum mimulum
plants.form: A small to medium white-lipped leek orchid with a single tubular, green leaf with a purplish base.
plants.flowers: 5-20 on a short, crowded spike, white petals with mauve suffusions that widen towards the apex, lateral sepals fused or partly fused. A bright-white labellum, crisped at the margins, strongly recurved in the middle with a short, greenish, fleshy callus.
plants.habitat: Relatively common in sub-alpine heathland and sedgeland in northern Tasmania.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum olidum
plants.form: A slender, green-brown leek orchid with relatively long tapered tepals with a single tubular yellowish-green leaf.
plants.flowers: A dense spike of 10-30 bright green to brownish-green flowers with long, free lateral sepals. An elliptical labellum, strongly recurved in the middle with slightly irregular margins and a shiny yellowish-green callus. Strongly fragrant.
plants.habitat: Known from only one site in moist, sandy native grassland in the Tasmanian midlands.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum pulchellum
plants.form: A small, slender white-lipped leek orchid.
plants.flowers: 3-12 small light-green flowers, petals with reddish suffusions. An oblong, white, irregularly-crisped labellum, sharply recurved in the middle with a shiny, dark-green callus that lightens to cream towards the apex.
plants.habitat: Uncommon. Found in widely scattered coastal sites growing on poorly-drained teatree sedgeland and heathland.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum robustum
plants.form: A sturdy white-tipped leek orchid, a single tubular dark-green leaf, 300-850 long.
plants.flowers: 15-30 relatively large, widely-spreading flowers, lateral sepals free and abruptly narrowed into distinctive horns at the apex through which a crinkled, white labellum projects. A fleshy, green callus extends to the midpoint.
plants.habitat: Uncommon. Found in several widely-dispersed, coastal sites in shrubby eucalypt forest in northern Tasmania.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum rostratum
plants.form: A slender green-brown leek orchid, single, tubular green leaf, 200-400mm long.
plants.flowers: 1-30 widely-opening, greenish-brown to maroon flowers, on a moderately crowded brown stem. A sharply-recurved, tapered labellum, pinched in at the midpoint, projects back through the lateral sepals and is distinguished by a shiny, thick, green callus that extends almost to the apex. Mildly fragrant.
plants.habitat: Widespread and fairly common in the north and west of Tasmania, growing in teatree sedgeland and heathland.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum secutum
plants.form: Light-greenish-brown leek orchid with a single, tubular leaf.
plants.flowers: 9-30 greenish-brown flowers, labellum whitish, margins entire, the broad green callus extending past the labellum curve. Strongly scented.
plants.habitat: Occurs in northern Tasmania in dense coastal scrub in the swales of stabilised sand dunes.
plants.notes: Apparently flowers only after summer fires.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum stellatum
plants.form: A robust white-lipped leek orchid, single, tubular dark-green leaf, dark purple at the base, 300-700mm long.
plants.flowers: 10-20 moderately large flowers, widely spreading segments. A white labellum with crinkled margins, recurved abruptly against the base and a fleshy, greenish-yellow callus with a notched, white apex.
plants.habitat: Found in a few alpine and sub-alpine areas in well-drained grassy Eucalyptus delegatensis forest in the north-east.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum taphanyx
plants.form: A tiny green-brown leek orchid, single, tubular, dark-green leaf, 200-300mm long, often withered at flowering.
plants.flowers: 15-25 tiny cream-to-greenish flowers with pinkish-mauve petals. A pink labellum, sharply reflexed, is restricted above the middle.
plants.habitat: Only found at one site in the Northern Midlands in remnant native grassland.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum truncatum
plants.form: A slender, fragrant, late-flowering white-lipped leek orchid, single tubular, dark-green leaf with a purplish base.
plants.flowers: 10-20 greenish, often purple-tinged flowers, well-spaced, white petals with a purplish midline and wavy margins. A white labellum, sharply recurved, with a callus ending just beyond the bend, apex notched.
plants.habitat: Locally common in native grasslands and shrubby forest from coastal to alpine and sub-alpine areas, often growing in disturbed sites.
plants.notes: Flowering enhanced by fire.

plants.name: Paraprasophyllum tunbridgense
plants.form: A robust, white-lipped leek orchid with a single, tubular bright green leaf, base purplish, 200-300mm long.
plants.flowers: 10-25 large, crowded, fragrant flowers with projecting ovaries and a large, oblong, labellum with strongly crinkled margins, strongly recurved in the middle. A yellowish-green callus ends just beyond the labellum bend.
plants.habitat: Known from only a few areas of remnant native grassland in the Tasmanian Midlands

plants.name: Parietaria cardiostegia
plants.form: Annual herb, softly hairy, without stinging hairs.
plants.fruit: Achene – about1.5 mm long, brown, shining.
plants.habitat: Recorded only from an island in the Furneaux Group.

plants.name: Parietaria debilis
plants.form: Slender annual herb with branches 10-30cm long; succulent leaves with soft hairs on slender stalks.
plants.flowers: Crowded and borne in the leaf axils, on twin stems with 3 flowers.
plants.habitat: Among muttonbird rookeries, in the salt spray zone on cliffs and rocks, on grazed pasture and grassland and on sand dunes in Northern Tasmania and the Bass Strait islands.
plants.notes: Tolerant of salt spray.

plants.name: Parsonsia brownii
plants.form: Vigorous, woody, twining climber with branches to 4-5cm in diameter. Leaves are opposite, lance-shaped, glossy on top and yellow-green to greyish underneath, 5-10cm long.
plants.flowers: Dull greenish-yellow, with the tube bearded at the throat, about 7mm in diameter. Many flowers, borne in broad clusters.
plants.habitat: Widespread in deep gullies, wet forest and rainforest.
plants.notes: Hardy; recommended to grow on mature trees or a frame for support, as it tends to smother shrubs. Suitable as a hedge or screening plant.

plants.name: Patersonia fragilis
plants.form: Tufted or tussock forming herb. Flower stems shorter than the leaves.
plants.flowers: Blue-mauve, 6-lobed. 3 outer lobes: large, rounded, spreading; 3 inner: tiny and erect.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – angular, breaking into 3 segments, curling back still enclosed in big brown bracts. Capsule contains many seeds which change from cream to red-brown at maturity.
plants.habitat: Common on sandy or gravelly soils near coasts, frequent in wet parts of coastal heaths.

plants.name: Patersonia occidentalis var. occidentalis
plants.form: Tufted herb.
plants.flowers: The tubes of the mauve flowers barely protrude beyond bracts.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – cylindrical; containing many seeds which change from cream to shiny red-brown at maturity.
plants.habitat: Found in wet heathland habitats near the coast.

plants.name: Pauridia glabella var. glabella
plants.form: Small herbaceous perennial with underground corms and dark-green grasslike leaves.
plants.flowers: One or two yellow or greenish-yellow flowers, 1.5-2.5 cm across, on stems up to 19 cm long.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – open at maturity to release the reddish-brown seed through a horizontal split.
plants.habitat: Grassy herb-lands and coastal heath; widely distributed.
plants.notes: Protect from snails and slugs.

plants.name: Pauridia vaginata var. vaginata
plants.form: Small herbaceous perennial with underground corms and dark-green leaves to 10 cm long and 2 mm wide.
plants.flowers: One or two yellow flowers, 3-4 cm across, on stems up to 10 cm long.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – open at maturity to release the seed through a horizontal split.
plants.habitat: Widespread in a variety of wetter situations.
plants.notes: Protect from slugs and snails.

plants.name: Pelargonium australe
plants.form: Perennial herb with persistent rootstock which forms erect leafy stems.
plants.flowers: Several in a stalked cluster, pinkish-white with reddish markings, 5 free petals.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – seeds with long awns attached are partially enclosed in papery bracts.
plants.habitat: Widespread, in crevices between rock, on rocky river banks and cliffs, coastal and inland to mountains.

plants.name: Pelargonium inodorum
plants.form: Annual herb with erect stems and opposite leaves, both covered in hairs. Lower leaf surface sometimes reddish.
plants.flowers: 3-15 small flowers with narrow, deep rose pink petals, sometimes with darker veins.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – long, slender; containing 4-5 dark brown or black seeds.
plants.habitat: Occasional, widespread from coasts to the Central Plateau.

plants.name: Pelargonium littorale
plants.form: Erect perennial herb with red stems.
plants.flowers: Deep pink.
plants.fruit: Schizocarp – long, slender; containing 4-5 dark brown or black seeds.
plants.habitat: Usually on sandy, coastal soils.

plants.name: Pellaea calidirupium
plants.form: Terrestrial species with creeping rhizome densely clothed with dark scales. Stipes persistent.
plants.habitat: A species from inland rocky areas of low to moderate rainfall. Will withstand dry and sunny conditions. Best planted amongst rocks where a good balance can be achieved between soil moisture and drainage.

plants.name: Pellaea falcata
plants.form: Terrestrial fern in clumps, fronds, 20-75cm long, erect or arching, pinnae falcate, dark green above, paler below, margins entire or short-toothed.
plants.habitat: Locally common in the north and east of Tasmania. Occurs on margins of wet sclerophyll forest and in fern gullies, particularly on their higher slopes. Usually occurs below 300m.
plants.notes: Mossy soil over rock.

plants.name: Pentachondra ericifolia
plants.form: Small heath-like shrub, dwarf, spreading to erect with hairy young growth.
plants.flowers: White, solitary, near ends of branches. Short scattered hairs on outside of corolla tube.
plants.fruit: Drupe – small, splitting into 5 parts when ripe.
plants.habitat: Found in alpine and sub-alpine habitats of the Central Plateau and at Mr. Dromedary. Requires acidic soils which do not dry out readily. Hardy to frost and snowfalls.
plants.notes: Rare in cultivation. Will require exceptionally good drainage in acid soils which do not dry out. Has potential for use in rockeries in temperate regions. A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. A sunny site will enhance flowering.

plants.name: Pentachondra involucrata
plants.form: Small shrub with hairy branches which may be erect or prostrate.
plants.flowers: Large, white and hairy, in groups of 1-3 near the ends of branches.
plants.fruit: Drupe – tiny, hidden in the persistent base of the sepals.
plants.habitat: A sub-alpine plant on kunanyi/Mt. Wellington, locally abundant. Also found on acid moors in the Upper Huon Valley and on the east coast at Eaglehawk Neck, Swanport and Schouten Island and in the extreme south at Whale Head.

plants.name: Pentachondra pumila
plants.form: Prostrate woody plant growing in dense matted patches up to 1m diameter.
plants.flowers: Usually white, solitary at the end of short branches.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in alpine heath and sedgeland in the southern most western mountains.

plants.name: Pentapogon quadrifidus var. parviflorus
plants.form: Similar to Pentapogon quadrifidus var. quadrifidus, but usually shorter.
plants.flowers: Flowerhead up to 5 cm long.

plants.name: Pentapogon quadrifidus var. quadrifidus
plants.form: Slender, erect or kneed annual or short lived perennial; variable.
plants.flowers: Flower head up to 5cm long (20cm var. quadrifidus), and contain fewer, smaller spikelets.
plants.habitat: Sedge and grasslands, heath, rock crevices, boulder slopes and stream banks. From sea level on the east coast and in the south-west, to 1200m altitude in the Central Highlands and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Persicaria decipiens
plants.form: Annual or perennial herb with slender, prostrate stems up to 60cm long, rooting at the base and sparingly branched. The leaves often have a black blotch near the middle, and the veins and margins are hairy.
plants.flowers: Flowers are slender, 2.5-3.5mm long and found at the end of the main branches. The flower tube is green and the petals are pale to deep pink, sometimes white.
plants.fruit: Nut – 3mm long, dark brown and shining.
plants.habitat: Banks of rivers and streams, most common in the north, including Cataract Gorge.

plants.name: Persicaria hydropiper
plants.form: Annual herb with reddish-green, slender stems, usually branched from the base. Leaves are 2-9cm long and lance-shaped.
plants.flowers: 1-3 flowers occur together in most of the leaf axils, and in slender spikes at the ends of the branches. Flower heads often droop at the tip. Flowers have dot-like markings, and green lobes with white or pale pink margins.
plants.fruit: Nut – 3-3.5mm long, dark brown or black.
plants.habitat: Damp places and stream margins in the north of the State.

plants.name: Persicaria praetermissa
plants.form: Annual herb with slender yellowish or greenish-brown stems, 60-150cm long. Leaves are 3-6cm long and variable in shape, ranging from arrow-shaped to lance-shaped. The midrib and veins on the underside of the leaves are bristly.
plants.flowers: Flowers occur in the axils of the upper leaves and on the ends of the stems. Flowers are 3mm long.
plants.habitat: Margins of streams and rivers in the north of the State.

plants.name: Persicaria subsessilis
plants.form: Perennial herb with few branches and erect stems. Leaves are narrow, 6-10cm long, with stiff, erect hairs on both surfaces and a long, pointed tip.
plants.flowers: Flower heads occur at the ends of the branches, in 2-4 slender spikes. Flowers are pink and 3mm long.
plants.habitat: Under Melaleuca ericifolia scrub and in wet and rocky places in the north of the State, including Cataract Gorge.

plants.name: Persoonia gunnii
plants.form: Dense shrub, upright to spreading.
plants.flowers: White, tubular with recurved petals, fragrant.
plants.fruit: Drupe – purplish-black, ovoid, 6-10 mm long; edible, semi-sweet but mealy.
plants.habitat: Occurs in the central highlands but Rare.

plants.name: Persoonia juniperina
plants.form: Erect to decumbent shrub. Young branches sparsely to densely hairy.
plants.flowers: Yellow, tubular with recurved petals.
plants.fruit: Drupe – purplish-black, ovoid, 6-10 mm long, edible but tasteless.
plants.habitat: Widespread in Tasmania growing on siliceous soils from sea level to 700m.
plants.notes: Adaptable to a variety of conditions. Bird attracting. Good protection for bird nesting.

plants.name: Persoonia moscalii
plants.form: Prostrate shrub with branches turning upwards at tips.
plants.flowers: Yellow, single in leaf axes.
plants.fruit: Drupe – spherical to ovoid, 10 mm long, 8 mm wide.
plants.habitat: Confined to a few mountains in the far south-west of the state.

plants.name: Persoonia muelleri subsp. angustifolia
plants.form: Erect shrub with a covering of greyish or tawny hairs.
plants.flowers: Yellow to cream, pointed at the tip and moderately hairy on the outside.
plants.fruit: Drupe – purplish-black, ovoid, 8–12 mm long; edible, semi-sweet but mealy and tasteless.

plants.name: Persoonia muelleri subsp. densifolia
plants.form: Erect, dense shrub, leaves crowded towards the ends of the branches.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow
plants.fruit: Drupe – purplish-black, ovoid, 8–12 mm long; edible, semi-sweet but mealy and tasteless.
plants.habitat: Local to common in coastal heaths and shrubberies and on higher ground adjacent to the coast, in the south-west of the state, from sea-level to about 1000m.

plants.name: Persoonia muelleri subsp. muelleri
plants.form: Shrub with young branchlets densely hairy, hairs greyish. Leaves not crowded.
plants.flowers: Mostly subtended by scale leaves, tepals 15- 22mm long, yellow to cream, hairy on outside.
plants.fruit: Drupe – purplish-black, ovoid, 8–12 mm long; edible, semi-sweet but mealy and tasteless.
plants.habitat: Occurs chiefly north-east of Lake St. Clair – Derwent River with a single collection known from Mt. Field. Grows in alpine heath and sclerophyll forest on dolerite from 700 to 1200m alt.
plants.notes: P. muelleri susbsp. muelleri apparently intergrades with subsp. angustifolia in the area between Lake St. Clair and Macquarie Harbour, also in the Lake Dove-Cradle Mountain and Adamsons Peak-South Cape areas.

plants.name: Phebalium daviesii
plants.form: Slender shrub. Leaves glossy 2-3cm long. Indented central vein ending in a v-shape.
plants.flowers: Flowers in terminal umbels. Petals white to deep cream; exterior with silvery or rusty scales.
plants.habitat: Known only from eastern coast of the north-east region at George River near St Helens.
plants.notes: In cultivation it has adapted well in free draining, acidic soils, semi shade or partial sun. Suited to containers.

plants.name: Pheladenia deformis
plants.form: Leaf narrowly linear, bright green, sparsely hairy.
plants.flowers: 1, rarely 2, bright blue flowers, 20-30 mm across, widely spreading petals. A tri-lobed blue labellum densely covered with slender, curved blue calli.
plants.habitat: Heathy and grassy open eucalypt forest, often with bulloak. Sunny heaths with a range of soil types.
plants.notes: The only small blue Caladenia-like orchid in Tasmania. Uncommon.

plants.name: Pherosphaera hookeriana
plants.form: Dark green, dense, much-branched shrub, branchlets often short and stiff.
plants.flowers: Separate male and female plants. Female cones 2-4mm long on short, usually pendulous branches (hence the common name of ‘drooping pine’) become fleshy and red when mature.
plants.fruit: Cone – Male cones – solitary, terminal with scales purplish-brown. Female cones – woody, solitary, terminal, pendulous with 2-5 fertile scales. Seed ripens with a hard brown covering.
plants.habitat: Abundant as dominant or co-dominant in areas of coniferous heath at Mt. Field; rarely encountered elsewhere.

plants.name: Philotheca freyciana
plants.form: Erect, compact shrub with slender, warty green stems, covered with oil glands.
plants.flowers: Solitary, on short stalks in the leaf axils. The flowers are pink in the bud stage, and white with five petals when open.
plants.fruit: Capsule – pointed tip. Seeds black, shiny and 4mm long.
plants.habitat: Grows on skeletal granite soils, and in the cracks of granite slabs and boulders. Known only from The Hazards and Cape Tourville on the Freycinet Peninsula.

plants.name: Philotheca verrucosa
plants.form: Small shrub, sprawling or erect. Extremely variable.
plants.flowers: White or pink, 5+ petals, 1.5cm across, solitary on numerous leaf axils near end of branch.
plants.fruit: Capsule – dry; separates into one-seeded parts which are dehiscent. Smooth, black seeds are released on maturity.
plants.habitat: Found in the eastern part of the state mainly on rocky hillsides or sandy areas in heath or eucalyptus forest.

plants.name: Philotheca virgata
plants.form: Erect shrub
plants.flowers: Flowers with 4-5 petals, white, may be tinged with pink, to 1.5 cm across.
plants.fruit: Capsule – dry; separates into one-seeded parts which are dehiscent. Smooth, black seeds are released on maturity.
plants.habitat: Near the coast in the east, south-west and west.

plants.name: Phlegmariurus varius
plants.form: Fern ally with stems erect or hanging, sometimes branching, leaves in spiral, overlapping, upright, lance-shaped.
plants.habitat: Widespread in Tasmania but seldom locally abundant. A variable species ranging from stunted upright plants on the coast and on mountain summits above 1000m to long pendulous plants in deep shade within rainforest. Usually terrestrial, but may be lithophytic and sometimes epiphytic.
plants.notes: Epiphytic, Lithophytic. Fern fibres, pine bark, orchid bark, charcoal and coarse gravel are suitable.

plants.name: Phragmites australis
plants.form: Vigorous, emergent aquatic resembling bamboo.
plants.flowers: Plume-like, at the top of the tall, straight stems.
plants.habitat: Common in lowland areas on the margins of streams, rivers, lakes and dams, sometimes found in irrigation and drainage ditches, and in brackish water and tidal systems.
plants.notes: Requires full sun and a large pool, needs to be contained within a large box. Cut back in winter, as stems die down after flowering. The underground stems can be eaten, and taste like bamboo shoots. Uses: making reed pens, and leaves are sometimes used for weaving. …

plants.name: Phyllachne colensoi
plants.form: Densely tufted, perennial plant with erect, closely packed stems, which forms a hard, mat-like cushion.
plants.flowers: Solitary, 4mm in diameter, barely raised above the cushion surface.
plants.habitat: Exposed slopes of mountains at altitudes of 1000m, recorded from Mt. Field West, Mount Rufus and Mount Pelion East.
plants.notes: Difficult to grow.

plants.name: Phyllangium distylis
plants.form: Small annual herb with erect stems, and pairs of light green, blunt, opposite leaves which are joined across the stem at their bases.
plants.flowers: Flowers are solitary and bell-shaped, with white, blunt-lobed petals, and borne on thread-like stalks.
plants.habitat: Boulders and rocky situations, muddy soaks and hollows in sandy heaths which are prone to flooding, in the north and north-east.

plants.name: Phyllangium divergens
plants.form: Annual ephemeral plant. Very similar in form to P. distylis; distinguished by elliptical leaves, larger flower tube and brown/grey seeds with a fine network of veins running over the surface.
plants.flowers: Whorls of bracts surrounding the flowers have 8 or 9 veins, compared to Phyllangium distylis which has 6-veined bracts.
plants.habitat: Open habitat on periodically wet, sandy and clay soils which often overlie rock, largely in the east of the State.

plants.name: Phyllanthus australis
plants.form: Undershrub with a woody base and slender, wiry stems, leaves 3-7mm long.
plants.flowers: Small, in the axils, on slender stalks.
plants.fruit: Capsule – hard, 4-5mm in diameter, changes from green to brown when mature.
plants.habitat: On roadsides and in open places, especially in the north, east and centre of the state.
plants.notes: Grows in most soils.

plants.name: Phyllanthus gunnii
plants.form: Erect slender shrub with rounded, short-stalked leaves in opposite rows.
plants.flowers: 4-5mm in diameter, green, occurring in the axils on slender stalks.
plants.fruit: Capsule – hard 4-5mm in diameter, changes from green to brown when mature.
plants.habitat: In shaded places, especially near the coast in the east and north.
plants.notes: Grows in most soils.

plants.name: Phyllocladus aspleniifolius
plants.form: Tree with lower branches whorled and spreading horizontally.
plants.flowers: Male: insignificant. Female: a seed-bearing scale which becomes pink and fleshy.
plants.fruit: Fleshy cone – seed ripens with the covering hard and greenish-black, becoming surrounded by a white fleshy aril.
plants.habitat: Occurs as a dominant in rainforest, an understorey species in eucalypt forest and occasionally as a shrub in alpine vegetation. It is confined to areas of high rainfall and low fire frequency.
plants.notes: Slow growing. Prefers moist, cool, acidic soil. A valuable commercial timber that does not shrink when dried.

plants.name: Phylloglossum drummondii
plants.form: Tiny, terrestrial fern ally; rootstock tuberous; leaves in an erect tuft; fruiting spike 3-5cm tall ending in ovoid, yellowish “cone”.
plants.habitat: Rare in Tasmania. Found only on northern coastline (also King and Flinders Islands) at or near sea level. Grows in wet, peaty soils. Requires regular disturbance and is usually found in areas that have been burnt.

plants.name: Phyllota diffusa
plants.form: Small shrub, ascending and much-branched.
plants.flowers: Numerous pea flowers, wings yellow, keel red/yellow, above claw sometimes streaked green.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – egg-shaped, 4-6mm long containing one or, rarely, two seeds.
plants.habitat: Local in sandy heaths near the east coast and in the north-west.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pilularia novae-hollandiae
plants.form: Tiny terrestrial fern forming mats. Rootstock threadlike; fronds simple, 2-7cm long, narrowly linear, coiled when young.
plants.habitat: Aquatic or semi-aquatic growing in the mud or silt of shallow and slow-moving rivers and on seasonally inundated margins of lakes and depressions. Establishes freely in man-made lakes.
plants.notes: Prefers a sunny position and tolerates light to moderate frost.

plants.name: Pimelea axiflora subsp. axiflora
plants.form: Small to medium shrub with few, slender branches.
plants.flowers: White to cream, exterior hairy, in few-flowered clusters in axils.
plants.habitat: Local on the islands of Bass Strait. Usually found in moist habitats from the coast to inland mountain ranges.
plants.notes: Plants grow best in moisture retentive, moderately well-drained, acidic soils in semi-shade or dappled shade. Hardy to most frosts and light snowfalls. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea cinerea
plants.form: Straggling shrub, branches and lower surfaces of leaves covered with long hairs.
plants.flowers: White to greenish-white, about 0.5cm long, exterior hairy, bisexual.
plants.habitat: Known from scattered localities in the south, west and north. Grows in the understorey of rainforest and wet forest at all altitudes.
plants.notes: Should adapt well to free-draining soils with good moisture retention. Likes semi-shaded aspect, is hardy to most frosts and tolerates snowfalls. It has potential as a cut foliage crop and as a hedging plant. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea curviflora
plants.form: Dwarf shrub with pale to dull green densely hairy leaves with incurved margins.
plants.flowers: Many flowered compact heads of greenish-yellow flowers at end of side branches.
plants.habitat: Recorded often in forest and often in sandy soil.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea drupacea
plants.form: Straggling shrub, with slender, silky-hairy branches.
plants.flowers: White or pale cream, to about 0.6cm in terminal heads in upper axils, sometimes profuse.
plants.fruit: Drupe – usually black, may be red; poisonous.
plants.habitat: Widespread and fairly frequent in wet forests.
plants.notes: Hardy to most frosts and withstands extended dry periods. Likes free draining acidic soils and a sunny to somewhat shaded site. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea filiformis
plants.form: Prostrate/scrambling, small flat clumps; light brown/grey bark.
plants.flowers: Clusters of 6-9 flowers at end of branch, very slender stems. Flowers, 5mm, white to deep pink; tubular.
plants.habitat: Known only from a few localities in northern Tas.
plants.notes: Occurs in heavy or light acidic soils and does best in a semi-shaded site but will tolerate plenty of sunshine. Also tolerates slightly alkaline soils. Excellent as a ground cover beneath shrubs and for growing over rocks and embankments. Attracts butterflies. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea flava subsp. flava
plants.form: Shrub with slender erect branches arising in whorls below the previous year’s flowers.
plants.flowers: Heads bright buttercup yellow of many tubular flowers surrounded by four wide green bracts. Male with wider spreading lobes, 2 orange stamens.
plants.habitat: Abundant but local near east and north coasts.
plants.notes: Likes moderately well-drained soils and a semi-shaded site. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea glauca
plants.form: Dwarf spreading shrub arising from tap root.
plants.flowers: Creamy-white, sweetly scented in heads to about 3cm across, terminal, erect, profuse.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent on coasts and occasional in dry places inland.
plants.notes: Occurs in a range of soils and habitats. Grows well in moderately to well-drained sites in semi-shaded or sunny positions. Will tolerate extended dry periods. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea humilis
plants.form: Small, tufted, many erect branches. Leaves 1cm, dark green, in opposite pairs.
plants.flowers: Heads many-flowered, white tubular at ends of branches, outside covered with short hairs.
plants.habitat: Widespread in sclerophyll forests and fairly dry places.
plants.notes: Flowers attract nectar seeking butterflies on sunny days. Found in a variety of soil types and adapts very well to cultivation. Likes moderately well-drained soil, sunny or semi-shaded site, is hardy to most frosts and withstands extended dry periods. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea leiophylla
plants.form: Small, erect to spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: Erect, compact terminal, or sometimes lateral, head of 10–25 white to pale creamy yellow flowers.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, local in open, dry forests and scrubby heaths, on granitic soils and gravels on Freycinet Peninsula and Schouten Island; from sea-level to 450m.

plants.name: Pimelea ligustrina subsp. ligustrina
plants.form: Shrub with glabrous stems or very sparse hairs near flower heads.
plants.flowers: Semi-globular flower heads to about 4cm, erect, terminal. Whitish/cream, profuse, moderately fragrant.
plants.habitat: Found from coast to about 1400m in altitude, mainly in open forest and wet sclerophyll forest. Grows in a range of freely to moderately well-drained acidic soils.
plants.notes: Tolerates plenty of sunshine but prefers a semi-shaded site. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea linifolia
plants.form: Dwarf to small shrub, slender branches. Branchlets yellow to reddish brown.
plants.flowers: Heads about 4cm, terminal, semi-compact. Flowers white, pink, rarely yellow. Bracts 4 green/red.
plants.habitat: Widespread from coastal to mountain regions.
plants.notes: Attracts butterflies. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea micrantha
plants.form: Small shrub, densely branched.
plants.flowers: Compact heads of 3–9 flowers, dull yellow or yellowish-brown.
plants.habitat: Very localised in remnant native grassland vegetation on basalt soils in the Central Midlands.

plants.name: Pimelea milliganii
plants.form: Low, much-branched silvery shrub. When looked at from above leaves form a cross.
plants.flowers: Heads to about 1.5cm across, few-flowered. Flowers white, exterior densely hairy.
plants.habitat: Occasional in alpine heath at altitudes of 900m to 1250m near the west coast.
plants.notes: Not usually cultivated and plants may not flower well at low altitude. Best results are likely to be achieved in well-drained acidic soils, sunny or semi-shaded sites. Hardy to most frosts and snowfalls. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea nivea
plants.form: Shrub, slender leafy branches. Leaves dark green, shining, surface glabrous, abaxial surface densely white.
plants.flowers: 10 or more white or pinkish heads of flowers at ends of main branches. Tubular.
plants.fruit: Drupe – dry, surrounded by long hairs.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread on rocky hillsides to 1000m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Attracts butterflies. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Traditional Palawa use: the bark was used for string.

plants.name: Pimelea pauciflora
plants.form: Small to medium shrub.
plants.flowers: Yellow to yellow-green, glabrous.
plants.fruit: Drupe – small, deep yellow to scarlet.
plants.habitat: Grows on mainly clay soils at altitudes of 500-1000m.
plants.notes: Lacks ornamental value but used for revegetation in the north-east; should adapt to a range of acidic soils in sunny or semi-shaded sites. Hardy to moderate frosts. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea pygmaea
plants.form: Cushion-like dwarf shrub.
plants.flowers: Flowers to about 0.8cm long, white, solitary, terminal, often profuse, exterior free of hairs.
plants.habitat: Occurs in sub-alpine moorland in central Tasmania.
plants.notes: Could be a very useful plant for rockeries or containers but may not flower well at lower altitudes. Must have an open aspect to succeed. Tolerates frost and heavy snowfalls and requires acidic soils. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

photos.credit: K and D Storey – Natural Values Atlas

plants.name: Pimelea sericea
plants.form: Shrub with many erect stems and leaves almost round.
plants.flowers: White to pale pink many-flowered heads at end of branches.
plants.fruit: Dry, nut-like – appear in clusters but are not prominent.
plants.habitat: Found in alpine heath in the eastern and central mountains, often on dolerite boulder-fields.
plants.notes: Requires moist, well drained acidic soils with plenty of organic matter. Tolerates sunshine but prefers semi-shade. Withstands heavy frosts and snowfalls. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea serpyllifolia subsp. serpyllifolia
plants.form: Dwarf to small shrub, branchlets may be slightly spiny.
plants.flowers: Flowers in terminal, compact heads, yellow, white or rarely yellow-green, without hairs.
plants.habitat: Found on the Bass Strait Islands. Most common on calcareous soils in woodland and scrubland.
plants.notes: Flowers for most of the year. Valuable for revegetation in its natural range although it is not particularly ornamental. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pimelea sp. Tunbridge
plants.form: Densely branched shrub; branches wiry
plants.flowers: Compact heads of up to 16 flowers, the heads axillary or terminating short branchlets. The butter-yellow flowers lack petals. Floral tube long and slender.
plants.habitat: Grows in native grassland dominated by Themeda triandra and what would have originally been Eucalyptus pauciflora grassy woodland.

plants.name: Pittosporum bicolor
plants.form: Erect shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Yellow or red flowers flushed with deep crimson or purple hanging on stalks.
plants.fruit: Woody Capsule – rounded and compressed, at first yellowish-green then woody, 8-10mm broad; the valves woody, opening flat into 2 valves leaving the seeds in a red pulp in the centre. 8-20 seeds per capsule.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet forests and gullies, sea level to 1500m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Bee attracting. Good hedge plant. Moderate flammability.

plants.name: Planocarpa nitida
plants.form: Dark green shrub with many individual erect stems.
plants.flowers: White, solitary in axils of upper branches.
plants.fruit: Drupe – black, shiny, flattened, 5–7 mm diameter.
plants.habitat: Confined to heath on the sand dunes of the Central Plateau around Lake Augusta. Grows in shallow, stony soils.
plants.notes: Prefers dappled shade.

plants.name: Planocarpa petiolaris
plants.form: Grey-green shrub with many individual erect stems. Can be discriminated from Planocarpa sulcata by leaf size and the pattern of hairiness on the inside of the flower.
plants.flowers: White, hairy on the inner surface.
plants.fruit: Drupe – red or red-black, surface dull, round, flattened, 4–7 mm diameter
plants.habitat: Common in exposed alpine heath and coniferous heath on shallow soils in the eastern and central mountains.
plants.notes: Growth habit and fruit make this an ideal plant for containers and gardens. Should do best in well drained, light to medium soils with dappled shade.

plants.name: Planocarpa sulcata
plants.form: Grey-green shrub with many individual erect stems with leaves in clusters around.
plants.flowers: White, hairy on the inside but not towards the ends.
plants.fruit: Drupe – red, shiny, flattened, 5–7 mm wide.
plants.habitat: Common in exposed alpine heath, coniferous heath and deciduous heath on shallow soils in the western mountains.

plants.name: Plantago antarctica
plants.form: Perennial herb with a stout tap-root and leaves with 3-5 longitudinal veins forming a flat rosette or arising from the base of the stem.
plants.flowers: Flowers in cylindrical spikes, on hairy flowering stems twice as long as the leaves.
plants.habitat: Alpine and sub-alpine grassland on the Central Plateau.

plants.name: Plantago bellidioides
plants.form: Perennial herb with a long, slender taproot, and flat leaves which are intermingled with brownish silky hairs spreading in a basal rosette.
plants.flowers: Flowers are green or thin, dry and translucent, and usually borne in cylindrical spikes, on erect flowering stems which are longer than the leaves. Flowers during the first year.
plants.habitat: Sandy places near the east, west and north-west coasts.

plants.name: Plantago brownii
plants.form: Perennial herb with a long, stout taproot, and somewhat fleshy, bright green leaves, 3-4cm long, arranged in a spreading, flat rosette.
plants.flowers: Flowers occur in groups of 1-4 in short dense spikes or heads. These are borne on flowering stems which are sparsely hairy and at least as long as the leaves.
plants.habitat: Rocks and other coastal places prone to salt spray.

plants.name: Plantago debilis
plants.form: Perennial herb with a slender taproot and erect leaves which are hairy on both surfaces. Leaves are arranged in a basal rosette, and the leaf margins are usually toothed.
plants.flowers: Flowers are very small and are found towards the ends of long slender stalks.
plants.habitat: Boulder crevices and wet and dry forest and woodland, on the east coast and in the north-east.

plants.name: Plantago gaudichaudii
plants.form: Erect perennial plant with soft narrow linear leaves, and fine brown hairs on the leaf bases.
plants.flowers: Tiny brown flowers in dense, compact spikes up to 10cm long.
plants.habitat: Known from one grassy dry sclerophyll forest site, at Rosny Point in the south-east.

plants.name: Plantago glabrata
plants.form: Perennial herb with a stout taproot and radical, spreading, lance-shaped leaves with distinct midribs.
plants.flowers: Flowers are borne in cylindrical spikes which are up to 2.5cm long, on erect, slender and wiry flowering stems which are longer than the leaves.
plants.habitat: Frequently growing in alpine and sub-alpine grassland with Plantago paradoxa, Central Plateau.
plants.notes: Attracts the migratory Meadow Argus butterfly (Junonia villida calybe), which lays its eggs on the leaves.

plants.name: Plantago glacialis
plants.form: Stout, perennial, mat-forming herb, with flat, thick, lance-shaped leaves and golden-brown hairs in the leaf axils.
plants.flowers: 1-4 greenish flowers in a flower head at the end of the stems.
plants.habitat: Short alpine herbfields associated with snow patches, in the central and western mountains.

plants.name: Plantago gunnii
plants.form: Small perennial herb with slender stems, forming rosettes of leaves 1.5cm in diameter. The leaf stalk is often longer than the blade, which is thick and covered with long, erect hairs.
plants.flowers: Flowers are usually solitary, on short, hairy stalks which become longer than the leaves in the fruiting stage.
plants.fruit: Capsule – opens by a lid. Usually only 1 or 2 seeds mature.
plants.habitat: Grows in cushion plants, including Donatia novae-zealandii and Pterygopappus lawrencii, on mountains of the Central Plateau and west of the State.

plants.name: Plantago leptostachys
plants.form: Perennial herb with elliptical leaves, 2-5cm long, arising from the base of the stem. The base of the leaf is narrowed into a stalk which is about as long as the leaf blade.
plants.flowers: Flowers are borne in a narrow, cylindrical spike, up to 2.5cm long.
plants.habitat: Cushion plant communities on mountains above 1200m altitude.

plants.name: Plantago paradoxa
plants.form: Perennial herb with a short rootstock and lance-like leaves with blunt teeth on the margins, 1.5-5cm long and arranged in a flat rosette. The upper surface of the leaves often have tufts of hairs on wart-like swellings near the teeth.
plants.flowers: 2-4 flowers occur together in heads, on hairy flowering stems which are only a few mm long at the time of flowering. In the fruiting stage, the flowering stems become upright and longer than the leaves.
plants.habitat: Widespread in alpine and sub-alpine grassland.
plants.notes: Attracts the migratory Meadow Argus butterfly (Junonia villida calybe), which lays its eggs on the leaves.

plants.name: Plantago tasmanica var. archeri
plants.form: Rounded leaves, densely hairy on both leaf surfaces.
plants.flowers: Flowers on short cylindrical spikes on stalks longer than the leaves.
plants.habitat: Widespread in moist alpine heathland.

plants.name: Plantago tasmanica var. tasmanica
plants.form: Perennial herb with leaves arising from the base of the stem, interspersed with long silky hairs. Leaf stalks are short, wide, thick and toothed. Leaf blades are broadest above the middle, and sparingly covered with stiff, bristle-like hairs.
plants.flowers: Flower stems are downy, curve upwards, and are scarcely longer than the leaves. The flowers are born in short, narrow cylindrical spikes.
plants.habitat: Widespread on mountains.

plants.name: Plantago varia
plants.form: Perennial herb which is very variable in size and form. Leaves are erect or half-spreading and arise from the base of the stem. The leaf are pale greyish-green, have 1-5 prominent longitudinal veins, and range in length from 1-30cm.
plants.flowers: Flowers are usually in cylindrical spikes, sometimes in heads or reduced to 2-3 flowers, and borne on erect flowering stems which are usually longer than the leaves.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in lowland habitats.
plants.notes: Attracts the migratory Meadow Argus butterfly (Junonia villida calybe), which lays its eggs on the leaves.

plants.name: Platylobium obtusangulum
plants.form: Slender shrub, spreading or erect.
plants.flowers: Pea flower on short stalks almost hidden by bracts. Large kidney-shaped standard yellow and red.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oblong (20mm long, 12mm wide), flat and almost stalkless.
plants.habitat: Widespread but local in dry soil.
plants.notes: Hardy in most soils and aspects provided they are kept reasonably dry. Interesting triangular leaves.

plants.name: Platylobium parviflorum
plants.form: Slender shrub with downy, wiry, branches. Some forms are prostrate.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, solitary or 2-3 together, the large standard is notched. Stem has brown bracts.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – 2-4cm long, oblong, flat and stalked with upper edge winged.
plants.habitat: Local in shady places in sandy heaths in the north.
plants.notes: Hardy plant in most soils and aspects provided that they are not too wet. Common in cultivation. Natural regeneration is from seed, particularly after fire. Useful in providing low-level cover (up to 2m) in mixed species windbreaks.

plants.name: Platylobium triangulare
plants.form: Wiry spreading shrub with broad triangular leaves.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, yellow standard, reddish-brown on back, red on front, keel is reddish-purple.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – flattened, oblong (25mm long, 10mm wide) and winged on upper edge.
plants.habitat: Local in sandy soil in the south-east, east and north.

plants.name: Pleurosorus rutifolius
plants.form: Lithophytic or grows in crevices and rocky ledges.
plants.habitat: Found in dry habitats; this species desiccates in summer.

plants.name: Pneumatopteris pennigera
plants.form: Clump-forming fern; rootstock erect, short trunk; fronds, 40-110cm long, erect in tussock; pinnae broad-based, deeply lobed, lower pinnae reduced.
plants.habitat: Very rare in Tasmania. Restricted to several sites in the north-west and King Island. Found in riparian situations or soaks. Will tolerate boggy soils and most frosts.
plants.notes: Can be grown successfully with regular addition of lime.

plants.name: Poa clelandii
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial grass with green or purplish stems, purplish leaf sheaths and folded leaves up to 25cm long.
plants.flowers: In a 10cm long flower head of spikelets, which is contracted at first and spreading later.
plants.habitat: Wide range of habitats, including coastal sands in the north-east, under light eucalypt forest in the Midlands, and poorly drained sites in grass-sedgeland in the Central Highlands and south-west.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting. Attracts seed-eating birds and provides cover for small lizards. Lowland plants are taller, with strongly flattened stems; plants from higher altitudes are smaller with less flattened stems.

plants.name: Poa clivicola
plants.form: Slender, tufted, green to grey-green grass with very fine leaves, mostly 0.2-0.4mm wide, which are rough to touch.
plants.flowers: Spikelets are strongly flattened, and the flower head is 2-12cm long.
plants.habitat: Highland grasslands on fertile soils, usually basalt or limestone, 700-1000m altitude.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting; attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

photos.credit: Queensland Herbarium, D. Sharp CC BY

plants.name: Poa costiniana
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial grass with smooth stems and rolled, 45cm-long leaves which narrow to a stiff sharp tip.
plants.flowers: In flower heads of green or purplish spikelets, up to 15cm long.
plants.habitat: Above the tree line, in grassland, heathland and open areas. Mostly over 1000m in the north-east, Ben Lomond, Central Highlands and south-west.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

photos.credit: ANBG photo C. Totterdell CC BY

plants.name: Poa fawcettiae
plants.form: Erect, tufted, rather rigid perennial grass with smooth stems and stiff, tightly folded bluish-green leaves with sharp tips.
plants.flowers: Flower heads are pyramid-shaped and up to 20cm long, and bear green or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Sub-alpine areas in heath, grassland and open situations, usually over 1100m altitude, in the north-east and Central Highlands.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

photos.credit: ANBG photo C. Totterdell CC BY

plants.name: Poa gunnii
plants.form: Very variable, smooth, tufted perennial grass, with in rolled or folded leaves up to 30cm long, and smooth, slender stems.
plants.flowers: Flower head 1.5-8cm long, bearing green or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Common in sub-alpine habitats from 800-1400m altitude, but extending to near sea level in the south of the State.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards. An important habitat and food plant for the endangered and endemic Ptunarra Brown Butterfly (Oreixenica ptunarra) in the Central Highlands. …

photos.credit: Queensland Herbarium, D. Sharp CC BY

plants.name: Poa halmaturina
plants.form: Small, erect perennial plant, with very fine, long stems and thread-like, pale or yellowish green leaves.
plants.flowers: Flower head is up to 3cm long, with short, erect branches, bearing pale green, straw-coloured or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Restricted to coastal dunes and heath on King Island, the Furneaux Group and in the south-west of the State.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

plants.name: Poa hiemata
plants.form: Smooth, tufted grass with fine, soft leaves up to 25cm long which are rolled or folded.
plants.flowers: Flower heads up to 12cm long with green or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Sub-alpine heath, grassland and open areas, in the Central Highlands and Ben Lomond, usually above 1000m altitude.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

plants.name: Poa hookeri
plants.form: Small, tufted perennial grass with in rolled leaves, 3-30cm long, and long, slender stems.
plants.flowers: Flower head 3-12cm long, containing green or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Dry situations in open woodland to about 700m altitude, in the Midlands, east coast, Ben Lomon and Central Highlands.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

plants.name: Poa jugicola
plants.form: Densely or loosely tufted perennial grass with fine, soft, mostly basal leaves and long, slender stems.
plants.flowers: Flower head is 10-25cm long with flattened green or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Occurs in open, rocky situations, mostly above 900m altitude, on Quamby Bluff and the Western Tiers.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

plants.name: Poa labillardierei var. acris
plants.form: Perennial dense tussock, shorter, denser blades than usual type. Alpine.
plants.flowers: Panicle with green or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Grass herbfields of Central highlands, 600 to 1100m.

plants.name: Poa labillardierei var. labillardierei
plants.form: Perennial grass with green to blue-green leaves rolled into a tube, forming dense tussocks. Can grow to only 20cm in sub-alpine areas and coastal sands.
plants.flowers: Panicle 10 -30cm long. Green or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant, favours damp situations.
plants.notes: Cut back or burn in autumn or every couple of years to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards. Self-seeds vigorously in the garden. …

plants.name: Poa mollis
plants.form: Loosely tufted perennial grass, basal leaf sheaths straw-coloured, upper sheaths grey-green to blue-green, densely covered with soft hairs.
plants.flowers: 2-4 flowers in spikelets, green or tinged with purple.
plants.habitat: Dry open hillsides and cliffs in the north-west and Midlands, mostly around Launceston.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

plants.name: Poa poiformis var. poiformis
plants.form: Tufted perennial; leaf sheaves often smooth. Variable in size, colour and texture. Coastal.
plants.flowers: Panicles up to 25cm long, usually contracted and linear.
plants.habitat: Coastal and estuarine areas of east coast and Furneaux Group.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards. Tolerant of salt spray.

plants.name: Poa poiformis var. ramifer
plants.form: Similar to Poa poiformis var. poiformis, except it branches from the lower nodes, and the leaf sheaths and internodes are often purple.
plants.flowers: Panicles up to 25cm, usually contracted and linear.
plants.habitat: Shores and offshore islands, east coast and Furneaux Group.

plants.name: Poa rodwayi
plants.form: Green or greyish-green tussock grass, with tightly rolled leaf blades up to 30cm long. Sheaths of basal leaves are straw-coloured and shining, upper sheaths green with short dense hairs.
plants.flowers: Panicles 3-15cm long, loosely contracted, later spreading.
plants.habitat: Common in dry open habitats under light eucalypt cover, most common in lowland areas, near sea level to 1300m altitude.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

photos.credit: Queensland Herbarium, D. Sharp CC BY

plants.name: Poa sieberiana var. hirtella
plants.form: Grey-green to blue-green, densely tufted perennial grass.
plants.flowers: Panicle 3-20cm long, contracted to spreading at maturity. Green – purplish.

plants.name: Poa sieberiana var. sieberiana
plants.form: Grey-green to blue-green, densely tufted perennial grass.
plants.flowers: 2-7 flowers borne in a green to purplish spikelet. Yellow or purplish anthers.
plants.habitat: Wide range of habitats, from sea level to over 1300m. Open grassland and light forest, usually on dry hillsides, but also tolerant of damper conditions. North-west, north-east, west coast, Central Highlands, east coast and south-west.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

plants.name: Poa tenera
plants.form: Trailing, perennial tussock grass with long, smooth, slender stems producing clusters of shoots from the nodes. Leaves are floppy, linear and 5-20cm long.
plants.flowers: Flower heads 1-12cm long and pyramid-shaped when mature, bearing pale green or purplish spikelets.
plants.habitat: Moist, well-drained and shaded situations, from sea level to 800m.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

plants.name: Podocarpus lawrencei
plants.form: Yellowish-green shrub, branches usually spreading over dolerite boulders.
plants.fruit: Fleshy cone – Male plants have tiny cones which scatter pollen in season. Female plants have small red fruits with the seed attached to the end.
plants.habitat: Widespread but local on mountains on stabilised talus at about 900-1300m.
plants.notes: Leaves have a pine-like fragrant scent when crushed.

plants.name: Podolepis decipiens
plants.form: Herbaceous undershrub with perennial rootstock.
plants.flowers: Daisy-like flowers, solitary or few heads per group. Ray florets bright yellow; disc, yellow.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent from sea level to mountain summits. Tolerates most frosts.
plants.notes: Has excellent potential as a plant for borders, containers and floral displays. Roots are edible and were used by early European settlers and Aboriginal people.

plants.name: Polyphlebium venosum
plants.form: Small epiphytic fern in dense masses, rootstock; creeping, thread-like; fronds,5-15cm long, dark green, 1-2 times pinnate, translucent.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common from sea level to 600m. Typically epiphytic on live trunks of Dicksonia.
plants.notes: Easily grown if given constant high humidity and daily misting. Requires protection from drying winds, in a shady position. May also be cultured in a bottle, terrarium or aquarium.

plants.name: Polystichum proliferum
plants.form: Rootstock forms a short trunk with age; fronds, 30-150cm long, bi-pinnate, oblong in outline, often with bulbil near apex. Spreads to tussock.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant from sea level to at least 1300m in a wide range of habitats. Will tolerate salt laden winds in coastal situations.
plants.notes: Very hardy; clump forming; suitable for growing in large container. Will tolerate moderate exposure to sun and dry periods once established. Excellent for planting under established trees.

plants.name: Pomaderris apetala subsp. apetala
plants.form: Tall shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Numerous, small (without petals), cream to greenish-brown in pyramid shaped terminal racemes.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent on the margins of wet eucalypt forest and in wet gullies.
plants.notes: Moist, well drained acidic soil with shade. Good for stabilising banks of streams. Good screen plant. Bird attracting. Bee attracting. Low flammability.

plants.name: Pomaderris apetala subsp. maritima
plants.form: Medium shrub.
plants.flowers: Numerous, small (without petals), cream to greenish-brown in pyramid shaped terminal racemes.

plants.name: Pomaderris aspera
plants.form: Leafy erect shrub or slender tree.
plants.flowers: Greenish – masses in terminal sprays.
plants.habitat: In forests on moister slopes and near streams throughout the eastern ranges. Sensitive to drought.
plants.notes: In cultivation generally hardy. Appreciate good drainage and full sun to part shade. Fast growing. Important in maintaining stream bank stability. Bird attracting. Small insectivorous birds (e.g. wrens) nest in the foliage. The flowers provide food for insects. …

plants.name: Pomaderris elachophylla
plants.form: Slender shrub
plants.flowers: Small about 1mm long in few-flowered clusters, terminal and in the axils of upper leaves.
plants.habitat: Local in scattered localities from sea level to about 900m.
plants.notes: In cultivation generally hardy. Appreciate good drainage and full sun to part shade.

plants.name: Pomaderris elliptica var. diemenica
plants.form: Shrub or small tree.
plants.flowers: Yellow, profuse, in terminal clusters. Petals usually present.
plants.notes: Hardy; can tolerate sun or semi shade.

plants.name: Pomaderris elliptica var. elliptica
plants.form: Shrub or small tree.
