plants.flowers: Yellow, profuse, in terminal clusters. Petals usually present.
plants.notes: Hardy; can tolerate sun or semi shade.

plants.name: Pomaderris intermedia
plants.form: Open shrub
plants.flowers: Yellow in tight clusters, shorter stalks towards the top of the cluster.
plants.fruit: Capsule – small capsules that are brownish, papery and dry. Seed is light brown.

plants.name: Pomaderris oraria subsp. oraria
plants.form: Small shrub
plants.flowers: Small, in dense compound clusters sometimes reduced to 5 or 6 flowers.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – small capsules that are brownish, papery and dry. Seed is light brown.
plants.habitat: Local near the north and north-east coasts and on the islands of Bass Strait.

plants.name: Pomaderris paniculosa subsp. paralia
plants.form: Compact much-branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Flowers are on short stalks, with greenish-brown sepals to 2.5 mm long and a deeply trifid style; there are no petals.
plants.fruit: Capsule – dry, about 3 mm long, opening by three valves to release pale-brown flattened seeds.
plants.habitat: Occurs in coastal sites in the north-east, the Furneaux Group and King Island, where it grows in exposed sites along cliff lines and within dune scrubs.

plants.name: Pomaderris phylicifolia subsp. ericoides
plants.form: Woody shrub
plants.flowers: Small, yellowish and numerous, on short flower stems at the ends of the branches.

plants.name: Pomaderris phylicifolia subsp. phylicifolia
plants.form: A woody shrub with numerous, erect, hairy branches.
plants.flowers: In short clusters, oldest flowers near the top, in axils of upper leaves of the many branches.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – small, brownish, papery and dry. Seed is light brown.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in the north and east especially on the banks of the Mersey, St Paul’s and Prosser rivers.

photos.credit: H & A Wapstra – Natural Values Atlas

plants.name: Pomaderris pilifera subsp. pilifera
plants.form: Shrub resembling Pomaderris elliptica.
plants.flowers: Small, creamy yellow, conspicuous; 5 petals; in pyramid shaped panicles.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – small, brownish, papery and dry. Seed is light brown.

plants.name: Pomaderris pilifera subsp. talpicutica
plants.form: Small diffuse shrub with numerous stems arising from a single rootstock.
plants.flowers: Small golden yellow flowers.

plants.name: Pomaderris racemosa
plants.form: Small woody shrub
plants.flowers: In loose, compound clusters, terminal and in the axils of upper leaves.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – small, brownish, papery and dry. Seed is light brown.
plants.habitat: Local, usually on the banks of streams and lakes as along the South Esk River at Fingal and Avoca, Tooms Lake and lakes on the Central Plateau.

plants.name: Poranthera microphylla
plants.form: Small herb with slender, sometimes thread-like branches, 2-20cm long. Leaves are distant, with flat leaf blades which are thin and flexible in lowland plants and somewhat fleshy in plants at high altitudes.
plants.flowers: On slender stalks, in small, leafy flower heads. Petals are white, pale pink or tinged with green.
plants.habitat: Open habitats, roadsides, hills and mountains, from sea level to about 1150m altitude.

plants.name: Poranthera petalifera
plants.form: Spreading perennial herb 20-30cm long annual stems, which scramble over rocks and plants. The leaves are lance-shaped and in opposite pairs, and the margins bend under.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, on stalks in the upper leaf axils. Male flowers are white and female flowers have greenish-white sepals surrounding the clear petals.
plants.fruit: Capsule – almost spherical, about 2mm wide, and contains 6 pale, smooth, orange-brown seeds.
plants.habitat: Known only from a dolomite ridge which runs north and north-east of Mount Anne, 750-1000m altitude.
plants.notes: Rare alpine that only occurs in small population on Mt Anne.

plants.name: Portulaca oleracea
plants.form: Annual herb with purplish, spreading stems.
plants.flowers: Yellow flowers, with 4-6 petals joined at the base, may be solitary or a few together.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule – seeds are black and shiny.
plants.habitat: Locally common as a weed in cultivated ground; prominent on floodplains.
plants.notes: All parts of the plant are edible and may be eaten raw or cooked; frequently eaten by Aboriginal people, especially the seeds.

plants.name: Posidonia australis
plants.form: Perennial marine herb with 2-3 flat, thin, leaves per shoot, each 60cm long.
plants.flowers: Flower head contains 2-6 spikes, up to 6.5cm long.
plants.habitat: Just below the low water mark on coasts of the north-west, north-east and Furneaux Group.
plants.notes: Sea grass.

plants.name: Potamogeton australiensis
plants.form: Perennial aquatic herb, with stout stems to 3m long and a creeping rhizome.
plants.flowers: Small flowers produced in dense spikes, on stalks up to 20cm long.
plants.fruit: Achene – 4 in number, buoyant in water.
plants.habitat: Rivers, creeks, lakes and lagoons, King Island, Furneaux Group, north-west, north-east, Midlands and east coast.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Potamogeton cheesemanii
plants.form: Perennial aquatic herb, with leafy stems and a creeping rhizome.
plants.flowers: Small flowers produced in dense, cylindrical, 3cm long spikes, on long stout stalks.
plants.fruit: Achene – 4 in number, buoyant in water.
plants.habitat: Rivers, creeks, lakes, lagoons and farm dams, from sea level to 1000m altitude.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Potamogeton crispus
plants.form: Perennial aquatic herb, with compressed stems and toothed leaf margins.
plants.flowers: Small flowers produced in floppy, 1-2cm long spikes. Flower stalks often curve backward in fruit.
plants.fruit: Achene – 4 in number, buoyant in water.
plants.habitat: Rivers, lagoons and farm dams in the north-west, Midlands and east coast.

plants.name: Potamogeton ochreatus
plants.form: Perennial aquatic herb, with stems round in cross section or compressed, rounded leaf tips and a creeping rhizome.
plants.flowers: Small flowers produced in dense, 1.5mm long spikes.
plants.fruit: Achene – 4 in number, buoyant in water.
plants.habitat: Rivers, creeks, lagoons and farm dams, from sea level to 1000m altitude, all Tasmanian regions except Ben Lomond, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Potamogeton perfoliatus
plants.form: Perennial aquatic herb, with stems to 3m long and round in cross-section, translucent leaves and a creeping rhizome.
plants.flowers: Small flowers produced in 1-3cm long, cylindrical spikes.
plants.fruit: Achene – 4 in number, buoyant in water.
plants.habitat: Rivers and lagoons in the north-west, Midlands and east coast.

plants.name: Prasophyllum abblittiorum
plants.form: A tiny yellowish-green leek orchid with a single dark-green, tubular leaf, purple at the base, 180-250mm long.
plants.flowers: Up to 10 sparsely crowded lemon flowers, a slightly paler labellum lacking a callus.
plants.habitat: Only found at two moisture-retentive sites in peaty soil near Arthur River, north-west Tasmania.

plants.name: Prasophyllum elatum
plants.form: A robust species with a smooth tubular leaf 200–1000mm long.
plants.flowers: Up to 100 greenish-yellow to purplish-black flowers 10–15 mm across. The pinkish-white, crisped labellum has a prominent green callus plate with raised edges.
plants.habitat: Locally common, growing in coastal sandy, sandy-clay and lateritic soils in heathlands, woodlands and shrublands.
plants.notes: Flowers best in the season following summer fire.

plants.name: Prionotes cerinthoides
plants.form: Climbing shrub with long slender branches on ground or epiphytic on trunks of trees.
plants.flowers: Pendulous, stalked, tubular flowers, crimson or pink, about 2cm long, with long stamens.
plants.fruit: Woody capsule opening by 5 valves with many seeds in each part.
plants.habitat: Frequent in rainforests especially in the west and south-west of the State.
plants.notes: Slow growing. Requires reasonable shade, plenty of moisture, but excellent drainage.

plants.name: Prostanthera lasianthos
plants.form: Upright shrub to small tree with a bushy spreading crown when grown in the open.
plants.flowers: Prolific white or pale lilac spotted with deep purple.
plants.fruit: Nut – splits into four segments each with own seed at maturity – 4 together in “ice-cream cone”. Seed is slightly flattened, brown or grey and up to 2mm long; turns from green to grey when ripe.
plants.habitat: Needs protection from strong winds. Margins of streams to sea level, abundant on mountain slopes in openings in wet forest.
plants.notes: Fast growing. Useful as a screen plant if protected from strong winds. Prostantheras require full sun and excellent drainage. Even in ideal conditions they are not long-lived. …

plants.name: Prostanthera rotundifolia
plants.form: Much-branched aromatic shrub.
plants.flowers: Lilac to purple in showy sprays.
plants.fruit: Nutlet – split into four segments each with own slightly flattened, brown or grey seed, up to 2mm long.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in north and east, along river banks and on adjacent rocky hillsides.
plants.notes: Prostantheras require full sun and excellent drainage. Even in ideal conditions they are not long-lived. To overcome the problem, the Australian National Botanic Gardens began, in the 1970s, to graft Prostanthera on to Westringia fruticosa rootstock. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Pseudanthus divaricatissimus
plants.form: Procumbent to prostrate spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: Pink to red flowers solitary in axils of upper leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule – ovoid, 4.5 mm long, glabrous. Seed broadly ovoid, 2.5 mm long, pale tan to dark brown.
plants.habitat: Local on heathland and heathy woodland on the east coast near Coles Bay.
plants.notes: Flowering and fruiting through the year, peak flowering in spring.

plants.name: Pseudanthus ovalifolius
plants.form: Compact procumbent shrub.
plants.flowers: Creamy-white flowers solitary in axils of upper leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule – ovoid, 3.5–4.0 mm long. Seed ovoid, 2.5–2.8 mm long, tan-brown.
plants.habitat: Found on heathland and heathy woodland on the Furneaux Islands.
plants.notes: Flowering and fruiting through the year, peak flowering in spring

plants.name: Pseudopanax gunnii
plants.form: Sparsely branched shrub with slender branches covered by coarse hairs. Stalked leaves divided into 3-7 leaflets, 2-8cm long.
plants.flowers: Numerous small flowers with 5 greenish-white petals.
plants.fruit: Berries or drupes – succulent, purplish-black, about 5mm long and 8mm wide. 2 seeds per fruit, enclosed in the hard inner layer of the fruit wall.
plants.habitat: Occasional in temperate rainforest in the west and south-west.

plants.name: Psychrophila phylloptera
plants.form: Rosette herb, hairless, with prostrate leaves which have two vertical wings emerging from blade. Rootstock, stout.
plants.flowers: Creamy yellow, held in the centre of the rosette.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – persistent, usually short, styles.
plants.habitat: Known from short alpine herbfield in the eastern and central mountains. Sometimes growing in cushion plants. Also found in wet flushes on scree.
plants.notes: Needs snow patch habitat to grow.

plants.name: Pteridium esculentum subsp. esculentum
plants.form: Fronds, up to 300 cm (but usually about 90cm tall), stiffly erect, leathery, glabrous on upper surface, appressed fine hairs under. Lobe present where segment joins stalk.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant across most of Tasmania but broadly absent from the highlands and parts of the Midlands. Occurs in well-drained soils of most vegetation types but not usually in rainforest, wet sclerophyll forest and dark fern gullies.
plants.notes: Has moderate flammability. Sporelings are rarely seen except occasionally on burnt sites. Most growth is by spreading rhizomes.

plants.name: Pteris epaleata
plants.form: Terrestrial fern, rhizome tufted, erect; rhachis yellowish; fronds dark-green with netted interconnected veins of pinnules.
plants.habitat: Common in north-west Tasmania, rare elsewhere. Grows in wet and often boggy soils in rainforest, wet sclerophyll forest and fern gullies. Occurs in very sheltered lowland sites besides small watercourses or within drainage lines. Has also been observed in wooded bogs amidst coastal sand dunes.
plants.notes: Resents disturbance.

plants.name: Pteris tremula
plants.form: Terrestrial fern, rhizome tufted, erect; rhachis brown and polished; fronds, up to 200cm, narrow upright, pale, fine and lacy.
plants.habitat: Uncommon across northern and eastern Tasmania to 300m in well-drained, fertile soils on the margins of fern gullies and along ephemeral creeks and drainage lines. Has quite a high light requirement.
plants.notes: Fast growing in a wide variety of habitats. Plants from some areas are reputed to be short-lived.

plants.name: Pterostylis alata
plants.form: A winter-flowering erect, green and white-striped greenhood, leaf rosette absent on flowering plants.
plants.flowers: Flower with bold green and white stripes. A short curved hood, tepals brown at the apex. Lateral sepals extending well above the galea (hood). Pointed labellum protruding prominently from a broadly notched sinus when in set position.
plants.habitat: Widespread near the coast in the east, particularly common in the south-east.

plants.name: Pterostylis aphylla
plants.form: A tiny greenhood, 2-7 leaves in a rosette and a fleshy stalk.
plants.flowers: 1-3 crowded, plump, green white and brown scabrous flowers and a dark, hidden labellum.
plants.habitat: Widespread but uncommon in coastal heathland, sedgeland and buttongrass plain in moisture retaining soils and gravels.

plants.name: Pterostylis atriola
plants.form: A tiny slender multi-flowered greenhood with a wiry scape, 3-6 dark green rosette leaves, margins entire.
plants.flowers: 1-10 tiny green white and brown-striped flowers. 2-4 open at once. Dorsal sepal similar length to petals. Labellum hidden.
plants.habitat: Occurs in the north and east on generally stony soil in dry to damp sclerophyll forest, typically with an open understorey e.g. shrubby Eucalyptus obliqua forest, shrubby/heathy Eucalyptus amygdalina forest. …

plants.name: Pterostylis commutata
plants.form: A medium ruddyhood with a rosette of 6-10 leaves encircling the scape, often dried off by time of flowering.
plants.flowers: 1-5 large, erect, pale-green to translucent flowers with some dark-green markings. Sepals with long, thin filamentous points. An oblong labellum covered with small bristles.
plants.habitat: Restricted to a few sites in the Tasmanian Midlands on native grassland and grassy woodland, often on poor dry soil.

plants.name: Pterostylis concinna
plants.form: A slender wiry greenhood, a rosette of 3-6 dark green leaves encircling the base.
plants.flowers: Small, green and white-striped flower with reddish-brown markings on top of petals. Long erect lateral sepals, protruding just above the hood. A forked labellum just visible above a shallow sinus.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common in moist coastal and near-coastal sand dunes, grasslands and Melaleuca scrub.

plants.name: Pterostylis curta
plants.form: A stout greenhood, a rosette of 2-6 dark green leaves encircling the scape, margins entire or crinkled.
plants.flowers: Single green, white and brown flower with a short blunt hood, a bulging sinus and prominent cream to brown labellum, twisted towards the apex.
plants.habitat: Locally common in heathy and shrubby eucalypt forest in the east and north-east, including the Furneaux Islands. Often in colonies in moist, sheltered areas.

plants.name: Pterostylis decurva
plants.form: Relatively large, erect, slender green white and brown-striped greenhood. Rosette often held above the ground on a separate stalk.
plants.flowers: Boldly striped, white and dark green or brown greenhood. Long, thin, curving dorsal sepal. Dark curved or kinked labellum protruding prominently in the set position.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally common from the coast to foothills and sub-alpine areas, often in stony soils derived from dolerite rock.

plants.name: Pterostylis dubia
plants.form: A relatively large, stout greenhood with 3-5 fleshy, dark-green leaves, loosely encircling the stem.
plants.flowers: A large, single, boldly-striped, green and white flower, a bulging and deeply-notched sinus, tapered short free-points extending just above the hood and a blue-green curved labellum.
plants.habitat: Localised and sometimes common growing in moist moss and litter in alpine and sub-alpine areas in central and southern Tasmania.

plants.name: Pterostylis furcata
plants.form: A slender, erect, moderately large green and white striped greenhood; 4-6 dark-green leaves, usually in a loose rosette.
plants.flowers: Moderately large green and white striped greenhood; hood held obliquely erect to erect. A curved labellum protruding prominently from deeply notched sinus.
plants.habitat: Uncommon orchid, growing in moist habitats around streams and soaks in the north of Tasmania.

plants.name: Pterostylis melagramma
plants.form: A tall greenhood with 5-7 stem leaves, basal rosette of 3-6 leaves on separate basal stalk.
plants.flowers: 1-20 shiny, translucent pale green flowers with indistinct darker green stripes. Long, oblong, yellowish-cream labellum with a dark-brown basal mound and central stripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common, growing in a variety of habitats from moist forest litter to rocky outcrops from the coast to the mountains.

plants.name: Pterostylis nana
plants.form: Tasmania’s only snail greenhood. 4-8 oval leaves, forming a rosette at the base and 1-2 stem leaves. Slender, smooth to slightly rough stem.
plants.flowers: Small, bright green and white-striped flower held erect. Lateral sepals erect, protruding well above the hood. Labellum hidden.
plants.habitat: Relatively common in coastal and near coastal heathland and scrub in the south-east, east and north and Bass Strait islands.

plants.name: Pterostylis nutans
plants.form: A medium-sized, strongly-nodding greenhood; a rosette of 3-6 dark-green crinkled, oval leaves. Often forming clonal colonies.
plants.flowers: Single, translucent pale-green flower, often orange-brown towards the apex; a curved, bristled, green and brown labellum protruding prominently.
plants.habitat: Common and widely distributed from the coast to alpine and sub-alpine areas in a variety of moist, sheltered habitats.

plants.name: Pterostylis parviflora
plants.form: A small, slender autumn-winter flowering tiny greenhood; 3-10 bright green, oval leaves form a basal rosette with 2-5 leaves closely sheathing the stem.
plants.flowers: 1-6 tiny, inwardly-facing, green and white-striped flowers (occasionally brownish at apex). Lateral sepals not protruding above the hood. Labellum can sometimes just be seen protruding from the sinus.
plants.habitat: Common in sandy soils in coastal and near-coastal heathland and scrub in the east and the north.

plants.name: Pterostylis pedunculata
plants.form: A small, slender greenhood, dark green rosette of oval leaves with prominent veins on sterile plants only. Fleshy stem. Often forms clonal colonies.
plants.flowers: A single green and white striped flower, distinctive brownish-maroon markings at the apex. A dark-red labellum is just visible through the sinus opening.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common in a range of moist habitats from the coast to alpine and sub-alpine areas.

plants.name: Pterostylis pratensis
plants.form: A slender midget greenhood with a rosette of 4-8 dark-green, almost round leaves.
plants.flowers: 2-12 densely crowded flowers, translucent green with prominent green stripes. A protruding oblong labellum with a darker broad, blunt beak.
plants.habitat: Grows in native grasslands in sub-alpine areas of the Tasmanian Highlands in moist loam soils.

plants.name: Pterostylis rubenachii
plants.form: A tiny, multiflowered midget greenhood with 4-6 broad, dark-green leaves, tapered at each end, forming a rosette at the base.
plants.flowers: 2-7 densely crowded, green flowers with darker green veins, irregularly toothed petal margins, lateral sepals deeply pouched. Light-green labellum, oblong with a darker recurved appendage and a short, narrow central ridge.
plants.habitat: Restricted to a few areas around Arthur River in Tasmania’s north-west, growing on both dry coastal dunes and moister wet heathland sites.

plants.name: Pterostylis scabrida
plants.form: Slender greenhood; 3-5 dark-green, fleshy leaves in a loose rosette or scattered up the scabrous (rough) stem.
plants.flowers: Single, narrow green and white-striped flower; a deeply notched sinus and erect free points extending just above the hood. Darker green curved labellum protruding prominently from the sinus in the set position.
plants.habitat: Widespread from lowlands to highlands, more common in sub-alpine woodlands, growing amongst moist grass, shrubs and ferns.

plants.name: Pterostylis stenochila
plants.form: A tall greenhood with 5-6 stem leaves, basal rosette of 3-5 leaves on separate basal stalk.
plants.flowers: 1-7 shiny, translucent green flowers with darker green stripes. Long, oblong light green labellum with a darker, emerald green central stripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread but localised, growing in freely draining soils in open forest and heathland from the coast to the foothills in the east and south-east of Tasmania.

plants.name: Pterostylis straminea
plants.form: A medium, upright bearded greenhood, a rosette of 8-20, crowded light green leaves with darker green veins and wavey margins, often extending up the stem.
plants.flowers: A solitary translucent dark green flower; thin pointed hood, parallel lateral sepals, thin and deflexed. A long labellum with pale yellow hairs and a large knob at the apex protrudes prominently from the hood.
plants.habitat: Relatively common in in woodland and grassland in the east.

photos.credit: H & A Wapstra – Natural Values Atlas

plants.name: Pterostylis wapstrarum
plants.form: A small, sturdy, midget greenhood, 4-7 broad, broad, thick, fleshy dark green leaves forming a rosette at the base.
plants.flowers: 5-15 densely crowded, green flowers with darker green veins and irregularly toothed petal margins. Light-green labellum, with a darker recurved appendage and a narrow central ridge.
plants.habitat: Highly localised, restricted to just a few sites in the Tasmanian south-east and Southern Midlands where it grows in well-drained soil in open forest and grassland .

plants.name: Pterostylis williamsonii
plants.form: A slender tall greenhood.
plants.flowers: 1-9 pale, shiny, translucent green flowers with darker green striping. Labellum tapered, dark brown with a darker basal mound sloping backwards and a darker central stripe.
plants.habitat: Locally common, growing among shrubs and bracken and under sheoaks in freely draining gravels and clay loams.

plants.name: Pterostylis ziegeleri
plants.form: A comparatively robust midget greenhood with a rosette of 4-7 green leaves.
plants.flowers: 3-8 densely crowded flowers, narrow, pale green with darker green stripes. Labellum has a dark-green appendage at its base with a small beak.
plants.habitat: Widespread but localised. Growing on coastal sand dunes in the east, north-east and north-west as well as grasslands in the midlands. Vulnerable to predation by snails.

plants.name: Pterygopappus lawrencei
plants.form: Tufted soft cushion herb with sage green leaves clothed with white hairs and stems densely packed.
plants.flowers: Solitary small white flower heads which emerge from the centre of hexagonal leaf formations.
plants.fruit: Achene – flattened, pappus bristles 6 or fewer, shortly feathered.
plants.habitat: Found in bolster heath on most mountains in the state. Frequent on wet screes and exposed places on mountain summits where snow lies for several months of the year.
plants.notes: Has very attractive foliage.

plants.name: Ptilotus spathulatus
plants.form: Perennial herb, spreading prostrate stems.
plants.flowers: Vertical from ground, fluffy spikes 3-7cm long, covered with long straight hairs, green/yellow.
plants.fruit: 2-3cm long, fluffy seed heads, lose green tinge and turn off-white; small utricle enclosed in rounded end of fruit.
plants.habitat: Occasional in dry grassy places.

plants.name: Puccinellia perlaxa
plants.form: Annual or perennial grass with smooth, erect stems and very slender, in rolled leaves, 2-15cm long, which taper to a fine point.
plants.flowers: The flower head is up to 15cm long, with wide-spreading branches.
plants.habitat: Known only from a creek bed in a saline area of a paddock in the Midlands.

plants.name: Puccinellia stricta
plants.form: Stiffly erect, perennial grass with smooth, stiff stems and erect, in rolled leaves, 2-25cm long.
plants.flowers: In flower heads up to 15cm long, with branches that spread slightly at maturity, bearing spikelets which are circular in cross-section.
plants.habitat: Saltmarshes, estuarine mud flats, saline lagoons and saline areas in agricultural land. King Island, Furneaux Group, north-west, north-east, Midlands and east coast.

plants.name: Pultenaea daphnoides
plants.form: A slender erect shrub with wedge-shaped leaves.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers mainly yellow with a red-brown petal at the base clustered at ends of branches.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oval, flattened with fine hairs. Pods turn from green to red-brown and seeds become almost black and hard when ripe, 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Common in the more shady parts of woodlands. Also found in a more dense form as a component of coastal heathlands.
plants.notes: Fast growing and apparently short-lived. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea dentata
plants.form: Heath-like shrub.
plants.flowers: Yellow, purple-veined pea flowers in small dense heads with very short stalks.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oval, flattened, silky, turns from green to red-brown. Seeds become black and hard when ripe, with 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent in peaty heaths.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea fasciculata
plants.form: Prostrate much-branched undershrub.
plants.flowers: Yellow, solitary, pea-flower growing in the axils of a few of the upper leaves.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oval, flattened, turns from green to red-brown. Seeds become almost black and hard when ripe, with 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Local on the Central Plateau at altitudes of about 700-1000m.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea gunnii subsp. gunnii
plants.form: Small, hairy, soft woody shrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, small orange-brown in terminal heads.
plants.habitat: Widespread from sea level to 1000m.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea humilis
plants.form: An undershrub with short thick woody stem and branches.
plants.flowers: Pea flower, orange-yellow on short stems crowded into clusters near ends of branches.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oval, downy, turns from green to red-brown. Seeds become almost black and hard when ripe, with 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Local on sandy banks in the midlands and north.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea juniperina
plants.form: An erect, much-branched, prickly shrub.
plants.flowers: Orange-yellow petalled pea flowers with dark purple-brown keels.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – short, fat, ovate, less than 1cm long, turns from green to red-brown. Seeds become almost black and hard when ripe; 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Understorey of forests from sea-level up to the sub-alpine woodland. Particularly abundant in dry forests at low altitudes and under the tall forests at mid altitudes.
plants.notes: A shrub which can form extensive thickets over a large area due to its suckering habit. Bird attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea mollis
plants.form: Small-leaved shrub almost prostrate or erect.
plants.flowers: Orange-yellow pea flower with darker keel, in dense heads at ends of short lateral branches.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oval, downy, turns from green to red-brown. Seeds become almost black and hard when ripe; 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Very local in the north-east.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea pedunculata
plants.form: A prostrate or creeping undershrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flower, wings yellow, keel deep orange or crimson.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oval, swollen, downy, turns from green to red-brown. Seeds become almost black and hard when ripe; 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in sandy heaths and dry places.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea prostrata
plants.form: Small shrub with branches prostrate or spreading on ground with tips ascending.
plants.flowers: Pea flower, yellow streaked with red; wings yellow, keel red.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oval, softly hairy, turns from green to red-brown. Seeds become almost black and hard when ripe; 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Local in grasslands in the midlands.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea sericea
plants.form: Small, straggling shrub with hairy branches.
plants.flowers: Yellow pea flowers borne in short, dense racemes or heads at the end of branches.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – flattened pod, covered in silky hairs.
plants.habitat: Near the coast in the north-east.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea stricta
plants.form: An erect or ascending shrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, wings yellow, streaked purple; keel purplish-brown.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – triangular-oval, flattened, downy, turns from green to red-brown. Seeds become almost black and hard when ripe; 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant in damp heaths.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pultenaea tenuifolia
plants.form: Prostrate shrub with branches along ground, tips ascending.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers, yellow and red at the base; wings yellow, keel red.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – obliquely oval, sometimes flattened, turns from green to red-brown. Seeds become almost black and hard when ripe; 1-2 seeds per pod.
plants.habitat: Local, usually in sandy soil on coastal granite rocks in the east and north-east.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Pyrorchis nigricans
plants.form: Colony forming orchid with a large fleshy heart-shaped ground-hugging basal leaf. The plants turn black on drying.
plants.flowers: Up to 8 flowers, 2-3cm across, white with prominent dark reddish stripes; large strongly hooded dorsal sepal and a whitish deeply fringed labellum.
plants.habitat: Heathy eucalypt woodland, teatree scrub, sedgeland and heathland on moderately to well-drained sandy soils. Widespread and locally abundant in coastal and near coastal lowland on the Tasman Peninsula and in northern Tasmania, including Bass Strait Is. …

plants.name: Ranunculus acaulis
plants.form: Small perennial herb, glabrous, fleshy often forming mats. Stolons long, slender; leaves in rosettes.
plants.flowers: Solitary on stems, 5-8 petals, narrow, sometimes toothed, twice as long as sepals.
plants.fruit: Achene – usually few in number. Seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Local on west and north-west coasts in areas of seepage on the seaward sides of dunes. Was previously found in wet sand at Lake Pedder.

plants.name: Ranunculus amphitrichus
plants.form: Perennial herb growing in shallow water, with floating or submerged round and deeply divided leaves, and stoloniferous stems.
plants.flowers: Flowering stems are slender and erect, and bear 1-3 pale golden yellow flowers with 5-7 petals.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Still to slow-flowing, shallow fresh water throughout the State.

plants.name: Ranunculus collicola
plants.form: Rosette herb with stolons and with trifoliate leaves 2-4 cm long.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow, 5-8mm in diameter, petals with shallow nectary pocket.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Known only from short alpine herbfield around lagoons near Lake Augusta.
plants.notes: Distinguished from Ranunculus collinus by the shape of the leaves and the hairiness of the sepal.

plants.name: Ranunculus collinus
plants.form: Rosette herb with stolons; leaves have three leaflets or are deeply 3-segmented each having 3 blunt teeth.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow, borne singly 8-15mm in diameter, sepal covered with pressed hairs.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Common in seepage areas in short alpine herbfield and sedgeland, especially in eastern and central mountains.

plants.name: Ranunculus decurvus
plants.form: Perennial hairy rosette herb, leaves divided into 3-5 leaflets.
plants.flowers: Pale greenish-yellow, below leaves, 5-8mm in diameter, nectary, crescent-shaped.
plants.fruit: Achene – smooth, no marginal ridges, stylar beak short, straight to recurved. Seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Found in wet grassland and bog in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Ranunculus diminutus
plants.form: Rhizomatous, basically terrestrial perennial. Leaves in basal rosettes.
plants.flowers: Bright yellow flowers on stems 1–4cm long.
plants.fruit: Achene – in a globular head, flattened-obovoid, 1.0–1.8 mm long. Beak slender, erect, about 1 mm long.
plants.habitat: Known from a single collection made in 1975 which came from Badger Island, Furneaux Group.

plants.name: Ranunculus glabrifolius
plants.form: Perennial rosette herb with stolons and dull, leathery, hairless or almost hairless leaves, with 3 sharply- toothed lobes.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow flowers on stems, 1–3-flowered, to about 25 cm long.
plants.fruit: Achene – inflated, lateral faces with 3-4 coarse, oblique ridges. Seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: In aquatic vegetation and short alpine herbfield in the eastern and central mountains.
plants.notes: Has adapted well to cultivation.

plants.name: Ranunculus gunnianus
plants.form: Rosette herb with thick rootstock and stalked leaves, which are divided into thick linear segments and tipped by small gland.
plants.flowers: Large, with white or yellow petals, some purple on outside, on flowering stem longer than leaves.
plants.fruit: Achene – flattened. Seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in mountain bogs at altitudes of 1000m.

plants.name: Ranunculus jugosus
plants.form: Rosette herb with leaves in 3-5 distant leaflets, each often with 3-pointed lobes. Leaf blades hairless, stalks reddish-brown.
plants.flowers: Pale yellow, with 5-6 petals, inconspicuous, held below leaves.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Known only from the Central Plateau growing in short alpine herbfield near rivers and soaks.

plants.name: Ranunculus lappaceus
plants.form: Perennial herb, usually with spreading or appressed hairs; short erect rootstock; stems to 40cm; leaves, numerous, trifoliate or palmately trifoliate.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow flowers to 3cm in diameter.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in grasslands and sclerophyll forests from sea level to about 900m. Grows in most soils.

plants.name: Ranunculus nanus
plants.form: Small perennial herb, leaves 3-5 lobed or divided, in radical rosette, glabrous or with scattered hairs.
plants.flowers: Solitary, 8-15mm in diameter on scapes about as long as the leaves; 5 golden yellow petals.
plants.fruit: Achene – smooth or minutely dimpled. Seeds turn from green to yellowish and have broad and tapered beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Widespread on the Central Plateau and in the eastern mountains from about 900-1200m in swamps and bogs subject to intermittent flooding.
plants.notes: May be distinguished from Ranunculus triplodontus by the length of the flowering stem in relation to the leaves and from Ranunculus lappaceus by the shape of its petals, petal nectaries and its generally smaller habit.

plants.name: Ranunculus pascuinus
plants.form: Rosette herb with hairs pressed tightly on to leaves and flowering stems. Leaves in 3 segments.
plants.flowers: Golden-yellow, single on stalks longer than leaves.
plants.fruit: Achene – smooth, flattened with marginal ridge. Seeds turn from green to yellowish, with stylar beak suberect to recurved.
plants.habitat: Grassland and grassy heath in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Ranunculus pimpinellifolius
plants.form: Herb with rosette of hairy leaves, each with 3-5 toothed leaflets. Stems 2-25cm long.
plants.flowers: Golden-yellow, 1-2 per stem. Stems longer than leaves.
plants.fruit: Achene – flattened, smooth or slightly warty. Seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small stylar beak, erect or recurved.
plants.habitat: Wet grassland and wet grassy heath on the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Ranunculus prasinus
plants.form: Small, perennial, mat-forming herb. The grass-green leaves form a basal rosette, and are covered in long, soft hairs.
plants.flowers: Flowers are pale yellow, solitary and on a stalk longer than the leaves.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Occurs from Tunbridge to Campbell Town in the Midlands, on the margins of grassland wetlands.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Ranunculus pumilio var. pumilio
plants.form: Annual herb, leaves deeply divided.
plants.flowers: Small flowers on single stalks.
plants.fruit: Achene – usually hairy, faces covered with sharp tubercles. Seeds with beaks prominent recurved, turn from green to yellowish.
plants.habitat: Chiefly in wet places, from sea level to altitudes of about 900m.

plants.name: Ranunculus scapiger
plants.form: Rosette herb, leaves orb-shaped, not usually deeply dissected and with soft, spreading, pressed hairs.
plants.flowers: Golden yellow, may have red flushing, stalks longer than leaves. Sepals pointing down.
plants.fruit: Achene – smooth with narrow marginal rib. Beak coiled at apex and often purplish. Seeds turn from green to yellowish.
plants.habitat: Local at lower elevations in the eastern mountains in damp alpine grassland.

plants.name: Ranunculus sessiliflorus var. sessiliflorus
plants.form: Slender annual plant, tufted. Leaves on slender stems, 3-lobed or divided, segments again lobed.
plants.flowers: Very small, leaf-opposed.
plants.fruit: Achene – pale brown with green margins and faces covered with sharp tubercles. Beak very short, recurved.
plants.habitat: Widespread from sea level to about 300m.

plants.name: Ranunculus setaceus
plants.form: Rosette herb with rhizomes; leaves erect, linear sometimes with two lobes near extremities.
plants.flowers: Single, cream or pale greenish-yellow, on stalks shorter than leaves.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Local on mountains of the Western Tiers and eastern mountains, in depressions subject to intermittent flooding at altitudes of about 1200m.

plants.name: Ranunculus triplodontus
plants.form: Rosette herb, leaves variable in shape, not hairy.
plants.flowers: Pale yellow on stalks shorter than leaves. Either 2-3 pale petals or five glossier ones.
plants.fruit: Achene – seeds turn from green to yellowish and have small beak-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Wet grassland and short alpine herbfield in the eastern mountains.
plants.notes: Can be distinguished from Ranunculus decurvus by the lack of hairs on its leaves and from Ranunculus nanus by its nectary which is a crescentic pocket with a small lobe below, and by the relative lengths of leaves and flowering stems.

plants.name: Rhagodia candolleana subsp. candolleana
plants.form: Straggling or erect shrub to 2.5m wide, leaves greyish-green, shiny on the upper surface and white underneath, 1-2.5cm long with a short stem, slightly succulent.
plants.flowers: Terminal flower spikes of small, green flowers surrounded by white hairs. Flowers most of the year.
plants.fruit: Small red berries which occur in terminal clusters.
plants.habitat: Saltmarshes and coastal vegetation.
plants.notes: Hardy plant in coastal and inland areas, useful as a screen and tolerant of salt spray. Fruits are edible but bitter; leaves are also edible and can be cooked and eaten like spinach.

plants.name: Rhodanthe anthemoides
plants.form: Perennial herb with woody rootstock from which rise many erect unbranched stems.
plants.flowers: White flower heads with small yellow discs 15-25mm wide and white papery outer bracts.
plants.fruit: Achene – densely silky hairy, pappus bristles not joined at the base.
plants.habitat: Widespread, occasional in the south, frequent in the north at sea level; abundant in alpine and sub-alpine grassland of the Central Plateau.
plants.notes: Prefers a well-drained, sunny position. Has merit as a basket plant. A variable species with selected forms commercially available.

plants.name: Rhytidosporum inconspicuum
plants.form: Dense, prostrate shrub with rhizomes. Leaves elliptical hairless.
plants.flowers: Single on hairy stalks terminating branches.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 2-valved, slightly flattened, up to 4 mm long, up to 5.4 mm wide, light brown at maturity. Seed about 1.7 mm long, brown, several per fruit.
plants.habitat: Rare in alpine heath on the Central Plateau.

plants.name: Rhytidosporum procumbens
plants.form: Tiny shrub with small, dark green, linear to linear-oblong leaves.
plants.flowers: Starry white, sometimes fringed with crimson, about 1cm in diameter.
plants.fruit: Capsule – broader than long, the valves having fine transverse wrinkles. Seeds ovoid, deeply wrinkled.
plants.habitat: Common in sandy heaths and dry sclerophyll forests.

plants.name: Richea acerosa
plants.form: Rigid shrub with leaves only on stems of current season’s growth.
plants.flowers: White, cream or light pink, in small spikes at ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent on flat damp ground on northern mountains. Also found on mountains of the Central Plateau and west.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some overhead shade is desirable.

plants.name: Richea alpina
plants.form: Low growing sparsely branching shrub with annular scars below leaves.
plants.flowers: Numerous heads crowded into a triangular terminal spike.

plants.name: Richea dracophylla
plants.form: Erect slightly branched shrub.
plants.flowers: White in large dense terminal spikes 13cm long with large brown bracts protruding from head.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in Alpine and Sub-alpine forests.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some overhead shade is desirable.

plants.name: Richea gunnii
plants.form: Shrub with widely diverging branches.
plants.flowers: Flowers, usually white, 3-5 together on lateral branches.
plants.habitat: Dominates bog in eastern and central mountains.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some overhead shade is desirable.

plants.name: Richea milliganii
plants.form: Sparsely branched, erect shrub.
plants.flowers: Yellow, in short, nodding spikes.
plants.habitat: Found in heath at lower altitudes on the western mountains and at Lake Belcher in Mt. Field National park.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some overhead shade is desirable.

plants.name: Richea pandanifolia subsp. pandanifolia
plants.form: Tree, usually unbranched with lower trunk bare or clothed with dead leaves.
plants.flowers: Red or pink flowers in dense stalked heads in leaf axils. Caps of petals shed to show stamens.
plants.habitat: Frequent in wet Alpine and Sub-alpine forests and gullies, extending in a stunted form to mountain plateaux at altitudes of c1200m
plants.notes: A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some overhead shade is desirable. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi. Old leaves are used by contemporary basket weavers contributing interesting curling effects.

plants.name: Richea pandanifolia subsp. ramulosa
plants.form: Slender shrub with branches.

plants.name: Richea procera
plants.form: Shrub, sparingly branched.
plants.flowers: Solitary, the base of flower surrounded by 2-6 bracts, the 2 outer ones prominently keeled.
plants.habitat: Occasional and locally frequent from sea level to about 800m. Rare in low altitude alpine heath in the eastern mountains, more common in sub-alpine woodland and forest.
plants.notes: Very similar to Richea sprengelioides but with narrower, more lax leaves. A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some overhead shade is desirable.

plants.name: Richea scoparia
plants.form: Erect, much-branched shrub , rounded bushes in windy places on mountains.
plants.flowers: Flower spikes from white, through pink to red or orange. Opens when rice-like caps fall off.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant on mountains in alpine heaths and bog.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some overhead shade is desirable.

plants.name: Richea sprengelioides
plants.form: Shrub forming a compact rounded bush in exposed situations.
plants.flowers: Cream, in spikes at ends of branches. Petals form cap which does not open but falls away.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common on mountains, especially on rocky slopes.
plants.notes: Very similar to Richea procera but has wider more rigid leaves. A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some overhead shade is desirable.

plants.name: Richea x curtisiae
plants.form: Small shrub with spreading branches, the tips crowded with a rosette of leaves. Has the appearance of a hybrid of Richea scoparia and Richea pandanifolia but has none of the usual indicators of hybridity. …
plants.flowers: Flower spike, erect at ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Alpine heath in the southwestern mountains.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some overhead shade is desirable.

plants.name: Ricinocarpos pinifolius
plants.form: Erect shrub
plants.flowers: Stalked, white, 4-6 petals. Male flowers more conspicuous than female.
plants.fruit: Hairy capsule – ripe fruits red, burr-like, spherical. Seeds mottled brown, 5mm long with a fleshy white swollen knob at one end.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant on coastal heaths in the north and east.

plants.name: Roepera billardierei
plants.form: Perennial herb with much-branched stems spreading over the ground and bright green, fleshy, Y-shaped leaves.
plants.flowers: Usually 4 yellow flowers, 1cm in diameter, occurring singly in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Capsule – drooping, four-angled; contains 4 brown, almost triangular seeds. The seeds are covered with a gelatinous coating, which glues the seed to the soil when wet.
plants.habitat: Calcareous sands, forest, wetlands and heath on the Furneaux islands.

plants.name: Rorippa dictyosperma
plants.form: Perennial herb, decumbent at base, branched and erect above.
plants.flowers: Flowers about 1.2cm in diameter, petals narrowly obovate and white, stamens 6.
plants.fruit: Capsule (siliqua) more or less erect, borne on spreading stalks about 1cm long. Valves have one conspicuous vein. Seeds – 1 row per locule, oval and with thin, translucent margins.
plants.habitat: Common in moist shady places.

plants.name: Rorippa gigantea
plants.form: Herb with coarse, erect or ascending branches.
plants.flowers: Small, with white, obovate, spreading petals.
plants.fruit: Capsule 2.5-4 cm long on stalks about 1cm long, spreading. Seeds oval with ridges running longitudinally and pits between, with narrow membranous wing.
plants.habitat: Occasional in moist forests.

plants.name: Rubus gunnianus
plants.form: Matt-forming perennial herb, with rosettes connected by trailing stems, often below the soil. May spread to 60-80 cm in diameter.
plants.flowers: Single cream flowers, 2 cm in diameter, on short stalk emerging from the centre of the rosette.
plants.fruit: Drupelet – soft and red when mature.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in all alpine vegetation types except aquatic, at altitudes of 900-1500m. Grows in most soils.
plants.notes: Likely to get blackberry rust when grown at lower altitudes.

plants.name: Rubus parvifolius
plants.form: Slender, straggling plant with erect or spreading branches and hooked prickles.
plants.flowers: With five round reddish-pink petals, shorter than the hairy sepals.
plants.fruit: Drupelet – small clusters of 4-10 orange-red drupelets. Soft and red when mature.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant, common on rocky hillsides and near coasts.
plants.notes: Very hardy and may be trained as a climber. Resistant to salt spray. Used as canes by contemporary basket weavers.

plants.name: Rumex bidens
plants.form: Stout aquatic herb with spreading, floating stems. Leaves are stalked near the base of the plant and have blunt tips. Upper leaves are narrower and have sharper tips.
plants.flowers: The numerous, erect flowering stems are thick and hollow.
plants.fruit: Nut – small and fawnish-brown, with teeth or spines on the margins.
plants.habitat: Marshes and drainage channels, especially in the north of the State.
plants.notes: If Rumex is allowed to set seed, it can become weedy. Seed is eaten by waterbirds. Important in traditional medicine, rich in Vitamin C and can be used as leafy greens, although shouldn’t be consumed in large amounts.

plants.name: Rumex brownii
plants.form: Perennial herb with stalked basal leaves, 9-15cm long with scalloped edges, and narrower, shorter upper leaves.
plants.flowers: Flowering stem is erect, and flowers occur in whorls.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally frequent.
plants.notes: If Rumex is allowed to set seed, it can become weedy. Seed is eaten by waterbirds. Important in traditional medicine, rich in Vitamin C and can be used as leafy greens, although shouldn’t be consumed in large amounts. Can be used in stir-fries, for seasoning soups and in omelettes.

plants.name: Rumex dumosus
plants.form: Perennial herb with numerous widely spreading flowering branches and erect stems. Basal leaves are stalked and lance-shaped, and up to 10cmm long, upper leaves get progressively smaller.
plants.flowers: In whorls of 1-4 flowers.
plants.habitat: Grassy places in the Midlands.
plants.notes: If Rumex is allowed to set seed, it can become weedy. Seed is eaten by waterbirds. Important in traditional medicine, rich in Vitamin C and can be used as leafy greens, although shouldn’t be consumed in large amounts.

plants.name: Rumohra adiantiformis
plants.form: Has long, creeping, scaly rhizome; glossy, leathery , triangular fronds up to 120cm long, semi-erect; stipes grooved on upper surface.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant to 500m (rarely 900m). Sometimes epiphytic on Dicksonia and a range of tree species and rotting logs. Will tolerate salt laden winds in coastal situations.
plants.notes: Very hardy; clump or slow spreading. Easily raised from spores. Very easy to grow once established. Resents disturbance and is best grown on a slab or hanging basket in epiphyte mixture.

plants.name: Ruppia megacarpa
plants.form: Submerged aquatic herb, perennial, with stems often zig-zagged and slender leaves.
plants.flowers: Two small flowers in terminal spikes. Flowering stalk varies in length depending on water depth, and coils after pollination.
plants.fruit: Achene – usually 2-6mm long; turn black when mature.
plants.habitat: Coastal creeks, estuaries and lagoons on the east coast.
plants.notes: Aquatic plant.

plants.name: Ruppia polycarpa
plants.form: Submerged aquatic herb, with erect stems and slender leaves.
plants.flowers: Two small flowers in terminal spikes. Flowering stalk up to 60cm long, and coils after pollination.
plants.fruit: Achene – usually 2-6mm long; turn black when mature.
plants.habitat: Coastal creeks, estuaries, coastal and inland saline lagoons, all Tasmanian coasts and inland lagoons in the Midlands.
plants.notes: Aquatic plant from brackish waters.

plants.name: Ruppia tuberosa
plants.form: Submerged slender aquatic herb, perennial, with stems up to 2cm long and thread-like leaves.
plants.flowers: Two small flowers in terminal spikes. Flowering stalk up to 30cm long, regularly shorter where plants are exposed at low tides.
plants.fruit: Achene – 2mm long; turn black when mature.
plants.habitat: Holes and channels in saltmarshes, Ralphs Bay and Blackman Bay, east coast.
plants.notes: Aquatic annual plant. Commonly produces turions, fleshy storage organs which overwinter and then start growth in the spring.

plants.name: Rytidosperma australe
plants.form: Densely tufted perennial grass, spreading by short rhizomes (underground stems). Leaves are smooth, 4cm long, folded or in rolled, and tapering to a fine point.
plants.flowers: Flower heads are 1.5cm long and stiffly erect.
plants.habitat: Damp places and late snow areas above 1000m, in the Central Highlands and Mt. Field.

plants.name: Rytidosperma caespitosum
plants.form: Perennial grass forming clumps or tussocks.
plants.flowers: Spikelets 4-7-9 flowered, green or tinged purple, bracts exceeding florets except for exerted awns.
plants.habitat: Widespread in open situations or light woodland in lowland areas and up to about 1000m. Drought tolerant.
plants.notes: Rejuvenation occurs after burning, especially if followed by heavy rain. Wallaby-grass species are amongst the most valued native grasses in pastoral areas of Australia, due to their persistence, palatability and productivity. …

plants.name: Rytidosperma carphoides
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial grass, with hairless stems longer than the leaves.
plants.flowers: In a flower head of erect spikelets.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, in lowland areas in the Midlands and on the east coast.

plants.name: Rytidosperma diemenicum
plants.form: Tufted or shortly rhizomatous perennial grass with stems much taller than tuft of basal leaves.
plants.flowers: Panicle bearing up to 10 spikelets, spikelets 10-18mm long, 4-6 flowered.
plants.habitat: Occurs in open, rocky or damp situations in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Rytidosperma dimidiatum
plants.form: Slender, erect or bent perennial grass with stems very slender, smooth below, finely-ribbed above with 2 to 4 nodes.
plants.flowers: Panicle with 4-20 spikelets, spikelets 4-7 flowered, bracts greenish with wide purple margins.
plants.habitat: Occurs in open situations from sea level to 1150m on the east coast, Midlands, Central Highlands, west coast, north-east, Ben Lomond, south-west.

plants.name: Rytidosperma fortunae-hibernae
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial grass growing from a short rhizome.
plants.flowers: Spikelets up to 11mm long, 3-4 flowered, florets about two-thirds as long as bracts.
plants.habitat: Occurs in highland areas, on the west coast, Central Highlands and Mt. Field at 650-1450m altitude and in the south-west from 80m.

plants.name: Rytidosperma geniculatum
plants.form: Tufted, erect or bent perennial grass with hairless leaf sheaths and blades tightly in rolled.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence about 5cm long, spikelets 4-6 flowered with florets a little shorter than bracts.
plants.habitat: Coastal and lowland areas of the north-east, Midlands and east coast.

plants.name: Rytidosperma gracile
plants.form: Erect or bent tufted perennial with slender, finely ribbed stems.
plants.flowers: Spikelets usually 3-flowered, florets about two thirds as long as the bracts.
plants.habitat: In heath or on the margins of rainforest on the west coast, Central Highlands, south-west between the Pieman and Gordon Rivers from sea level to about 700m.

plants.name: Rytidosperma indutum
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial grass with in rolled leaves; ribs on the upper surface that feel rough to touch.
plants.flowers: The flower head is higher than the rest of the plant, 7-15cm long, and bears straw-coloured or purple-tinged spikelets.
plants.habitat: Open sclerophyll woodlands to about 300m altitude, in the Midlands and east coast.

plants.name: Rytidosperma laeve
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial with stems smooth and hairless.
plants.flowers: Spikelets green, tinged purple, 4-7 flowered with divergent florets.
plants.habitat: Found on the west coast, Central Highlands, Midlands, Ben Lomond, north-east, east coast and south-west from sea level to sub-alpine areas, on dry hillsides and wet shady places. Also occurs on stream banks.

plants.name: Rytidosperma nitens
plants.form: Tufted perennial grass. Similar to Rytidosperma nivicola which has stiffer, less hairy flowering stems and a hairier bract.
plants.flowers: Spikelets with 4-6 flowers, lower flower bract hairless except for 1 or 2 sparse tufts at sides.
plants.habitat: Occurs at lower altitude in damp grassy vegetation in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Rytidosperma nivicola
plants.form: Tufted grass with very rigid, shiny flowering stems. Similar to Rytidosperma nitens which has laxer, more hairy flowering stems and a less hairy bract; also similar to Rytidosperma nudiflorum which has larger spikelets and lateral lobes longer than the body of the bract.
plants.flowers: Spikelets with 3-5 flowers, 5.5 to 8mm long, bracts sometimes shiny with marginal hair tufts.
plants.habitat: Wet tussock grassland in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Rytidosperma nudiflorum
plants.form: Tufted or mat-forming grass with very rigid flowering stems and leaf blades. Similar to Rytidosperma nivicola which has smaller spikelets and lateral lobes shorter than the body of the bract.
plants.flowers: Spikelets with 5-6 flowers, 8-13mm long, bract shiny, hairs confined to tufts on margins.
plants.habitat: Wet tussock grassland in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Rytidosperma pauciflorum
plants.form: Tufted grass with rhizomes. Similar to Rytidosperma fortunae-hibernae but smaller in all parts.
plants.flowers: Spikelets with 3 flowers, bract 4-7mm long, richly brown.
plants.habitat: Found widely as an epiphyte in bolster heath.

plants.name: Rytidosperma penicillatum
plants.form: Slender, tufted grass often with nodding flowering stems.
plants.flowers: Spikelets with 4-6 flowers, purplish.
plants.habitat: Grassy vegetation in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Rytidosperma pilosum
plants.form: Erect, perennial grass.
plants.flowers: Spikelets 6-8-9 flowered, straw-coloured or greenish, florets tightly packed, shorter than bracts.
plants.habitat: From sea level to about 1100m in the Furneaux Group, north-west, Central Highlands, Midlands, north-east, Ben Lomond, east coast, and south-west.

plants.name: Rytidosperma racemosum var. racemosum
plants.form: Slender, erect, tufted perennial
plants.flowers: Spikelets pale green or straw coloured, purple tinge.
plants.habitat: Open situations or under light forest cover, sea level to 850m.

plants.name: Rytidosperma remotum
plants.form: Loosely tufted glabrous perennial.
plants.flowers: Spikelets purple, brown.
plants.habitat: Recorded only from the west coast on the summit of Hibbs Pyramid, 70m on dolerite.

plants.name: Rytidosperma semiannulare
plants.form: Erect tufted perennial with ribbed leaf sheaths.
plants.flowers: 4-6 flowered spikelets.
plants.habitat: Widespread in lowland areas, mostly coastal. Up to about 600m above sea level in open or semi-shaded situations (dry or moist).

plants.name: Rytidosperma setaceum
plants.form: Slender, erect, tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Spikelets, golden-brown.
plants.habitat: Widespread in open situations and under light eucalypt cover, up to 400m.

plants.name: Rytidosperma tenuius
plants.form: Erect, tufted perennial.
plants.flowers: Spikelets green tinged, purple, margins purple.
plants.habitat: Coastal areas, up to 1000m.

plants.name: Sagina diemensis
plants.form: A glaucous perennial herb, the stems four angled, branched, spreading.
plants.flowers: Conspicuous white flower up to 10mm diameter. Flowering shoots brittle.
plants.habitat: Very restricted plant occurring in difficult to access regions.

plants.name: Sagina namadgi
plants.form: A glaucous perennial herb, the stems four angled, branched, spreading.
plants.flowers: Flowering shoots brittle.
plants.habitat: Local in marshes in the north. Specimens are variable in habit and the size of their parts.

plants.name: Salicornia blackiana
plants.form: Undershrub with horizontal, rooting stems and numerous, erect, segmented and fleshy branches which have a blue-green waxy coating.
plants.flowers: Flowers do not have petals, but the white styles and stigmas are visible. Flowers are borne in fleshy spikes throughout most of the year.
plants.fruit: Fruiting perianth spongy. Seed is egg-shaped and somewhat flattened.
plants.habitat: Grows in saltmarshes with Salicornia quinqueflora, but less abundant, and usually on higher ground.
plants.notes: Important food plant for migratory birds. The Tasmanian Sarcocornia species are often parasitised by gall-gnats, which cause segments or short branches to turn bright red.

plants.name: Salicornia quinqueflora subsp. quinqueflora
plants.form: Small succulent undershrub with green to red upright, segmented stems and greenish rooted prostrate stems.
plants.flowers: Flowers do not have petals, but the white styles and stigmas are visible. Borne in fleshy spikes, on upper segments of upright stems.
plants.fruit: Seed is oval and somewhat flattened, with slender spreading hairs.
plants.habitat: Moderately saline and frequently flooded communities, usually in estuaries.
plants.notes: Important food plant for migratory birds. The Tasmanian Sarcocornia species are often parasitised by gall-gnats, which cause segments or short branches to turn bright red.

plants.name: Salicornia quinqueflora subsp. tasmanica
plants.form: Small succulent tufted plant with green to red upright, segmented stems and greenish rooted stems.
plants.flowers: Flowers do not have petals, but the white styles and stigmas are visible. Borne in fleshy spikes, on upper segments of upright stems.
plants.fruit: Seed is oval and somewhat flattened, with short acute curved hairs.
plants.habitat: Scattered in coastal areas on rocky substrates that are flooded by the sea.
plants.notes: Important food plant for migratory birds. The Tasmanian Sarcocornia species are often parasitised by gall-gnats, which cause segments or short branches to turn bright red.

plants.name: Salsola australis
plants.form: Compact, somewhat fleshy annual shrub.

plants.name: Sambucus gaudichaudiana
plants.form: Woody plant with annual branches arising from perennial rootstock.
plants.flowers: White, cup-shaped with a short tube and 4 spreading lobes about 10mm across.
plants.fruit: Almost translucent drupe, 3mm long with 3-4 stones. Clusters of drupes turn from green to white or yellow when ripe.
plants.habitat: Local in gullies and on alluvial flats in the north of the state and on King Island.

plants.name: Samolus repens var. repens
plants.form: Perennial, prostrate herb, with wiry stems to 60cm which often root in the substrate. Basal leaves up to 5cm long, others smaller and narrower.
plants.flowers: White or pink, with five rounded petals about 1.5cm in diameter, arising from leaf axils.
plants.habitat: Widespread in salt and brackish marshes, and around cliff seepages.
plants.notes: Good plant for wet conditions such as bog gardens or the sides of ponds; grows in sun or part shade. Spreading, salt-tolerant groundcover.

plants.name: Sarcochilus australis
plants.form: A small, pendulous, epiphytic orchid, with a tuft of 3-10 linear leathery, dark-green leaves and long roots.
plants.flowers: Pendulous racemes of 2-14 sweetly fragrant pale green or brown flowers; lateral sepals are brilliant white externally with mauve stripes internally, forming a pouch below the labellum.
plants.habitat: Most commonly found in sheltered, shady and permanently moist gullies, where it grows on a range of shrubs and trees, usually at about eye level, but also in rainforest and other moist forest types. It is occasionally found on low boulders. …

plants.name: Saxipoa saxicola
plants.form: Hairless, tufted, erect or abruptly bent perennial grass with slender stems and flat, linear, often floppy leaves.
plants.habitat: Widespread in sub-alpine meadows, herb fields and open woodlands, usually 800-1400m altitude, on the west coast, Central Highlands, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.
plants.notes: Cut back in autumn to promote new growth. Bird attracting: attracts seed-eating birds. Provides cover for small lizards.

plants.name: Scaevola aemula
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.flowers: Terminal flowers, pale mauve to pale purplish-blue, fan-shaped corolla lobes divided.
plants.habitat: Local in the east of the State.
plants.notes: Bird attracting. Also good for attracting insects.

plants.name: Scaevola albida
plants.form: Perennial, slender, creeping herb, with erect stems covered in scattered hairs.
plants.flowers: Blue or white with a yellow or white centre, 1-2cm long, solitary and stalkless, borne in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Drupe – spherical or egg-shaped, 3mm long, containing 2 seeds.
plants.habitat: Heath communities, dune vegetation and rough pastures in The Furneaux Group and at Temma on the West Coast.

plants.name: Scaevola hookeri
plants.form: Prostrate – creeping perennial herb; stems to 30cm long.
plants.flowers: Shortly stalked with 5 white petals each with red or brown on the back.
plants.fruit: Drupe – white, slightly fleshy, in two parts with one seed in each part.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet heaths, sea level to alpine and sub-alpine and on margins of coastal lagoons and saltmarshes.

plants.name: Scapisenecio albogilvus
plants.form: Perennial rosette herb with stolons.
plants.flowers: Single flower head borne terminally on vertical stem.
plants.habitat: Widespread in most non-aquatic alpine vegetation types.

plants.name: Scapisenecio leptocarpus
plants.form: Rosette herb with stolons.
plants.flowers: A single yellow-orange flower head, terminal on vertical flowering stems.
plants.habitat: Widespread in most non-aquatic alpine vegetation types.

plants.name: Scapisenecio papillosus
plants.form: Perennial herb with leaves pressed to the ground in a basal rosette.
plants.flowers: Flower heads solitary, terminal about 2.5cm in diameter. Florets yellow, ray florets in 1 row.
plants.fruit: Achene – ribbed, pappus of fine hairs.
plants.habitat: Understorey of coniferous heath in the most southerly of Tasmanian mountains.

plants.name: Scapisenecio primulifolius
plants.form: Perennial herb with leaves crowded at base of erect, woolly hairy stem.
plants.flowers: Yellow, single at end of flowering stalk.
plants.fruit: Achenes without hairs, pappus hairs minutely barbed.
plants.habitat: Found in the understorey of alpine heaths and sedgeland in the southern most mountains.

plants.name: Schenkia australis
plants.form: Hairless, annual herb, with erect stems and stalkless, oblong or lance-shaped leaves, 1-2cm long.
plants.flowers: Pink flowers with fused petals are borne at the tops of the stems, on flower stalks 2-5mm long.
plants.habitat: Cleared forest pasture, rainforest or wet sclerophyll forest and heathland, in the East and North.

plants.name: Schizacme archeri
plants.form: Prostrate. Alpine cushion plant with creeping, densely leafy stems forming small mats. Leaves are circular and shiny, with a hard, transparent margin, and resemble stacked dinner plates.
plants.flowers: White and solitary.
plants.habitat: On mountains of the Central Plateau and the west of the State.

plants.name: Schizacme montana
plants.form: Prostrate perennial herb with much-branched stems and crowded leaves.
plants.flowers: White and solitary.
plants.habitat: Alpine, wet peats and at sea level in the south-west of the state.

plants.name: Schizaea asperula
plants.form: Fern with fertile fronds tall, thin, very flattened, branched up to 4 times, rough, lanky with small combs. Sterile fronds forked, fan-shaped.
plants.habitat: Rare in Tasmania. Occurs at or near sea-level in sandy soils of heathland or dry sclerophyll forest.
plants.notes: Transplanting of most species is very difficult as they do not tolerate disturbance of the root system which is often buried deep in the soil. Plants from a wet habitat over rock are most likely to succeed. Once established they can be maintained in conditions similar to the original habitat.

plants.name: Schizaea bifida
plants.form: Fertile fronds unbranched (or branched once), short, thick, slightly flattened, smooth with large combs. Sterile fronds (rare) unbranched.
plants.habitat: Locally common below 200m in near-coastal sites. Grows in peaty, gravelly or sandy soils in dry sclerophyll forest or heathland.
plants.notes: Transplanting of most species is very difficult as they do not tolerate disturbance of the root system which is often buried deep in the soil. Plants from a wet habitat over rock are most likely to succeed. Once established they can be maintained in conditions similar to the original habitat.

plants.name: Schizaea fistulosa
plants.form: Fronds erect, entirely smooth, undivided, almost terete; sterile fronds undivided. Stipes terete, entirely smooth.
plants.habitat: Common in western and southern Tasmania from forest margins and heathland at sea level, to alpine moors and bogs. At lower altitudes has same distribution as Schizaea bifida, the two species frequently occurring together.
plants.notes: Transplanting of most species is very difficult as they do not tolerate disturbance of the root system which is often buried deep in the soil. Plants from a wet habitat over rock are most likely to succeed. Once established they can be maintained in conditions similar to the original habitat.

plants.name: Schoenoplectus pungens
plants.form: Summer-green perennial sedge with triangular, sharp-edged stems and blue-grey to lime leaves.
plants.flowers: A head of 1-5 spikelets, bright purplish-brown.
plants.fruit: Nut – egg-shaped, smooth dark brown, 3mm long. Seed heads turn brown when seed is ripe.
plants.habitat: Saltmarshes, wetlands and fresh and brackish swamps near the coasts and inland at low altitudes.
plants.notes: Dies down in winter.

plants.name: Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani
plants.form: Stout perennial sedge with erect, smooth rush-like leaves, 2m or more long.
plants.flowers: An umbel with many spikelets.
plants.fruit: Nut – seed heads turn brown when seed is ripe.
plants.habitat: On edges of lagoons on King Island, and on some river banks in the Midlands.
plants.notes: Frog habitat.

plants.name: Schoenus absconditus
plants.form: Small, densely tufted perennial sedge with erect leaves and very short stems.
plants.flowers: 2-4 flowers per spikelet.
plants.habitat: Rarely collected, known from the Midlands near Ross and Tunbridge, the back of dunes at Triabunna on the east coast, and the Clyde River Falls near Bothwell.

plants.name: Schoenus apogon
plants.form: Densely tufted, leafy perennial sedge with slender, unbranched stems, variable in size. Deep reddish-brown at the base of the leaves.
plants.flowers: Flower heads vary, spikelets usually contain 2-3 flowers and are dark purplish-brown to almost black.
plants.habitat: Usually in damp places, abundant in a range of soils, from coasts to mountains.

plants.name: Schoenus biglumis
plants.form: Small perennial sedge with erect, threadlike stems on obscure angles, and rather thick leaves.
plants.flowers: Solitary spikelet on the end of the flowering stems, about 4mm long.
plants.fruit: Nut – cream to pale brown, three narrow dark brown longitudinal bands, 1mm long.
plants.habitat: In wet heaths on the west coast and south-west.

plants.name: Schoenus brevifolius
plants.form: Perennial sedge with erect stems, 2mm in diameter, with a single narrow channel.
plants.flowers: In a narrow, stiff flower head on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – cream to light red-brown, 1.5mm long.
plants.habitat: In shallow water at the edges of lagoons in the north-east.

plants.name: Schoenus calyptratus
plants.form: Densely tufted perennial sedge with bristly, rigid leaves much longer than stems.
plants.flowers: Stems have 1-3 spikelets, each spikelet containing 1 flower.
plants.fruit: Nut – cream and shiny, sometimes with greenish ribs, 1.2-1.8mm long,.
plants.habitat: Open alpine and sub-alpine habitats, in the Central Highlands, south-west, Mt. Field and kunanyi/ Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Schoenus carsei
plants.form: Perennial sedge with wiry, erect, densely crowded stems, less than 1mm in diameter.
plants.flowers: A loose flower head on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.habitat: Wet heaths in the Furneaux, west coast and south-west.

plants.name: Schoenus fluitans
plants.form: Densely tufted, much-branched perennial sedge with leafy, floating stems, usually growing submerged.
plants.flowers: In spikelets on the end of flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Nut – brown to grey-black with yellowish green ribs, 1-1.2mm long.
plants.habitat: In still fresh water, in the Furneaux, north-east, Central Highlands, east coast, south-west and Mt. Field.

plants.name: Schoenus latelaminatus
plants.form: Small, tufted annual sedge with slender stems and grass-like, pale green leaves.
plants.flowers: Solitary spikelets of 3-6 flowers on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.habitat: Known from the margin of a roadside soak near Epping Forest in the Midlands.

plants.name: Schoenus lepidosperma subsp. lepidosperma
plants.form: Shortly rhizomatous or loosely tufted perennial sedge.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Schoenus maschalinus
plants.form: Slender tufted perennial sedge, with many threadlike, leafy stems.
plants.flowers: Spikelets of flowers in leaf axils or on short stalks.
plants.fruit: Nut – white to pale grey, 1mm long.
plants.habitat: Marshy places from sea level to alpine and sub-alpine areas.

plants.name: Schoenus nitens
plants.form: Hairless perennial sedge with stiffly erect flowering stems, erect leaves and a slender creeping rhizome.
plants.flowers: In clusters of chestnut brown spikelets, each spikelet containing 2-3 flowers.
plants.fruit: Nut – smooth, shining and yellowish-brown to chestnut-brown, 1.5-1.8mm long.
plants.habitat: Sandy flats and near the coast.

plants.name: Schoenus pygmaeus
plants.form: Very small tufted perennial sedge with erect or spreading stems and clustered leaves.
plants.flowers: Solitary, single-flowered spikelets on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.habitat: Wet sub-alpine moors and bogs in the Central Highlands, south-west, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Schoenus tesquorum
plants.form: Tufted, leafy perennial sedge with erect, threadlike, unbranched stems, and threadlike leaves.
plants.flowers: A small cluster of spikelets on the end of the flowering stems.
plants.habitat: In shallow standing water, like drainage ditches, in the north-east, Central Highlands, Midlands and south-west.

plants.name: Schoenus turbinatus
plants.form: Tufted perennial sedge with slender, erect stems and stiff, shorter leaves.
plants.flowers: A dense cluster of spikelets at the end of the flowering stems.
plants.habitat: Well-drained heathlands on sand or quartzite in the Furneaux, north-west, north-east, east coast and south-west.

plants.name: Scleranthus biflorus
plants.form: A small tufted perennial herb with bright green leaves and short decumbent stems. Usually forming dense masses.
plants.flowers: Flowers very small, cream with 4-5 petals.
plants.fruit: Nutlet -tiny, green, in pairs, turn cream as mature.
plants.habitat: Common in dry pastures and in heaths through a wide range of altitudes.

plants.name: Scleranthus brockiei
plants.form: Dense, compact, cushion-like perennial with stems up to 12mm long, and inward-curved leaves.
plants.flowers: A pair of stalked flowers, 5-18mm long.
plants.habitat: Grasslands and woodlands in sub-alpine to alpine habitats. Key sites include Mt. Inglis and Parkside, St. Helens.

plants.name: Scleranthus diander
plants.form: A small perennial herb, the rootstock tufted, almost woody, the stems much-branched, erect or ascending. Leaves crowded.
plants.flowers: The stalkless flowers are clustered in groups of 3 or 4.
plants.habitat: Pastures and dry banks in the north of the State.

plants.name: Scleranthus fasciculatus
plants.form: A small tufted perennial herb with short decumbent stems and leaves in clusters. Straggly and open.
plants.flowers: Flowers very small, yellow to green, in pairs.
plants.habitat: Inter-tussock spaces in tussock grassland and grassy woodland, only recorded from a few sites in the Midlands and the south-east.

plants.name: Scutellaria humilis
plants.form: Vigorous suckering perennial herb with creeping basal stems, leaves bluntly toothed, 8-15mm long, with scattered hairs along the veins on the lower surface.
plants.flowers: Solitary, pale pink or purplish with a conspicuous lip.
plants.fruit: Nutlet – small, spherical, 1.5mm in diameter. Turns from green to tan when ripe, and becomes brittle. Seed also changes from green to light brown at maturity.
plants.habitat: Local in moist, shaded places, especially in the north of the state.
plants.notes: Low maintenance plant. Plant at 50cm intervals.

plants.name: Sebaea albidiflora
plants.form: Annual, hairless, somewhat fleshy herb with an erect stem and leaves 3-10mm long, in opposite pairs.
plants.flowers: White or cream, cylindrical floral tube with four petals and blunt sepals. Occur in dense terminal flower heads.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 4-5mm long. Seed small and numerous.
plants.habitat: Coastal, in sandy soil and on the landward edges of saltmarshes.

plants.name: Sebaea ovata
plants.form: Annual, hairless herb with an erect, 4-angled stem, and leaves 6-15mm long, in opposite pairs.
plants.flowers: Yellow floral tube, 4mm long with five petals, and acute sepals.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 5mm long. Seed small and numerous.
plants.habitat: Widespread, in pastures, on roadside banks and grass hillsides.

plants.name: Selaginella gracillima
plants.form: Wispy, annual, fern ally; stems erect, simple or forking once or twice; leaves scattered, lanceolate with margins entire.
plants.habitat: Rare in Tasmania. Grows in tufts in seasonally moist or inundated soils of swamp margins, seasonal lagoons and heathland depressions usually in coastal districts.

plants.name: Selaginella uliginosa
