plants.form: Fern ally with stems pinnately branched, erect, simple, or usually fanlike; leaves 2-3mm broad, spreading, keeled, pointed; underground rhizome .
plants.habitat: Abundant in coastal heath and often inland up to 500m, less common on margins of dry sclerophyll forest. Grows in exposed or semi-exposed positions. In dry seasons the tops of the stems may die and become papery.

plants.name: Senecio biserratus
plants.form: Short-lived perennial herb with erect leafy flowering stems. Leaves not stem clasping.
plants.flowers: Numerous yellow flower heads in loose terminal clusters.
plants.fruit: Achene – dark brown, short and cylindrical with broad ribs separated by narrow grooves from which a double row of short hairs project.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant from sea level to mountain plateaux.

plants.name: Senecio glomeratus subsp. glomeratus
plants.form: Stout annual or short-lived perennial herb, stems erect, sparingly branched.
plants.flowers: Heads shortly cylindrical, yellow or orange-yellow florets, phyllaries green or purplish.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent, most abundant in lowland habitats.

plants.name: Senecio gunnii
plants.form: Bluish herb with stolons, stems first prostrate and rooting then erect.
plants.flowers: Yellow flowers in terminal groups.
plants.habitat: Common in grassy heath and grassland in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Senecio hispidulus
plants.form: Stout annual or short-lived perennial herb, stems erect, sparingly branched.
plants.flowers: Flower heads long-stalked, narrow; florets yellow.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent, most abundant in lowland habitats.

plants.name: Senecio linearifolius var. linearifolius
plants.form: Perennial undershrub, stems erect, simple or sparingly branched.
plants.flowers: Large fat clusters of golden flower heads at the ends of stems.
plants.fruit: Achene – cylindrical, scarcely 2mm long, pappus bristles soft.
plants.habitat: Along roads and on hillsides especially in moderate rainfall areas where it springs up quickly after fires.

plants.name: Senecio odoratus
plants.form: Robust leafy bush with tough downy stems. Faintly scented.
plants.flowers: Broad, branched terminal clusters of very small heads; 10-12 florets, tubular.
plants.habitat: Local on coasts in the north-east, north and north-west.

plants.name: Senecio pinnatifolius var. pinnatifolius
plants.form: Erect perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Terminal loose heads of single yellow daisies.
plants.habitat: Widespread and adaptable.
plants.notes: Short lived.

plants.name: Senecio quadridentatus
plants.form: Short-lived perennial undershrub. Stems woody at base, finely striate, hairy.
plants.flowers: Heads numerous in loose terminal clusters; florets yellow; green or purplish phyllaries.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant on roadsides, waste places and in a variety of habitats.

plants.name: Senecio spathulatus var. spathulatus
plants.form: Perennial herb with many branches, erect/prostrate rooting at base then ascending.
plants.flowers: Flower heads 2.5-3.5 cm across, solitary or in irregular few-flowered terminal clusters; florets yellow.
plants.fruit: Achene – ridged, pappus bristles very fine and silky.
plants.habitat: Common on sandy foreshores in the south, west and north of the State and abundant on islands in the south-west and in Bass Strait.

plants.name: Senecio squarrosus
plants.form: Annual or short-lived perennial herb, stem striate, leaves with triangular marginal lobes.
plants.flowers: Flower heads few in loose terminal clusters; florets deep yellow.
plants.fruit: Achene- blackish, ribs densely covered with short hairs.
plants.habitat: Widespread

plants.name: Senecio vagus subsp. vagus
plants.form: Robust rounded bush.
plants.flowers: Relatively few dark yellow daisies in loose terminal clusters; black glands on green calyx.
plants.habitat: Sheltered forests.

plants.name: Sicyos australis
plants.form: Scrambling herb with rough, broad, stalked leaves and slender stems, 1-4m long.
plants.flowers: Flowers are greenish, either male or female and 5-7cm diameter. Male flowers are found on the stem, and female flowers occur in small dense clusters on short flower stalks.
plants.fruit: Leathery, 1mm long and covered densely with barbed prickles.
plants.habitat: Coastal shrubbery on rocky limestone ground and coastal grasslands on alkaline sand, Inner Sister Island. The species was historically collected from eastern Flinders Island.
plants.notes: Seedlings are very susceptible to grazing by garden snails in cultivation.

plants.name: Siloxerus multiflorus
plants.form: Slender annual herb, stems erect and threadlike.
plants.flowers: Shining white heads, shortly-stalked, with about 25 florets in the terminal head, less in lateral ones.
plants.fruit: Achene – softly hairy. The outer ones each carry 8 conspicuous white pappus scales.
plants.habitat: Local on rocks near the mouth of the River Tamar at George Town and West Head.

plants.name: Solanum laciniatum
plants.form: Shrub, erect (appears herbaceous when small). Long, narrow leaves to 25cm.
plants.flowers: Long-stalked bluish purple flowers 5cm across, petals joined.
plants.fruit: Berry – fleshy, egg-shaped, 3cm long, orange-yellow when ripe. Seed 2mm.
plants.habitat: Common in damp, shaded places.
plants.notes: Colonises disturbed sites, relatively short lived (4-7 years). Bird attracting. Spread by birds.

plants.name: Solanum opacum
plants.form: Prostrate annual or short-lived perennial herb, with green or purple-tinged stems, and alternate, deep green or purple-tinged hairy leaves.
plants.flowers: White, occasionally tinged with purple, and star-shaped. Flowers are borne in clusters of 2-4, each with an individual stalk.
plants.fruit: Berry – spherical and up to 1cm wide; mostly green when mature (rarely black).
plants.habitat: Small number of collections only from King Island and the north of the state, from sea-level to about 100m.

plants.name: Solanum vescum
plants.form: Resembles Solanum laciniatum (kangaroo apple), but has narrower leaves, often with margins rolled under.
plants.flowers: Flowers bluish-purple and up to 5cm in diameter.
plants.fruit: Berry – large, soft, egg-shaped, fleshy, green or ivory white when ripe. Contains many reddish-brown seeds.
plants.habitat: In the south-west at Port Davey and in Kent and King Islands in Bass Strait.

plants.name: Solenogyne gunnii
plants.form: Perennial herb, leaves in basal rosette, roots numerous thick and spreading.
plants.flowers: Heads terminal, solitary; outer florets 2-lipped, inner ones regular, corolla, tubular.
plants.fruit: Achene – flattened, 2-2.5mm long, without a beak. Sometimes the corolla remains attached simulating a slender beak.
plants.habitat: Frequent and widespread in open forests and grassland.

plants.name: Sowerbaea juncea
plants.form: Perennial herb with tuft of blue-green solid leaves.
plants.flowers: Flower-heads pale pinkish-mauve, each with pale pink papery bracts and yellow stamens.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – pale brown, 2-3mm long containing 3-6 seeds. Seeds are dull and brown to black when mature.
plants.habitat: Grows on sandy and peaty soils, in coastal and near-coastal areas in the north-east, near Gladstone.

plants.name: Sphaerolobium minus
plants.form: Small, soft, rush-like shrublet.
plants.flowers: Pea, small, yellow often with red markings, in long terminal sprays, arranged in twos or threes.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – globular, turns from green to grey brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Widespread in heathlands.

plants.name: Sphaerolobium vimineum
plants.form: Small, erect, leafless shrub.

plants.name: Spinifex sericeus
plants.form: Creeping silvery perennial growing in coastal sands.
plants.flowers: Separate male and female plants. Female flower a 30cm diameter porcupine like sphere.
plants.habitat: Frontline coastal and estuarine sands on King Island, Furneaux Group, north-west, north-east and east coast.
plants.notes: Useful for binding sand dunes.

plants.name: Spiranthes australis
plants.form: Summer flowering orchid with a loose basal rosette of 3-5 dark green, shiny leaves.
plants.flowers: 10-60 brilliant pink and white (rarely completely white) flowers arranged in a dense spiral up the wiry stem. Labellum is 3-lobed with a fringed margin.
plants.habitat: Grows in wet to poorly drained marshes and sedgelands on peaty or silty soils that are usually waterlogged in winter and spring. In drier areas plants typically grow around marshes in a narrow strip between dry ground and the permanently inundated centre. …

plants.name: Sporadanthus tasmanicus
plants.form: Dioecious, rhizomes shortly creeping.
plants.flowers: Male and female flowers.
plants.habitat: Heath and sedgeland, buttongrass plains, sea level to 800m.

plants.name: Sporobolus virginicus
plants.form: Perennial, hairless, tussock-forming grass, arising from a stout creeping rhizome.
plants.flowers: Flower head 1 to 6cm, may be enclosed in upper leaf sheath, spike-like, grey.
plants.habitat: Creeping in coastal sands in the Furneaux group, north-east and east coast.

plants.name: Sprengelia distichophylla
plants.form: Usually prostrate scrambling shrub with branches 2-5cm long.
plants.flowers: Solitary at ends of branches, white or pink.
plants.habitat: Local in mountains of the west coast, south of Moore’s Lookout.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out.

plants.name: Sprengelia incarnata
plants.form: Short shrub occasionally taller with erect branches.
plants.flowers: 5 petals, white or pale pink, occasionally darker, in heads ending main stems and side branches.
plants.habitat: Found in heaths and wet places from sea level to mountains.
plants.notes: A well-composted peaty soil is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Full sun or part shade needed and plants need good drainage. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Sprengelia montana
plants.form: Usually a small spreading shrub branched from the base, branches ascending.
plants.flowers: 5 petals, white or pink.
plants.habitat: Frequent in alpine and sub-alpine heaths.
plants.notes: Sprengelia montana is described as an extreme variable form of Sprengelia incarnata. It has less strongly pointed smaller leaves than S. incarnata. Intermediate forms occur in which the characters are combined in different ways. …

plants.name: Spyridium eriocephalum
plants.form: Shrub with spreading, linear leaves, with a narrow, hard point. The upper surface is shining or slightly rough, and the lower surface is woolly.
plants.flowers: Flowers are 2mm in diameter, in small, dense heads.
plants.habitat: Dry places at Risdon in the south-east of the State, under Eucalyptus amygdalina woodland on mudstone.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Spyridium gunnii
plants.form: Shrub; occasionally grows to 8m.
plants.flowers: 4-5mm in diameter in dense heads, clustered in small compound heads. Petals hood shaped.
plants.fruit: Paper capsule – up to 3mm wide releasing brown-black small seeds from valves when mature.
plants.habitat: In scattered localities near Tasman Peninsula and mountains of the west at altitudes of about 900m; margins of eucalypt forest.
plants.notes: Suitable for dry to moist shrubberies. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Spyridium lawrencei
plants.form: Small, erect or wiry, much-branched shrub with thick, leathery leaves 2-4mm long. The veins are indented on the upper surface of the leaves, and the lower surface is covered in short hairs.
plants.flowers: Flowers are 2mm wide, and occur in small dense heads on the ends of lateral branches. Whitish floral leaves resembling petals surround the flower heads.
plants.habitat: Often associated with outcropping rocks and plates, or on generally open ground. Central east coast at Douglas-Apsley National Park and the Swan River, and the eastern Midlands along the St. Pauls River.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Spyridium obcordatum
plants.form: Prostrate or decumbent shrub with slender wiry branches up to 40cm long forming dense mounds .
plants.flowers: Small, 3-6 together in dense heads surrounded by brown bracts and silky hairs.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in several areas near Beaconsfield in northern Tasmania and near Spring Bay on the east coast.
plants.notes: Seed stored in soil responds to disturbance. Can sprout after grazing and probably after fire. Attracts butterflies. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Spyridium obovatum var. obovatum
plants.form: Medium shrub to small tree.
plants.flowers: Cream flowers, 4-5mm across in compact heads in leaf axils. Elliptical floral leaves, notched apex.
plants.habitat: Dry rocky sites on Flinders and Maria Islands and east coast.

plants.name: Spyridium obovatum var. velutinum
plants.form: Medium shrub to small tree.
plants.flowers: Pale yellow flowers, 4-5mm across in compact heads in leaf axils. Elliptical floral leaves, notched apex. Upper surface densely hairy.

plants.name: Spyridium parvifolium var. molle
plants.form: Erect, much branched shrub. Leaves greyish-green covered with soft, velvety hairs.
plants.flowers: Salmon pink, 3mm diameter, clustered in heads. Each head surrounded by brown bracts with one or more densely hairy floral leaves. Distinctive honey smell.
plants.habitat: Variety of habitats including riparian, rocky slopes, open woodland and heath.

plants.name: Spyridium parvifolium var. parvifolium
plants.form: Erect, much-branched shrub, with grey-green, softly hairy leaves which have prominent veins.
plants.flowers: Salmon pink, 3mm wide, clustered in heads, with a distinctive honey smell.
plants.habitat: Occurs in riparian, open woodland and heath habitats, and on rocky slopes.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Spyridium ulicinum
plants.form: A bushy shrub with many ascending branches.
plants.flowers: White with brown bracts, numerous, grouped near ends of branches. Sweetly scented.
plants.habitat: Local in several widespread situations in north and south on rocky hillsides and along river banks.
plants.notes: Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Spyridium vexilliferum var. vexilliferum
plants.form: Slender, twiggy shrub.
plants.flowers: Button-like heads. Individual flowers white, 1.5 mm in diameter, 5 sepals, 5 petals forming hoods over stamens. Each head has 1-3 conspicuous white, velvety, floral bracts.
plants.habitat: Locally common in sandy heaths, on river banks and rocky slopes in the east, north and west.
plants.notes: Requires full sun. Resistant to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Stackhousia monogyna
plants.form: Herb, usually branched from the base.
plants.flowers: White flower spike.
plants.habitat: Widespread and extending well into the mountains. Found on shady cliff edges. Often prominent after fires. Flowering in spring in the lowlands through to early autumn in the highlands. Coastal forms probably frost tender.
plants.notes: Attracts butterflies.

plants.name: Stackhousia pulvinaris
plants.form: Prostrate, mat-forming plant with small, light-green leaves.
plants.flowers: Profuse, yellow to cream, solitary star-shaped flowers.
plants.habitat: Local in alpine and sub-alpine regions, including the Middlesex Plains and Western Tiers.

plants.name: Stackhousia spathulata
plants.form: Small perennial herb, much-branched at the base. Thick, light green, 3cm long spoon-shaped leaves.
plants.flowers: White flowers in dense terminal heads, producing 4mm long fruitlets.
plants.habitat: Local on sea coast in north, west, south-west, and islands of Bass Strait.
plants.notes: Requires a well-drained, sunny position.

plants.name: Stackhousia subterranea
plants.form: Smooth perennial herb with solitary aerial shoots and a creeping rhizome.
plants.flowers: Similar to Stackhousia monogyna, except with a strongly disagreeable smell, and petals deep cream or yellowish.
plants.habitat: Sandy pastures in the Midlands and the north.

plants.name: Stackhousia viminea
plants.form: Perennial herb which branches from the base, with horizontal or upward sloping stems and alternate leaves which are linear or wedge-shaped.
plants.flowers: Yellow and tubular, clustered in groups of 2-3 along the end of the stem. The oldest flowers occur at the bottom of the flower head.
plants.habitat: Damp sandy heathland and pastures in the north-west.
plants.notes: Requires a well-drained, sunny position.

plants.name: Stellaria angustifolia subsp. angustifolia
plants.form: A glaucous perennial herb, the stems four angled, branched, spreading.
plants.flowers: Flowering shoots brittle.
plants.habitat: Local in marshes in the north of the State. Variable in habit and the size of the plant parts.

plants.name: Stellaria flaccida
plants.form: A perennial herb, the stems much-branched, procumbent or ascending.
plants.flowers: Flowers solitary, axillary.
plants.habitat: Common in damp shaded places.

plants.name: Stellaria multiflora subsp. multiflora
plants.form: A glabrous annual herb, branching, often tufted with several erect or ascending stems.
plants.flowers: Flowers axillary on pedicels shorter than the leaves.
plants.habitat: Local in dry pastures and stoney places.

plants.name: Stellaria pungens
plants.form: A perennial herb, the stems much-branched, short or ascending against shrubs or rocks.
plants.flowers: Flowers solitary in upper axils on pedicels longer than the leaves.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common.

plants.name: Stenanthemum pimeleoides
plants.form: Prostrate undershrub, woody base, slender branches. Shiny dark green leaves.
plants.flowers: White flowers 2mm wide tightly packed at branch ends surrounded by 2-3 conspicuous white leaves.
plants.habitat: Local in drier parts of Midlands and east, stony ground or ironstone gravel.

plants.name: Stenanthera pinifolia
plants.form: Small, stiff shrub. Branches erect or ascending, with many needle-like leaves.
plants.flowers: Long yellow tubular bells, 15-18mm long constricted at the throat.
plants.fruit: Seed enclosed in hard, woody, oval-spherical drupe, 10-15mm long, covered with a fleshy layer.
plants.habitat: Coastal heaths. Also inland in north, east and south.

plants.name: Stenopetalum lineare
plants.form: Annual herb with few branches, erect, slender, hairless.
plants.flowers: Petals clawed, tapering to a point, often long and twisted after flowering, yellowish/brown.
plants.fruit: Capsule (silicula) cylindrical or oval with 8-12 seeds in each loculus.
plants.habitat: Local in sandy heaths.

plants.name: Sticherus lobatus
plants.form: Fern with creeping rhizome; fronds erect or straggling, form 1-3 tiers; pinnules (margins entire) set at right-angles to rhachis.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in Tasmania, mainly restricted to the north-west up to 280m. Occurs typically as a vigorous groundcover as well as in the more usual Sticherus habitats such as creek banks, waterfalls and road cuttings.
plants.notes: Resents disturbance.

plants.name: Sticherus tener
plants.form: Fern with creeping rhizome; fronds erect or straggling; pinnules set at 90° to midrib, pinnule margins entire.
plants.habitat: Very common and widespread in Tasmania (west coast to inland) in permanently wet soils; also along sheltered streams in dry sclerophyll forest and coastal scrub. Will tolerate boggy soils.
plants.notes: Resents disturbance.

plants.name: Sticherus urceolatus
plants.form: Lanceolate shaped ultimate frond segments; all pinnules acutely angled to the midrib.
plants.habitat: Mostly on the east coast, abundant near sea level.

plants.name: Stonesiella selaginoides
plants.form: Slender erect shrub.
plants.flowers: Pea flowers bright yellow with reddish markings, wings yellow, keel with reddish tip.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – long shaggy hairs. Seeds green with darker green markings.
plants.habitat: Local in the east as on the bank of the Apsley River at the Lilla Villa Bridge.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Stuckenia pectinata
plants.form: Perennial aquatic herb growing completely submerged, in dense masses. Rhizomes grow from hook-shaped turions, or over-wintering buds. Stems are slender, leafy and much branched.
plants.flowers: A few small flowers, produced in spikes.
plants.fruit: Achene – 4 in number, buoyant in water.
plants.habitat: Commonly coastal or near the coast, occasionally inland in fresh or brackish water less than 2m deep. King Island, Furneaux Group, north-east, Midlands and east coast.
plants.notes: Requires brackish waterways.

plants.name: Stylidium armeria subsp. armeria
plants.form: Perennial herb growing in tufts. Leaves in a dense basal rosette.
plants.flowers: A long spike of pink to magenta flowers; small white projection at the throat. Flower has trigger action.
plants.fruit: Capsule – cylindrical 8–15 mm long. Seeds reddish-brown 1–2 mm.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally common in open woodlands, heaths and shrubberies, nearer coastal area, extending to higher altitudes inland.
plants.notes: Unpredictable in the garden – best treated as an annual.

plants.name: Stylidium beaugleholei
plants.form: Small, ephemeral herb with few, linear leaves, 2-4mm long, which are arranged in a basal rosette.
plants.flowers: Small, white with a tinge of pale pink, and situated at the top of the erect flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Capsule – dry, narrow, circular, taper towards the base, 5-8mm long. Turn from green to tan-brown, and become brittle as they ripen. Seeds are brown, 0.2mm long and pointed at both ends. Seeds tend to ripen progressively along the flower stem. Hundreds of fine seed per fruiting stem.
plants.habitat: Hollows, wet areas and soaks, often with a peat soil, in sandy heathlands on Cape Barren Island, the north-east coast and west coast.
plants.notes: Rare ephemeral plant from Bass Strait Islands.

plants.name: Stylidium despectum
plants.form: Small ephemeral herb with reddish, somewhat fleshy stems.
plants.flowers: Very pale pink to white flowers on erect flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 6-7mm long, turn from green to tan-brown, and become brittle as they ripen. Seeds tend to ripen progressively along the flower stem. Seeds turn from green to red-orange at maturity. Hundreds of fine seed per fruiting stem.
plants.habitat: Sandy heaths, in roadside soaks and the margins of ditches in the north, north-east and south-east.

plants.name: Stylidium graminifolium
plants.form: Herb, variable in size, resembling a tuft of grass.
plants.flowers: One or more spikes of pink or lilac flowers to 75mm high.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – small, turn from green to tan-brown and become brittle as they ripen. Seeds tend to ripen progressively along the flower stem. Seeds turn from green to red-orange at maturity. Hundreds of fine seed per fruiting stem.
plants.habitat: Found in sedgeland and wetlands. Widespread and abundant in a wide range of soil-types from sea level to mountain plateaux.
plants.notes: Difficult to establish in open-ground situations. Of interest because of the “trigger” mechanism for ensuring cross-pollination. Attracts butterflies. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Stylidium perpusillum
plants.form: Tiny, slender, ephemeral herb with a rigid, erect, thread-like stem, scattered with hairs, and few, slightly spoon-shaped leaves arranged in a basal rosette.
plants.flowers: White, solitary, and borne at the top of the stems.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 1.5-2mm in diameter, nearly spherical. Turn from green to tan-brown, and become brittle as they ripen. Seeds turn from green to red-orange at maturity. Hundreds of fine seed per fruiting stem.
plants.habitat: In hollows in sandy heath which retain water after rain, in the north and north-east.
plants.notes: Rare ephemeral annual plant. Seeds tend to ripen progressively along the flower stem. This species can be distinguished from the other short-lived Stylidium species by its spherical, rather than linear, capsules.

plants.name: Styphelia adscendens
plants.form: Small shrub, branches ascending or prostrate forming a mat of flat leaves.
plants.flowers: Greenish-yellow tubular, fairly conspicuous flowers. Petals with hairy lobes.
plants.fruit: Drupe – a thin fleshy layer and stone with 5 or fewer sections, each with one seed.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in dry pastures and heaths. Scattered in districts mainly near the coast. Sometimes on dry sites, but also on damp peaty sites.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil that is well-drained is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. Some shade is desirable.

plants.name: Styphelia ericoides
plants.form: Slender shrub with spreading branches.
plants.flowers: White, tubular with spreading bearded lobes in short dense spikes along great lengths of stem.
plants.fruit: Drupe – greenish-black, dryish, ovoid, often curved; may be prominently ridged and sparsely hairy.
plants.habitat: Widespread, abundant in sandy and peaty heaths.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained in cultivation. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial. This formula is not the total answer. …

plants.name: Styphelia esquamata
plants.form: Small shrub with numerous erect branches.
plants.flowers: White, 2-3 together on short stalks. Disk lacking 5 scales typical of others in the species.
plants.fruit: Drupe – approximately 4 mm long, glabrous, brown, in 2-3 segments.
plants.habitat: Local in central Flinders Island.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained in cultivation. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial.

plants.name: Styphelia humifusa
plants.form: Small much-branched shrub, usually prostrate and forming a small mat.
plants.flowers: Inconspicuous, red, tubular flowers partly hidden by the leaves.
plants.fruit: Seed is enclosed in a hard woody drupe covered with fleshy green layer; 8–10 mm long, ovoid; the flesh is sweet, edible.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in dry heaths and pastures.
plants.notes: The fruits are sweet and edible. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Styphelia nesophila
plants.form: Small, shrubby plant, branched from the base, with slender, wiry branches.
plants.flowers: White, solitary on short stalks with the inner surface of the flower tube bearded.
plants.fruit: Fleshy yellowish-orange drupe with 4-5 sections; 3–4 mm diameter, spherical, glabrous.
plants.habitat: Local in upland grassland and on the margins of swamps.
plants.notes: Not easily maintained in cultivation. It is suggested that most species require a well-drained, well-composted soil with cool root run provided by large flat stones or a thick mulch. Some shade is also considered beneficial.

plants.name: Suaeda australis
plants.form: Upright or spreading low shrub, with succulent, opposite or alternate leaves, to 3cm long. Lower leaves often larger and red to purple, upper leaves yellowish. Stems are reddish.
plants.flowers: Small and pale green, about 3mm wide, in clusters arising from the axils.
plants.fruit: Achene – seed flattened, shiny and black.
plants.habitat: Widespread on the edges of coastal saltmarshes, also found in intertidal rock crevices.
plants.notes: Thrives in moist, saline conditions. Fast-growing, good for stabilising saltmarsh and tidal creek edges. Also provides habitat for wading birds. …

plants.name: Swainsona lessertiifolia
plants.form: Perennial herb with trailing or ascending stems.
plants.flowers: Showy purple pea flowers, 12-25 in axillary sprays, each flower on a short stalk.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – oblong, inflated (15-30mm long, 5-8mm wide) and hairy.
plants.habitat: Local in the north-west at Woolnorth. Mainly a plant of the coastal sand-hills but occasionally extending inland.

plants.name: Taraxacum aristum
plants.form: Rosette herb, leaves, 6cm long x 1cm wide, less serrated than introduced Taraxacum. No leaves on flowering stem.
plants.flowers: Yellow, single on end of stalk which is taller than the leaves.
plants.fruit: Achene – seed grey about 4mm long excluding the windmill-like attachment.
plants.habitat: Occurs in alpine grassland and grassy heath in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Tasmannia lanceolata
plants.form: A much-branched shrub or small tree with red stems and leaf stalks.
plants.flowers: Narrow yellow or cream petals. Male and female on different plants. Male flowers are larger; noticeable.
plants.fruit: A 2-lobed lustrous black berry containing many small angular seeds.
plants.habitat: Grows sea level to sub-alpine in high rainfall areas and in alpine and sub-alpine grasslands and shrubberies.
plants.notes: Currently being used in specialised food lines. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi. High flammability.

plants.name: Tecticornia arbuscula
plants.form: Erect, woody shrub with green or reddish branches. The stem fuses with leaves to appear segmented.
plants.flowers: Minute flowers, often 3 together, arise at upper projecting edge of several segments.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in saltmarshes, swamps, estuaries and on low rocky shingly islands which are occasionally inundated. More common in the south.
plants.notes: Highly tolerant of salt and moisture.

plants.name: Telopea truncata
plants.form: Shrub with stout spreading branches or a small tree.
plants.flowers: Flower heads 5-8cm across with 15-20 small, scarlet, red or, rarely, yellow or pink florets.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – dark brown woody follicle containing two rows of winged seeds.
plants.habitat: Mountain forests at altitudes between 600 and 1200m.
plants.notes: As with all other Proteaceae, waratahs have a root association with a particular fungus. Beware of transplanting diseases!! Not easy to keep alive in cultivation in the south-east of the state. Best results at higher altitudes. Grows reliably in the north-west. …

plants.name: Tetracarpaea tasmannica
plants.form: Small, erect shrub with thick, serrated leaves which are broadest above the middle, 1.5-3cm long.
plants.flowers: Flowers are small, each with four white, erect petals, and occur at the ends of the flowering stems.
plants.fruit: Seed follicle – numerous. The outer seed coat is loose and almost winged.
plants.habitat: Sub-alpine habitats.

plants.name: Tetragonia implexicoma
plants.form: Succulent trailing plant, leaves 5cm long, produces juicy orange-red to blackish globular fruit.
plants.flowers: Small, stalked flowers with 4 yellow, strongly scented petals.
plants.fruit: Orange-red to black spherical berries or drupes containing 2-3 brown seeds.
plants.habitat: Widespread on coasts.
plants.notes: Good plant to grow on sandy banks, position at 1m intervals for dense cover. Fruits taste salty sweet, and leaves are also edible. Low maintenance, resistant to salt spray.

plants.name: Tetragonia tetragonoides
plants.form: Robust prostrate herb with stems up to 1m long and succulent, stalked leaves which are shaped like a broad arrowhead, 3-8cm long.
plants.flowers: Greenish-yellow, borne in the leaf axils.
plants.fruit: Indehiscent, dry horned fruits 5-12mm long with hard endocarp containing 2-4 seeds.
plants.habitat: Rocky headlands in the north and north-west.
plants.notes: Can be used as a green vegetable.

plants.name: Tetrarrhena acuminata
plants.form: Variable grass, slender and scrambling in shaded places, or with shorter stems and more crowded leaves in more open situations. Leaves hairless, up to 2.5cm long, and prominently ribbed on the upper surface.
plants.flowers: An erect spike-like flower head, 1.5-2.5cm long, containing 5-7 spikelets.
plants.habitat: Damp, shaded places, or more open sites in areas of higher rainfall, Furneaux Group, Ben Lomond, Central Highlands, south-west and west coast, from sea level to 750m altitude.

plants.name: Tetrarrhena distichophylla
plants.form: Very variable grass with branching stems. The lower stems are prostrate and rooting at the nodes, and the upper stems are erect. Leaves are 4.5cm long, with the upper surface strongly ribbed and densely covered with long and short hairs.
plants.flowers: Flower head is erect and spike-like, 1-2cm long and bearing 4-12 plump spikelets.
plants.habitat: Wide range of habitats, open or sparsely treed, in damp situations or dry situations prone to winter inundation, from lowland areas to 200m altitude. King Island, north-east, Midlands, east coast and west coast.

plants.name: Tetrarrhena juncea
plants.form: Straggling grass with wiry stems up to 6m long which scramble over supporting vegetation. Leaves are up to 13cm long and rough on the upper surface, with a prominent midrib.
plants.flowers: Flower head erect and spikelike, 5cm long.
plants.habitat: Uncommon, but forming extensive colonies scrambling over the understorey in coastal eucalypt forest, in the north-west and on the west coast.

plants.name: Tetrarrhena oreophila var. minor
plants.form: Straggling grass with wiry stems up to 6m long which scramble over supporting vegetation.
plants.flowers: Flower head 0.75-2cm long.
plants.habitat: Rarer than Tetrarrhena oreophila var. oreophila, occurring in similar habitats. South-west, Mt. Field and Central Highlands.

plants.name: Tetrarrhena oreophila var. oreophila
plants.form: Hairless, tufted grass with erect stems and flat leaves, which are whitish above and darker green below.
plants.flowers: Flower head 2-3cm long.
plants.habitat: South-west, Mt. Field and Central Highlands.

plants.name: Tetratheca ciliata
plants.form: Undershrub, erect or spreading, slender branches.
plants.flowers: Large 1cm long, solitary, lilac to purple.
plants.fruit: Capsule – shape varies, contains seed 2-3mm long, hairy.
plants.habitat: Very local near north coast. Sandy heaths.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Tetratheca gunnii
plants.form: Undershrub with slender spreading branches. Leaves alternate, usually linear, margins revolute.
plants.flowers: Petals pale lilac to deep pink, less than 5mm. The anther tube is the main feature distinguishing Tetratheca gunnii from other special of Tetratheca. The tube terminates at the widest point and is shorter than that of other species.
plants.fruit: Capsule – compressed with 2 or 3 sections and sparse cover of gland-tipped hairs.
plants.habitat: Restricted to serpentine outcrops at the Dazzler Range near Beaconsfield.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Tetratheca labillardierei
plants.form: Small hairy undershrub.
plants.flowers: Mauve
plants.fruit: Capsule – shape varies, contains seed 2-3mm long.
plants.habitat: Widespread in heaths and light forests from sea level to mountain foothills.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Tetratheca pilosa subsp. pilosa
plants.form: Slender, spreading branches to 60cm, leaves narrow linear 10mm.
plants.flowers: White to deep purple, 4 petals, black stamens, around ends of stems.
plants.fruit: Capsule – shape varies, contains seed 2-3mm long.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread in heaths and dry sclerophyll forests at all altitudes.
plants.notes: Can be short-lived in the garden. Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Tetratheca procumbens
plants.form: Small undershrub, many slender branches to 20cm near base, long narrow leaves 6mm.
plants.flowers: White to deep purple, solitary.
plants.fruit: Capsule – shape varies, contains seed 2-3mm long, hairy.
plants.habitat: Widespread and abundant in alpine and sub-alpine habitats, heaths at all altitudes, wet forests.
plants.notes: Susceptible to Phytophthora cinnamomi.

plants.name: Teucrium corymbosum
plants.form: Erect perennial herb with opposite leaves, rigid square stems and toothed or lobed leaves. The undersides of the leaves are covered with grey hair.
plants.flowers: White, 8-10mm long, with 5 spreading lobes. Borne in loose groups of 3-7 flowers.
plants.fruit: Nutlet – small, papery, about 1.5mm long, brown and dry when mature. Splits and releases fine seed which is brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Allocasuarina verticillata woodlands, Eucalyptus viminalis woodlands and native grasslands in the east of the State.

plants.name: Thelionema caespitosum
plants.form: Perennial herb with grass-like leaves, often in small tussocks.
plants.flowers: Usually pale yellow/cream or blue (much less common, apparently confined to the north of the state). Star-like with 6 stamens, yellow and bent in the open flower.
plants.habitat: Very common in coastal heaths and wet soaks, also under light forest cover, sea level to about 700m altitude.

plants.name: Thelionema umbellatum
plants.form: Similar to Thelionema caespitosum, but smaller; leaves up to 35cm long and 1-5mm wide.
plants.flowers: Cream, yellow or blue, with six petals.
plants.fruit: Capsule – seeds are dark brown to black, shiny, oblong and 2.5mm long.

plants.name: Thelymitra aggericola
plants.form: A short, pale greyish-blue sun orchid with a channelled dark-green, often curved leaf.
plants.flowers: Up to five freely opening, slate-blue flowers, long curved column ending with a pale yellowish-brown cap. Column arms erect and ending in a dense white tuft of hairs.
plants.habitat: Uncommon. Occurs in rock outcrops in the Arthur River area.

plants.name: Thelymitra aristata
plants.form: A robust blue sun orchid, large fleshy, leathery, ribbed, dark-green leaf.
plants.flowers: Up to 40 blue flowers with darker blue veins and a white column with a narrow, strap-like, irregularly-toothed hood and converging column arms with white hair tufts.
plants.habitat: Common in poorly -drained soil in open heathland and coastal scrub. Flowering promoted after fire.

plants.name: Thelymitra cyanea
plants.form: A veined, late-flowering usually blue sun orchid, fleshy dark-green leaf, often black on margins.
plants.flowers: 1-5 readily opening blue, rarely pink or white, with darker veins on the tepals. Labellum larger and wider than other segments, margin often wavy. Column white, scrolled column arms yellow lacking tufts.
plants.habitat: Fairly common from coastal heathland to alpine moorland on poorly drained soils often at the sides of streams or waterways.

plants.name: Thelymitra flexuosa
plants.form: A yellowish, swamp-dwelling sun orchid with a wiry stem and a single narrow, often twisted leaf.
plants.flowers: Up to four prominently cupped, lemon-yellow flowers 12–15mm across. A cream column with small, knob-like lobes and a prominent yellow anther.
plants.habitat: Locally common in coastal areas on poorly drained soils in heathland and open scrub in the north, east and south-east.

plants.name: Thelymitra imbricata
plants.form: A medium-sized, blue sun orchid with a solitary fleshy, channelled, dark-green leaf.
plants.flowers: 1-8 freely opening, sky-blue flowers. A bluish, inflated column with a brown collar and yellow hood, column arms with white hair tufts.
plants.habitat: Uncommon on dry native grasslands in the Tasmanian Midlands.

plants.name: Thelymitra ixioides
plants.form: A slender to stout blue, spotted sun orchid, with a single, flesh, channelled, dark-ground leaf.
plants.flowers: 2-10 pale to dark blue flowers, 30-35 mm across, usually with small, darker blue spots on the dorsal sepal and petals. Column bluish with a dark reddish blue collar, topped with irregular yellow glands; column tufts that are usually white.
plants.habitat: Common in lowland sites, in open woodlands and heathlands.

plants.name: Thelymitra jonesii
plants.form: A slender, light-blue sun orchid with a fleshy, channelled, ribbed, dark-green leaf, 150-300mm long.
plants.flowers: 1-8 flowers, azure blue with darker veins. Column lobes separated by an inward fold, with lobes and fold adorned with fleshy yellow glands and untidy white tufts on the converging column arms.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in dry native grassland in a number of near-coastal sites.

plants.name: Thelymitra nuda
plants.form: A moderately tall but slender, dark blue to purple sun orchid, with a relatively short, fleshy, channelled dark-green leaf.
plants.flowers: 1-12 clear dark blue to purplish flowers. Column pale blue with a dark brown collar and a tubular, strongly notched bright yellow apex. Column arms converging with toothbrush-like white hair tufts. Opens freely on warm, humid days.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally common in a variety of habitats from coastal grasslands to sub-alpine woodland below 1000 altitude.

plants.name: Thelymitra polychroma
plants.form: A small, slender sun orchid with a channelled, dark-green leaf, 100-200mm long.
plants.flowers: 1-4 upwardly-facing flowers, blue with mauve suffusions and darker veins and a few spots on the petals. A colourful blue column suffused with mauve and a yellow keyhole-shaped rim. Dense white hair tufts. Only opens on warm days. Self-pollinating.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in coastal and near-coastal heathland and open teatree scrub.
plants.notes: Flowering enhanced by summer fires.

plants.name: Thelymitra rubra
plants.form: A small, slender salmon-pink sun orchid with a solitary deeply-channelled green leaf.
plants.flowers: 1-5 small salmon-pink flowers, column irregularly toothed, yellow apex with short yellow column arms, often with a few short yellow hairs.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common in coastal and near-coastal heathland and open scrub.

plants.name: Thelymitra silena
plants.form: A tall robust blue sun orchid with a solitary thick, fleshy green to yellowish leaf, 150-200mm long.
plants.flowers: 3-15 crowded sky-blue flowers with darker veins. A deeply cleft orange to yellowish capped column. The column arms converge with white hair tufts.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in a few areas of coastal and near-coastal heathland in eastern Tasmania and the Furneaux Islands.

plants.name: Thelymitra spadicea
plants.form: A small, spotted blue sun orchid with a solitary fleshy, channelled, dark-green leaf, 100-220mm long.
plants.flowers: 1-4 blue spotted flowers with a dark tubular apex divided into two distinct spade-like yellow, occasionally brown, lobes. Column arms parallel, projecting horizontally, with white, mop-like hair tufts.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in poorly drained coastal heathland.

plants.name: Thelymitra sparsa
plants.form: A slender sun orchid with a solitary fleshy, channelled dark-green leaf, 60-250mm long.
plants.flowers: 1-6 readily opening blue flowers with darker blue spots. Column bluish white with two distinct bluish brown lobes, usually but not always tipped with yellow. Hair tufts sparse.
plants.habitat: Uncommon on sedgey open forest at higher altitudes.

plants.name: Thelymitra viridis
plants.form: A clumping or solitary sun orchid with a single fleshy ribbed, mid-green leaf.
plants.flowers: 1-6 pale blue to purple flowers, exterior pale green, a wide yellow column opening and column arms converging with white, mop-like hair tufts.
plants.habitat: Relatively common in seasonally wet areas and around swamp margins.

plants.name: Themeda triandra
plants.form: Deep rooted tussocky perennial grass.
plants.flowers: Stalked clusters of green and purple spikelets with long purple bracts, rusty-brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: May be seen in large patches along roadsides and in openings in the forest where the stocking rate is low, sea level to alpine and sub-alpine.
plants.notes: With direct seeding, herbicides may be needed in weed-infested areas. Provides moderate forage value, and a useful green ‘pick’ after summer rainfall. Valuable for stock fodder when other more palatable grasses have been consumed. …

plants.name: Thismia rodwayi
plants.form: A small fleshy saprophyte often flowering above the surface of the soil. Roots vermiform.
plants.flowers: Flowering stems erect, 0.5–3.0cm long, arising in the axil of a minute scale leaf.
plants.habitat: Seldom seen but widespread in damp humus and litter in wet forests, recorded in association with roots of Bedfordia salicina, Olearia argophylla and Coprosma quadrifida. Ben Lomond, south-west, Mt Field and kunanyi/Mt Wellington.
plants.notes: Saprophytic plant.

plants.name: Threlkeldia diffusa
plants.form: Prostrate, mat-forming undershrub with branches up to 40cm long, and crowded, light green, fleshy leaves with pointed tips.
plants.flowers: Tiny, hidden flowers, fruit enclosed at the base of the flower tube. Flowers throughout most of the year.
plants.fruit: Red egg-shaped berry, 3-4mm long, ribbed and black when mature.
plants.habitat: Seashores in the north-east and Bass Strait islands.
plants.notes: The tiny red fruits and the leaves are edible.

plants.name: Thryptomene micrantha
plants.form: Shrub with slender, spreading branches.
plants.flowers: White, to 5mm across, usually 2-3 together, petals orb-shaped.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent on the east coast at Freycinet Peninsula.
plants.notes: In cultivation requires reasonably good drainage, full sun to part shade and a good mulch.

plants.name: Thynninorchis nothofagicola
plants.form: A tiny, thin, leafless elbow orchid.
plants.flowers: Greenish to reddish with small, sharply-reflexed sepals and petals. Labellum glandular, insect-like, hinged on the end of a stalk.
plants.habitat: Known from a solitary site in the State’s south-west. Vegetation at the site consists of tall mixed forest, with Eucalyptus delegatensis over an understorey of Nothofagus cunninghamii, Phyllocladus aspleniifolius and Dicksonia antarctica.

plants.name: Thyridia repens
plants.form: Small herbaceous plant, with stem creeping and rooting forming mats.
plants.flowers: Small, purple widely tubular flowers, inside of throat hairy, yellow and white spotted red.
plants.habitat: Wet ground, brackish marshes and shores of saline lagoons.

plants.name: Thysanotus patersonii
plants.form: Herbaceous plant with long, thin, spirally twining stem and very few leaves.
plants.flowers: Bears many solitary, purple flowers with fringed flower petals.
plants.fruit: Capsule – containing 4-6 more or less spherical seeds, 1.5mm in diameter. Seed changes from creamy-green to black when mature.
plants.habitat: Heaths and open woodland, coastal near sea level, and inland to 1000m, in the north-east, Midlands and east coast.
plants.notes: Likes a well-drained, sunny position where the stem can be supported by rocks or other plants. A cluster of edible white, watery tubers is found at the base of the lily stem, which Aboriginal people (Victoria) probably would have cooked before eating.

plants.name: Tmesipteris elongata
plants.form: Fern ally with thick fleshy rhizome usually buried deeply in host; stems, up to 30cm, angular bearing simple ovate leaf-like appendages.
plants.habitat: Uncommon in Tasmania. Largest populations in rainforests of the north-west with only scattered occurrences elsewhere. Observed as an epiphyte on Dicksonia only.
plants.notes: Have been successfully grown in inflated plastic bags with rhizomes covered by moist sphagnum moss. Rhizomes are very brittle and resent disturbance.

plants.name: Tmesipteris obliqua
plants.form: Fern ally with thick fleshy rhizome usually buried deeply in host; stems angular bearing simple ovate leaf-like appendages.
plants.habitat: Widespread and common from sea level to 600m in rainforest, wet sclerophyll forest and fern gullies. Sometimes on mossy logs, rock or soil amongst exposed roots. Epiphytic on dicksonia (Rarely cyathea).
plants.notes: They have been successfully grown in inflated plastic bags with rhizomes covered by moist sphagnum moss. Rhizomes are very brittle and resent disturbance.

plants.name: Tmesipteris parva
plants.form: Fern ally with rhizome thick fleshy usually buried in host. Stems, up to 10cm, very small crowded with curved, narrow leaf-like appendages.
plants.habitat: Very rare in Tasmania, known only from King and Flinders Islands. Small pendulous epiphyte on Dicksonia and Cyathea. Most common in higher, drier side gullies or drainage channels.
plants.notes: They have been successfully grown in inflated plastic bags with rhizomes covered by moist sphagnum moss. Rhizomes are very brittle and resent disturbance.

plants.name: Todea barbara
plants.form: Fern with massive, broad trunk, black and fibrous outside; fronds erect, numerous, bipinnate, leathery.
plants.habitat: Common and widespread particularly in the north and west of the state. Occurs below 300m in rainforest, wet and dry sclerophyll forest, heathland and, less commonly, up to 500m on wet rock faces. Will tolerate boggy soils and salt laden winds in coastal situations. …
plants.notes: Slow growing; very hardy; clump forming; easily grown in a protected position in the ground; suitable for growing in large container.

plants.name: Townsonia viridis
plants.form: Small fragile orchid with a fleshy stem growing in beech forests; single oval leaf, often around the midpoint of the stem.
plants.flowers: Small green and red flowers borne on a fleshy scape. 1-4 often slightly nodding flowers, green with maroon markings. Labellum heart-shaped.
plants.habitat: Prefers rainforest and tall open eucalypt forest with rainforest understorey, usually growing in moss or rotting logs, at the base of trees and occasionally on boulders. Widespread and quite common in the western half of the state from lowland to 1000m; also at Mt Maurice in the north-east. …

plants.name: Trachymene composita var. composita
plants.form: Biennial or short-lived perennial herb with a stout taproot, finely grooved stem and deeply divided leaves.
plants.flowers: Many 2-3cm wide, white-petalled flowers produced per umbel.
plants.habitat: Widespread and locally abundant in wet sandy heaths.

plants.name: Trachymene humilis subsp. humilis
plants.form: Perennial herb with stout rootstock and numerous leaves arranged in a rosette, arising from the root.
plants.flowers: White or pale pink petals, less than 2mm long.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in wet alpine and sub-alpine grasslands.

plants.name: Tricoryne elatior
plants.form: Perennial herb with grass-like leaves and thick roots.
plants.flowers: Yellow, in flower heads on the ends of stems. After flowering the petals twist spirally, then fall off.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 1-3 black, firm seeds are found within each fruit. The fruit is still green when the seeds are ripe.
plants.habitat: Grassy areas below 200m altitude, in the north-east and Midlands.

plants.name: Tricostularia pauciflora
plants.form: Tufted perennial sedge with rather stiff stems, circular in cross-section.
plants.flowers: In 4-5mm long spikelets.
plants.habitat: Sandy heaths and dunes, heath on clay soils, and coastal areas in the Furneaux, north-east and east coast.

plants.name: Triglochin minutissima
plants.form: Annual herb
plants.flowers: Blackish
plants.habitat: Fresh or brackish mudflats or margins of swamps in lowland, mostly coastal areas.
plants.notes: Aquatic annual plant.

plants.name: Triglochin mucronata
plants.form: Annual herb
plants.flowers: Raceme is up to 1.5 cm long, usually few-flowered, sometimes just a solitary terminal flower.
plants.habitat: Recorded from the Furneaux Group.
plants.notes: Aquatic annual plant. Not seen since 1976.

plants.name: Triglochin nana
plants.form: Annual herb
plants.flowers: Blackish
plants.habitat: Margins of swamps from sea level to 200m and damp areas in drier situations.

plants.name: Triglochin striata
plants.notes: Semi-aquatic herb.

plants.name: Trisetum spicatum subsp. australiense
plants.form: Tufted perennial grass with flat or folded leaves, stems with small, soft erect hairs towards the bottom, and velvety towards the top.
plants.flowers: Spike-like, green or purplish flower head, 2-7cm long.
plants.habitat: On skeletal soils, rock clefts, cliff ledges, heaths, alpine shrubbery and grass-herb woodland. From 800-1500m, in the Central Highlands, south-west, Ben Lomond and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Trithuria filamentosa
plants.form: Very small aquatic/semi aquatic annual alpine/sub-alpine herb with erect leaves 1-2cm long, forming clumps several cm in diameter.
plants.flowers: Minute, crowded on the end of the flower stem, which is much shorter than the leaves. Often has separate male and female flower heads.
plants.habitat: Local and uncommon, found submerged in lakes at Mt Field National Park and in the Central Highlands, also in swamps in the south-west.

plants.name: Trithuria submersa
plants.form: Small tufted aquatic/semi aquatic annual alpine/sub-alpine herb with thread-like leaves, growing more or less submerged in fresh water. Leaves are 1-3cm long, clustered at the base of the stem, bright red in open places and green in shaded situations.
plants.flowers: Numerous, tiny, and closely packed, borne on stalks longer than the leaves.
plants.fruit: Egg-shaped and 0.5-0.8mm long. Seeds are rough and white.
plants.habitat: Marshes in the Midlands, Bass Strait Islands and north-east of the State.

plants.name: Trochocarpa cunninghamii
plants.form: Low, scrambling, wiry and straggly shrub ; may spread over a large area
plants.flowers: Crowded in terminal spikes. Bell-shaped pink or white with one tuft of hairs at the base.
plants.fruit: Drupe – purplish-blue/black, the stone separating into about 10 parts; 10–13 mm diameter; edible.
plants.habitat: Common in rainforest in the west of the State, also in alpine woodland and sometimes rocky habitats at high altitudes.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil that is well-drained is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. A damp shady spot is important. Very slow growing.

plants.name: Trochocarpa disticha
plants.form: Tall spreading shrub.
plants.flowers: Pink, tubular, crowded in cylindrical terminal spikes.
plants.fruit: Drupe – pale to deep purple, pithy, 6–10 mm diameter, separating readily into segments.
plants.habitat: Local in the extreme south of the state at Recherche Bay and near Lune River.
plants.notes: A well-composted soil that is well-drained is essential and care should be taken to prevent plants from drying out. A damp shady spot is important.

plants.name: Trochocarpa gunnii
plants.form: Tall shrub, which forms twisted spreading branches in the understorey.
plants.flowers: Small, sweetly scented pinkish-white in short dense spikes near the ends of branches.
plants.fruit: Drupe – globular, 5mm in diameter, pale to dark blue, occasionally orange.
plants.habitat: Widespread, but not common, in rainforests of south, centre and west. Extends into sub-alpine habitats especially near quartzite outcrops.

plants.name: Trochocarpa thymifolia
plants.form: Much-branched shrub.
plants.flowers: Small, white, sweet-scented 3-5 together in dense clusters.
plants.fruit: Drupe – bluish-purple (occasionally white), spherical, about 8mm in diameter, clustered at the ends of branches.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in alpine and sub-alpine habitats.
plants.notes: May be difficult to grow on at lower altitudes.

plants.name: Typha domingensis
plants.form: Vigorous perennial aquatic, emergent rush-like leaves 5-15mm wide.
plants.flowers: Spear-like flower spikes, female flower head cinnamon brown.
plants.habitat: Throughout the State in farm dams, creeks, ponds and slow-moving rivers.
plants.notes: Not recommended for planting as it can take over large dams and wetlands. Identified as having weedy potential by the Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania, although not declared at present. In Victoria, the floury rhizomes of bulrushes traditionally provided a staple food. …

plants.name: Typha orientalis
plants.form: Vigorous perennial aquatic, emergent rush-like leaves 15-25mm wide.
plants.flowers: Spear-like flower spikes, female flower head chestnut brown.
plants.fruit: Seed contained in old flower spike, each of which can contain up to 200,000 seeds.
plants.habitat: Throughout the State in farm dams, creeks, ponds and slow-moving rivers.
plants.notes: Not recommended for planting as it can take over large dams and wetlands. Identified as having weedy potential by the Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania, although not declared at present. In Victoria, the floury rhizomes of bulrushes traditionally provided a staple food. …

plants.name: Uncinia compacta
plants.form: Loosely tufted perennial sedge with stiff leaves and erect, cream-ribbed stems which lengthen as the fruits mature.
plants.flowers: In a dense oblong spike.
plants.habitat: Mountains of the west coast, Central Highlands, Ben Lomond, south-west, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Uncinia elegans
plants.form: Tufted perennial sedge with erect or curved stems, forms small mats.
plants.flowers: Flowers in 2-7cm long spikes.
plants.habitat: Central Highlands, Midlands, east coast and south-west.

plants.name: Uncinia flaccida
plants.form: Densely tufted perennial sedge with erect but flexible, triangular stems with sharp, rough edges, and thin leaves with curved tips when dry.
plants.flowers: In a narrow oblong spike.
plants.habitat: Mountain moors and plateaux on the west coast, Central Highlands, south-west, Mt. Field and kunanyi/Mt. Wellington.

plants.name: Uncinia nervosa
plants.form: Tufted perennial with round-tipped, stiff leaves and erect, needle-like stems which are round in cross-section.
plants.flowers: In 1.5-2.5cm long spikes.
plants.habitat: Open alpine and sub-alpine moors, alpine and sub-alpine forests and sometimes fern gullies in the Central Highlands, Ben Lomond, south-west, kunanyi/Mt. Wellington and Mt. Field.

plants.name: Uncinia riparia
plants.form: Tufted, spreading perennial sedge with erect, triangular, rough-edged stems, and leaves up to 60cm long. Forms large clumps.
plants.flowers: In spikes, 2-8cm long.
plants.habitat: Fern gullies, wet sclerophyll and rain forests in the Central Highlands, Midlands, south-west, Mt. Field, kunanyi/Mt. Wellington and on the west coast in wet, shaded places.

plants.name: Uncinia tenella
plants.form: Very slender, tufted perennial sedge with very slender stems and floppy, threadlike leaves.
plants.flowers: In 6-12 cm long narrow oblong spikes.
plants.habitat: Gullies and forests, growing on the ground or with moss on the roots of trees and the trunks of Dicksonia.

plants.name: Urtica incisa
plants.form: Perennial herb with stiff stinging hairs on slender stems and serrated leaves.
plants.flowers: Small and green, arranged in spikes.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in moist shady places, including fern gullies.

plants.name: Utricularia australis
plants.form: Carnivorous, aquatic herb with free-floating stems and finely divided leaves holding small bladders which trap minute aquatic animals.
plants.flowers: Yellow flowers with brownish spots on the prominent lip. Flowers are about 1.5cm long, and occur in groups of 3-6, held erect above the water surface by slender stems which are 8-16cm long.
plants.habitat: Marshy habitat, in still or slow-flowing water up to a few metres deep. Widespread distribution, ranging from the Gordon River in the south-west to the northern part of Flinders Island in the far north-east; also reportedly from the Derwent River in the State’s south.
plants.notes: Grow in still, clear water with a pH of 5-6 which has been seeded with swamp water, to provide a healthy community of microscopic fauna. Position in high light situation but do not allow water to get too hot. Grows easily in a pond in a sunny position. Anchor in place with a stone.

plants.name: Utricularia dichotoma subsp. dichotoma
plants.form: Small perennial, carnivorous herb. When leaves are present, they are arranged in a rosette.
plants.flowers: 1, 2 or more deep purple flowers with a yellow centre, borne on long bare stalks.
plants.habitat: Peaty areas, sea level to mountain plateaux in waterlogged soil.
plants.notes: This plant traps and digests minute aquatic or soil animals such as water fleas and insect larvae in small bladders attached to thin stems lying at or below the surface of the soils.

plants.name: Utricularia dichotoma subsp. monanthos
plants.form: Herb with slender erect flowering stalk, and upward pointing traps.
plants.flowers: Purple, usually solitary, on the end of the flowering stalk. The lower lip has yellow markings.
plants.habitat: Occasional but widespread in wet sandy ground, from sea level to about 1100m.
plants.notes: Grown by division, may grow faster if kept partially submerged in 5mm of water.

plants.name: Utricularia lateriflora
plants.form: Small semi-aquatic herb with tiny leaves and a thread-like, erect, wiry flowering stem.
plants.flowers: 3-6 small purple or lilac flowers.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant in wet heaths.
plants.notes: Grown by division, may grow faster if kept partially submerged in 5mm of water. Keep in a well-lit position.

plants.name: Utricularia tenella
plants.form: Tiny annual herb with an erect, thread-like flowering stem and few narrow, spoon-shaped leaves on the base of the stem.
plants.flowers: One or two pale pink, four-lobed flowers, with yellow or white throats. Utricularia tenella flowers can be distinguished from other Utricularia species by the four sepals on the flowers (other species only have two sepals).
plants.habitat: In wet heaths on the islands of the Bass Strait.
plants.notes: Some species may grow faster if kept partly submerged in 5mm of water. Do not allow moss to grow as the seedlings will be smothered. It has been recommended that the flowers be hand pollinated when grown in cultivation, to ensure viable seed for the next growing year.

plants.name: Utricularia uniflora
plants.form: Perennial, terrestrial stoloniferous herb.
plants.flowers: Inflorescence erect, solitary, with a single pink, mauve or lilac flower or rarely an opposite pair, 10-20cm high.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 3mm in diameter. Seeds obovoid to ellipsoid, 0.3–0.4 mm long.
plants.habitat: Widespread but local in wet areas in the western half of the state, to about 500 m.

plants.name: Utricularia violacea
plants.form: Small, terrestrial, annual herb.
plants.flowers: Solitary, tiny violet flower.
plants.fruit: Capsule – 1.4-2 mm in diameter. The seeds are minute, 3-dimensional and approximately 0.3 mm in diameter.
plants.habitat: Swamp verges with areas free of rushes and sedges.

plants.name: Vallisneria australis
plants.form: Tufted perennial herb with ribbon-like leaves to 2m long, submerged in flowing fresh water.
plants.flowers: Small white female flowers borne on spiralling stems in summer, and very small male flowers on separate plants. As the fruits mature, they are pulled down to the pond floor by the spiralling stem.
plants.fruit: Fruits with viable seed are not found in most populations.
plants.habitat: Locally frequent in rivers, e.g. Jordan River at Bridgewater, in the Macquarie River at Ross and the South Esk River.
plants.notes: A good pond plant. Useful for large cold-water and tropical tanks.

plants.name: Veronica calycina
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender rhizomes, may be procumbent, spreading widely, rooting at the nodes, or ascending or erect.
plants.flowers: Flowers few and variable in size. Reddish purple corolla.

plants.name: Veronica ciliolata subsp. fiordensis
plants.form: Hard cushion herb. Forms dense, compact cushions up to 40-50cm in diameter.
plants.flowers: White, solitary open-petalled, tubular flowers among the leaves.
plants.habitat: Within open heath on very rocky ground at altitudes of 1470–1530m above sea level. Only known in one location in Tasmania on Ben Lomond.
plants.notes: Needs organically rich, well-structured soil.

plants.name: Veronica derwentiana subsp. derwentiana
plants.form: Perennial herb
plants.flowers: White or pale blue in terminal clusters.
plants.habitat: Favours shady coastal habitats around Hobart but is also found on the mountains. Coastal in Rocky Cape Nat. Park on quartzite and inland in Guilford area south of Hampshire on the Murchison Highway.
plants.notes: Needs roots shaded if growing in exposed site. Old stems should be removed when flowering is finished.

plants.name: Veronica formosa
plants.form: Shrub with slender erect branches.
plants.flowers: 4-petalled, pale to lilac-blue with two long purplish stamens in loose spikes at tips of stem.
plants.fruit: Papery capsule – 2-lobed inflated capsules which split from the top and remain on bushes long after seed has been shed.
plants.habitat: Widely distributed on rocky hillsides in the north and along some river banks in the east; coastal to about 1250m.
plants.notes: Hardy small plant for well drained sites. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Veronica gracilis
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender rhizomes or runners; wiry, erect aerial stems .
plants.flowers: Few pale blue flowers in upper leaf axils on stalks longer than the leaves.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent, especially in grassy places.

plants.name: Veronica nivea
plants.form: Small, soft, much-branched herbaceous shrub with smooth, deeply divided leaves which are 6-12cm long.
plants.flowers: Small but conspicuous, white to pale lilac-blue.
plants.fruit: Capsule 2-3.5mm long, and contains numerous seeds.
plants.habitat: Mountain moors and plateaux, especially the Central Plateau.

plants.name: Veronica notabilis
plants.form: Perennial herb with creeping stems and erect or ascending flowering branches.
plants.flowers: Very pale lilac with purple striations.
plants.habitat: Occurs in the Mount Arthur Regional Reserve.

plants.name: Veronica novae-hollandiae
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender rhizomes creeping below or just above the ground surface.
plants.flowers: Pale lilac-pink sometimes with crimson streaks.
plants.habitat: Grows on the west and south-west coasts, where it grows in sandy littoral banks and herbfields.

plants.name: Veronica plebeia
plants.form: Perennial herb, usually procumbent, spreading widely; sometimes rooting at the nodes.
plants.flowers: Few and variable in size, corolla reddish purple.
plants.fruit: Capsule 2-3.5 mm long containing numerous seeds.
plants.habitat: In Tasmania recorded only from limestone rocks at the River Gordon, Macquarie Harbour.

plants.name: Viminaria juncea
plants.form: Shrub, usually erect.
plants.flowers: Small, yellow pea flowers, in loose spikes.
plants.fruit: Seed pod – small and oval, enclosing ripe seed, turn a dull matt black when seed is mature. Seed is hard and golden or pale brown, solitary.
plants.habitat: In Tasmania, known only from one locality on the east coast, near Coles Bay.
plants.notes: Very quick growing. Bird attracting.

plants.name: Viola betonicifolia subsp. betonicifolia
plants.form: Perennial herb with rosette, leaves much longer than wide, erect rootstock.
plants.flowers: Resembles small cultivated violets. Has a short spur sticking out behind the flower.
plants.fruit: Capsule – releases seed from valves. Small seeds turn from cream to dark maroon or pale brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Common in damp places, mainly on Central Plateau.
plants.notes: Will seed itself readily. Can also form seed without showing petals.

plants.name: Viola caleyana
plants.form: Perennial herb with weak stems, straggling or ascending.
plants.flowers: Petals white 2-3 times as long as sepals, the anterior one having a short broad spur.
plants.fruit: Capsule – releases seed from valves. Small seeds turn from cream to dark maroon or pale brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Occasional near the east and north coasts.
plants.notes: Can form seed without showing petals.

plants.name: Viola cleistogamoides
plants.form: Small rosette herb with long-stalked, rounded leaves from 5-15mm long.
plants.flowers: Variable. Usually white with a purple or mauve centre, but also all purple or rarely all white. Flower stalks held up above the leaves.
plants.fruit: Capsule – small seeds turn from cream to dark maroon or pale brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Common in a range of habitats, from sea level to mountains.

plants.name: Viola cunninghamii
plants.form: Rosette herb with rhizomes and blade of leaves about as long as wide.
plants.flowers: White or violet on the end of stalks longer than the leaves. Rear petal with a short, blunt spur.
plants.fruit: Capsule – releases seed from valves. Small seeds turn from cream to dark maroon or pale brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: In short alpine herbfield, grassland and grassy heath in the higher parts of eastern and central mountains.

plants.name: Viola curtisiae
plants.form: Stoloniferous perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Blue-violet to violet externally, cream internally with faint markings.
plants.fruit: Capsule – dehiscing into three boat-shaped valves, sometimes explosively, with two to many seeds.
plants.habitat: Recorded from Mount Field and the Wellington Range. Grows in sub-alpine Eucalyptus coccifera woodland at 1050-1200m above sea level.

photos.credit: Threatened Species Section DPIPWE – Natural Values Atlas

plants.name: Viola fuscoviolacea
plants.form: Perennial herb; stems short; stolons well developed.
plants.flowers: Petals dark violet in the bud, often paler at maturity; lower petal lacking a spur.
plants.habitat: Widespread – found on stream, river and lake margins, damp areas in grass and sedgeland, gravely and sandy soils, near sea level to 1080m.

plants.name: Viola hederacea subsp. hederacea
plants.form: Perennial herb; stems short; stolons well developed.
plants.flowers: Violet and white; petals 5.5–10 mm long; anterior petal without a spur.
plants.fruit: Capsule 4-6 mm long, stained purple at maturity.
plants.habitat: Widespread in a variety of mostly moist habitats from coastal dunes to alpine shrubberies at 1200m.

plants.name: Viola serpentinicola
plants.form: Perennial, often mat-forming, stoloniferous herb.
plants.flowers: Violet near the centre and much paler at the apices; petals 5–9 mm long; anterior petal without a spur.
plants.fruit: Capsule 6-7 mm long, green mottled purple.
plants.habitat: Endemic to areas of serpentinite geology in western Tasmania, where it is common on exposed ground and disturbed areas.

plants.name: Vittadinia australasica var. oricola
plants.form: Stout herb with woody rootstock.
plants.flowers: Flowers are solitary, bluish-mauve, on the ends of 2 to 5 cm stalks that arise from the ends of the branches.
plants.habitat: Known from only one site on coastal dunes on the north-west coast of Tasmania.

plants.name: Vittadinia burbidgeae
plants.form: A tufted perennial herb.
plants.flowers: Flowers are small and mauve in colour with a yellow centre.

plants.name: Vittadinia cuneata var. cuneata
plants.form: Perennial undershrub, stems herbaceous but woody at base. Stems and leaves hispid.
plants.flowers: Heads solitary, terminal. Ray florets with narrow mauve ligules about 5mm long.
plants.fruit: Achene – 4-7mm long, usually finely striate, downy, capillary bristles fawn or pale reddish-brown.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent especially in dry stony places.

plants.name: Vittadinia gracilis
plants.form: Perennial undershrub, stems and leaves with soft woolly hairs.
plants.flowers: Heads in loose leafy clusters.
plants.fruit: Achene – 4-7mm long, usually finely striate, downy, capillary bristles fawn or pale reddish-brown.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent especially in dry stony places.

plants.name: Vittadinia muelleri
plants.form: Small bright green herbaceous perennial.
plants.flowers: Small mauve daisy on long stalks.

plants.name: Wahlenbergia ceracea
plants.form: Perennial herb with slender branching rhizome. Leaves crowded near base of stem.
plants.flowers: Tube pale blue (rarely white), mid-vein of each lobe dark blue. Solitary, terminal, nodding in bud stage.
plants.habitat: Occasional in dry grassland in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Wahlenbergia gracilenta
plants.form: Slender annual or ephemeral herb with tap root bearing many slender laterals.
plants.flowers: Corolla usually pale blue, 2-3mm in diameter tube up to 3mm long, lobes narrow-oblong, spreading.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent especially in dry places and in sandy soil near the coasts.

plants.name: Wahlenbergia gracilis
plants.form: Perennial herb with erect or ascending stems, branched, often with basal leafy runners.
plants.flowers: Solitary on slender stems, corolla pale blue, funnel-shaped, lobes longer than tube, spreading.
plants.habitat: Roadsides and grassy places.

plants.name: Wahlenbergia gymnoclada
plants.form: Perennial herb with aerial stem erect or ascending and leaves confined to lower part of the stem.
plants.flowers: Usually solitary, terminal. Corolla blue sometimes with yellowish throat, tube about 4mm long.
plants.habitat: Open forests and coastal scrub, also on the Central Plateau at altitudes of about 700m.

plants.name: Wahlenbergia littoricola subsp. littoricola
plants.form: Perennial herb with one to many stems, erect or ascending, stout with the lower part ridged, sometimes hairy.
plants.flowers: Corolla funnel-shaped, pale or lilac blue, sometimes yellowish at base. Stalks much-branched.
plants.habitat: Frequent in grassy places and open eucalypt forests.

plants.name: Wahlenbergia multicaulis
plants.form: Perennial herb with one to many stems, erect or ascending, stout with the lower part ridged, sometimes hairy.
plants.flowers: Corolla funnel-shaped, pale or lilac blue, sometimes yellowish at base. Stalks much-branched.
plants.habitat: Frequent in grassy places and open eucalypt forests.

plants.name: Wahlenbergia saxicola
plants.form: Rosette herb with rhizome and occasional scattered leaves on prostrate aerial stems.
plants.flowers: Pale blue, 18-22mm in diameter on ends of vertical flowering stems.
plants.habitat: Occasional in grassy open heath and grassland in the eastern mountains.

plants.name: Wahlenbergia stricta subsp. stricta
plants.form: Perennial herb with tap-root, thick and fleshy in old plants. Stems- several, branched at base. Leaves usually on lower half of stem.
plants.flowers: Solitary on stems, pale blue, tube 4-5mm long, lobes erect and half-spreading.
plants.habitat: Widespread and frequent in grassy places.

plants.name: Westringia angustifolia
plants.form: Shrub with rigid, slender, spreading branches. Leaves with pointed tips, arranged in whorls of 3, upper surface scabrous (rough to touch), lower surface soft and downy.
plants.flowers: Showy flowers with 5 very short pointed calyx lobes, white or pale lilac, near the ends of the branches.
plants.fruit: Nutlet – each contains 4 seeds which are 2mm long, brown or grey and slightly flattened.
plants.habitat: Dry, shrubby vegetation on rocky (often dolerite) hillsides, from sea level to about 900m altitude.

plants.name: Westringia brevifolia
plants.form: Rounded, much-branched shrub with branchlets and lower leaf surfaces covered with silvery-white hairs. Leaves 4-10mm long and 1.2-3mm wide, occurring in whorls of 4.
plants.flowers: Solitary, near the ends of the branches. 5 calyx lobes more than half the length of tube.
plants.fruit: Nutlet – contains 4 seeds which are 2mm long, brown or grey and slightly flattened.
plants.habitat: Occasional in the north and on the west coast.

plants.name: Westringia rigida
plants.form: Rigid bushy shrub. Leaves mainly in whorls of 3.
plants.flowers: Mauve white flowers, with magenta dots around the throat and on lower 3 petals.
plants.fruit: 4 nutlets surrounded by the persistent papery calyx.
plants.habitat: Locally abundant on foredunes and rocky outcrops on the east coast, from Friendly Beaches to Southport Lagoon.

plants.name: Westringia rubiifolia
plants.form: Much-branched, dense shrub. Leaves in whorls of 4.
plants.flowers: Small, open, 2-lipped, lower lip 3-lobed and spreading. White or pale pink spotted with lilac.
plants.fruit: Nutlet – splits into 4 segments at maturity, each with own seed.
plants.habitat: Widespread in wet eucalypt forests, along creeks and in alpine and sub-alpine areas.

plants.name: Wilsonia backhousei
plants.form: Prostrate perennial shrub with a woody rhizome, with spreading stems 4-15cm long. Narrow, green, succulent leaves, 5-15mm long.
plants.flowers: Single, white, erect tubular flowers grows from leaf axils, 1.5cm long with petals bent backwards.
plants.habitat: Upper edges of coastal saltmarshes.

plants.name: Wilsonia humilis
plants.form: Slender shrub with prostrate stems which spread 15-30 cm or more before rooting at the tips, and spreading again. Leaves are crowded, grey green, and silky hairy with rounded tips, pressed together and overlapping.
plants.flowers: Single, stalkless flowers with white floral tubes and 5 petals.
plants.habitat: Coastal saltmarshes in the east of the State.

plants.name: Wilsonia rotundifolia
plants.form: Small perennial shrub with low-growing, branching stems and dark-green, almost round leaves.
plants.flowers: Yellow or white tubular flowers with spreading lobes.
plants.habitat: Coastal and inland saltmarshes in the east of the State.

plants.name: Winifredia sola
plants.form: Rhizome elongated
plants.flowers: Male inflorescences red-brown.
plants.habitat: Heathland, margins of buttongrass plains, peaty soil, sea level to 100m.

plants.name: Wolffia australiana
plants.form: Tiny, free-floating, rootless aquatic herb, up to 1.2mm long. Upper surface green and flat, lower surface translucent and greatly inflated to form a keel.
plants.flowers: One male and one female flower produced in a flowering cavity on the upper surface.
plants.habitat: Dams, lagoons, marshes and still pools in rivers and streams, north-west, King Island, Midlands and east coast.

plants.name: Wurmbea biglandulosa subsp. biglandulosa
plants.notes: Only occurs in a small population on Flinders Island.

plants.name: Wurmbea dioica subsp. dioica
plants.form: Small erect herb; generally has separate male and female plants.
plants.flowers: Flower stem bearing 3-5 white-petalled flowers, each with a purple band near the base. Female flowers can be distinguished by a purple ovary at the centre of each flower; males have six obvious stamens.
plants.fruit: Capsule – seeds turn from cream to red-brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Grasslands and sedgelands, dry woodland edges, in wind-pruned coastal shrubbery, often persisting in poor quality pasture. North-east, east coast, Central Highlands and the south-west.

plants.name: Wurmbea latifolia subsp. vanessae
plants.form: Small, smooth herb; has separate male and female plants.
plants.flowers: Spike of 2-9 star-shaped flowers, with a white or pale band.
plants.fruit: Capsule – spherical, smooth and brown. Seeds turn from cream to red-brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Localised in the north-west of state, only known from a single collection near Woolnorth growing in a near-coastal short grassland dominated by Poa rodwayi.
plants.notes: Only grows on one remote private property. Recorded in 1836 and ostensibly the same location in 2010.

plants.name: Wurmbea uniflora
plants.form: Small erect herb, with well-separated leaves, corm 8-10mm wide.
plants.flowers: One or occasionally two flowers, with yellow anthers.
plants.fruit: Capsule – seeds turn from cream to red-brown when ripe.
plants.habitat: Peaty wet ground, including buttongrass plains, mostly in the north of the state. Grasslands and sedgelands. Heaths and coastal shrubberies. Sea level to 800m altitude.

plants.name: x Phelodia tutelata
plants.form: Narrowly elliptical, sparsely hairy obliquely erect leaf.
plants.flowers: Solitary purple-blue flower with a heart shaped labellum that has 2-4 basal calli and numerous shorter calli towards the apex.
